text: kindness careful hopeless slowly
qs: What does the ending mean in kindness? What does kindness mean?
What does the ending mean in careful? What does careful mean?
key: -ness means being or state of. kindness means being kind.
-ful means full of. careful means full of care.

title: Read the Story
desc: a 262-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: Nora had practiced her song for three weeks. Tonight was the school talent show, and she had butterflies in her stomach. She peeked around the curtain. Every se
key: 262 words. Time 1 minute and mark errors and self-corrections on your own copy. Let the student finish the passage.

Fall grade 3 benchmark: about 83 words correct per minute (Hasbrouck and Tindal 2017, fall 50th percentile). The passage length is set from the highest grade 3 figure on that same table, the spring 90

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice and let the rhymes show.
text: The Rain The rain comes down, drip, drop, drop. It taps on the roof and it will not stop. The puddles grow wide and the ducks come to play. They splash and they
key: 36 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm and expression at the ends of lines: a pause at the end of each line or where the punctuation is.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: Nora had practiced her song for three weeks. Tonight was the school talent show, and she had butterflies in her stomach. She peeked around the curtain. Every se
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: Prove It
desc: story questions answered with evidence from the text
dir: Answer out loud. Look back at the story to find your answer.
text: Nora had practiced her song for three weeks. Tonight was the school talent show, and she had butterflies in her stomach. She peeked around the curtain. Every se
qs: How did Nora feel before she went on stage? Find the words in the story that show it.
What did Leo do to help Nora? Use the story to answer.
key: Nervous or scared. Points to “butterflies in her stomach,” “I can’t do it,” or “My legs feel like jelly.” (RL.3.1)
He told her to look at him in the front row and pretend they were at home, and he waved both arms from his seat. (RL.3.1)

title: Word Meanings
desc: literal and nonliteral word and phrase meanings in a story
dir: Answer out loud.
qs: Nora had “butterflies in her stomach.” What does that mean? Were there real butterflies?
Leo said the song would be “a piece of cake.” What did he mean?
key: She felt nervous. No real butterflies: it is not literal. (RL.3.4)
It would be easy. (RL.3.4)

title: Ask and Answer
desc: asking and answering questions to show understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers
dir: Read the text to yourself or out loud. Then ask your teacher questions about it. Answer your teacher’s questions with words from the text.
text: Pia packed her backpack for the hike. She put in a map, two apples, and a rain coat. At the top of the trail, dark clouds rolled in. Pia pulled out her coat jus
key: Say: “Ask me one question about the text that the text can answer.” (asks a real question; you answer it from the text)
Say: “Ask me a second question that starts with why or how.” (asks a real question that needs more than one word to answer)

title: Use the Text
desc: questions about an informational text answered from the text
dir: Read both texts to yourself. Then answer out loud.
text: Text 1: A Coat of Fur Sea otters live in the cold water of the Pacific Ocean. Most sea animals have a thick layer of fat to keep them warm. But sea otters do no
qs: Why do sea otters clean their fur so often? Use Text 1 to answer.
How does an otter open a shell? Use Text 2 to answer.
key: Clean fur traps tiny bubbles of air next to the skin, and the air keeps the cold water out. Answer comes from Text 1. (RI.3.1)
It floats on its back and uses a rock to crack the shell. Answer comes from Text 2. (RI.3.1)

title: Same and Different
desc: comparing and contrasting two texts on the same topic
dir: Think about both texts. Answer out loud.
qs: Both texts tell how sea otters stay warm. What is the same in both texts? What is different?
Say the most important point of Text 1 in one sentence. Then say the most important point of Text 2 in one sentence.
key: Same: both say otters live in cold water and need to stay warm. (RI.3.9, compare)
Different: Text 1 says thick, clean fur traps air. Text 2 says eating a lot of food gives the body energy to stay warm. (RI.3.9, contrast)

title: Ask and Answer
desc: asking and answering questions to show understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers
dir: Read the text to yourself or out loud. Then ask your teacher questions about it. Answer your teacher’s questions with words from the text.
text: A volcano is a mountain with a hole at the top. Deep in the earth, rock gets so hot that it melts. The hot melted rock is called magma. When magma rises and flo
key: Say: “Ask me one question about the text that the text can answer.” (asks a real question; you answer it from the text)
Say: “Ask me a second question that starts with why or how.” (asks a real question that needs more than one word to answer)

title: Note Catcher
desc: taking brief notes from two texts and sorting them into given categories
dir: Look back at the two texts. Write your notes on your paper and hold it up.
text: Text 1: A Coat of Fur Sea otters live in the cold water of the Pacific Ocean. Most sea animals have a thick layer of fat to keep them warm. But sea otters do no
key: Fur box: a fact from Text 1, such as thickest fur of any animal, no layer of fat, cleans fur for hours, clean fur traps air, air keeps cold water out. (W.3.8, gathers information and sorts it)

Food box: a fact from Text 2, such as eats one fourth of its body weight each day, dives for crabs, clams, and sea urchins, cracks shells with a rock, food gives energy to stay warm. (W.3.8, gathers i

title: Remember and Take Notes
desc: recalling information from experience and taking brief notes on a source, sorting the evidence into categories
dir: Write on your paper. First, remember a time from your own life and write about it. Then take notes on the text and sort them.
text: Read the text. Take brief notes. Sort your notes into two groups: Birds and Fish. A robin builds a nest of twigs and grass. A hawk hunts mice from the sky. A tr
qs: Think about a time you worked on something hard. Write two or three sentences about what you did.
Take brief notes on the text. Write short notes, not whole sentences. (for example: nest of twigs, hunts mice)
key: Gives a real experience and at least two details about what they did, in complete sentences.
Short notes in the student’s own words, not copied sentences.

title: Listen Up
desc: the main idea and two details of a text read aloud
dir: Listen to your teacher read. Then answer out loud.
text: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about the moon. Then tell the main idea and two details.
key: Main idea: the moon looks like it changes shape because we see different amounts of its sunny side as it moves around Earth. (SL.3.2)
Detail 1, such as: the moon does not make its own light; it goes around Earth about once a month; full moon is the whole sunny side. (SL.3.2)

title: Read the Chart
desc: determining main ideas and supporting details from information presented visually and quantitatively
dir: Look at the chart. Answer your teacher’s questions out loud.
text: Class pets: number of students Choice Students Dog 9 Cat 12 Fish 6 Bird 3
qs: What is the main idea of this chart? Tell it in one sentence.
Which choice did the most students pick? How many?
key: The chart shows how many students chose each kind of class pets. The most popular is Cat.
Cat, 12

title: Grammar
desc: spoken grammar items (verb tense, comparing words, agreement, joining sentences)
dir: Say each sentence out loud with the correct word.
qs: The children ____ to the bus yesterday. (run)
Tomorrow she ____ a cake. (bake)
key: ran (L.3.1, irregular past tense)
will bake (L.3.1, simple future)

title: Word Parts
desc: meanings of words with a prefix or suffix
dir: Answer out loud.
qs: What does misread mean?
What does careless mean?
key: To read something wrong. mis- means wrong or badly. (RF.3.3)
Without care, not careful. -less means without. (RF.3.3)

title: Each Other
desc: using reciprocal pronouns such as each other and one another correctly
dir: Choose the word that fits. Say it or write it.
qs: The twins hugged ___ at the door. (each other / one another)
The students in the class helped ___ with spelling. (each other / one another)
key: each other (reciprocal pronoun for two)
one another (reciprocal pronoun for more than two). Each other is also accepted by many writers.

title: Write It in Cursive
desc: writing legibly in cursive or joined italics with margins and correct spacing between letters in a word and words in a sentence
dir: On your paper, write this sentence in cursive or joined writing. Leave a margin and keep space between your words.
text: Write this sentence: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
key: Letters are joined within each word (cursive or joined italics, not separate print letters)
Letters are formed so another person can read them

title: What Does the Word Do?
desc: explaining the function of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs in particular sentences
dir: Read the sentence. Then answer out loud. Tell what job each word does.
qs: Read: “She quickly ate the red apple.” What does the word She do? What kind of word is it?
What does the word quickly do? What kind of word is it?
key: She is a pronoun. It takes the place of a girl’s name.
Quickly is an adverb. It tells how she ate.

title: Tell Me About It
desc: reporting on a topic with facts and details, speaking clearly
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly.
text: Tell me about an animal you know a lot about. What it is Facts Details
key: Gives facts that fit the topic (SL.3.4)
Adds relevant, descriptive details (SL.3.4)

title: Write About It
desc: an opinion writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Was Leo a good brother? Write your opinion. Give reasons from the story. Write 4 or 5 sentences. Say your opinion Give reasons Use a linking word: because, sinc
key: Introduces the topic and states an opinion (W.3.1)
Gives reasons that support the opinion (W.3.1)

title: Write About It
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Write to teach someone how sea otters stay warm. Use facts from the two texts. Write 4 or 5 sentences. Name your topic Give facts and details Use a linking word
key: Introduces the topic: how sea otters stay warm (W.3.2)
Develops the topic with facts and details from the texts, such as thick fur, clean fur traps air, eating a lot gives energy (W.3.2)

title: Write About It
desc: a narrative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Write about a time you felt nervous, like Nora. It can be real or made up. Write 4 or 5 sentences. First Next Last
key: Sets up the situation and who is in the story (W.3.3)
Events happen in a clear order, with time words like first, then, after that (W.3.3)

title: Multiply
desc: explaining multiplication as equal groups
dir: Look at the stars. Write your equation on your paper and hold it up. Say your story problem out loud.
qs: Write a multiplication equation for this picture. What does each number mean?
Tell a story problem for 4 × 6.
key: 3 × 5 = 15: 3 rows (groups) of 5 stars, 15 in all. 5 × 3 = 15 read as 5 columns of 3 is also correct. Partial: the equation right with no meaning for each number is approaching. (3.OA.A.1)
A story with 4 equal groups of 6, or 6 groups of 4, 24 in all. Partial: a story with the right numbers but no equal groups is approaching. (3.OA.A.1)

title: Divide
desc: explaining division as equal shares or equal groups
dir: Say your story problem out loud.
qs: Tell a story problem for 20 ÷ 5. What does the answer mean in your story?
28 shells are packed into bags with 7 shells in each bag. Write the division equation. What does the answer count?
key: A story where 20 things are shared into 5 equal groups, or put into groups of 5. Partial: a story with the right numbers but no equal sharing is approaching. (3.OA.A.2)
Says the 4 is the number in each group, or the number of groups, to match the story. Partial: naming 4 with no match to the story is approaching. (3.OA.A.2)

title: Tell a Story for a Quotient
desc: interpreting a whole-number quotient as the number in each share and as the number of shares
dir: Tell your teacher a story that fits the division. Do it two ways.
qs: Tell a story where 24 ÷ 6 means the number of objects in each share.
Tell a story where 24 ÷ 6 means the number of shares.
key: 24 things shared equally among 6 people; each share has 4.
24 things put into groups of 6; there are 4 groups (shares).

title: Round It
desc: rounding to the nearest 10 and 100
dir: Say each answer out loud.
qs: Round 67 to the nearest 10.
Round 342 to the nearest 10.
key: 70. Partial: 60 rounds down when the ones digit is 7 and does not count. (3.NBT.A.1)
340. Partial: 350 rounds up when the ones digit is 2 and does not count. (3.NBT.A.1)

title: Two-Step Problems
desc: two-step word problems with an equation and an estimate
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work and hold it up.
qs: Mia has 3 packs of pencils with 8 pencils in each pack. She gives 7 pencils to her class. How many pencils does she have left? Write an equation with a letter for the unknown. Then solve.
A school ordered 198 red shirts and 305 blue shirts. Then 96 shirts were handed out. How many shirts are left? Estimate first. Then solve.
key: Problem 1 equation with a letter: 3 × 8 − 7 = p, or 3 × 8 = 24 and 24 − 7 = p. Partial: the right answer with no letter for the unknown is approaching. (3.OA.D.8)
Problem 1 answer: 17 pencils. Partial: 24 stops at the packs and leaves the 7 out, so it is approaching. (3.OA.D.8)

title: Area
desc: finding area by counting tiles and by multiplying
dir: Look at the rectangle. Answer out loud.
qs: Each small square is 1 square unit. What is the area of this rectangle? How did you find it?
Another rectangle is 7 cm long and 5 cm wide. What is its area?
key: 24 square units. Partial: 24 with no square unit named is approaching. (3.MD.C.7)
Counts the tiles or rows, or multiplies 6 × 4. Partial: counting the tiles one at a time counts here, and the multiplying is the thing to note. (3.MD.C.7)

title: Area Models and L-Shapes
desc: relating area to multiplication and addition, using the distributive property with area models, and finding areas of rectilinear figures by adding non-overlapping rectangles
dir: Draw on your paper. Show your work. Tell how you know.
qs: Tile a rectangle 4 rows by 7 columns, or draw it. Show that the area is 4 × 7. What is the area?
Break a 4 by 7 rectangle into a 4 by 5 part and a 4 by 2 part. Write the area as 4 × 5 + 4 × 2. What is the total?
key: 28 square units. 4 × 7 = 28 and the tiles show 4 rows of 7.
20 + 8 = 28. The two parts add to the same area (distributive property).

title: Fraction Shapes
desc: naming fractions and unit fractions of a whole
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud.
qs: Shape A: What fraction is shaded? What fraction is one part?
Shape B: Is this shape split into fourths? Why or why not?
key: 3/4 is shaded. Partial: 3 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.NF.A.1)
One part is 1/4. Partial: naming 4 parts with no fraction for one part is approaching. (3.NF.A.1)

title: Equal Parts
desc: splitting a shape into equal parts and naming the unit fraction
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up. Then answer out loud.
qs: On your paper, draw a rectangle and split it into 6 equal parts. What fraction of the whole is each part?
Now draw a circle and split it into 4 equal parts. What fraction of the whole circle is each part?
key: Draws 6 parts that are about equal in area. Partial: 6 parts drawn that are plainly not equal in area is approaching. (3.G.A.2)
Each part is 1/6. Partial: 6 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.G.A.2)

title: Number Line
desc: fractions on a number line
dir: Look at the number lines. Answer out loud.
qs: Line 1: What fraction is at the dot?
Line 2: Which letter is at 2/6?
key: 3/4. Partial: 3 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.NF.A.2)

title: Compare Fractions
desc: equivalent fractions and comparing fractions
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know. For the last one, write the fraction on your paper. Then hold it up.
qs: 1/2 = ?/4. How do you know?
Which is greater: 3/8 or 5/8?
key: 2/4. Explains with a picture, same size, or same point on a number line. Partial: 2/4 right with no explanation is approaching. (3.NF.A.3)
5/8: same size parts, more of them. Partial: naming 5/8 with no reason is approaching. (3.NF.A.3)

title: Compare With Symbols
desc: comparing fractions with the same numerator or denominator, recording the results with the symbols >, =, or <, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know. You can draw a model.
qs: Which is greater, 3/8 or 5/8? Write the comparison with >, = or <. Tell how you know.
Compare 1/4 and 1/6 with a symbol. Tell how you know. Draw a model if it helps.
key: 5/8 > 3/8 (or 3/8 < 5/8). Same denominator, so the one with more parts of the same size is greater.
1/4 > 1/6. Same numerator, so the one with fewer, bigger parts (fourths) is greater.

title: Fractions on a Number Line
desc: representing a fraction on a number line diagram by partitioning 0 to 1 into equal parts and marking off lengths
dir: Draw on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
qs: Draw a number line from 0 to 1. Cut it into 4 equal parts. Mark and label 3/4.
On the same number line, where is 1/4? Mark and label it.
key: The line from 0 to 1 has 4 equal parts. 3/4 is marked at the end of the third part. The interval from 0 to 3/4 is 3 parts of size 1/4.
1/4 is at the end of the first part, one part from 0.

title: Measure It
desc: measuring lengths to the nearest half and fourth of an inch, including generating measurements of real objects with a ruler
dir: Look at the rulers. Each ruler shows inches. Say each length out loud. For the last one, get a ruler and measure.
qs: How long is gold bar A?
How long is gold bar B?
key: 2 1/2 inches. The bar ends on the half-inch mark between 2 and 3. Partial: 2 inches or 3 inches rounds to a whole and is approaching. (3.MD.B.4)
3 1/4 inches. The bar ends on the first small mark after 3. Partial: 3 inches rounds to a whole and is approaching. (3.MD.B.4)

title: Plot It
desc: showing measurement data on a line plot marked in fourths of an inch
dir: Tell your teacher where each X goes. Your teacher will click for you.
text: Here are four more gold bars. Put all six gold bars on the line plot. Gold bar C D E F Length in inches 3 3 2 3/4 3
qs: Where does the X go for each gold bar? Use bars A, B, C, D, E, and F.
key: How to mark: click above a number on the line plot to add an X as the student tells you. Use Undo last X to fix a click.
Whole inches: three Xs stacked above 3, for bars C, D, and F. Partial: two of the three Xs placed right is approaching. (3.MD.B.4)

title: Sense, Brain, Act
desc: using a model to show how an animal takes in information, processes it, and responds
dir: Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your model on your paper. Then hold it up.
text: The ship’s cat is asleep on the warm planks of the dock. A gull lands behind her. She turns her head toward the sound.
qs: Which body part took in the information about the gull?
Something happens between hearing the sound and turning her head. What is it, and which body part does that work?
key: Her ears. An ear is a sense organ, and it takes in sound. (3-LS1-1)
The information travels to her brain, and the brain works out what it means and decides what to do. (3-LS1-1)

title: Why Groups Help
desc: building an argument from data that forming a group helps animals survive
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: The crew counted fish caught by dolphins off the reef for one hour. Dolphins Fish caught by each dolphin one dolphin hunting alone 3 a pod of six dolphins hunti
qs: Which dolphins caught more fish each?
Make an argument that being in a pod helps a dolphin survive. Use a number from the table.
key: The ones in the pod, 7 fish each against 3 for the dolphin alone. (3-LS2-1)
The claim yes, with the numbers attached: each dolphin in the pod got 7 fish and the one alone got 3, so a dolphin in a pod gets more food. A yes with no number from the table is not yet an argument.

title: Passed Down and Shaped
desc: reading trait data for parents and offspring, naming the variation, and telling when the surroundings shaped a trait
dir: Look at both tables. Answer out loud.
text: Table 1: a pair of green parrots on the island and their four chicks. Bird Tail color Tail length in cm parent 1 green 10 parent 2 green 12 chick A green 9 chic
qs: Both parents have green tails and so does every chick. What does that tell you about where the color came from?
The four chicks do not have tails of the same length. What is that difference called. Does it mean one of them is not their chick?
key: It was inherited from the parents. A trait both parents have and every offspring has is passed down. (3-LS3-1)
Variation. They are all still their chicks: inherited traits vary from one offspring to the next, so a group of similar organisms is not identical. (3-LS3-1)

title: Clues in the Cliff
desc: reading fossil data to say which organisms lived in a place and what the place was like
dir: Look at the table of rock layers. Answer out loud.
text: The crew dug into a cliff above the beach and wrote down the fossils in each layer. The top layer is the youngest. Layer Fossils found top fern leaf prints, a b
qs: Name two organisms that lived where this cliff now stands.
What kind of place was the bottom layer, dry land or shallow sea? Use the fossils as your evidence.
key: Any two the table names: a fern, a beetle, a fish, a clam, coral, a sea urchin. (3-LS4-1)
A shallow sea. Coral and sea urchins live in sea water, and naming them is the evidence. An answer with no fossil named is not yet using the data. (3-LS4-1)

title: A Useful Difference
desc: explaining how a variation among individuals of one species gives an advantage
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Shore crabs on this beach eat snails, and a snail has to be cracked open first. The crew measured claws and counted shells. Crabs Claw width Shells opened in a
qs: Which crabs opened more shells in a day?
Explain why a wider claw is an advantage for a crab on this beach. Use the table.
key: The wide-clawed crabs, 9 shells against 3. (3-LS4-2)
A wider claw cracks more shells, so the crab gets more food on a beach where the food is locked inside shells, and it is more likely to survive. The explanation has to lean on the data. (3-LS4-2)

title: Who Survives, and What Would Help
desc: arguing from data who can survive in a changed habitat, then judging the merit of a solution
dir: Read the table. Answer out loud.
text: A storm pushed a long sand bar across the mouth of the lagoon. Cool sea water no longer flows in, and the lagoon is now warm and shallow. The crew checked it ev
qs: Which living thing survived well in the changed lagoon? Give the evidence.
Which one could not survive there at all. Which one survived less well?
key: The eelgrass. It grew thickly in warm shallow water, so the change suited it. (3-LS4-3)
The reef crab could not survive at all, none were found. The spotted shore fish survived less well, fewer every month. (3-LS4-3)

title: A Season of Weather
desc: reading and making a graphical display of typical weather for one season
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your graph on your paper. Then hold it up.
text: The island has a wet season. Here are the rainy days counted in each of its four months. Month Rainy days first 14 second 18 third 21 fourth 12
qs: Which month of the wet season had the most rainy days?
About how many rainy days does a typical month of this wet season have? Use the table.
key: the third month, 21 rainy days (3-ESS2-1)
About 16. Anything from 14 to 18 counts if the student used the numbers. The point is a typical value for the season, not one single month. (3-ESS2-1)

title: Two Parts of the World
desc: combining information to describe the climates of two different regions of the world
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Two places, far apart on the globe. Region Warm season average Cool season average Rain in a year this island, near the middle of the globe 29 C 26 C 190 cm a h
qs: Which region is warm all year long?
In which region would you expect snow. What in the table tells you?
key: the island, 29 C in its warm season and 26 C in its cool season (3-ESS2-2)
The mountain region. Its cool season average is below freezing, 4 C below zero, so water there turns to ice and snow. (3-ESS2-2)

title: Ready for the Storm
desc: making a claim about the merit of a design that reduces the impact of a weather hazard
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A big storm pushes sea water up the beach. Water runs across the sand. It soaks everything in the camp. The crew decides to rebuild the sleeping huts on posts.
qs: Which weather hazard is this design meant to reduce?
Make a claim. Does raising the huts on posts have merit? Give your reason.
key: flooding, from a storm pushing sea water up the beach (3-ESS3-1)
Yes, with a reason attached: water running across the sand passes underneath the floor instead of into it. A yes with no reason is not yet a claim. (3-ESS3-1)

title: Balanced or Not
desc: planning an investigation of balanced and unbalanced forces acting on an object
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A heavy supply crate sits on the sand with a rope tied to each end. Two crews pull, one on each rope, in opposite directions. The crate does not move.
qs: Are the forces on the crate balanced or unbalanced? How do you know?
One crew lets go of its rope. What happens to the crate. What changed about the forces?
key: Balanced. Equal pulls in opposite directions add up to no change in motion, and the crate staying still is the evidence. (3-PS2-1)
It moves toward the crew that is still pulling. The forces are now unbalanced. (3-PS2-1)

title: Predict the Next Roll
desc: using a pattern in motion data to predict where an object will be later
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: A barrel rolls along the flat planks of the dock. The crew marked where it was at the end of each second. Seconds Distance from the start 1 3 m 2 6 m 3 9 m
qs: Describe the pattern in the table.
Where will the barrel be at 5 seconds? How do you know?
key: It travels 3 m in every second, the same distance each time. (3-PS2-2)
15 m, because five seconds of 3 m each is 15 m. The reason has to be the pattern, not a guess. (3-PS2-2)

title: Ask About the Pull
desc: asking questions about cause and effect in magnetic interactions between objects not touching
dir: Answer out loud. Your two questions have to be questions, not statements.
text: A compass lies flat on the table. When an iron nail is slid across the table toward it, the compass needle swings. The nail never touches the needle. Two magnet
qs: The nail never touches the needle, yet the needle turns. What does that tell you about this force?
Ask two questions about it that you could actually investigate.
key: The force acts across a distance, with no contact between the objects. (3-PS2-3)

Any two real investigable questions: how close does the nail have to be, does a longer nail swing the needle further, does a copper nail do anything, does a thick book between them change it, what hap

title: A Problem for a Magnet
desc: defining a design problem that magnets can solve, with criteria for success and constraints
dir: Answer out loud. For the third one you may write your two sentences on your paper.
text: A ring of iron keys slipped off the chest. The keys fell into shallow water between sharp rocks. Reaching in cuts your hands.
qs: Say the problem in one sentence that begins: The problem is.
Why is a magnet a sensible idea here? Would the same tool lift a wooden spoon dropped in the same spot?
key: A problem statement about lifting iron keys out of shallow water without putting hands between sharp rocks. The problem has to be about the keys and the rocks, not about the chest. (3-PS2-4)
The keys are iron, and a magnet pulls iron without touching it, so it can lift them from outside the rocks. A wooden spoon is not pulled by a magnet, so no. (3-PS2-4)

title: Three Ways to Do It
desc: comparing several possible solutions against stated criteria and constraints
dir: Look at the table and the three rules. Answer out loud.
text: Water has to be carried from the spring to camp. Three carriers are on the table. Design Holds Weight empty Water lost on the walk clay jar 8 L heavy none canva
qs: Which design holds the most water?
Which design meets all three rules? Explain using the table.
key: the wooden bucket, 10 L (3-5-ETS1-2)
The canvas bag. It holds 6 L, loses only half a cup, and is light. Another choice counts only if the student argues it against all three rules using the table. (3-5-ETS1-2)

title: Make the Test Fair
desc: judging whether a test is fair, naming controlled variables, and identifying a failure point
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two canvas bags were tested to see which one leaks less. Bag Water put in Path walked bag A 6 L flat sand, 100 steps bag B 3 L over rocks, 40 steps
qs: Is this a fair test? Say why.
Name two things to keep the same so the test is fair.
key: No. Two things were different at once, the amount of water and the path, so a leak cannot be pinned on the bag. (3-5-ETS1-3)
Any two controlled variables: the same amount of water, the same path, the same number of steps, the same carrier, the same weather. (3-5-ETS1-3)

title: Maps and Places
desc: using a map grid and a table to describe physical and human features and where they sit
dir: Use the map grid and the table. Answer out loud.
text: A map grid of the island. North is the top row. west middle east north ridge spring palm grove middle forest camp rope bridge south beach dock store hut Place S
qs: What is directly north of the camp?
Which direction do you walk to get from the camp to the store hut? Name both directions you need.
key: the spring (HSS-3.1)
south and east, in either order. The store hut sits in the south row and the east column. Partial: one of the two directions is approaching. (HSS-3.1)

title: The First Nations Here
desc: describing how the American Indian nations of California used the land long ago and how a nation is part of the state today
dir: Answer out loud. Use what is on the screen and what you have learned.
text: Oak trees grow across much of California. Many nations have their homelands here. In the fall they gathered acorns. They dried them. They ground them into flour
qs: The screen names four things nations did with acorns before cooking them. Name all four, in order.
Nations here held a ceremony of thanks before the acorn harvest began. What does that tell you about what the people believed about the land?
key: Gathered the acorns in the fall. Dried them. Ground them into flour. Rinsed the flour with water. All four, in that order. Partial: three of the four steps named, or all four out of order, is approach
That the land was not only a food supply to them. Their religious beliefs tied them to it, so the harvest was treated as something to give thanks for and not only a job to get done. Accept any answer

title: A Town Over Time
desc: sequencing local historical events and describing the mark each period left on the land
dir: Look at the timeline. Answer out loud.
text: A timeline for the town of Harbor Bend. Year What happened 1850 a trading post opens where the river meets the sea 1878 a sawmill is built, and the forest on th
qs: Put these three in order, earliest first: the park, the sawmill, the rail line.
Which event changed the hill. What did it do to it?
key: sawmill, rail line, park. Partial: two of the three in the right order is approaching. (HSS-3.3)
the sawmill in 1878, which cut the forest off the hill for lumber. Partial: naming the sawmill with no account of what it did to the hill is approaching. (HSS-3.3)

title: Rules, Laws and Government
desc: telling rules from laws and naming the basic parts and levels of United States government
dir: Answer out loud.
text: On the ship there are rules. In a town there are laws. The country keeps two documents under glass in Washington. The Declaration of Independence, signed in 177
qs: What is the difference between a rule in your own house and a law?
The United States government has three parts. One makes the laws, one carries them out, and one decides what the laws mean. Which part makes the laws?
key: A rule is set by a family, a class or a crew and applies in that place. A law is made by a government, applies to everyone there, and the government decides what happens when it is broken. Partial: de
Congress, the lawmaking part, also called the legislative branch. (HSS-3.4)

title: Choices and the Local Economy
desc: basic economic reasoning about scarce money, trade-offs, goods and services
dir: Look at the price list. Answer out loud.
text: The store hut on the island sells supplies and it also sharpens tools for a fee. The crew has 8 coins. Item Price rope 4 coins lantern 7 coins dried fruit 2 coi
qs: Can the crew buy both the lantern and the rope with 8 coins? What do they give up if they buy the lantern?
You pick one thing over another. There is a name for what you give up. Explain that idea in your own words.
key: No. The lantern and the rope together cost 11 coins and they have 8. Buying the lantern leaves 1 coin, so they give up the rope and the dried fruit as well. Partial: saying no with nothing named that

The idea of a trade-off, or opportunity cost: choosing one thing means doing without another, because money and goods are limited. The idea matters more than the term at this grade. Partial: naming th

title: Word Flip
desc: reading long words with prefixes, roots, and suffixes
dir: Read each word out loud. The last two are made-up words. Just sound them out.
key: Read each word. dismortable and replanicate are made-up words: listen for the prefix, the middle, and the suffix (dis-mort-a-ble, re-plan-i-cate).
Watch for: prefixes (dis-, un-, re-, mis-, inter-, sub-), roots (micro, scope, tele, phone, bio, graph), suffixes (-ance, -able, -tion, -ior), and whether the student breaks long words into syllables

title: Read the Sentences
desc: reading multisyllabic words accurately in context using letter-sound correspondences, syllable patterns, and word parts
dir: Read each sentence out loud. Take your time with the long words.
text: The explorers discovered an enormous cavern beneath the mountain. Her curiosity led her to examine the unfamiliar footprints.
key: Listen for these six words read correctly in the sentences: explorers, discovered, enormous, cavern, curiosity, unfamiliar. Mark each one.
A word that is self-corrected on a second try counts as correct. Note words the student breaks into syllables to decode.

title: Read the Story
desc: a 170-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: The summer sun beat down on the empty lot behind Maple Street. Weeds stood as tall as Jada’s little brother, and broken bottles glittered in the dirt. “This is
key: 170 words. Time 1 minute and mark errors and self-corrections on your own copy.
Fall grade 4 benchmark: about 94 words correct per minute (50th percentile).

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice. Let the rhythm and the rhymes show.
text: Thunder Walk The storm is rolling over the hill, With a rumble that rattles the window sill. The lightning flashes, a silver thread, And the thunder booms above
key: 43 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm, pauses at the end of lines or punctuation, and a voice that fits the mood of the poem.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: The summer sun beat down on the empty lot behind Maple Street. Weeds stood as tall as Jada’s little brother, and broken bottles glittered in the dirt. “This is
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: Prove It
desc: questions answered with details and examples from a story
dir: Answer out loud. Look back at the story for details.
text: The summer sun beat down on the empty lot behind Maple Street. Weeds stood as tall as Jada’s little brother, and broken bottles glittered in the dirt. “This is
qs: How did Leo feel about the job at noon? Give details from the story.
Why did so many neighbors show up? Use a detail from the story.
key: Tired and ready to quit. Details: his arms felt like wet noodles, the lot looked almost the same, he dropped his rake, he said “This is hopeless.” (RL.4.1, explicit)
They heard about the garden and came to help. Detail: “Word had spread through the neighborhood like wildfire.” (RL.4.1, inference)

title: Word Meanings
desc: meanings of words and phrases in a story, including one from mythology
dir: Look back at the story. Answer out loud.
qs: What does “a Herculean effort” mean? Who was Hercules?
What does “Leo’s arms felt like wet noodles” mean?
key: A huge effort that takes great strength. Hercules was a very strong hero in Greek myths. (RL.4.4, allusion to mythology)
His arms were tired and weak. (RL.4.4)

title: Use the Text
desc: questions answered with details from informational texts
dir: Read both texts to yourself. Then answer out loud.
text: Text 1: Underground Helpers Earthworms spend their lives tunneling through the soil. Their tunnels let air and water reach the roots of plants. As they dig, ear
qs: How do earthworms help plants? Give two details from Text 1.
Why would a worm be in danger on a hot, dry sidewalk? Use details from Text 2.
key: Any two: tunnels let air and water reach roots; they eat dead leaves; castings add nutrients to the soil. (RI.4.1, explicit)
Its skin would dry out, and it breathes through its skin, so it could not breathe. (RI.4.1, inference)

title: Put It Together
desc: putting together information from two texts on the same topic
dir: Think about both texts. Answer out loud.
qs: Use both texts. Explain how an earthworm’s body helps it do its job in the soil.
Text 2 says an earthworm stays underground during the day so its skin will not dry out. Use Text 1 to explain why that habit is good news for a garden.
key: Uses Text 2: muscles and bristles let it push and grip to move through dirt. (RI.4.9)
Connects to Text 1: that digging makes tunnels that bring air and water to roots, and its eating makes castings. (RI.4.9)

title: Explorer’s Notebook
desc: taking notes in their own words, sorting the notes, and listing sources
dir: Look back at the two texts. Write your notes on your paper and hold it up.
text: You are gathering facts for a report about how earthworms live. Look back at the two texts Text 1: Underground Helpers Earthworms spend their lives tunneling th
qs: Write two notes about earthworms, one from each text. Keep them short and use your own words.
Sort your notes. Write a heading above each note: Helping the Soil or Body Parts.
key: Two short notes, one from each text, in the student’s own words and not copied sentences. Examples: worm tunnels bring air and water to roots; worms breathe through damp skin. (W.4.8: gathers informat

Each note sits under the heading that fits. Text 1 facts (tunnels, eating dead leaves, castings) go under Helping the Soil. Text 2 facts (no eyes or legs, muscles, bristles, breathing through skin) go

title: Listen and Retell
desc: retelling a text read aloud in their own words
dir: Listen to your teacher read. Then tell it back in your own words.
text: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about rainbows. Then tell it back in your own words.
key: Tells the main idea: raindrops bend sunlight and spread it into colors. (SL.4.2)
Includes 2 or more key details: sunlight is made of many colors; light bends going in, bounces, and bends coming out; the sun must be behind you with rain in front. (SL.4.2)

title: Say It in Your Own Words
desc: paraphrasing information presented visually and quantitatively
dir: Look at the chart. Tell your teacher what it shows in your own words. Do not read it word for word.
text: Hours of sleep by age Item Amount 6 to 8 years 10 hours 9 to 12 years 9 hours 13 to 18 years 8 hours
qs: Tell what the chart is about in your own words.
Tell two important facts from the chart in your own words.
key: A paraphrase of the main point in the student’s own words (not reading the numbers aloud in order).
Two accurate facts or comparisons put in new words (for example, which is greatest or smallest and about how much).

title: Grammar Fix
desc: spoken grammar items (relative pronouns, progressive tense, adjective order, fragments, confused words)
dir: Say each sentence out loud the correct way.
qs: The girl ____ won the race is my cousin. (who or which)
Right now I ____ my bike. (ride)
key: who (L.4.1, relative pronoun)
am riding (L.4.1, progressive tense)

title: Cursive Writing
desc: writing fluidly and legibly in cursive or joined italics
dir: Write this sentence on your paper in cursive or joined writing. Write smoothly and keep it neat.
text: Write this sentence: The little brown rabbit hopped across the meadow.
key: Letters are joined within words (cursive or joined italics)
Writing is legible: another reader can read each word

title: Tell Me How
desc: explaining how to do something out loud in an organized way
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly.
text: Tell me about something you know how to do well. Explain it so I could do it too. What it is Steps or facts Details
key: Tells it in an organized order (SL.4.4)
Gives facts that fit the topic (SL.4.4)

title: Write About It
desc: an opinion writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Should every neighborhood have a community garden? Write your opinion. Write 5 or 6 sentences. State your opinion Give reasons with facts or details Use linking
key: Introduces the topic and states an opinion (W.4.1)
Gives reasons supported by facts and details (W.4.1)

title: Write About It
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: How do earthworms help a garden? Write to explain it. Use facts from the two texts. Write 5 or 6 sentences. Introduce your topic Give facts, details, or example
key: Introduces the topic clearly (W.4.2)
Develops the topic with facts, details, or examples from the texts, such as tunnels, air and water for roots, or castings (W.4.2)

title: Write About It
desc: a narrative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Write a story about a job that was too big for one person. It can be real or made up. Write 5 or 6 sentences. Start by telling who is in the story and where the
key: Sets up the situation and introduces a narrator or characters (W.4.3)
Events unfold in a clear order, with transition words like first, later, finally (W.4.3)

title: Place Value
desc: place value and how a digit is worth 10 times as much one place to the left
dir: Look at the number. Answer out loud.
qs: In 7,700, how does the 7 in the thousands place compare to the 7 in the hundreds place?
key: It is 10 times as much (7,000 vs 700). Partial: naming the two values with no comparison is approaching.
10. Partial: 100 counts two places instead of one and does not count.

title: Round It
desc: rounding multi-digit numbers to a given place
dir: Say each answer out loud.
qs: Round 83,549 to the nearest thousand.
Round 83,549 to the nearest hundred.
key: 84,000. Partial: 83,000 rounds down when the hundreds digit is 5 and does not count.
83,500. Partial: 83,600 rounds up when the tens digit is 4 and does not count.

title: Times As Many
desc: multiplication as a comparison (times as many)
dir: Say number 1 out loud. Write 2 and 3 on your paper and hold it up.
qs: 35 = 5 × 7. Finish the sentence: 35 is ____ times as many as 7.
Write an equation for this: 24 is 4 times as many as 6.
key: 5. The blank is 5 and only 5, because 35 is 5 groups of 7. Do not accept 7 here. (The sentence “35 is 7 times as many as 5” is also true, but it is a different sentence and not an answer to this one.)
24 = 4 × 6. Or: 4 × 6 = 24 written the other way round counts equally.

title: Units
desc: sizes of measurement units and changing a larger unit to a smaller unit
dir: Answer out loud.
qs: How many centimeters are in 3 meters?
How many minutes are in 2 hours?
key: 300 cm. Or: 3 × 100 = 300. Partial: 30 cm uses tens instead of hundreds and does not count.
120 minutes. Partial: 120 with no unit named is approaching.

title: Area and Perimeter
desc: area and perimeter of rectangles
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work and hold it up.
qs: A garden is 9 feet long and 6 feet wide. Find the area and the perimeter.
A room has an area of 56 square feet. It is 7 feet wide. How long is it?
key: Area: 54 square feet (9 × 6). Partial: 54 with no square unit named is approaching.
Perimeter: 30 feet (9 + 9 + 6 + 6). Or: 2 × 9 + 2 × 6 = 30. Partial: 54 given as the perimeter is the area and does not count.

title: Pounds and Ounces
desc: knowing the relative sizes of pounds and ounces, converting a larger unit to a smaller unit, and recording equivalents in a table
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work.
qs: How many ounces are in 1 pound?
A bag of flour weighs 3 pounds. How many ounces is that?
key: 16 ounces
48 ounces (3 × 16)

title: Lines and Angles
desc: sorting shapes by parallel sides, perpendicular sides, and right angles
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud with the letters.
qs: Which shapes have parallel sides?
Which shapes have perpendicular sides?
key: A and C. Partial: one of the two shapes named is approaching.
A and B. Partial: one of the two shapes named is approaching.

title: Triangles by Their Sides
desc: classifying triangles as equilateral, isosceles, or scalene by their side lengths
dir: Answer out loud. For the drawing questions, draw on your paper.
qs: A triangle has sides of 5 cm, 5 cm, and 5 cm. What kind of triangle is it?
A triangle has sides of 6 cm, 6 cm, and 4 cm. What kind of triangle is it?
key: Equilateral (all three sides equal)
Isosceles (two sides equal)

title: Special Four-Sided Shapes
desc: classifying quadrilaterals as rhombus, trapezoid, parallelogram, rectangle, or square by parallel sides, equal sides, and angles
dir: Answer out loud. Draw if you need to.
qs: A shape has four equal sides and two pairs of parallel sides, but no right angles. What is it?
A shape has exactly one pair of parallel sides. What is it?
key: A rhombus
A trapezoid

title: Equal Fractions
desc: explaining and making equivalent fractions
dir: Look at the two bars. Answer out loud. Write your fractions on your paper.
qs: Do these show the same amount? Explain using the number of parts and the size of the parts.
Write two fractions that are equal to 2/3.
key: Yes, the same amount is shaded. Partial: saying yes with nothing said about the parts is approaching.
Explains: the second bar has 4 times as many parts, and each part is 4 times smaller, so the amount is the same. Partial: naming the number of parts with nothing said about their size is approaching.

title: Compare Fractions
desc: comparing fractions with different numerators and denominators
dir: Show your thinking on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Which is greater: 2/3 or 3/5? Show how you know.
Which is greater: 3/8 or 1/2? Show how you know.
key: 2/3. Shows 10/15 and 9/15, or another valid reason. Or: compare both with 1/2, since 2/3 is further above it than 3/5. Partial: naming 2/3 with no reason is approaching.
1/2. 1/2 is 4/8, and 3/8 is less than 4/8 (benchmark). Partial: naming 1/2 with no reason is approaching.

title: Compare With Symbols
desc: comparing fractions with different numerators and denominators, recording the results with symbols, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know.
qs: Compare 2/3 and 3/4. Use a common denominator or a benchmark. Write the comparison with >, = or <.
Compare 3/8 and 1/2 with a symbol. Tell how you know.
key: 3/8 < 1/2 (3/8 is less than the benchmark 1/2, which is 4/8)

title: Fractions and Decimals
desc: writing tenths and hundredths as decimals and fractions
dir: Write your answers on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Write 7/10 as a decimal.
Write 0.62 as a fraction.
key: 62/100. Or: 0.62 is 6 tenths and 2 hundredths, which is 60/100 + 2/100.

title: Compare Decimals
desc: comparing decimals to hundredths
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
qs: Which is greater: 0.5 or 0.45? How do you know?
key: 0.5 is greater. Partial: naming 0.5 with no reason is approaching.
Reason: 0.5 is 50 hundredths and 0.45 is 45 hundredths, or uses a model. Partial: naming the hundredths with no comparison made is approaching.

title: Compare Decimals
desc: comparing two decimals to hundredths, recording the results with the symbols >, =, or <, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know. You can use a number line or a grid.
qs: Compare 0.45 and 0.5 with a symbol. Tell how you know.
Compare 0.7 and 0.07 with a symbol.

title: Built to Survive
desc: arguing that named plant and animal structures do a job that supports survival or growth
dir: Look at the two living things. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: A palm leans over the beach where the map says to dig. A land crab lives in a burrow under it. A structure is a part of a living thing. Some structures are on t
qs: Name one outside structure of the palm and say what job it does for the tree.
The crab has a hard shell on the outside and gills on the inside. Pick one and say what job it does.
key: Any real palm structure with a matching job: roots take in water and hold the tree down, the trunk holds the leaves up high, the leaves catch sunlight to make food, the fruit carries seeds to new plac
The shell covers and protects the soft body and keeps it from drying out. The gills take oxygen out of the water. Either one, with the job stated. (4-LS1-1)

title: Built to Survive
desc: modelling the path from sense organ to brain to response in an animal
dir: Read what happens, then answer. You may draw your model.
text: A parrot sits on a low branch eating fruit. A coconut drops onto the sand behind it. The parrot flies up to a higher branch and then goes back to eating.
qs: Which sense took in the information, and which body part took it in?
What did the parrot's brain do between taking in the sound and moving its wings?
key: Hearing, taken in by the ears. Accept a student who says the parrot heard the thump. (4-LS1-2)
The brain processed the information: it worked out what the sound meant and chose a response. Look for the idea that the brain decided, not that the ears made the wings move. (4-LS1-2)

title: Layers in the Sea Cliff
desc: reading rock layers and the fossils in them as evidence of landscape change
dir: Study the cliff. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The crew digs into a cliff beside the beach. The layers are stacked like pages, newest on top. Layer What the rock is like Fossils found in it top loose sand no
qs: Which layer formed first? Point to the evidence in the chart.
Two layers hold fossils of things that lived in the ocean. What does that tell you about this spot long ago?
key: The bottom layer. Layers pile up from the bottom, so the lowest one was already there before the others landed on it. (4-ESS1-1)
This spot was under sea water during the time those two layers formed. Sand dollars and fish live in the ocean, so the water must have been here. (4-ESS1-1)

title: Layers in the Sea Cliff
desc: using measurements to compare how fast water, wind and plant roots change the land
dir: Look at the measurements. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The crew built four trays of the same sand, each one 30 centimetres long. They treated each tray for ten minutes and then weighed the sand that washed or blew o
qs: Which tray lost the most sand? What did the water do to that sand?
Compare tray 2 and tray 4. What did the grass do to the rate of erosion?
key: Tray 2, 41 grams. The fast water carried the loose grains away and moved them off the end of the tray. (4-ESS2-1)
The grass slowed it down a lot: 41 grams without grass and only 9 grams with it. Roots hold the grains in place so moving water cannot pick them up as easily. (4-ESS2-1)

title: Reading the Map
desc: interpreting map data to describe a pattern in Earth's features
dir: Study the chart of the islands. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: Eight islands sit in a line from south to north. The chart gives what the map shows at each one. Island Tallest point Cone shaped peak? 1 south end 40 m no 2 12
qs: Describe the pattern in the heights as you read from island 1 to island 8.
Where on the chain are the cone shaped peaks? Say it as a pattern, not as a list.
key: The heights rise from the south end to the middle and then fall again toward the north end. Island 5 is the tallest at 1,240 metres. (4-ESS2-2)
They are all grouped in the middle of the chain, islands 3 to 6, which are also the tall ones. A student who only reads the list back is approaching. (4-ESS2-2)

title: Reading the Map
desc: generating and comparing solutions that reduce the impact of a natural Earth process
dir: Read the two plans. Answer out loud or in writing.

qs: Give one more idea of your own that would reduce the mud in the garden.
Compare plan A and plan B. Which would you choose. What does the chart say that backs your choice?
key: Any workable idea: dig a channel that carries the water past the garden, move the garden to higher ground, build raised beds, lay a bank of sandbags before the wet season, spread gravel. It has to red

Either plan, judged on the chart. Plan A works the first season and costs the most. Plan B costs little and keeps improving but is weak in its first year. The choice itself is not what is rated: the r

title: Fuel for the Voyage
desc: describing where energy and fuels come from and how using them affects the environment
dir: Study the chart. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The crew keeps a chart of everything that gives them energy on the island. Source Where it comes from Can it run out? One effect of using it ship's diesel oil p
qs: Pick two sources from the chart and say which natural resource each one is made from.
Which two sources will not run out? What is it about them that keeps them coming?
key: Any two read correctly: diesel from oil under the ground, firewood from trees, the wind pump from moving air, the sun panel from sunlight. (4-ESS3-1)
The wind pump and the sun panel. The wind keeps blowing and the sun keeps shining, so the supply is renewed instead of used up. (4-ESS3-1)

title: Speed and Crashes
desc: using evidence to explain how the speed of an object relates to its energy
dir: Look at the results. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The crew rolled the same loaded cart down a plank three times and let it hit a wooden block at the bottom. They measured how fast the cart was going and how far
qs: What happens to the distance the block slides as the cart's speed goes up?
Which try had the most energy in the moving cart? Use the measurements as your evidence.
key: It goes up: 4 cm, then 11 cm, then 26 cm. (4-PS3-1)
Try 3, the fast one. It pushed the block 26 cm, farther than the other two, so it had more energy to give the block. (4-PS3-1)

title: Speed and Crashes
desc: asking a question and predicting the energy change in a collision
dir: Answer out loud or in writing. You do not need the real answer for your prediction, just a reason.
text: Two carts of the same size sit on a flat deck. One is loaded with stones. The crew will roll the loaded cart into the empty one, which is standing still.
qs: Ask one question about this collision that a test could answer.
Predict what happens to the empty cart. What happens to the loaded cart's speed.
key: Any testable question: how far will the empty cart go, will it go faster if the loaded cart starts higher up, what happens if both carts are loaded, does the sound get louder with a faster crash. A qu
The empty cart is pushed and moves away. The loaded cart slows down. Either half is credit toward this; both halves is the full prediction. (4-PS3-3)

title: Energy on the Move
desc: matching observations to energy transferred by sound, light, heat or electric current
dir: For each observation, say how the energy travelled. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: Four things the crew noticed in one evening. What they noticed 1 The cook hits a metal pan and everyone across the beach looks up. 2 A lamp is lit in the cabin
qs: How did the energy travel in observation 1?
How did it travel in observation 2?
key: By sound, through the air from the pan to everyone's ears. (4-PS3-2)
By light, from the lamp across the room to the wall. (4-PS3-2)

title: Energy on the Move
desc: designing, testing and improving a device that converts energy from one form to another
dir: Draw your device and label it. Then answer out loud or in writing.
text: The crew needs a light at the cabin door that works without matches. Design a device that turns one kind of energy into light. You may use a small hand crank, a
qs: Draw and label your device. Show where the energy goes in and where the light comes out.
Name the kind of energy going in and the kind coming out.
key: Any labelled drawing with a path through it: a crank turning, wire, and a bulb; or sunlight, a panel, wire, and a bulb. Labels are what make it a design rather than a picture. (4-PS3-4)
Going in: motion from the crank, or light from the sun. Coming out: light, and heat as well. Naming both forms is the heart of this standard. (4-PS3-4)

title: Waves, Light and Signals
desc: using a wave model to describe amplitude and wavelength and the effect on a floating object
dir: Look at the two waves. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The crew drew the water at the shore on a calm day and on a windy day. The dotted line is the flat water level.
qs: Which letter marks the amplitude of the calm day wave. Which marks the wavelength?
Compare the two drawings. Which measurement changed on the windy day, and did it get bigger or smaller?
key: A marks the amplitude, the height from the flat line up to the top. B marks the wavelength, the distance from one wave to the next one like it. (4-PS4-1)
The amplitude got bigger. The waves are taller on the windy day. The wavelength is the same in both drawings, which is worth asking about if the student does not notice. (4-PS4-1)

title: Waves, Light and Signals
desc: modelling how light reflects from an object into the eye so the object can be seen
dir: Answer out loud or in writing. You may draw arrows.
text: A gold coin sits on the table in the cabin. The lamp is lit and the crew can see the coin. Then the lamp is covered and the room is completely dark.
qs: Draw or tell the path the light takes when the crew sees the coin. Name every place it goes.
In the completely dark room the coin is still on the table. Why can nobody see it?
key: Light leaves the lamp, travels to the coin, reflects off the coin, and travels into the eye. All three legs are needed: lamp to coin, coin to eye, and the eye taking it in. (4-PS4-2)
There is no light to reflect off the coin, so no light reaches the eye. Seeing needs light coming into the eye, not just an object being there. (4-PS4-2)

title: Waves, Light and Signals
desc: comparing two solutions that use patterns to send information
dir: Read the two codes. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The camp and the ship need to send three messages across the water at night: all is well, send the boat, and we are moving camp. Code How a message is sent Need
qs: How does a pattern carry the information in each code? Say it for both.
Which code works better for a message sent at night? Give your reason from the chart.
key: In the flash code the pattern is the number and length of the flashes. In the flag code the pattern is which shape is flying. Either way an agreed pattern stands for a message, which is how informatio
The lantern flashes, because flags need daylight and a clear view while a lantern can be seen in the dark. (4-PS4-3)

title: Build It and Test It

Write two criteria: how will the crew know the fix worked?

Any two testable criteria: the jug stays upright when the deck tilts, no water spills, the crew can still lift the jug to pour, it holds through a whole trip. (3-5-ETS1-1)

title: Build It and Test It
desc: generating and comparing solutions against the criteria and constraints

qs: Which fix breaks a constraint? Name the constraint it breaks.
Compare fix 1 and fix 3 against the criteria. Which is likely to hold the jug better?
key: Fix 2. It needs nails and the crew has none, and it also takes longer than one afternoon of work allows. (3-5-ETS1-2)

Fix 1, the lashing, because tying the jug to the rail holds it when the deck tilts, while a flat coil only keeps it from sliding on a small tilt. A student who argues for fix 3 on the grounds that the

title: Build It and Test It

qs: Plan the test. What will you measure?
Name two things you must keep the same in both tries so the test is fair.
key: Any measured outcome: the tilt angle at which the jug falls, how many rocks it survives, how much water spills, counted or measured the same way for both. (3-5-ETS1-3)
Any two: the same jug with the same amount of water in it, the same plank tilted the same amount, the same number of rocks, the same speed of rocking, the same person doing the rocking. Changing only

A pothole on your street needs fixing. Which level of government would handle it, and why that one?

title: Word Flip
desc: reading long words with prefixes, suffixes, and roots

title: Read the Sentences
desc: reading unfamiliar multisyllabic words accurately in context using letter-sound correspondences, syllable patterns, and morphology

desc: saying the first sound of a pictured word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the first sound.
key: Model first: Cider. The first sound in cider is /s/. Now you try.
Point to the cake. Say: Cake. What is the first sound in cake? (/k/)

title: Rhyme Buzz
desc: making a rhyme for a given word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say a word that rhymes.
key: Model first: Pie, sky, my. They rhyme. They sound the same at the end.
Point to the hen. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with hen. (ten, pen, men, when, zen, len)

title: Put the Parts Together
desc: blending syllables and single sounds into a word with picture support
dir: Listen to the slow buzzy voice. Say the whole word.
key: Say: The bee talks very slowly. Put the parts together and tell me the word. The pictures can help you.
Say with a pause in the middle: ap ... ple. (apple)

title: Penny and the Apple
desc: questions about the character, the order of events, and what happens next in a story read aloud
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
key: Read the story out loud. Stop after the third sentence, when Penny still cannot reach.

Ask at the stopping place: What do you think will happen next? (Any guess that fits the story, like Penny gets a ladder, shakes the tree, asks a friend for help, or the apple falls.) Then read the res

title: First Letter
desc: writing the letter for a beginning sound (b, p, f)
dir: Listen for the sound. Write the letter on your paper and hold it up.
key: Point to the bee. Say: Bee starts with /b/. Write the letter that makes the /b/ sound. Hold it up. (b or B)
Point to the pear. Say: Pear starts with /p/. Write the letter for /p/. (p or P)

title: Farm Stand Sign
desc: writing letters to label a drawing
dir: Draw something to sell at the farm stand. Write letters to tell what it is. Hold it up.
key: Say: Let's make a sign for the farm stand. Draw one thing you would sell, like apples, pie, or honey. Then write a word or some letters to tell what it is. Hold it up and tell me what you wrote.
Look for: writing that is separate from the drawing (letters or marks that look like letters, not only a picture).

title: What Is It?
desc: naming objects, actions, and describing words from pictures
dir: Look at each picture. Answer out loud.
key: Picture 1. Say: What is this? (basket)
Picture 2. Say: What is this? (butterfly)

title: Mystery Basket
desc: asking questions and follow-up questions to find out information
dir: Something is hiding in the basket. Ask your teacher questions to find out what it is.
key: Your secret: a rabbit is hiding in the basket. Do not tell.
Say: Something is hiding in my basket. Ask me questions to find out what it is. You can ask things like: Is it a food? What does it feel like?

title: Pick One
desc: sharing an opinion with a reason and details
dir: Pick one. Tell your teacher why.
key: Say: Would you rather climb the ladder and pick apples, or bake an apple cake? Tell me which one and why.
Look for: tells an opinion (picks one).

title: How an Apple Grows
desc: making an inference, making a connection, and asking a question about an informational text read aloud
dir: Listen to your teacher read about apple trees. Then answer out loud.
key: If picture supports are on, point to the three pictures first. Say: This is the order an apple grows in. First a flower, then a bee, then an apple. Then read the facts out loud.
Ask: What if no bees at all came to the orchard in the spring? What do you think would happen? (Not many apples would grow, or no apples would grow. The facts never say this part, so the child has to

title: Count the Rows
desc: counting 10 or more real objects one by one where the teacher can see, then counting rows of 10, 12, 13, and 14 objects one by one on the screen
dir: First count some small things from near you. Then count the pictures on the screen.
key: Start with real things, before the screen. Say: Go and get ten small things you can hold, like spoons, blocks, socks or crayons, and set them on the table where I can see them. Then say: Move each one

Say: Push them back into a pile, add a few more, and count the whole lot again the same way. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down

title: Mixed Up Count
desc: counting mixed-up groups of 10, 11, 12, and 13 objects one by one
dir: These are all mixed up. Count each group out loud.
key: Box 1. Say: These are not in a row. Count the ladybugs. (10 ladybugs)
Box 2. Say: Count the bees. (11 bees)

title: Basket Numbers
desc: naming the numerals 1 to 10
dir: Say the name of each number.
key: Say: Each basket has a number on it. What number is this? Click Next after each one.
The order is 2, 4, 1, 5, 3, 7, 10, 8, 6, 9. Correct means the child says the number name. Write down the ones missed.

title: Which Has More?
desc: comparing two groups by counting (more, same, fewer)
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
key: Box 1. Say: Are there more apples or more pears? How do you know? (More apples. 6 apples and 2 pears.)
Box 2. Say: Which group has fewer, the bees or the flowers? (Fewer bees. 3 bees and 5 flowers.)

title: Sign Shapes
desc: naming, describing, and drawing circles, squares, rectangles, and triangles
dir: Look at the signs. Answer out loud. Then draw one on your paper.
key: Say: The farm stand has signs in lots of shapes. What shape is the green sign? (circle)
Say: What shape is the red sign? (triangle. It still counts as a triangle when the point is at the bottom.)

title: Orchard Hide and Seek
desc: position words (in, over, next to, behind, in front of)
dir: Look at the picture. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Where is the bird? (In the tree, or up in the tree. Look for a position word, not only pointing.)
Say: What is in the basket? (apples)

title: Apple Vote
desc: reading, copying, and adding to a picture chart with three groups
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud. Then make marks on your paper.
key: Say: Some children picked the fruit they like best: a red apple, a green apple, or a pear. Each hand is one child. How many children picked the red apple? (5)
Say: Which fruit got the most picks? (The green apple. It has 7.)

title: Sort the Apples
desc: sorting eight objects by color, by size, and by two attributes at once
dir: Look at the tray of apples. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Eight apples came in from the orchard on this tray. Sort them by color in your head. How many red? How many green? (4 red and 4 green)
Say: Now forget the color. Sort them by size. How many big? How many small? (4 big and 4 small)

title: What Comes Next?
desc: extending three repeating patterns and naming the part that repeats
dir: Look at each row. Say what comes next.
key: Row 1. Say: Apple, leaf, apple, leaf, apple, leaf, apple. What comes next? (a leaf)
Row 2. Say: Look at this row. What comes next? (an apple. The pattern is apple, apple, pear, pear, and the row ends with the second pear.)

title: Tree Line
desc: ordering five objects by height
dir: Look at the five trees. Answer out loud.
key: Point to the trees. Say: Five apple trees grow in a row at the orchard. Which tree is the tallest? (C)
Say: Which tree is the shortest? (B)

title: Uppercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 uppercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts.

title: Lowercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 lowercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
b, d, p and q are the ones to watch. Write down which way a mix-up went, such as said d for b.

title: Letter Sounds
desc: saying the most common sound for all 26 letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What sound does this letter make? Mark each correct sound.
For a, e, i, o and u the short sound is what is expected. The long sound is also correct.

title: Look at the Sign
desc: print concepts (where to start reading, counting words, telling a letter from a word)
dir: Look at the sign and the cards. Answer out loud.
text: We pick red apples. t jam 6
key: Ask: I want to read the sign. Do I start at the bee or at the crate? (at the bee. Reading starts on the left.)
Ask: How many words are on the sign? (4. You may slide your pointer under the sign, but do not count for the student.)

title: Book Parts
desc: print concepts (finding the title, where to start, which way to read, and the first and last word of a line)
dir: Look at the page. Point or answer out loud.
text: The Apple Tree I see a red apple It is on the tree
key: Say: This is a page from a book. Point to the title. (the big words in the banner at the top: The Apple Tree. If the student cannot point on the screen, they can tell you where it is.)
Ask: Where do I start reading? Point to it. (the first word of the top line, on the left: I)

title: Rhyme Hive
desc: hearing and making rhymes
dir: Listen to your teacher. Answer out loud.
text: bee tree apple crate
key: Ask: Do bee and tree rhyme? (yes)
Ask: Do apple and crate rhyme? (no)

title: Clap and Listen
desc: clapping syllables, blending word parts, and saying first sounds
dir: Clap the parts you hear. Then listen for sounds.
key: Say: Clap the parts in apple. (2 claps: ap-ple)
Say: Clap the parts in tree. (1 clap)

title: Squirrel Story
desc: asking and answering questions about key details in a story read aloud
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer your teacher’s questions.
key: Ask: Who wanted the apple? (Pip the squirrel)
Ask: Where was the apple? (at the top of the tree, up high)

title: Sound Apples
desc: saying the sounds of letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: The student says the most common sound for each letter: n /n/, c /k/, h /h/, l /l/, k /k/, w /w/, j /j/, v /v/, e as in egg, u as in up. The letter name is not needed here.
Long vowel sounds for e and u are also fine. Write down any sounds that were missed.

title: First Sound Match
desc: matching first sounds to letters
dir: Listen to the word. Tell which letter makes the first sound.
text: 1 t h m 2 c s p 3 n l s 4 u n w
key: Say: Number 1 is honey. Which letter makes the first sound in honey? (h, the middle letter)
Say: Number 2 is cow. Which letter makes the first sound in cow? (c, the first letter)

title: Cider Time
desc: answering questions and asking for help after listening to spoken information
dir: Listen to your teacher. Then answer out loud.
key: Ask: What do the farmers do first? (pick the apples)
Ask: What happens to the apples after they are picked? (they are washed in cold water)

title: Draw and Write
desc: an informative draw-and-write piece about apples
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Draw an apple. Write a letter or a word to name it. Then write or tell one thing you know about apples.
key: Names what the piece is about: an apple. The student may say it, label the picture, or write a letter or word for it.
Gives at least one piece of true information about apples, such as: Apples grow on trees. Apples can be red.

title: Say It Right
desc: spoken grammar items (plural nouns, question words, complete sentences)
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say your answer out loud.
key: Say: One apple, two ____. (apples)
Say: One peach, two ____. (peaches)

title: Write Letters
desc: printing uppercase and lowercase letters
dir: Write each letter your teacher says. Hold up your paper.
key: Say: Write the first letter of your name. (a letter you can recognize)
Say: Write an uppercase H. (H)

title: Where Is It?
desc: using in, on, and under to tell where something is
dir: Look at each picture. Say your answer out loud.
key: Ask: Look at picture 1. Where is the bee? (in the box. in or inside counts)
Ask: Look at picture 2. Where is the bee? (on the table. on or on top counts)

title: Picnic Chat
desc: describing a familiar food with details
dir: Tell your teacher out loud. Use lots of details.
text: Tell me about a food you like to eat.
key: Names a food and tells something about it
Adds a detail when you ask: What does it look like? How does it taste?

title: What the Facts Say
desc: asking and answering questions about key details in an informational text read aloud
dir: Listen to the facts about bees. Then answer out loud.
key: Read the facts out loud once. Read them again if the student asks.
Ask: What sticks to a bee's legs? (pollen, the yellow dust)

title: Answer the Question
desc: answering a question using information from a text just heard and from the student's own experience
dir: Answer your teacher out loud. You may draw on your paper too.
text: How do bees help the apple trees?
key: Say: Here is our question. How do bees help the apple trees? Use the facts we just heard.
Look for: pulls at least one fact from the reading, such as bees carry pollen, or bees go flower to flower.

title: Little Apple Book
desc: reading an eight-line emergent-reader text out loud and telling what it is about
dir: Read the little book out loud. Point to each word as you read.
text: I See an Apple I see an apple. It is red. I see a pear. It is not red. The apple is big. The pear is little. I can get an apple. I like it.
key: Count the words the student reads correctly, out of 31, and enter the number in the box. A word the student fixes without help counts. Write down the words that were missed.
Say: This is a little book about an apple and a pear. Read it out loud and point to each word.

title: Which Do You Like?
desc: an opinion draw-and-write piece with a topic and a reason
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Which do you like better, picking apples or drinking cider? Draw it. Then tell or write which one you like and why.
key: Names the topic: tells you the two things the piece is about, picking apples or cider.
States an opinion: says or writes which one, such as I like cider. Drawing plus telling counts.

title: What Happened
desc: a narrative draw-and-write piece with two events in order and a reaction
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Draw one thing that happened to you outside. Then tell what happened first and what happened next, and how you felt.
key: Tells about one real thing that happened. Any event counts, at an orchard or anywhere outside.
Tells two things in the order they happened. Listen for order words such as first, then, next, or after that.

title: Climb and Count
desc: counting out loud by ones
dir: Count out loud. Start at 1. Go as high as you can.
key: Say: Climb the ladder with your voice. Start at 1 and count as high as you can. Check: counts 1 to 10 in order with no skips.
Counts 11 to 20 in order. Listen for skipped teen numbers such as 13, 15, and 16.

title: Crates of Ten
desc: counting by tens
dir: Count by tens out loud.
text: 10 apples in every crate
key: Say: Every crate holds 10 apples. Count by tens, one crate at a time. Check: says 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 for the top row.
Keeps going for the bottom row: 60, 70, 80, 90, 100. Write the last number said in order.

title: How Many
desc: counting objects and telling how many
dir: Count out loud. Your teacher will point for you.
qs: Count the apples in the row. How many?
One more apple rolls in. How many apples now?
key: 7. Says one number for each apple as you point.
8, without counting them all again

title: Count On
desc: counting forward from a given number
dir: Start at the number your teacher says. Count out loud.
qs: Start at 3. Count to 8.
Start at 5. Count to 10.
key: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Starts at 3 and does not go back to 1.

title: Fill the Crates
desc: comparing two groups of objects (more, fewer, the same)
dir: Look at the two groups. Answer out loud.
key: Card 1. Ask: Are there more apples or more pears? (pears. 5 is more than 3.)
Card 2. Ask: Which group has fewer, the bees or the flowers? (the flowers. 4 is fewer than 6.)

title: Fruit Sort
