desc: sorting objects into groups, counting each group, and ordering the groups by count
dir: Look at the fruit. Count out loud.
qs: How many apples?
How many pears?
key: 5 apples
6 pears

title: Farm Stand Shapes
desc: naming shapes in a picture and telling where things are (above, beside, below)
dir: Look at the farm stand. Answer out loud.
qs: What shape is the roof?
What shape is the door?
key: Triangle
Rectangle

title: Apples In, Apples Out
desc: adding and subtracting within 10 in word problems
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud. You may draw to help.
key: Point to the two groups of apples. Say: Pip put 5 apples in the basket. Then he put in 3 more. How many apples are in the basket now? (8)
Say: 8 apples were in the basket. Pip took 2 out for lunch. How many apples are left? (6)

title: Two Crates
desc: breaking 7 into two parts in more than one way
dir: Look at the 7 apples and the two crates. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Here are 7 apples and two crates. Put some in crate 1 and the rest in crate 2. Tell me how many go in each. (any pair that makes 7: 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4, 4 and 3, 5 and 2, 6 and 1, and 0 and
Say: Now do it a different way. Tell me another pair that uses all 7 apples. (a second pair that makes 7, different from the first one)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: seeing a teen number as ten ones and some more ones
dir: Look at the full crate and the loose apples. Answer out loud.
key: Say: This crate is full. How many apples are in a full crate? (10)
Say: Count the loose apples beside it. How many? (4)

title: Split It
desc: breaking a number up to 10 into two parts in more than one way and recording each way
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Here are 8.
key: Say: Show me one way to split these 8 into two groups. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 3 + 5 = 8. (a drawing with two groups, or an equation, that makes 8)
Say: Now show me a different way. (a second pair of parts that make 8. The same two numbers in the other order do not count as different.)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: showing a number from 11 to 19 as a ten and some more and recording it
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Look at the full ten frame and the extra ones.
key: Say: Show 16 as a ten and some more. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 16 = 10 + 6. (a drawing of a ten and 6 more, or the equation)
Ask: How many ones are left after the ten? (6)

title: Longer and Heavier
desc: comparing two objects directly by length and by weight, and describing the difference
dir: Look at the poles and the baskets. Answer out loud.
key: Point to the two picking poles. Say: Both poles start at the same line. Which pole is longer? (A)
Say: Now tell me about pole B. Use a word that ends in er. (B is shorter. Shorter than A is even better.)

title: Flat or Solid
desc: telling flat two dimensional shapes from solid three dimensional shapes
dir: Look at the four cards. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Two of these shapes are flat, like a shape drawn on paper. Which two are flat? (1 and 2, the circle and the square)
Say: Two of them are solid. You could hold them in your hand. Which two are solid? (3 and 4, the cube and the can shape)

title: What Living Things Need
desc: telling what plants and animals need to stay alive
dir: Look at each row. Answer out loud.
text: An apple tree and a hen both live at the apple tree. Living things need certain things to stay alive.
qs: The apple tree needs two of these to grow. Which two? Sunlight, water, or a ladder?
The hen needs two of these. Which two? Food, water, or a bell?
key: sunlight and water. A ladder is for the picker, not for the tree.
food and water. A bell is not something a hen needs.

title: Weather at the Orchard
desc: describing a weather pattern from a week of observations
dir: Look at the week of weather. Answer out loud.
text: Here is one week of weather at the apple tree. Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri
qs: How many cloudy days were there?
How many days had rain?

title: Weather at the Orchard
desc: telling how a living thing changes its surroundings to get what it needs
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A squirrel at the apple tree wants to save acorns to eat later.
qs: The squirrel digs a hole in the ground and buries the acorns in it. Did the squirrel change the ground, or did the ground change the squirrel?
Tell me one way a person changes the land to grow food.
key: The squirrel changed the ground. It dug a hole that was not there before.
Any sensible answer about changing land on purpose: digging it up, pulling weeds, watering it, planting seeds, putting a fence around it.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Land
desc: matching animals to the places that give them what they need
dir: Match each animal to the place it lives. Answer out loud.
text: Animals live at the apple tree. Each one lives in one place. It gets what it needs. Here are the places. A hive. A hole in the ground. A hollow in an old tree.
qs: Where does the mouse live?
Where does the bee live?
key: a hole in the ground. Accept a burrow or a tunnel.
a hive

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Land
desc: telling what a weather forecast is for
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The farmer listens to the weather report the morning before picking day.
qs: Why does she listen to the weather report? To find out if strong wind is coming, or to find out what day of the week it is?
What could the farmer do if strong wind was coming?
key: to find out if strong wind is coming.
Any sensible answer: pick early, tie the ladder down, cover the crates, wait for a calm day.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Land
desc: telling one way people can take better care of the land and water
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two helpers fill watering cans at the apple tree tap.
qs: One helper turns the tap off as soon as her can is full. The other walks away and leaves the tap running. Which choice takes better care of the water?
Name one more thing people can do to take care of the water.
key: turning the tap off as soon as the can is full
Any sensible answer: pick up litter, do not pour things down a drain, reuse a bag, plant something, put food scraps in a compost pile.

title: Pushes and Pulls
desc: telling a push from a pull, and comparing a hard push with a gentle one
dir: Answer out loud. Let the student say the word push or pull first.
text: A push moves something away from you. A pull brings it toward you.
qs: You hold the handle of a wagon of apples and bring it along behind you. Is that a push or a pull?
You slide a heavy crate of apples across the barn floor, away from you. Is that a push or a pull?
key: a pull
a push

title: Pushes and Pulls
desc: deciding whether a change made a thing move faster or in a new direction
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The helpers rolled the same apple along two different paths and counted the steps it rolled. Path How far the apple rolled a smooth board 9 steps the grass 2 st
qs: Which path sent the apple farther?
An apple is rolling along the ground. You put your hand in its way and push back on it. What happens to the apple?
key: the smooth board, 9 steps
It slows down and stops, or it rolls back the other way. Either answer counts. The push changed how the apple was moving.

title: Sun and Shade
desc: telling what sunlight does to the things it shines on
dir: Answer out loud. If you can, feel a sunny spot and a shady spot together first.
text: Two buckets of water sit out at the apple tree all morning. One is in an open row. One is under an apple tree.
qs: What warms the water in a bucket, the sun or the wind?
Which bucket is warmer by lunchtime, the one in the open row or the one under the tree?
key: the sun
the one in the open row

title: Sun and Shade
desc: designing and drawing something that keeps a spot cooler
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: The apples are on a table. It is the farm stand table. They go soft in the sun. The afternoon sun is hot. Draw something over the table to make shade, like a cl
qs: Draw your shade cover over the apple table.
Tell me how your cover keeps the apples cooler.
key: Any cover drawn ABOVE the table. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one still counts. A screen drawn beside the table is partial: ask where the sun is coming from.
Something like: it blocks the sun, the sun cannot reach the apples, it puts the table in a shadow.

title: Solving a Problem
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking about it
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem? Apples slip out of her arms and bruise, or the apples are red?
Ask me a question about the apples that would help you fix it.
key: Apples slip out of her arms and bruise on the ground.
Any real question: how many apples does she carry, how far away is the crate, how big are the apples, does she have a bag. A statement is not a question, so ask once more.

title: Solving a Problem
desc: drawing something whose shape would solve the problem
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw something Mira could use to carry the apples without dropping them, like a basket, a bag with a strap, or a bucket with a handle.
qs: Draw the thing you would use.
Tell me what you drew and how its shape holds the apples in.
key: Any container that would hold apples: a basket, a bag, a bucket, a box, a deep pocket, an apron pouch. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one earns credit.
Naming it is what shows intent. Something like: the sides hold them in, the bag closes around them, the handle leaves her hands free.

title: Solving a Problem
desc: comparing test results from two fixes for the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Mira tried two fixes and counted how many apples dropped each time. Fix Apples that dropped a basket with a handle 1 an open cloth bag 6
qs: Which fix lost fewer apples?
What on the chart shows that?
key: the basket with a handle
Because only 1 apple dropped with the basket and 6 dropped with the open bag. The reason has to come from the chart, not from liking baskets.

title: Rules and Doing Right
desc: following rules, knowing what happens when they are broken, and naming an honest choice
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What did Jonah choose to do? Give the coin back, or keep it and say nothing?
One rule at the apple tree is stay on the path. What might happen if people walk wherever they like?
key: He gave the coin back.
Young trees and new plants get stepped on, or someone gets lost between the rows. Any real consequence counts.

title: Maps and Places
desc: telling land from water on a map, using position words, and naming places in a neighborhood
dir: Look at the map. Answer out loud.
text: Here is a map of the orchard. the farm stand the apple rows the pond
qs: On a map, which color usually shows the water, and which color shows the land?
The pond is behind the apple rows. The farm stand is in front of them. Which one is behind the apple rows?
key: Blue is water. Green or brown is land. Pointing to each one as they say it counts.
the pond

title: Left and Right
desc: telling where things are with left and right, near and far, and in front and behind
dir: Look at each picture. Point or answer out loud.
text: A B C
key: Ask: Look at picture A. Point to the one on the left. (the apple)
Ask: Point to the one on the right. (the bee)

title: Our Flag and Long Ago
desc: recognizing the flag as a symbol of the country
dir: Answer out loud.
qs: What is this a picture of?
Our flag is a symbol. A symbol stands for something bigger than itself. What does our flag stand for?
key: a flag. Accept the flag of our country or the American flag.
our country, the United States, or all the people who live here. Any answer about the country counts.

title: Our Flag and Long Ago
desc: telling what a holiday honors and how life long ago was different from life today
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Farms had no tractors long ago. Americans still tell stories. They are about a man. He was called Johnny Appleseed. He walked for miles and miles. He had a bag
qs: Long ago, how did a farmer move a heavy load of apples, with a horse and wagon or with a tractor?
How does a farmer move a heavy load today?
key: a horse and wagon
Any real answer: a tractor, a truck, a forklift, a cart with wheels. Naming today's way is the then-and-now half of this standard.

title: Bee Buzz Sounds
desc: blending, isolating, and segmenting sounds in spoken words
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the sounds and words out loud.
text: Listen. Then say it.
key: Blend: /b/ /u/ /g/ (bug)
Blend: /sh/ /e/ /d/ (shed)

title: Long or Short?
desc: distinguishing long from short vowel sounds in spoken single-syllable words
dir: Listen to the word. Tell if the vowel sound is long or short.
qs: Is the vowel in cake long or short?
Is the vowel in cap long or short?
key: Long (says its name, /ā/).
Short (/a/).

title: Word Baskets
desc: reading words with short vowels, digraphs, and blends
dir: Read each word out loud. The last one is a silly word. Just sound it out.
key: Count each word read correctly. mip is a silly word: listen for all three sounds blended.
Watch for: short vowels (bud, sap, web, fix), digraphs (chop, moth, thick), blends (stem, twig, plum), tricky word (was).

title: Silent E and Vowel Teams
desc: reading words with final e and common vowel teams that make long vowel sounds
dir: Read each word out loud.
key: Mark each word read correctly. The first four use a silent e (long vowel with a silent e at the end). The last four use a vowel team (two vowels that work together, such as ai, ee, oa, ea).
If the student says the short vowel sound for a silent e word (for example cap for cape), mark it wrong.

title: How Many Parts?
desc: using the rule that every syllable has a vowel sound to find the number of syllables in a printed word
dir: Read the word to yourself. Tell how many syllables, or parts, it has. Clap it if that helps.
text: basket dog picnic fish
key: Point to “basket”. How many syllables? (2)
Point to “dog”. How many syllables? (1)

title: Truck on the Hill
desc: a 74-word decodable story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: The Red Truck Gus has a red truck. He fills it with bags. There are ten big bags. Each bag is full of apples. The apples are crisp and red. The truck goes up th
key: 74 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Note pace, expression, and whether the student rereads to fix a mistake.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: The Red Truck Gus has a red truck. He fills it with bags. There are ten big bags. Each bag is full of apples. The apples are crisp and red. The truck goes up th
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the story about? What happened first?” (a summary or answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: Plop! A Story
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about a story the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the story. Then listen to each question and answer out loud.
text: Plop! Meg had a big tin tub. She set it on the grass. Plop! A red plum fell in. Plop, plop, plop! Lots of plums fell in. Then a pig ran up. It got ten plums and
qs: What did Meg set on the grass?
What fell into the tub?
key: Her big tin tub
Plums. First one red plum, then lots of plums

title: Farm Stand Writer
desc: an opinion piece about the best apple treat
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Which apple treat is the best? Write what you think. Tell why. apple cake apple cider a fresh apple Write 2 or 3 sentences.
key: Names the topic: apple treats (W.1.1)
States an opinion: tells which treat is best (W.1.1)

title: Farm Stand Writer
desc: an informative piece with facts about apples
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write about apples. Tell 2 facts you know. colors where they grow how they taste Write 2 or 3 sentences.
key: Names the topic: apples (W.1.2)
Gives at least 2 facts about apples, such as color, where they grow, seeds inside, or how we eat them (W.1.2)

title: Farm Stand Writer
desc: a narrative about a day at an apple orchard
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write a story about a day at an apple orchard. It can be real or made up. Tell what happens first, next, and last. First Next Last Write 2 or 3 sentences.
key: Tells 2 or more events in order (W.1.3)
Includes some details about what happened (W.1.3)

title: Hen House Facts
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about hens. Then listen to each question and answer out loud.
text: Hens A hen sits on a nest. She has six eggs. She sits on them a lot. Then the eggs crack. Chicks pop up! A chick is soft and wet. It can peck and run.
qs: Where does the hen sit?
How many eggs does the hen have?
key: On a nest (on her eggs)
Six eggs

title: Sentence Spy
desc: naming the first word, capital letter, and end mark of a sentence
dir: Look at the sentences. Answer out loud.
text: The bug is on a stem. Can it hop?
qs: Read the first word of the first sentence. What kind of letter does it start with?
What is the mark at the end of the first sentence called?
key: The. It starts with a capital (uppercase) letter
A period

title: Fix It at the Farm
desc: spoken grammar items (plural nouns, matching verbs, a and an, pronouns, describing words, whole sentences)
dir: Listen to your teacher read each one. Say your answer out loud.
qs: One apple. Two ____.
Which sounds right? The bees buzz. The bees buzzes.
key: apples (plural noun)
The first one: bees buzz, with no -es on the verb

title: Which Word Fits?
desc: using indefinite pronouns such as everyone, anyone, someone, something, and nothing
dir: Listen to the sentence. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? ___ is knocking at the door. (Someone / Nothing)
Which word fits? ___ was wrong with the toy, so it did not work. (Something / Everyone)
key: Someone. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)
Something. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)

title: Whose Is It?
desc: using possessive nouns to show who owns something
dir: Listen. Say the answer. For the last one, you can point to the right one on paper.
qs: Sam has a bike. Whose bike is it? Say it with an apostrophe s.
The bird has a nest. Whose nest is it?
key: Sam’s bike. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)
the bird’s nest. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)

title: Commands and Big Feelings
desc: producing imperative (command) and exclamatory sentences in response to prompts
dir: Listen. Say your answer out loud in a full sentence.
qs: Tell me to sit down. Say it as a command.
Your team wins the game! Say one sentence that shows a big feeling.
key: A command such as “Sit down.”
An exclamation, for example “We won!” or “That was so fun!”

title: Print the Alphabet
desc: printing all upper- and lowercase letters
dir: On your paper, print each big letter and its small letter. Print them in order. Hold up your paper when you finish.
text: A a B b C c D d E e F f G g H h I i J j K k L l M m N n O o P p Q q R r S s T t U u V v W w X x Y y Z z
key: Look at the paper. Mark each letter pair where both the capital and the small letter are formed correctly and sit on the line. Letters may be uneven. Count a pair when each letter can be told from the
Check the tall letters (b, d, f, h, k, l, t), the letters that drop below the line (g, j, p, q, y), and the look-alikes (b and d, p and q).

title: Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow
desc: using verbs to show past, present, and future
dir: Listen. Say the sentence the new way.
qs: Say this sentence about yesterday: “Today I walk to the park.”
Say this sentence about tomorrow: “Today I walk to the park.”
key: Yesterday I walked to the park.
Tomorrow I will walk to the park.

title: Tell Me About It
desc: describing a favorite food with relevant details
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly.
text: Tell me about a food you love to eat. What does it look like? How does it taste? When do you eat it? How do you feel?
key: Names the food and gives 2 or more details about it, such as color, shape, or taste (SL.1.4)
Gives 1 or more details about when or where they eat it, and they stay on this one food (SL.1.4)

title: Look at the Sign
desc: using a picture sign to answer a question in writing
dir: Look at the sign. Write 1 sentence on your paper and hold it up.
text: What can you get at this farm stand? Tell 2 things from the sign.
key: Finds the answer on the sign. Your help is fine: point out the sign and read the question again (W.1.8)
Writes an answer that names 2 things from the sign: apples, eggs, nuts, or milk (W.1.8)

title: Person, Place, Thing, Event
desc: describing a person, a place, a thing, and an event with relevant details, and saying ideas and feelings clearly
dir: Listen to your teacher. Tell about each one. Use lots of details.
text: Tell about a person, a place, a thing, and something that happened.
key: Say: “Tell me about your best friend or a neighbor.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the person, such as who they are, what they look like, or what they do)
Say: “Tell me about your room or your backyard.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the place, such as what is there or what you do there)

title: Remember and Tell
desc: recalling information from experiences to answer a question
dir: Think about what happened to you. Tell your teacher your answer out loud. You can draw it, too.
qs: Think about your favorite place to play. Tell me what you do there.
Think about a time you helped someone. Tell me what you did.
key: Names a place and at least one thing they do there.
Tells one real time and what they did. (They may draw first, then tell. Write down what they say if you want a record.)

title: Orchard News
desc: answering questions about information heard out loud, and asking a question about it
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the orchard news. Then answer out loud.
text: Listen only. The news is not on your screen.
qs: What time does picking start?
Where does the wagon ride leave from?
key: Nine in the morning, on Saturday
The big red barn

title: Two-Step Directions
desc: giving, restating, and following simple two-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear, say it back, and give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do what your teacher says. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once, without repeating: “Pick up your pencil, then put it on your head.” (does both steps, in the right order)
Say once, without repeating: “Clap your hands, then touch your toes.” (does both steps, in the right order)

title: Ladder Count
desc: counting on from any number and reading numerals to 120
dir: Count and read the numbers out loud.
qs: Count out loud from 18 to 32.
Count out loud from 67 to 81.
key: 18, 19, 20 and on to 32. Watch the jumps past 19 and 29
67, 68, 69, 70 and on to 81. Watch the jumps past 69 and 79

title: Fill the Basket
desc: counting objects and writing numerals to 120
dir: Count the pictures. Write each number on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Count the apples. Write the number.
Count the bees. Write the number.
key: 23 apples (2 rows of ten and 3 more)
15 bees (3 rows of five)

title: Bee Hops
desc: counting on and counting back to add and subtract
dir: Count out loud like a hopping bee. Say each answer.
qs: Start at 4. Count on 2. Where do you land?
Start at 8. Count on 3. Where do you land? What adding sentence is that?
key: Counts 5, 6. Lands on 6
Counts 9, 10, 11. Lands on 11. 8 + 3 = 11

title: Farm Stand Math
desc: addition and subtraction word problems within 20
dir: Listen to each story problem. You can draw on your paper. Say your answer.
qs: There are 4 red apples and 3 green apples in a basket. How many apples in all?
Kai picks 6 apples. Then he picks 3 more. How many apples does Kai have now?
key: 7 apples (4 + 3 = 7)
9 apples (6 + 3 = 9)

title: Stack the Crates
desc: adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number or a multiple of 10
dir: Add. Say each answer. Show your work for the last one on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Look at the blocks. What is 23 + 4?
key: 27. Adds ones to ones: 3 + 4 = 7
46. Keeps 4 tens and adds the ones

title: Sort the Fruit
desc: sorting, counting, and comparing data in three categories
dir: Sort the fruit by kind. Write your numbers on your paper and hold it up. Then answer out loud.
qs: Count each kind of fruit: apples, pears, and peaches. Write the 3 numbers.
Which kind has the most? Which kind has the fewest?
key: Apples 7, pears 5, peaches 3. A tally chart, a list, or a drawing all count
Most: apples. Fewest: peaches

title: Make a Graph
desc: organizing and representing data with up to three categories, and answering questions about the total and about how many more or less
dir: Look at the list. Make a tally chart or a picture graph on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: Ten kids told us their pets at home. cat dog dog fish cat dog cat dog dog cat
key: A chart or graph with dog 5, cat 4, fish 1. Each item is counted once. Tally marks, pictures, or squares all work. Labels are on each group.
10 (the total of all three groups)

title: What the Digits Mean
desc: reading the tens digit and the ones digit of a two-digit number
dir: Look at the blocks. Answer out loud.
qs: How many tens and how many ones? What number is this?
In that number, what does the 4 stand for?
key: 4 tens and 6 ones. The number is 46
4 tens, which is 40. Not just four

title: Take Away Tens
desc: subtracting a multiple of ten from a multiple of ten
dir: Subtract. Say each answer out loud.
key: 40. Six tens take away two tens leaves four tens
50. Nine tens take away four tens leaves five tens

title: Swap and Group
desc: using the order of addends and grouping addends to add
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
qs: You know 4 + 9 = 13. So what is 9 + 4? How do you know without counting?
Add 8 + 2 + 6. Which two would you put together first, and why?
key: 13. The order of the two parts does not change the total, so there is nothing to count again
8 and 2 first, because they make 10. Then 10 + 6 = 16. The answer is 16. Any correct regrouping with a reason counts

title: How Many Cards Long
desc: measuring length as a whole number of same-size units
dir: Look at the twigs and the apple cards. Answer out loud.
qs: The apple cards are all the same size. How many cards long is twig A?
How many cards long is twig B?
key: 6 cards long
4 cards long

title: Orchard Clocks
desc: telling and writing time to the hour and half hour on analog and digital clocks
dir: Look at the clocks. Say each time out loud. Write the last one on your paper.
qs: Picking starts at this time. What time is it?
The wagon ride leaves at this time. What time is it?
key: 9:00, or nine o'clock
1:30, or half past one. The hour hand sits between 1 and 2, which is the usual place to slip

title: Equal Shares
desc: naming halves and fourths of a circle and a rectangle, and comparing the size of the shares
dir: Look at the apple pie and the crate top. Answer out loud.
qs: The pie is cut into 2 equal parts. What do we call one of those parts?
The crate top is cut into 4 equal parts. What do we call one of those parts?
key: A half, or one half. Two halves is also fine as a description of the whole pie
A fourth, or a quarter. One fourth of the crate top

title: Copy a Bird's Beak
desc: naming the job an animal body part does, then designing a tool that copies it to solve a human problem
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer the first out loud. Draw the second on your paper and hold it up.
text: A parrot has a thick beak. It curves down to a point. It hooks over a branch. It pulls the branch close. Then the bird can reach the fruit. The best apples are
qs: How does a curved, hooked beak help a parrot get to fruit it could not otherwise reach?
Draw a picking tool for the top of the tree that copies the parrot's hooked beak.
key: It hooks over the branch and pulls it closer, so the fruit comes to the bird. Any answer about hooking and pulling counts.
Any long tool with a hook or curve at the end: a pole with a crook, a bent wire on a stick, a hooked basket on a handle. A straight stick with no hook is partial, so ask what the beak's shape does.

title: Hen and Chicks
desc: finding a pattern in what a parent animal does and what the young do in answer, and saying how it helps the young
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What do the chicks do every single time the hen steps back from her scratching?
What do the chicks do when the hen stops clucking?
key: They run in and peck at the loose dirt. Every time is what makes it a pattern.
They stop walking and stand close to her feet.

title: Hen and Chicks
desc: making observations that young plants and animals are like their parents but not exactly like them
dir: Look at the two pairs. Answer out loud.
text: A young apple tree grown from a seed. The grown apple tree it came from. A chick. The hen that is its parent.
qs: Name one way the young apple tree is like the grown apple tree.
Name one way the young apple tree is not exactly like the grown apple tree.
key: Both have a stem or trunk, green leaves, and roots in the soil. Any likeness counts.
The young one is much shorter, it has a thin stem instead of a thick trunk, it has no apples. Any difference counts.

title: The Moon Over the Orchard
desc: finding a pattern in a log of sky observations and using it to predict what comes next
dir: Look at the moon log. Answer out loud.
text: The orchard keeper looked at the moon on four nights, one week apart each time. Night What the moon looked like first night a thin curve one week later half a c
qs: What did the moon look like on the first night?
What did it look like two weeks later?
key: a thin curve
a full round circle

title: The Moon Over the Orchard
desc: relating the number of hours of daylight to the time of year from observations made across a year
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The orchard keeper counted how many hours there was enough daylight to pick. Month Hours of daylight June 15 September 12 December 9
qs: Which month on the chart had the most hours of daylight?
How many fewer hours of daylight did December have than June?
key: June, 15 hours
6 fewer hours. 15 take away 9

title: Sound in the Barn
desc: planning an investigation showing that a shaking material makes sound and that a sound can make a material shake
dir: If you have string and an empty box, try the first part first. Either way, answer out loud.
text: Stretch a piece of string tight across an empty crate and pluck it once. Watch the string while you listen. Now tape a thin paper strip so it just touches the s
qs: While you hear the note, what is the string doing?
Press one finger on the string while it is still sounding. What happens to the sound, and why?
key: Shaking back and forth fast. Buzzing, wobbling, vibrating, going blurry, all count.
The sound stops, because the string is no longer shaking. No shaking means no sound.

title: In the Cellar
desc: accounting for why an object in darkness can be seen only when light shines on it
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The apple cellar is under the barn. It has no window, and the door fits tight.
qs: A crate of red apples is in the cellar with the door shut. Can you see them? Say why or why not.
What has to happen before you can see the apples down there?
key: No. No light gets into the cellar, and nothing can be seen unless light shines on it and comes back to your eyes.
Light has to get in: a lamp, a flashlight, a candle in a holder, or the door opened to let daylight in.

title: In the Cellar
desc: using test results to tell what happens when different materials are put in the path of a beam of light
dir: Look at the test results. Answer out loud.
text: In the dark cellar the keeper shone one flashlight beam at four things and wrote down what the beam did. What was put in the beam What the beam did a clean glas
qs: Which thing let the light go straight through?
Which thing made a dark shadow on the wall behind it?
key: the clean glass jar
the wooden crate lid

title: Calling Across the Rows
desc: designing a device that uses light or sound to send a message over a distance too far to shout
dir: Draw your answer on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: The orchard is twenty long rows wide. A picker at the far end cannot hear anyone shouting from the barn.
qs: Draw a device at the barn that tells every picker in every row that the water is ready. It has to use light or sound.
Say out loud what you drew, and say whether it works by light or by sound.
key: Any device that carries light or sound a long way: a bell on a post, a horn, a whistle, a drum, a bright lamp hoisted on a pole, a mirror catching the sun.
Names it and says which one it uses. Sound for a bell, a horn, a whistle, a drum. Light for a lamp or a mirror.

title: Fix the Bruised Apples
desc: naming a problem people want to change, asking a question about it, and saying what to observe first
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem the orchard wants to change?
Think like a builder. What is one question you would want answered before you fix it?
key: Apples get bruised when they are tipped into the hard crate, and bruised apples cannot be sold.
Any real question: how far do the apples fall, how hard is the bottom, how many go in at once, which apples bruise most. A statement is not a question, so ask once more.

title: Fix the Bruised Apples
desc: making a simple drawing of a fix and explaining how the shape of the object makes it work
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up. Then answer out loud.
text: Draw something that gets the apples into the crate without a hard drop.
qs: Draw your fix on the crate.
Point to the part that protects the apples and tell me its shape.
key: Any real fix: a soft pad in the bottom, a cloth lining up the sides, a sloping slide or chute into the crate, a smaller crate so the fall is shorter.
Names a shape: a soft flat pad, a sloping ramp, a curved chute, a deep soft nest.

title: Which Liner Worked
desc: comparing the data from tests of two objects built to solve the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The orchard tested two crate liners. Each liner got twenty apples tipped into it, and then the bruises were counted. Liner Bruised apples, out of 20 a thick str
qs: Which liner worked better in the test?
Read me the two numbers from the chart that show it.
key: the thick straw pad
Only 2 apples out of 20 bruised with the straw pad, and 11 out of 20 bruised with the paper. The numbers have to be in the answer.

title: The Stand Vote
desc: telling a right from a responsibility and naming the responsibility that goes with taking part in a vote
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: Everyone got a slip of paper and a say in the choice. Is that a right or a responsibility?
Counting the slips out loud where everyone can see is a job somebody has to do. Is that a right or a responsibility?
key: A right. It is something every person at the stand gets.
A responsibility. It is a job that has to be done, and done honestly.

title: The Orchard Map
desc: giving an exact grid location, describing a relative location, and telling a physical feature from a built one
dir: Look at the map grid. Answer out loud.
text: A map of the orchard, drawn on a grid. 1 2 3 A B C apple trees the hill the barn the pond the bridge
qs: Find the barn. Give its exact spot on the grid, the letter and the number.
Where is the pond compared to the barn? Use a word like above, below, left of, or right of.
key: B2. Both parts are needed.
Below the barn and to the left of it. Any correct position word counts, and down and over counts too.

title: The Orchard Map
desc: naming built features of a familiar place and recognizing that people in one place come from many different places
dir: Answer out loud about the town you live in.
text: The people who pick at this orchard come from six different towns, and three of them speak a second language at home.
qs: Name three things people built in the town where you live.
Do all the people who work in one place have to come from the same town? Say how you know from the story above.
key: Any three built things: stores, roads, a school, a library, houses, a bridge, a fire station, a park bench.
No. The pickers come from six different towns and some speak a second language at home.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: telling what a national symbol and a national tradition are, and why a country keeps them
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The Statue of Liberty stands up. She is on an island. A harbor holds the island. New York has the harbor. She holds a torch up high. She has stood there a long
qs: What does the Statue of Liberty hold up high?
People arriving by ship saw her first. What message do you think a torch held up high was meant to send them?
key: a torch
Welcome, you have arrived, there is light here, this is a free country. Any sensible welcoming meaning counts. This is the question that shows a symbol stands for an idea.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: comparing everyday life long ago with life today and telling what changed from what stayed the same
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Getting apples from the orchard to the market. Long ago Today how they travelled a horse pulled a wooden wagon a truck with an engine how long it took most of a
qs: Long ago, what pulled the apples to the market?
What carries them today?
key: a horse pulling a wooden wagon
a truck with an engine

title: Apple Word Baskets
desc: reading words with short vowels, blends, silent e, vowel teams, two syllables, an ending, and an irregular spelling
dir: Read each word out loud. The last two are silly words. Just sound them out.
key: Read each word. plome and fleep are silly words: listen for the long o (silent e) and the long e (ee) sounds.
Watch for: short vowels with blends and digraphs (stem, crunch), silent e (ripe, shade), vowel teams (sweet, pail, grow), two syllables (basket), the ending -ing (picking), an irregular word (said).

title: Two-Part Long Vowel Words
desc: decoding regularly spelled two-syllable words with long vowels
dir: Read each word out loud. Each word has two parts.
key: Mark each word read correctly. Each word has two syllables and at least one long vowel sound, such as pa-per, mu-sic, o-pen.
If the student breaks the word into syllables and then says it smoothly, count it correct.

title: Read the Lines
desc: decoding words with long vowels, vowel teams, prefixes, and suffixes in connected text
dir: Read each line out loud.
text: The pilot flew a paper plane. She opened the table and sat down.
key: Line 1: “The pilot flew a paper plane.” (every word read correctly)
Line 2: “She opened the table and sat down.” (every word read correctly)

title: Read the Story
desc: a 91-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: Nell and Omar went to the orchard on Saturday morning. The grass was still wet. Nell wanted the biggest apple on the tree. But it was at the very top. She jumpe
key: 91 words. Mark each missed word and each self-correction on the passage in the record sheet.
Note pace and expression in your notes.

title: Story Questions
desc: asking and answering when, where, what, how, and who questions about a story
dir: Look back at the story if you need to. Then answer each question out loud.
text: The Top Apple (click to open or close the story) Nell and Omar went to the orchard on Saturday morning. The grass was still wet. Nell wanted the biggest apple o
qs: When did Nell and Omar go to the orchard?
Where was the biggest apple?
key: On Saturday, in the morning
At the very top of the tree

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: Nell and Omar went to the orchard on Saturday morning. The grass was still wet. Nell wanted the biggest apple on the tree. But it was at the very top. She jumpe
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the text about? Tell me two things you remember.” (an answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: Tree Stump Tale
desc: retelling a fable in order and telling its lesson
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the fable. Then tell it back in your own words and answer out loud.
text: Squirrel and Hedgehog Squirrel and Hedgehog each had a pile of apples to take home before dark. Hedgehog put two apples in his basket and set off down the path.
qs: Tell what happened at the beginning of the story.
Tell what happened in the middle.
key: Squirrel and Hedgehog both had apples to take home before dark. Hedgehog carried two at a time. Squirrel said that was too slow.
Squirrel tried to carry all ten of his apples at once. He dropped them, and they rolled down the hill into the pond.

title: Pick and Write
desc: a short narrative with events in order, details, time words, and an ending
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Think of a time you made, picked, or cooked something to eat. Write a story about it. Tell what happened first, next, and last. Tell how you felt. Write 3 or 4
key: Tells about one event or a short set of events in order
Includes details about actions, thoughts, or feelings

title: Pick and Write
desc: a short informative piece with a topic sentence, facts, and a closing
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write to teach a friend about apples. Start by telling what you are writing about. Give 2 or more facts. End with a closing sentence. Write 3 or 4 sentences. Fa
key: Starts with a sentence that names the topic (apples)
Gives 2 or more facts about apples

title: Buzzing Bees
desc: asking and answering what, when, how, and why questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about bees. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Bees in the Orchard In spring, apple trees are covered with flowers. The flowers are white and pink. Bees fly from flower to flower. They drink sweet nectar. Ye
qs: What do bees drink from the flowers?
When are apple trees covered with flowers?
key: Nectar (sweet nectar)
In spring

title: Farm Stand Facts
desc: gathering information from a chart to answer questions
dir: Use the chart to find your answers. Say the first two out loud. Write the last one on your paper and hold it up.
qs: A cook wants to bake a pie. Which apple should the cook buy?
Which two apples taste sweet?
key: Granny Smith. The chart says it is best for pie.
Gala and Golden Delicious. Listen for both names.

title: Remember and Write
desc: recalling information from experiences to answer a question in writing
dir: Think about what happened to you. Write one sentence on your paper for each question. Hold it up when you finish.
qs: Think about a place you visited. Tell what you saw there.
Think about a game you played. Tell how you played it.
key: Names a real place and tells at least one thing seen. (a complete sentence)
Tells a real game and at least one rule or step. (a complete sentence)

title: Listen Up
desc: describing key details and retelling the steps from a text read aloud
dir: Listen first. Then answer your teacher’s questions out loud.
text: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about how apple cider is made.
key: Ask: “What do workers do to the apples first?” (wash them in cold water)
Ask: “What is mash?” (apples chopped into tiny bits)

title: Tell Me a Story
desc: telling about an experience in order, with facts and details, in clear complete sentences
dir: Tell your story out loud. Say what happened first, next, and last.
text: Tell me about a time you were outside and saw an animal or a bug. Where were you? What did it look like? What did it do? First Next Last
key: Tells what happened in an order that makes sense
Gives facts that fit the story (where, when, who, or what)

title: Longer Directions
desc: following three- and four-step oral directions, requesting clarification when something is not understood, and giving multi-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear. Ask a question if you are not sure what to do. Then give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do the steps in order. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once: “Get a pencil, write the number 8, and circle it.” (does all three steps in order)
Say once: “Clap two times, turn around, touch your toes, and sit back down.” (does all four steps in order)

title: Plan and Tell a Story
desc: planning and delivering a short narrative presentation that recounts an event with details, a logical sequence, and a conclusion
dir: Pick one idea. Plan what you will say: the start, the middle, and the end. Then tell your story out loud.
text: Pick one: a time you helped someone, a game or a sport you played, or a time something surprised you. Beginning Middle End
key: Plans first: says or draws what will happen at the start, the middle, and the end before telling (give about one minute to plan)
Tells one event with enough detail (who, where, and what happened)

title: Say It Right
desc: spoken grammar items (irregular plurals, irregular past tense, a group noun, making a sentence longer)
dir: Say each answer out loud.
qs: One leaf, two ____.
Today I eat an apple. Yesterday I ____ an apple.
key: leaf
ate

title: Write It Right
desc: written conventions (capital letters, an apostrophe in a contraction, a comma in a letter greeting, spelling a silent e word)
dir: Write each answer on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Fix this sentence: the orchard is in california
Write do not as one short word.
key: The orchard is in California. (capital T, capital C, and a period)
don’t (with the apostrophe)

title: Capital Letters
desc: capitalizing holidays, product names, and geographic names
dir: Listen while your teacher reads each sentence. Write it again with the right capital letters. Hold up your paper when you finish.
qs: Fix the capital letters: we watch fireworks on the fourth of july.
Fix the capital letters: she lives near the pacific ocean.
key: We watch fireworks on the Fourth of July.
She lives near the Pacific Ocean.

title: Use a Dictionary
desc: using a beginning dictionary and ABC order to check and correct spellings
dir: Listen. Answer out loud. If you have a beginning dictionary, you may use it.
qs: Put these words in ABC order the way a dictionary does: pig, cow, hen.
The guide words are fish and goat. Would the word frog be on this page? Tell why.
key: cow, hen, pig
Yes. frog comes after fish and before goat.

title: Adjective or Adverb?
desc: using adjectives and adverbs and choosing between them depending on what is to be modified
dir: Listen. Pick the word that fits and say it.
qs: Which word tells how he talks: loud or loudly? “He talks ___.”
Which word describes the box: heavy or heavily? “The ___ box fell.”
key: loudly
heavy

title: What I Think
desc: a short opinion piece with an opinion, a reason joined with because, and a closing
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Is it better to pick apples yourself at an orchard, or to buy apples at a store? Write what you think. Give one reason. Write 2 or 3 sentences. I think because
key: States an opinion: says clearly which one is better
Gives a reason for the opinion and joins it with a linking word such as because, and, or also

title: Bee Buddies
desc: telling odd from even for groups up to 20 and writing an even number as a double
dir: Buddies come in twos. Look at each group. Say odd or even. Write the adding sentences on your paper and hold them up.
qs: Is the number of apples odd or even?
Is the number of bees odd or even?
key: Even. There are 8 apples, and every apple has a buddy.
Odd. There are 13 bees, and one bee has no buddy.

title: Count the Crates
desc: skip-counting by 2s, 5s, 10s, and 100s and counting past 200
dir: Count out loud.
qs: Apples go in bags of 2. Skip count by 2s from 8 to 24.
Each basket holds 5 apples. Skip count by 5s from 25 to 60.

title: Read the Bar Graph
desc: reading a bar graph with four categories and solving compare and put-together problems from it
dir: Look at the bar graph. Answer each question out loud.
qs: How many baskets of green apples were sold?
Which color sold the most baskets?
key: Red (9 baskets)

title: Draw a Picture Graph
desc: drawing a picture graph from a table and solving compare and put-together problems from it
dir: Draw a picture graph on your paper. Draw one circle for each jug. Hold it up. Then answer out loud.
qs: Draw a picture graph that shows the cider sold each day.
How many more jugs were sold on Saturday than on Friday?
key: The graph has a row or column for each day with the day names written in. Friday has 3 circles, Saturday has 6, and Sunday has 4. The circles line up.

title: Draw a Bar Graph
desc: drawing a bar graph with a single-unit scale from a data set and solving put-together, take-apart, and compare problems
dir: Look at the table. Draw a bar graph on your paper. Count by ones up the side. Then answer out loud.
text: Favorite seasons: number of kids Choice Number of kids Winter 2 Spring 4 Summer 8 Fall 5
qs: Draw a bar graph of the table. Give it a title, label each bar, and number the side by ones.
How many kids chose Summer and Fall together?
key: A bar graph with bars of height 2 for Winter, 4 for Spring, 8 for Summer, 5 for Fall, a title, labels, and a side scale counting by ones that starts at 0.

title: One Step
desc: one-step addition and subtraction word problems within 100 (put together, add to, take from, compare)
dir: Listen while your teacher reads each problem. Solve it on your paper. You can draw or write a number sentence. Say your answer.
qs: A bowl has 9 red apples and 8 green apples. How many apples are in the bowl?
A cart has 34 apples. The farmer puts 25 more apples on the cart. How many apples are on the cart now?

title: Two Steps
desc: two-step addition and subtraction word problems within 100
dir: These problems have two steps. Listen while your teacher reads each one. Solve it on your paper and say your answer.
qs: Kai picked 12 apples. Then he picked 9 more. He fed 6 apples to a horse. How many apples does Kai have now?
A farm stand had 50 jars of honey. It sold 20 jars in the morning and 14 jars in the afternoon. How many jars are left?

title: Apple Trays
desc: finding the total of a rectangular array with rows of equal size, using repeated addition
dir: Look at the tray of apples. Answer out loud.
qs: How many rows are there, and how many apples are in each row?
Write an adding sentence that matches the rows. Say it out loud.
key: 4 rows with 5 apples in each row
5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20. Adding the columns instead, 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 20, is also correct

title: Read the Blocks
desc: naming the hundreds, tens, and ones in a three-digit number, and writing it as a numeral and in expanded form
dir: Look at the blocks. Answer out loud. Write the last one on your paper.
qs: How many hundreds, how many tens, and how many ones?
What number is on the mat? Say its name out loud.
key: 3 hundreds, 4 tens, and 6 ones
346. The name is three hundred forty-six. Three hundred AND forty-six is a common slip; the standard asks for the name without the and

title: Big Adding and Taking Away
desc: adding and subtracting three-digit numbers with regrouping
dir: Solve on your paper. You can use blocks or a drawing. Say your answer.
qs: The orchard counted 248 apples on Monday and 176 apples on Tuesday. How many apples is that in all?
There were 503 apples in the barn. 268 of them were sold. How many apples are left?
key: 424 apples (248 + 176 = 424). The ones make a new ten (8 + 6 = 14) and the tens make a new hundred (4 + 7 + 1 = 12)
235 apples (503 - 268 = 235). This one needs two trades, and the zero in the tens place is where the slip usually happens

title: Why Regroup?
desc: adding and subtracting within 1000 with place value, and explaining why a ten or hundred is composed or decomposed
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work. Then tell why you had to regroup.
qs: Solve 47 + 36. Tell why you had to make a new ten.
Solve 62 - 27. Tell why you had to take a ten apart.
key: 83. 7 + 6 = 13 ones, so 10 ones became 1 ten.
35. 2 ones is not enough to take away 7, so 1 ten was regrouped into 10 ones.

title: How Long
desc: measuring length in whole inches with a ruler, choosing the right tool for a longer object, and measuring a real object with a ruler
dir: Look at the rulers. Answer out loud. For the last one, get a real ruler and measure.
qs: How long is the twig?
How long is the leaf?
key: 4 inches
2 inches

title: Stand Clock
desc: telling time to the nearest five minutes and using a.m. and p.m.
dir: Look at the clocks. Say each time out loud.
qs: The wagon leaves at this time. What time is it?
The cider press starts at this time. What time is it?
key: 10:15. Quarter past ten is fine too
2:45. Quarter to three is fine too, as long as the student can also say 2:45

title: Coins at the Stand
desc: finding the value of a set of coins and solving a money word problem
dir: Look at the coins. Answer out loud. Write the last one on your paper.
qs: How much money is here in all?
A bag of apples costs 45 cents. If you pay with these coins, how much is left over?

title: Time Facts
desc: knowing relationships of time such as minutes in an hour, days in a month, and weeks in a year
dir: Listen. Answer out loud.
qs: How many days are in one week?
How many months are in one year?
key: 7 days
12 months

title: Shapes at the Stand
desc: naming shapes by their number of sides and angles, and drawing a shape with given attributes
dir: Look at the four signs. Answer out loud. Then draw on your paper.
qs: Which sign has 5 sides? What is that shape called?
How many angles does the last sign have? What is that shape called?
key: The third sign. It is a pentagon
6 angles. It is a hexagon. A shape has the same number of angles as sides

title: Three Young Apple Trees
desc: reading the results of a plant test and planning a fair test of one thing a plant needs
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Then answer out loud.
text: The orchard keeps young apple trees in pots for a year before planting them out. Three pots sat in different places for one month. Pot What it got How much the
qs: Which pot grew the most, and what did it get?
Pot B was watered every day. Why did it only grow 1 centimeter?
key: Pot A, 4 centimeters. It got both sunlight and water.
It was kept out of the sunlight. Water on its own was not enough, so sunlight is something a plant needs too.

title: Three Young Apple Trees
desc: making a simple model that does the job an animal does when it moves seeds
dir: Draw your model on your paper. Then tell your teacher about it.
text: Burrs come from the weeds. The weeds are at the end of the rows. They hook onto a sheep's wool. They get carried to a new field. There they fall off and grow. D
qs: Draw your model. Label the part that hooks the seed on and the part that lets it go.
Which animal job does your model copy, and why does the hooking part matter?
key: Any model with a grabbing part and a way to let go: hooks or bent pins on a mitten, a sticky pad, a loop of tape on a stick, a pocket with a flap. The two labelled parts are what to look for.
It copies an animal carrying seeds on its fur to a new place. The hooks matter because without them the seed falls off straight away and never gets anywhere new.

title: The Row and the Hedge
desc: comparing the kinds of living things found in two different habitats
dir: Listen while your teacher reads both lists. Answer out loud.
text: Two children walked the orchard for one hour and wrote down every kind of living thing they found in two places. A mowed row between the trees The wild hedge at
qs: How many kinds of living things are on the hedge list?
Which place has more different kinds of living things in it?
key: 14. Four wildflowers, two berry bushes, five beetles and bugs, two birds and one rabbit.
the wild hedge

title: Quick Change, Slow Change
desc: using two sources as evidence that some Earth events happen quickly and some happen slowly
dir: Listen while your teacher reads both notes. Answer out loud.
text: Two notes about the same farm, from two different places. Where it came from What it says the old orchard journal, written by hand The creek has moved about one
qs: Which note tells about a change to the land that happened quickly?
Which note tells about a change that is taking a very long time?
key: The weather report, the ditch washed across the field in one night.
The orchard journal, the creek moving one step every ten years.

title: Quick Change, Slow Change
desc: telling where water is found on Earth and whether it is solid or liquid
dir: Answer out loud.
text: There is water in more places on this farm than most people would guess.
qs: Name three places on this farm or nearby where you would find water.
Most of the water on Earth is in the ocean and it is salty. Name a place where the water is fresh instead.
key: Any three: the creek, the pond, the well, the rain barrel, rain in the clouds, frost or ice, under the ground, inside the apples.
A creek, a pond, a river, a lake, a well, rain. Fresh water is the kind people and crops can drink.

title: Holding the Soil, and a Map of the Farm
desc: comparing two things put in place to stop water from washing the land away
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Rain washes soil down the slope between two rows of trees. The farm tried two ways to hold it and measured the soil caught in a box at the bottom of the slope.
qs: Which one held the most soil on the slope?
How do you know, using the numbers in the chart?
key: the thick layer of straw
Only 1 kilogram of soil washed down with the straw, 3 kilograms washed down with the grass, and 9 kilograms washed down with bare dirt. The reason must come from the numbers.

title: Holding the Soil, and a Map of the Farm
desc: making a model of an area that shows the shapes of the land and the bodies of water in it
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up.
text: Make your own model map of the farm. Put in the hill the orchard sits on, the flat lower field, the creek, and the pond. Add a key that says which is which.
qs: Draw your model map with the hill, the flat field, the creek and the pond on it.
Show me your key. Which parts are land and which parts are water?
key: All four on the page and told apart by shape or colour: the hill as a bump or as rings, the flat field left flat, the creek as a line, the pond as a closed shape.
Points to each part and reads the key. The key is what makes this a model and not just a picture.

title: Sorting the Farm Stand Shelf
desc: describing materials by properties you can see or feel and sorting them into groups
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Four things from under the farm stand counter, and what the children noticed about each one. Item Material What they noticed a honey jar glass hard, smooth, you
qs: Sort the four items into a hard group and a group that bends easily.
You want a pile of things you can see through. Which item goes in it?
key: Hard: the glass honey jar and the metal funnel. Bends easily: the cloth sack and the paper envelope.
the glass honey jar

title: Sorting the Farm Stand Shelf
desc: using test data to choose the material that suits a job
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The farm stand needs a liner for its baskets so cut fruit does not leak through. Three materials were each loaded with 2 kilograms of fruit and half a cup of ju
qs: Which material is best for the basket liner?
Which two pieces of the chart make you sure?
key: the waxed paper
No juice leaked through it and it did not tear under 2 kilograms. Both columns have to be used, not just one.

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: telling how a thing built from a few pieces can be taken apart and built into something new
dir: Answer out loud. You may draw if it helps.
text: A drying rack is in the barn. It is made of 8 straight sticks. It has 6 rubber bands. One of the children untied it. She laid the sticks on the floor.
qs: The rack is gone. Are the sticks gone too? What is on the floor now?
Build something new in your head out of those 8 sticks and 6 bands. What is it, and how do the pieces go together?
key: No. All 8 sticks and all 6 bands are still there. They are the same pieces, just not tied together as a rack any more.

Any real thing from 8 sticks and 6 bands: a tent frame, a star, a ladder for a bean plant, a kite frame, a fence for a seed row. Listen for how the pieces join, because that is the evidence the same s

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: arguing with evidence that some heating and cooling changes can be undone and some cannot
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two things happened in the farm kitchen on the same afternoon. What happened A pat of butter was left in a warm pan and turned into a yellow puddle. Sliced appl
qs: Put the pan of melted butter somewhere cool. What happens to it?
Put the pot of apple sauce somewhere cool. Does it turn back into apple slices?
key: It goes hard again and is a pat of butter. Cooling undoes the melting.
No. It stays soft brown sauce. Nothing cool turns it back into slices.

title: The Baskets That Tip
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking a question about it
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the note. Answer out loud.
text: The farm stand sets its apple baskets out. They go on a long table. The table is by the road. A gust of wind comes along. Whenever it does a basket tips. The ap
qs: What is the problem the children want to fix? Say it in one sentence.
Ask one question that would help you fix it.
key: The baskets tip over in the wind and the apples roll off the table. Naming the tipping, not the picking up, is the problem.
Any real question: how tall are the baskets, how heavy is a full one, is the table flat, which way does the wind come from, are the empty ones the ones that tip. A statement is not a question, so ask

title: The Baskets That Tip
desc: drawing a design and telling how its shape does the job
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw something that would stop a basket tipping on that table. Think hard about its shape.
qs: Draw your fix.
Tell me how the shape of what you drew keeps the basket upright.
key: Any design that could really hold a basket: a ring or hole cut in a board that the basket sits down into, a rail along the table edge, a wide flat base under the basket, a crate the baskets stand insi
The shape is the part being checked. Something like: the ring holds the bottom so it cannot lean, the rail blocks it from going over the edge, a wide base is harder to tip than a narrow one.

title: The Baskets That Tip
desc: comparing test results from two designs built for the same problem
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Both fixes were tried for one whole windy Saturday. Fix Baskets that tipped that day a board with round holes cut for the baskets 0 a rail along the table edge
qs: Which fix worked better?
How do you know?
key: the board with round holes cut for the baskets
No baskets tipped with the board and 4 tipped with the rail. The reason has to come from the chart, not from liking one design.

title: Picking Then and Now
desc: telling things that happened long ago from things that happened in the last day or two
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the four lines. Answer out loud.
text: Four lines from the wall of the farm stand. Line What it says 1 Yesterday the children filled 40 baskets for the Saturday stand. 2 When this orchard was planted
qs: Which two lines tell about things that happened long ago?
Which two tell about things that happened in the last day or two?
key: Lines 2 and 4, the horse wagon and trading apples for cloth and nails.
Lines 1 and 3, filling the baskets yesterday and switching on the press this morning.

title: Where Things Are on the Farm
desc: giving an exact place on a map with a letter and a number, and using north, south, east, west and between
dir: Look at the farm map. Answer out loud.
text: The farm, drawn in nine squares. North is at the top. 1 2 3 A orchard rows bee hives hay field B packing shed farm stand machine barn C pasture pond hen house N
qs: Give the exact square the farm stand is in, using its letter and its number.
What is directly south of the farm stand?
key: B2
the pond, in square C2

title: Rules, Money and the Stand
desc: telling who makes rules at each level here, and how other countries choose a leader differently
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The farm stand has a sign that says what the rules are, and so does the county, and so does the country.
qs: Who leads a state? A governor, or a farm stand keeper?
A county rule says every farm stand must keep its scales honest. Why would a government make a rule like that?
key: a governor
So nobody is cheated. Any answer about fairness or keeping people safe counts. Rules are made to protect people who are buying.

title: Rules, Money and the Stand
desc: telling goods from services, spending a set amount of money, and saying why people trade
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the price list. Answer out loud.
text: The Saturday farm stand price list. What is on offer Price a basket of apples 60 cents a jar of honey 35 cents a loaf of bread 25 cents someone to carry your lo
qs: Three things on this list are goods and one is a service. Which one is the service, and how do you know?
You have 60 cents. You cannot buy everything. Name two things you could buy with it, and say what you give up.
key: Carrying your load to your car. It is help someone does for you, not a thing you take home.

Any pair that comes to 60 cents or less: honey and bread is 60 cents, bread and the carrying is 35 cents, apples on their own is 60 cents. The giving up is the part to listen for, because a set amount

title: Someone Who Made a Difference
desc: telling what one person from the recent past did and how it made a difference to others
dir: Listen to the story. Answer out loud.
text: Dr Martin Luther King Jr was a boy once. There were rules in many places then. They kept Black people and white people apart. Black children went to different s
qs: What did Dr King think was not fair?
What did he ask people to do instead of fighting?
key: The rules that kept Black people and white people apart. Any of the examples counts: different schools, having to sit at the back of the bus.
Change the rules in a peaceful way. Walking instead of riding the buses is the example in the passage. Accept speaking up, marching, or telling people it was wrong.

title: Apple Word Pick
desc: reading words with prefixes, suffixes, and more than one syllable
dir: Read each word out loud. If a word is long, break it into parts first.
key: Read each word: basket, blossom, orchard, unpack, refill, seedless, helpful, slowly, crunchy, unbroken, replanted, wonderful.

Watch for: two-syllable words (basket, blossom, orchard), prefixes un- and re- (unpack, refill, unbroken, replanted), suffixes -less, -ful, -ly, -y (seedless, helpful, slowly, crunchy), and three-syll

title: What Does the Ending Mean?
desc: identifying and knowing the meaning of common derivational suffixes and decoding words with Latin suffixes
dir: Read each word. Tell what the ending means and what the whole word means.
text: sadness helpful fearless quickly
qs: What does the ending mean in sadness? What does sadness mean?
What does the ending mean in helpful? What does helpful mean?
key: -ness means being or state of. sadness means being sad.
-ful means full of. helpful means full of help.

title: Tricky Words
desc: reading grade-appropriate irregularly spelled words
dir: Read each word out loud. Some of these words do not follow the usual rules.
key: Mark each word read correctly. These words do not follow the usual spelling patterns, so the student has to know them by sight.

title: Up the Ladder
desc: a 258-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: The Last Apple Tess and her neighbor, Mr. Park, picked apples all morning. By noon, six baskets were full. Only one apple was left on the old tree. It hung from
key: 258 words, not counting the title. Time 1 minute and mark errors and self-corrections on your own copy. Let the student finish the passage.

Fall grade 3 benchmark: about 83 words correct per minute (Hasbrouck and Tindal 2017, fall 50th percentile). The passage length is set from the highest grade 3 figure on that same table, the spring 90

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice and let the rhymes show.
text: The Kite My kite goes up in the wind so blue. It dips and it dances, it swings and it flew. I hold on tight to the long white string. I feel like a bird on the
key: 36 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm and expression at the ends of lines: a pause at the end of each line or where the punctuation is.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: The Last Apple Tess and her neighbor, Mr. Park, picked apples all morning. By noon, six baskets were full. Only one apple was left on the old tree. It hung from
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: The Last Apple
desc: story questions answered by pointing to the exact words in the text
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud. Look back at the story to prove each answer.
text: The Last Apple Tess and her neighbor, Mr. Park, picked apples all morning. By noon, six baskets were full. Only one apple was left on the old tree. It hung from
qs: How many baskets were full by noon? Read the sentence that tells you.
What three things did Tess try before she used the ladder? Look back at the story.
key: Six. Reads “By noon, six baskets were full.” (RL.3.1)
She stood on her toes, she jumped, and she shook the trunk. All three come from the second paragraph. (RL.3.1)

title: Ask and Answer
desc: asking and answering questions to show understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers
dir: Read the text to yourself or out loud. Then ask your teacher questions about it. Answer your teacher’s questions with words from the text.
text: Leo wanted to win the race. He ran fast and passed two friends. Then his shoe came untied. Leo stopped to tie it. Two friends passed him. He did not give up. He
key: Say: “Ask me one question about the text that the text can answer.” (asks a real question; you answer it from the text)
Say: “Ask me a second question that starts with why or how.” (asks a real question that needs more than one word to answer)

title: Cider Press Sayings
desc: literal and nonliteral meanings of phrases in a story
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Cider Day It was cider day at the orchard. “Can you lend me a hand?” called Aunt Jo. Mateo ran over. “I am all ears,” he said. “What do I do?” Aunt Jo showed hi
qs: Aunt Jo asks, “Can you lend me a hand?” Does she want Mateo’s real hand? What does she mean?
Mateo says, “I am all ears.” What does he mean?
key: No. She wants him to help her. It is not literal. (RL.3.4)
He is listening closely and is ready to hear what to do. (RL.3.4)

title: Sign Fixer
desc: fixing spoken grammar mistakes (plurals, verb tense, agreement, comparing words)
dir: Each sign has one mistake. Say the whole sentence the right way.
qs: Two mouses ran under the apple cart.
The bees is busy today.
key: Two mice ran under the apple cart. (L.3.1, irregular plural noun)
The bees are busy today. (L.3.1, subject-verb agreement)

title: Word Jobs
desc: spoken grammar items (plural nouns, future tense, agreement, verbs and adjectives)
dir: Answer out loud.
qs: Say the word for more than one: one leaf, two ____.
Say the sentence with the right verb: Tomorrow we ____ the apples. (wash)
key: leaves (L.3.1, irregular plural noun)
Tomorrow we will wash the apples. (L.3.1, simple future tense)

title: Each Other
desc: using reciprocal pronouns such as each other and one another correctly
dir: Choose the word that fits. Say it or write it.
qs: Mom and Dad smiled at ___. (each other / one another)
The dogs in the park chased ___. (each other / one another)
key: each other
one another or each other

title: Write It in Cursive
desc: writing legibly in cursive or joined italics with margins and correct spacing between letters in a word and words in a sentence
dir: On your paper, write this sentence in cursive or joined writing. Leave a margin and keep space between your words.
text: Write this sentence: Every kind word helps a friend smile.
key: Letters are joined within each word (cursive or joined italics, not separate print letters)
Letters are formed so another person can read them

title: Busy Bees
desc: asking and answering questions about an informational text using the exact words in the text
dir: Read the text. Then answer out loud. Look back at the text to prove each answer.
text: Bees at Work An apple tree cannot make apples all by itself. It needs help from bees. In spring, apple trees are covered with blossoms. Each blossom holds a yel
qs: Why does a bee land on an apple blossom? Which sentence tells you?
How does pollen get from one tree to another tree? Use the text.
key: To drink sweet nectar. Points to “A bee lands on a blossom to drink sweet nectar.” (RI.3.1)
Pollen sticks to the bee’s fuzzy body. When the bee flies to a blossom on another tree, some pollen rubs off. (RI.3.1)

title: Farm Stand Writer
desc: an opinion writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Which is the better apple treat: fresh apple slices or warm apple pie? Write your opinion. Give two reasons. Write 4 to 6 sentences. Say your opinion Give two r
key: Introduces the topic and states an opinion (W.3.1)
Gives reasons that support the opinion (W.3.1)

title: Farm Stand Writer
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Write to teach someone how apples become cider. Use the steps in the fact box. Write 4 to 6 sentences. Fact box: from apples to cider 1. Wash the apples 2. Grin
key: Introduces the topic: how apples become cider (W.3.2)
Develops the topic with facts and details from the fact box: wash, grind into mush, press out the juice, pour into jugs and keep cold (W.3.2)

title: Farm Stand Writer
desc: a narrative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: One morning, a friendly bee follows you all the way through the orchard. Write the story of what happens. Write 4 to 6 sentences. First Next Then Last Tell who
key: Sets up the situation and who is in the story (W.3.3)
Events happen in a clear order, with time words such as first, next, then, after that (W.3.3)

title: Note Baskets
desc: taking brief notes from a text and sorting them into given categories
dir: Read the text. Write your notes on your paper and hold it up.
text: An Apple Tree’s Year In spring, an apple tree grows pink and white blossoms. In summer, small green apples grow where the blossoms were. Farmers water the trees
key: Tree box: a fact about the tree, such as grows blossoms in spring, grows small green apples in summer, apples are ripe by fall, drops its leaves, rests in winter. (W.3.8, sorts evidence into the given
People box: a fact about people, such as farmers water the trees, workers climb ladders, workers fill baskets, farmers cut off old branches. (W.3.8, sorts evidence into the given category)

title: Remember and Take Notes
desc: recalling information from experience and taking brief notes on a source, sorting the evidence into categories
dir: Write on your paper. First, remember a time from your own life and write about it. Then take notes on the text and sort them.
text: Read the text. Take brief notes. Sort your notes into two groups: Birds and Fish. A robin builds a nest of twigs and grass. A hawk hunts mice from the sky. A tr
qs: Think about a place you visit often. Write two or three sentences about what you do there.
Take brief notes on the text. Write short notes, not whole sentences. (for example: nest of twigs, hunts mice)
key: Names a real place and at least two details.
Short notes in the student’s own words, not copied sentences.

title: Listen for the Main Idea
desc: finding the main idea and supporting details of information read aloud
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the guide's welcome. It is not on your screen. Then answer out loud.
text: Listen only. Your teacher will read the orchard guide's welcome once.
qs: What is the main idea of what you just heard?
Give two details that support that main idea.
key: How the apple picking tour works, from start to finish. Any wording that names the whole process counts. A single detail, such as a wagon, is not the main idea (SL.3.2)
Two of these: a wagon takes the group to the trees, a guide shows how to twist an apple off, you fill one bag yourself, the bag is weighed at the barn, what you pick is yours to keep (SL.3.2)

title: Tell Me About the Tools
desc: reporting on a topic with facts and descriptive details, in clear speech
dir: Talk for about a minute. Speak clearly and look up while you talk.
text: A worker picks apples at an orchard. Tell me what they need. What is each thing for? a ladder a bag or basket a crate
key: Names facts that fit the topic: a ladder to reach high branches, a bag or basket to carry what is picked, a crate to hold the apples, gloves, a wagon (SL.3.4)
Adds descriptive detail to at least one of them, such as how big it is, what it is made of, or how it is used (SL.3.4)

title: Read the Chart
