desc: determining main ideas and supporting details from information presented visually and quantitatively
dir: Look at the chart. Answer your teacher’s questions out loud.
text: Favorite lunch: number of students Choice Students Pizza 11 Sandwich 8 Salad 4 Soup 7
qs: What is the main idea of this chart? Tell it in one sentence.
Which choice did the most students pick? How many?
key: The chart shows how many students chose each kind of favorite lunch. The most popular is Pizza.
Pizza, 11

title: Two Ways to Pick
desc: comparing and contrasting the key points of two texts on the same topic
dir: Read both short texts. Then answer out loud. Look back at either text to prove your answer.
text: Picking by Hand At a small orchard, every apple is picked by hand. Workers carry canvas bags and climb ladders to reach the high branches. They twist each apple
qs: What is the same about the two ways of picking?
What is different about how long each way takes? Use a detail from each text.
key: Both are ways of getting the apples off the tree and into a bag or bin at harvest time. Any true point both texts share counts (RI.3.9)
Hand picking takes a long time. The machine empties one tree in about a minute. Both details are needed (RI.3.9)

title: Crates and Rows
desc: telling what the numbers in a multiplication equation mean with equal groups and rows
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud. Write your equations on your paper and hold them up.
qs: Picture A: How many crates are there? How many apples are in each crate?
Write a multiplication equation for Picture A. Tell what each number means.
key: 3 crates with 6 apples in each crate. Partial: one of the two counts given is approaching. (3.OA.A.1)

3 × 6 = 18. The 3 is the number of crates (groups), the 6 is the number of apples in each crate, and 18 is the total. Accept 6 × 3 = 18 when the student explains it. Partial: the equation right with n

title: Share the Harvest
desc: telling what the numbers in a division equation mean with equal shares and equal groups
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud. Write your equations on your paper and hold them up.
qs: Picture A: Share the 12 apples equally among the 3 crates. How many apples go in each crate?
Write a division equation for Picture A. Tell what each number means.
key: 4 apples in each crate. Partial: 4 with no account of what it counts is approaching. (3.OA.A.2)

12 ÷ 3 = 4. 12 is the total number of apples, 3 is the number of crates (equal shares), and 4 is the number of apples in each crate. Partial: the equation right with no meaning for each number is appr

title: Farm Stand Math
desc: matching multiplication to equal-group stories and drawings
dir: Answer out loud. For number 3, draw on your paper and hold it up.
qs: A farm stand has 6 bags. Each bag holds 5 apples. Which one tells how many apples in all: 6 + 5 or 6 × 5? Tell why.
Tell an orchard story problem for 3 × 9.
key: 6 × 5. There are 6 equal groups with 5 in each group, so 30 apples in all. Partial: choosing 6 × 5 with no reason is approaching. (3.OA.A.1)
A story with 3 equal groups of 9, or 9 groups of 3, and 27 in all. Example: 3 trees with 9 apples on each tree. Partial: a story with the right numbers but no equal groups is approaching. (3.OA.A.1)

title: Cider Jug Shares
desc: matching division to sharing and grouping stories and drawings
dir: Answer out loud. For number 4, draw on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Which story matches 30 ÷ 5? Story A: A shelf has 30 jugs of cider. Then 5 jugs are sold. Story B: 30 jugs of cider are put on 5 shelves, with the same number on each shelf.
Spot the mistake. Kai says, “10 ÷ 2 means 10 groups of 2.” Is Kai right? Tell why.
key: Story B. 30 jugs shared equally among 5 shelves is 6 jugs on each shelf. Story A is subtraction. Partial: choosing Story B with no reason is approaching. (3.OA.A.2)

No. 10 ÷ 2 means 10 things split into 2 equal groups (5 in each group) or into groups of 2 (5 groups). 10 groups of 2 is 10 × 2. Partial: saying no with no correct meaning given is approaching. (3.OA.

title: Two Steps
desc: two-step word problems solved with an equation using a letter, and checking that the answer is reasonable
dir: Solve on your paper. Write an equation with a letter for the unknown. Show your work and hold it up.
text: The cider stand started the day with 150 cider donuts. It sold 62 donuts before lunch and 45 donuts after lunch.
qs: Tess filled 7 baskets with 8 apples in each basket. She gave 15 of those apples to Mr. Park. How many apples does she have left? Write an equation with a letter for what you do not know.
Use rounding to show that your answer makes sense.
key: 41 apples. 7 × 8 = 56, then 56 - 15 = 41. An equation such as (7 × 8) - 15 = a, or 56 - 15 = a, counts. Or: 7 × 8 = b and b - 15 = a written as two equations, as long as the letter stands for the unkn
About 60 take away about 15 is about 45, so 41 is close to what we expect. Any rounding that lands near 41 counts. Partial: an estimate with no comparison to the answer is approaching. (3.OA.D.8)

title: Round It
desc: rounding whole numbers to the nearest ten and the nearest hundred
dir: Answer out loud.
text: 476 apples were picked on Saturday.
qs: Round 476 to the nearest ten.
Round 476 to the nearest hundred.
key: 480. The ones digit is 6, so it goes up. Partial: 470 rounds down when the ones digit is 6 and does not count. (3.NBT.A.1)
500. The tens digit is 7, so it goes up. Partial: 400 rounds down when the tens digit is 7 and does not count. (3.NBT.A.1)

title: Name the Fraction
desc: naming a fraction of a whole and finding a fraction on a number line
dir: Look at the pie bar and the number line. Answer out loud.
qs: The pie bar is cut into 6 equal pieces. 5 of them are shaded. What fraction is shaded?
What does the bottom number 6 tell you?
key: 5/6, five sixths. Partial: 5 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.NF.A.1)

The whole was cut into 6 equal parts, so each part is one sixth. The top number tells how many of those parts we have. Partial: naming the 6 parts with nothing said about the top number is approaching

title: Same Size, Different Name
desc: finding an equivalent fraction and comparing two fractions with the same numerator
dir: Look at the two bars. Answer out loud.
qs: The two bars are the same size. The top one shows 1/2 and the bottom one shows 2/4. Are those two fractions equal? How do you know?
Name a fraction with 8 on the bottom that is equal to 1/2.
key: Yes, they are equal. The shaded part of each bar covers the same amount of the same size whole. Partial: saying yes with no reason from the bars is approaching. (3.NF.A.3)
4/8. Partial: 2/8 or 8/8 does not count. (3.NF.A.3)

title: Compare With Symbols
desc: comparing fractions with the same numerator or denominator, recording the results with the symbols >, =, or <, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know. You can draw a model.
qs: Which is greater, 4/6 or 2/6? Write the comparison with >, = or <.
Compare 1/2 and 1/8 with a symbol. Tell how you know.
key: 4/6 > 2/6 (or 2/6 < 4/6). Same denominator, more parts.
1/2 > 1/8. Same numerator, and halves are bigger pieces than eighths.

title: Fractions on a Number Line
desc: representing a fraction on a number line diagram by partitioning 0 to 1 into equal parts and marking off lengths
dir: Draw on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
qs: Draw a number line from 0 to 1. Cut it into 6 equal parts. Mark and label 5/6.
Where is 1/6? Mark it.
key: 6 equal parts. 5/6 is at the end of the fifth part.
1/6 is at the end of the first part.

title: To the Nearest Quarter Inch
desc: measuring to the nearest quarter inch, generating measurements of real objects with a ruler, and reading a line plot of measurements
dir: Look at the ruler and the line plot. Answer out loud. For the last one, get a ruler and measure.
qs: How long is the twig on the ruler?
On the line plot, how many twigs measured 2 and a half inches?
key: 2 3/4 inches, two and three quarter inches. Partial: 3 inches rounds to a whole and is approaching. (3.MD.B.4)
4 twigs. Partial: counting the Xs above a different mark does not count. (3.MD.B.4)

title: Cover the Crate Lid
desc: finding the area of a rectangle by multiplying side lengths, and naming one of four equal parts as a unit fraction with its own area
dir: Look at the crate lid. Answer out loud.
qs: The crate lid is covered with square tiles. How many rows are there. How many tiles in each row?
What is the area of the lid in square tiles? How did you get it?
key: 4 rows with 6 tiles in each row. Partial: one of the two counts given is approaching. (3.MD.C.7)
24 square tiles. 4 × 6 = 24. Counting every tile gets the same number, so note whether the student multiplied. Partial: 24 with no square unit named is approaching. (3.MD.C.7)

title: Area Models and L-Shapes
desc: relating area to multiplication and addition, using the distributive property with area models, and finding areas of rectilinear figures by adding non-overlapping rectangles
dir: Draw on your paper. Show your work. Tell how you know.
qs: Tile a rectangle 3 rows by 8 columns, or draw it. What is the area? Show it as multiplication.
Break a 3 by 8 rectangle into a 3 by 5 part and a 3 by 3 part. Write the area as 3 × 5 + 3 × 3.
key: 24 square units, 3 × 8 = 24

title: Sense, Brain, Act
desc: using a model to show how an animal takes in information, processes it, and responds
dir: Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your model on your paper and hold it up.
text: A honeybee flies over the orchard rows. She has long antennae. They pick up scent out of the air. She passes two rows of bare branches. Then she turns sharply t
qs: Which part of the bee took in the information about the blossom?
The bee turned toward one row and not the others. What had to happen inside her before she could turn?
key: Her antennae, which pick up scent. Accept smelling with the antennae. (3-LS1-1)
The scent information went to her brain, and the brain worked out which way the strongest scent came from and decided to turn. (3-LS1-1)

title: A Hive Is a Group
desc: building an argument from data that forming a group helps animals survive
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Some bees live alone and some live in a hive of thousands. A beekeeper measured both through a cold week. Bees Warmest spot inside the nest Food still stored af
qs: Which nest stayed warmer through the cold week?
Make an argument that living in a hive helps a bee survive. Use a number from the table.
key: the hive, 33 C against 4 C (3-LS2-1)
The claim yes, with the numbers attached: the hive held 33 C while the lone bee’s stem was 4 C, and the hive still had food left, so a bee in a hive is more likely to live through cold. A yes with no

title: Passed Down and Shaped
desc: reading trait data for parents and offspring, naming the variation, and telling when the surroundings shaped a trait
dir: Look at both tables. Answer out loud.
text: Table 1: a red-fruited apple tree and four young trees grown from its seeds. Tree Fruit color Leaf length in cm parent tree red 9 young tree A red 7 young tree
qs: Every young tree has red fruit, the same as the parent. Where did that trait come from?
The leaf lengths are all different. What is that difference called. Does it mean one of the young trees came from a different parent?
key: It was inherited from the parent tree. A trait the parent has and every offspring has is passed down. (3-LS3-1)
Variation. They are all still its offspring: inherited traits vary from one offspring to the next, so a group of similar organisms is not identical. (3-LS3-1)

title: Clues in the Quarry
desc: reading fossil data to say which organisms lived in a place and what the place was like
dir: Look at the table of rock layers. Answer out loud.
text: Behind the orchard is an old stone quarry. A class wrote down the fossils in each layer. The top layer is the youngest. Layer Fossils found top pine cones, a be
qs: Name two organisms that once lived where this quarry is now.
Was the bottom layer once underwater or once dry ground? Use the fossils as your evidence.
key: Any two the table names: a pine, a beetle, a broad-leaved plant, a dragonfly, a clam, a snail, a fish. (3-LS4-1)
Underwater. Clams, snails and fish live in water, and naming them is the evidence. An answer with no fossil named is not yet using the data. (3-LS4-1)

title: A Useful Difference
desc: explaining how a variation among individuals of one species gives an advantage
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Ground beetles live under the orchard grass, and birds hunt them. A class measured legs and timed how fast each beetle crossed a path. Beetles Back leg length T
qs: Which beetles crossed the open path faster?
Explain why long back legs are an advantage for a beetle in this orchard. Use the table.
key: the long-legged beetles, 4 seconds against 9 (3-LS4-2)
Long legs cross the open ground faster, so fewer are caught, 3 against 14. A beetle that is not caught survives in a place where birds hunt. The explanation has to lean on the data. (3-LS4-2)

title: Who Survives, and What Would Help
desc: arguing from data who can survive in a changed habitat, then judging the merit of a solution
dir: Read the table. Answer out loud.
text: One autumn stayed cold and rainy for eight weeks. The orchard keeper wrote down what she found in the rows. Living thing What happened that autumn moss on the n
qs: Which living thing survived well in that cold wet autumn? Give the evidence.
Which one was gone from the orchard altogether. Which one only did worse?
key: The moss. It spread over twice its usual patch, so the cold and the wet suited it. (3-LS4-3)
The monarch butterflies could not survive there at all, none were seen. The honeybees survived less well, fewer flying and little food stored. (3-LS4-3)

title: A Season of Weather
desc: reading and making a graphical display of typical weather for one season
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your graph on your paper and hold it up.
text: The keeper records the highest temperature on the first day of every week of picking season. Week Highest temperature 1 24 C 2 22 C 3 18 C 4 16 C 5 15 C
qs: What is happening to the temperature across picking season?
A sixth week of picking season is coming. What temperature would you expect, and why?
key: It is falling week by week, from 24 C down to 15 C. (3-ESS2-1)
Somewhere near 14 C or 15 C, because the table drops a degree or two each week. Any answer in that range with the trend named as the reason. (3-ESS2-1)

title: Two Parts of the World
desc: combining information to describe the climates of two different regions of the world
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Apples grow well in some regions of the world and badly in others. Region Summer Winter Rain in a year a river valley where apples grow warm and dry cold, some
qs: Which region gets far less rain in a year?
Which region has frost in winter. What in the table tells you?
key: the desert region, 9 cm against 75 cm (3-ESS2-2)
the river valley, because the table says its winter is cold with some frost (3-ESS2-2)

title: Ready for the Hail
desc: making a claim about the merit of a design that reduces the impact of a weather hazard
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A hailstorm can bruise a whole row of apples. It takes ten minutes. The keeper stretches a net on poles above each row. It is high enough for a picker to walk u
qs: Which weather hazard is the net meant to reduce?
Make a claim. Does the net have merit? Give your reason.
key: hail, which bruises the fruit (3-ESS3-1)
Yes, with a reason attached: the hail strikes the net instead of the fruit, so the apples are not bruised. A yes with no reason is not yet a claim. (3-ESS3-1)

title: Balanced or Not
desc: planning an investigation of balanced and unbalanced forces acting on an object
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A cart loaded with apple crates stands on the sloped lane. The brake block is wedged under one wheel. The cart does not move.
qs: The slope is pulling the cart downhill. The cart stays still. Are the forces on it balanced or unbalanced? How do you know?
Someone pulls the brake block out. What happens, and what changed about the forces?
key: Balanced. The block pushes back exactly as hard as the slope pulls, and the cart staying still is the evidence. (3-PS2-1)
The cart rolls downhill. Now nothing balances the pull of the slope, so the forces are unbalanced. (3-PS2-1)

title: Predict the Next Apple
desc: using a pattern in motion data to predict where an object will be later
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Apples ride a sorting belt past a counting window. A class timed one apple as it passed the marks painted on the belt rail. Seconds Marks passed 4 1 8 2 12 3
qs: What is the pattern in the table?
Which mark will the apple be at after 20 seconds? How do you know?
key: One mark every 4 seconds, the same time for each one. (3-PS2-2)
mark 5, because 20 seconds divided into 4-second steps is five marks. The reason has to be the pattern, not a guess. (3-PS2-2)

title: Ask About the Pull
desc: asking questions about cause and effect in electric or magnetic interactions between objects not touching
dir: Answer out loud. Your two questions have to be questions, not statements.
text: A balloon is rubbed on a wool sleeve and held just above a dry apple leaf on the table. The leaf lifts off the table toward the balloon. The balloon never touch
qs: The balloon never touches the leaf, yet the leaf lifts. What does that tell you about this force?
Think of two questions about this that you could find out by testing.
key: The force acts across a distance, with no contact between the objects. (3-PS2-3)
Any two real investigable questions: how close does the balloon have to be, does rubbing it longer lift the leaf higher, does a wet leaf lift, does a plastic ruler work instead, does it still work on

title: A Problem for a Magnet
desc: defining a design problem that magnets can solve, with criteria for success and constraints
dir: Answer out loud. For the third one you may write your two sentences on your paper.
text: The steel pins that hold the picking ladders together keep working loose and dropping into the deep grass. They are hard to see. A pin left in the grass can go
qs: State the problem in one sentence. Start with the words: The problem is.
Why is a magnet a sensible idea here? Would the same tool find a dropped plastic cap in the same grass?
key: A problem statement about finding and picking up steel ladder pins out of deep grass. The problem has to be about the lost pins, not about the ladders being loose. (3-PS2-4)
The pins are steel, and a magnet pulls steel without touching it, so it can lift pins the eye cannot see down in the grass. A plastic cap is not pulled by a magnet, so no. (3-PS2-4)

title: Three Ways to Do It
desc: comparing several possible solutions against stated criteria and constraints
dir: Look at the table and the three rules. Answer out loud.
text: Pickers need something to carry apples in while both hands are up in the tree. Three designs are tried. Design Holds Hands free? Bruised apples out of 50 wire b
qs: Which design holds the most apples?
Which one meets all three rules? Use the table to explain.
key: the canvas bag, 35 apples (3-5-ETS1-2)
The canvas bag. It holds 35, leaves both hands free, and bruises only 3 out of 50. Another choice counts only if the student argues it against all three rules using the table. (3-5-ETS1-2)

title: Make the Test Fair
desc: judging whether a test is fair, naming controlled variables, and identifying a failure point
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two ladder feet were tested to see which one slips less on wet grass. Foot Ground Weight on the ladder wide rubber pad wet grass one picker narrow steel spike d
qs: Was that a fair test? Explain.
Which two things would you hold the same to make it fair?
key: No. Two things were different at once, the ground and the weight, so a slip cannot be pinned on the foot. (3-5-ETS1-3)
Any two controlled variables: the same ground, the same weight on the ladder, the same lean, the same ladder, the same weather. (3-5-ETS1-3)

title: Maps and Places
desc: using a map grid and a table to describe physical and human features and where they sit
dir: Use the map grid and the table. Answer out loud.
text: A map grid of the orchard and the land around it. North is the top row. west middle east north hills old oak wood well middle creek apple rows farm stand south
qs: What lies directly west of the apple rows?
Which two directions do you walk to get from the apple rows to the corn field?
key: the creek (HSS-3.1)
south and west, in either order. The corn field sits in the south row and the west column. Partial: one of the two directions is approaching. (HSS-3.1)

title: The First Nations Here
desc: describing how the American Indian nations of California used the plants around them long ago and how a nation is part of the state today
dir: Answer out loud. Use what is on the screen and what you have learned.
text: Many California nations are known for basket making. Weavers cut willow and other plants. They cut when the stems were right. That was one time of year. They sp
qs: The screen gives three steps the weavers took to make a basket. Name all three, in order, and say what the tightest baskets could do.
What does basket making tell you about what people here knew about the plants around them?
key: Cut the willow or other plants at the time of year when the stems were right, split them by hand, then wove them. The tightest baskets held water. Partial: the three steps right with nothing said abou

They knew their local plants closely: which ones to use, when in the year to cut them, and how to prepare them. Listen for knowledge of the local land rather than a memorized list. Partial: listing pl

title: A Town Over Time
desc: sequencing local historical events and describing the mark each period left on the land
dir: Look at the timeline. Answer out loud.
text: A timeline for the town of Mill Hollow. Year What happened 1844 a flour mill is built on the creek, and a pond is dug behind a dam 1869 farmers clear the oak fl
qs: Put these three in order, earliest first. The packing shed. The flour mill. The first apple rows.
Which event changed the oak flats. What did it do to them?
key: flour mill, first apple rows, packing shed. Partial: two of the three in the right order is approaching. (HSS-3.3)
the clearing in 1869, which took out the oaks and put apple rows in their place. Partial: naming the clearing with no account of what it did to the flats is approaching. (HSS-3.3)

title: Rules, Laws and Government
desc: telling rules from laws and naming the basic parts and levels of United States government
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The farm stand has a rule posted by the door. No fruit tasting until it is weighed. There is also a county law. It says every price has to be posted. A buyer mu
qs: What is the difference between the stand’s own rule and the county law?
The United States government has three parts. Which part makes the laws, and what is it called?
key: The stand’s rule is set by the owner and applies at the stand. The county law is made by a government, applies to every seller in the county, and the government decides what happens when it is broken.
Congress, the lawmaking part, also called the legislative branch. Accept the state legislature named for a state law. (HSS-3.4)

title: Choices and the Local Economy
desc: basic economic reasoning about producers and consumers, scarcity, and goods and services
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: The farm stand sells apples and cider, and for a fee it will press a customer’s own fruit into juice. Year Apples picked Price for a bag a good year 9,000 4 dol
qs: In which year was the price higher. What happened to the number of apples that year?
Why would fewer apples push the price up? Use the idea that there is not enough to go around.
key: the hail year, 7 dollars a bag, and there were far fewer apples, 2,000 against 9,000. Partial: the year named with no account of the number of apples is approaching. (HSS-3.5)

When there are fewer apples than people want, apples are scarce, and buyers will pay more for the few that there are. Accept scarcity explained in the student’s own words. Partial: saying the price go

title: Apple Word Pick
desc: reading long words with prefixes, roots, and suffixes
dir: Read each word out loud. The last two are made-up words. Just sound them out.
key: Read each word. Count a word as correct when the student reads it right on the first try or fixes it without help.
The last two are made-up words. Listen for the chunks: re-trind-a-ble and mis-floc-tion.

title: Read the Sentences
desc: reading multisyllabic words accurately in context using letter-sound correspondences, syllable patterns, and word parts
dir: Read each sentence out loud. Take your time with the long words.
text: The magnificent waterfall thundered over the ancient cliffs. The volunteers organized a celebration for the whole community.
key: Listen for these six words read correctly in the sentences: magnificent, waterfall, ancient, volunteers, organized, celebration. Mark each one.
A word that is self-corrected on a second try counts as correct. Note words the student breaks into syllables to decode.

title: Read Under the Apple Tree
desc: a 187-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.

key: 187 words. Time 1 minute and mark errors and self-corrections on your own copy.
Fall grade 4 benchmark: about 94 words correct per minute (50th percentile).

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice. Let the rhythm and the rhymes show.
text: Autumn Wind The autumn wind is running free, It shakes the branch of every tree. The orange leaves go twirling down, Red and yellow, gold and brown. They dance
key: 38 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm, pauses at the end of lines or punctuation, and a voice that fits the mood of the poem.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: Saturday was the last picking day at Hillcrest Orchard. Mina and her cousin Theo had one job. They had to fill the big wooden bin before the cider press started
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: Prove It
desc: questions answered with details and examples from a story
dir: Answer out loud. Look back at the story and point to the details that prove your answer.
text: Saturday was the last picking day at Hillcrest Orchard. Mina and her cousin Theo had one job. They had to fill the big wooden bin before the cider press started
qs: Why did Theo set each apple down so gently? Find the detail in the story.
How did Theo feel about the job at the start? Which details show it?
key: So the apples would not get bruised. Detail: bruised apples spoil quickly. (explicit)
He thought the job was too big and felt grumpy or discouraged. Details: he said they would never fill the bin, and he kicked a fallen apple down the row. (inference)

title: Word Detective
desc: meanings of words and phrases in a story, including one from mythology
dir: Look back at the story. Answer out loud.
text: Look back at the story Saturday was the last picking day at Hillcrest Orchard. Mina and her cousin Theo had one job. They had to fill the big wooden bin before
qs: The story says the bin was “titanic.” What does titanic mean here? Which words in the story help you? Bonus: titanic comes from the Titans in Greek myths. What do you think the Titans were like?
What does “Her stomach dropped to her shoes” mean?
key: Huge. Clue: Mina could have curled up inside it with room to spare. The Titans were giant, powerful beings in Greek myths. Tell the student if they do not know. (allusion to mythology)
She felt a sudden rush of fear when the ladder moved.

title: Use the Text
desc: questions answered with details and examples from informational texts
dir: Read both texts to yourself. Then answer out loud. Tell which details helped you.
text: Text 1: Why Apples Need Bees An apple starts as a blossom. In spring, each blossom holds a yellow dust called pollen. Before a blossom can turn into an apple, p
qs: How does pollen get from one apple tree to another? Give details from Text 1.
True or false: Every apple blossom turns into an apple. Prove it with a detail from Text 1.
key: Pollen sticks to the fuzzy body of a bee while it drinks nectar. At the next tree, some of the pollen rubs off. (explicit)
False. A blossom that gets no pollen dries up and falls off. (explicit)

title: Put It Together
desc: putting together information from two texts on the same topic
dir: Think about both texts. Answer out loud.
text: Look back at the two texts Text 1: Why Apples Need Bees An apple starts as a blossom. In spring, each blossom holds a yellow dust called pollen. Before a blosso
qs: Use both texts. Explain why a week of cold rain in spring could mean fewer apples in the fall.

A grower rents two hives for every acre. Text 2 calls that plenty of bees. But the grower plants only one kind of apple tree. Use both texts. Explain why that orchard would still grow very few apples.
key: Uses Text 2: honeybees stay in the hive when it is rainy or colder than about 55 degrees, and the blossoms are open for only about ten days.
Connects to Text 1: blossoms that get no pollen dry up and fall off, so fewer blossoms become apples.

title: Orchard Notebook
desc: taking notes in their own words, sorting the notes, and listing sources
dir: Look back at the two texts. Write your notes on your paper and hold it up.
text: You are gathering facts for a report about bees and apple trees. Look back at the two texts Text 1: Why Apples Need Bees An apple starts as a blossom. In spring
qs: Write two notes, one from each text. Keep them short and use your own words.
Sort your notes. Write a heading above each note: What Bees Do or What Growers Do.
key: Two short notes, one from each text, in the student’s own words and not copied sentences. Examples: bees carry pollen from tree to tree; growers rent hives for about ten days. (gathers information, ta

Each note sits under the heading that fits. Facts about pollen, nectar, and when bees fly go under What Bees Do. Facts about renting hives, trucks, and how many hives per acre go under What Growers Do

title: Fix-It Ladder
desc: spoken grammar items (relative pronouns, progressive tense, adjective order, run-ons, confused words)
dir: Say each sentence out loud the correct way.
qs: The ladder ____ leans on the tree is wobbly. (who or that)
Yesterday at noon, we ____ apples. (pick) Start with were.
key: that (relative pronoun)
were picking (progressive tense)

title: Cursive Writing
desc: writing fluidly and legibly in cursive or joined italics
dir: Write this sentence on your paper in cursive or joined writing. Write smoothly and keep it neat.
text: Write this sentence: A good book can take you anywhere you want to go.
key: Letters are joined within words (cursive or joined italics)
Writing is legible: another reader can read each word

title: Farm Stand Writer
desc: an opinion writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Would you rather spend a fall day picking apples in the trees or selling them at the farm stand? Write your opinion. Write 5 to 7 sentences. State your opinion
key: Introduces the topic and states an opinion
Gives reasons supported by facts and details

title: Farm Stand Writer
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: How do honeybees help an apple orchard? Write to explain it. Use facts from the two texts. Write 5 to 7 sentences. Introduce your topic Give facts, details, or
key: Introduces the topic clearly
Develops the topic with facts, details, or examples from the texts, such as pollen on the bee, blossoms turning into apples, or rented hives

title: Farm Stand Writer
desc: a narrative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Write a story about a day at an orchard when something went wrong and then got fixed. It can be real or made up. Write 5 to 7 sentences. Start by telling who is
key: Sets up the situation and introduces a narrator or characters
Events unfold in a clear order, with transition words like first, next, after that, finally

title: Tell It at the Farm Stand
desc: telling about an experience out loud in an organized way with facts and details
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly and take your time.
text: Tell me about a place you have visited. It could be a farm, a park, a market, or anywhere you like. Tell it so I can picture it. Where and when What happened, i
key: Tells it in an organized order with a beginning, middle, and end
Gives facts that fit the place and what happened

title: At the Press
desc: paraphrasing parts of an informational text read aloud
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about the cider press. It is not on your screen. Then say it back in your own words.
text: Listen only. Your teacher will read about the press at Hillcrest.
qs: In your own words, what happens to the apples before they are pressed?
Say the last sentence in your own words.
key: The apples ride up a belt into a grinder that chops them into a coarse mush. Count it correct only when the words are the student's own. Repeating pomace is fine as long as the rest is reworded (SL.4.
A ton of apples gives about 120 gallons of cider. Any accurate rewording counts (SL.4.2)

title: Say It in Your Own Words
desc: paraphrasing information presented visually and quantitatively
dir: Look at the chart. Tell your teacher what it shows in your own words. Do not read it word for word.
text: How far animals can run (miles per hour) Item Amount Cheetah 70 Horse 40 Human 15
qs: Tell what the chart is about in your own words.
Tell two important facts from the chart in your own words.
key: A paraphrase of the main point in the student’s own words (not reading the numbers aloud in order).
Two accurate facts or comparisons put in new words (for example, which is greatest or smallest and about how much).

title: Count the Crop
desc: place value and how a digit is worth 10 times as much one place to the left
dir: Look at the sign. Answer out loud and tell how you know.
qs: The number on the sign has three 5s. What is each 5 worth?
Compare the 5 in the thousands place to the 5 in the hundreds place. How many times as much is it worth? How do you know?
key: 5,000 and 500 and 50. Partial: two of the three values given is approaching.
10 times as much. 5,000 is 10 times 500, because each place is worth 10 times the place to its right. Partial: naming 10 with no reason from the places is approaching.

title: Round Up the Baskets
desc: rounding multi-digit numbers to a given place
dir: Say 1 to 4 out loud. For number 5, explain how you know.
qs: Round the number on the sign to the nearest ten.
Round the number on the sign to the nearest thousand.
key: 46,380. Partial: 46,370 rounds down when the ones digit is 5 or more and does not count.
46,000. Partial: 47,000 rounds up when the hundreds digit is below 5 and does not count.

title: Apple Pie Pieces
desc: explaining and making equivalent fractions
dir: Look at the two bars. Answer out loud. Write numbers 2 and 3 on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Do the two bars show the same amount? Explain. Talk about the number of pieces and the size of the pieces.
Fill in the missing number: 3/5 = ?/10
key: Yes. The second bar has 2 times as many pieces, and each piece is half as big, so the shaded amount is the same. Partial: saying yes with nothing said about the size of the pieces is approaching.
6 (3/5 = 6/10). Or: double the top and the bottom of 3/5 to get 6/10.

title: Cider Compare
desc: comparing fractions with different numerators and denominators
dir: Answer out loud and tell how you know. Write number 2 on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Which is greater: 2/5 or 7/10? How do you know?
Write >, <, or = to make it true: 3/4 ____ 5/6
key: 7/10. 2/5 is the same as 4/10, and 4/10 is less than 7/10. Partial: naming 7/10 with no common denominator shown is approaching.
3/4 is less than 5/6. Shows 9/12 and 10/12, or says 5/6 is closer to 1 whole. Or: compare both with 1 whole, since 5/6 is 1/6 short and 3/4 is 1/4 short.

title: Compare With Symbols
desc: comparing fractions with different numerators and denominators, recording the results with symbols, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know.
qs: Compare 3/5 and 1/2 with a symbol. Tell how you know.
Compare 5/8 and 3/4 with a symbol.

title: Times as Many
desc: reading and writing a multiplication equation as a comparison
dir: Answer out loud. Write the equations on your paper.
text: A crate holds 40 apples. The big wooden bin holds 400.
qs: Write a multiplication equation that compares the bin to the crate.
Say what your equation means, using the words times as many.
key: 400 = 10 × 40, or 40 × 10 = 400. Partial: 400 − 40 = 360 is a difference and not a multiplicative comparison, so it does not count. (4.OA.A.1)
The bin holds 10 times as many apples as the crate. Partial: naming the comparison without the words times as many is approaching. (4.OA.A.1)

title: Write It as a Decimal
desc: writing fractions with denominators of 10 and 100 as decimals, and decimals as fractions
dir: Answer out loud. Write each one on your paper.
qs: The grid has 100 squares and 45 are shaded. Write that as a fraction, then as a decimal.
Write 7/10 as a decimal.
key: 45/100 and 0.45. Partial: one of the fraction and the decimal given is approaching. (4.NF.C.6)
0.7. Writing 0.70 is correct too, and the student should be able to say why they are the same. Partial: 0.70 given with no account of why it is the same is approaching. (4.NF.C.6)

title: Which Is More
desc: comparing two decimals to hundredths and justifying the comparison
dir: Answer out loud. Use the words greater than, less than, or equal to.
qs: Which is greater, 0.7 or 0.68? Tell how you know.
Compare 0.3 and 0.30.
key: 0.7 is greater. 0.7 is the same as 0.70, and 70 hundredths is more than 68 hundredths. Saying 68 is a bigger number so 0.68 wins is the classic mistake. Partial: naming 0.7 with no reason from hundred
They are equal. 3 tenths is the same as 30 hundredths. Partial: saying equal with no reason is approaching. (4.NF.C.7)

title: Compare Decimals
desc: comparing two decimals to hundredths, recording the results with the symbols >, =, or <, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know. You can use a number line or a grid.
qs: Compare 0.36 and 0.4 with a symbol.
Compare 0.09 and 0.1 with a symbol.

title: Bigger Unit, Smaller Unit
desc: knowing relative sizes of units and changing a larger unit into a smaller one
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
qs: Finish the table. How many ounces are in 3 pounds? In 5 pounds?
Which is heavier, 40 ounces or 3 pounds? Tell how you know.
key: 48 ounces and 80 ounces (3 × 16 = 48, 5 × 16 = 80). Partial: one of the two rows right is approaching. (4.MD.A.1)

3 pounds is heavier. 3 pounds is 48 ounces, and 48 ounces is more than 40 ounces. The two have to be changed into the same unit before they can be compared. Partial: naming 3 pounds with no change int

title: Around and Inside
desc: using the area and perimeter formulas for a rectangle, including finding a missing side
dir: Look at the apple patch. Answer out loud. Show your work on your paper.
qs: What is the area of the patch?
How much fence goes all the way around it?
key: 84 square feet (12 × 7). Partial: 84 with no square unit named is approaching. (4.MD.A.3)
38 feet (12 + 7 + 12 + 7, or 2 × 12 + 2 × 7). Partial: 19 adds only one of each side and does not count. (4.MD.A.3)

title: Sign Shapes
desc: classifying figures by parallel and perpendicular sides and by angle type, including right triangles
dir: Look at the four signs. Answer out loud.
qs: Which sign has a right angle in it? What do we call that kind of triangle?
Which signs have two pairs of parallel sides?
key: Sign 1, and it is a right triangle. The little square in the corner marks the right angle. Partial: naming the sign with no name for the triangle is approaching. (4.G.A.2)
Signs 3 and 4. Sign 3 is a parallelogram and sign 4 is a rectangle. Sign 4 also has perpendicular sides. Partial: one of the two signs named is approaching. (4.G.A.2)

title: Triangles by Their Sides
desc: classifying triangles as equilateral, isosceles, or scalene by their side lengths
dir: Answer out loud. For the drawing questions, draw on your paper.
qs: A triangle has sides of 8 in, 8 in, and 8 in. What kind of triangle is it?
A triangle has sides of 7 in, 5 in, and 7 in. What kind of triangle is it?
key: Equilateral
Isosceles

title: Parts of the Orchard
desc: arguing that named plant and animal structures do a job that supports survival, growth or reproduction
dir: Look at the apple tree and the bee. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: An apple tree and a honeybee work together in the orchard. Every part of a living thing is a structure, inside or outside.
qs: The apple tree has bark on the outside and seeds inside the fruit. Name the job of each one.
A honeybee's body is covered in fine hairs. Build an argument that these hairs matter to the apple tree as well as to the bee.
key: Bark covers the trunk and protects the living wood underneath from drying out, insects and weather. Seeds carry the next generation of trees, so they support reproduction. Both parts named with a job.
Pollen sticks to the hairs while the bee drinks nectar, and rubs off at the next blossom. Without pollen moving between trees a blossom dries up instead of growing into an apple. Listen for the claim

title: Parts of the Orchard
desc: modelling the path from sense organ to brain to response in an animal
dir: Read what happens, then answer. You may draw your model.
text: The orchard dog is asleep by the barn door. A raccoon climbs into the apple bins across the yard. The dog lifts its head, turns toward the bins, and runs across
qs: Name two senses the dog could have used. The body part that takes in each one.
The dog had been asleep. What work did its brain do before its legs moved?
key: Hearing through the ears and smell through the nose. Accept sight through the eyes once the dog had its head up. (4-LS1-2)
The brain took in the signal, worked out what it meant and which direction it came from, and chose the response. The ears and nose only collect information, they do not decide. (4-LS1-2)

title: The Creek Bank
desc: reading rock layers and the fossils in them as evidence of landscape change
dir: Study the bank the creek has cut. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The creek at the edge of the orchard has cut down through four layers. Layers pile up with the newest on top. Layer What the rock is like Fossils found in it to
qs: Which layer is the oldest, and what in the chart tells you so?
The second layer is rounded gravel with river snails. What was happening at this spot while that layer formed?
key: The bottom layer, the lava rock. The newest layers rest on top, so the lowest one was there first. (4-ESS1-1)
A river or fast stream ran here. Gravel gets rounded by tumbling in moving water, and river snails live in moving water. (4-ESS1-1)

title: The Creek Bank
desc: using measurements to compare the rate of erosion under different conditions
dir: Look at the measurements. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The orchard road washes out every winter. The crew set four identical trays of soil on the same slope and ran water over each for five minutes, then weighed the
qs: Which cover slowed the erosion most? Use the numbers.
Compare tray 1 and tray 4. What does that pair show about the water itself?
key: Grass, 11 grams compared with 86 grams of bare soil. The roots hold the grains and the leaves break the force of the water. (4-ESS2-1)
Faster water erodes more: the same bare soil lost 86 grams at the slower speed and 159 grams at twice the speed. The speed of the water is what changed. (4-ESS2-1)

title: Mapping the Valley
desc: interpreting map data to describe patterns in Earth's features
dir: Study the chart from the county map. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: A county map gives the height of the land along a straight line of six places, from the river in the west to the ridge in the east. Place Height above sea level
qs: Describe the pattern in the land from place 1 to place 6.
At place 4 the map's height lines are drawn close together. What does that tell you about the land there?
key: The land climbs steadily from west to east, from 12 metres at the river to 910 metres at the ridge. (4-ESS2-2)
The land is steep there. Lines close together mean the height changes a lot over a short distance, which is why two creeks run down through it. (4-ESS2-2)

title: Mapping the Valley
desc: generating and comparing solutions that reduce the impact of a natural Earth process
dir: Read the two plans. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: Every few winters the creek rises and water stands in the lowest row of trees until the roots rot. The orchard can do one thing this year. Plan What it does Cos
qs: Add a third plan of your own that would reduce the effect of the flooding.
Compare plan A and plan B. Which would you choose. What in the chart supports your choice?
key: Any workable idea: plant that low row with a tree that tolerates wet roots, leave the low row as a flood basin on purpose, put in an underground drain line, widen the creek channel upstream, build a l

Either plan, judged on the chart. Plan A costs less and works at once but gives up a row of trees. Plan B keeps all the trees but costs the most and takes longer. The reason drawn from the chart is wh

title: Power for the Press
desc: describing where energy and fuels come from and how using them affects the environment
dir: Study the chart. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The cider press can be run four ways. The orchard keeps a chart before deciding. Way to run it Natural resource it comes from Runs out? One effect on the enviro
qs: Trace the petrol engine back to its natural resource. Where did that resource come from?
Two of these four will not run out. Name them and say why the supply keeps coming.
key: Petrol is refined from oil, which is pumped from deep underground. Oil formed from the remains of tiny living things buried for millions of years. Tracing it back to oil under the ground is enough at
The water wheel and the roof panels. Rain and snow keep refilling the creek and the sun keeps shining, so the supply is renewed rather than used up. (4-ESS3-1)

title: Down the Orchard Hill
desc: using evidence to explain how the speed of an object relates to its energy
dir: Look at the results. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The same loaded apple wagon was let go from three places on the orchard hill. At the bottom each one rolled into a hay bale and pushed it along the ground. Star
qs: What happens to the distance the bale is pushed as the speed goes up?
Which wagon carried the most energy? Name the measurement that is your evidence.
key: It gets much larger: 6 cm, then 23 cm, then 52 cm. (4-PS3-1)
The one from the top of the hill, at 6 metres each second. It pushed the bale 52 cm, farther than either other wagon, so it had more energy to give. (4-PS3-1)

title: Down the Orchard Hill
desc: asking a question and predicting the energy change in a collision
dir: Answer out loud or in writing. A prediction only needs a reason, not the right answer.
text: Apples roll down a wooden chute into a crate. A heavy apple is rolling down behind a light one, and it catches up and hits it.
qs: Ask one question about this collision that a test could answer.
Predict what happens to the light apple and to the heavy one when they hit.
key: Any testable question: how far does the light apple shoot forward, does the bruise get worse if the chute is steeper, does a padded chute change the sound, what happens if both apples are heavy. (4-PS
The light apple is pushed forward and speeds up. The heavy apple slows down. Both halves make the full prediction. (4-PS3-3)

title: Energy in the Barn
desc: matching observations to energy transferred by sound, light, heat or electric current
dir: For each observation, say how the energy travelled. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: Four things noticed in the packing barn in one afternoon. What was noticed 1 The press motor is switched on and the whole barn fills with a low hum. 2 A crate o
qs: How did the energy travel in observation 1?
How did it travel in observation 2?
key: By sound, through the air from the motor to every ear in the barn. (4-PS3-2)
By heat, carried in sunlight to the top apples and then along from apple to apple. Accept light as the way it crossed the yard and heat as what moved into the crate. (4-PS3-2)

title: Energy in the Barn
desc: designing, testing and improving a device that converts energy from one form to another
dir: Draw your device and label it. Then answer out loud or in writing.
text: The apple washing tub needs a small fan to dry the fruit. There is no outlet near the tub. Design a device that turns one kind of energy into the spinning of a
qs: Draw and label your device. Show the path from the energy going in to the fan turning.
Name the kind of energy going in and the kind coming out.
key: Any labelled drawing with a path: a paddle wheel in the creek, a belt, and the fan; or a battery, wire, and a small motor on the fan. Labels and a path through the device are what make it a design. (4
Going in: motion of the water or the crank, or electrical energy from the battery. Coming out: motion of the fan, plus some sound and heat. Both forms named. (4-PS3-4)

title: Ripples, Colour and Signals
desc: using a wave model to describe amplitude and wavelength and the effect on a floating object
dir: Look at the two drawings of the water. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: A leaf floats in the washing tub. The crew drew the surface twice: once when one apple was dropped in gently, and once when a full crate was tipped in.
qs: Which letter marks the wavelength, and which marks the amplitude?
Which measurement changed when the crate went in instead of one apple? Did it grow or shrink?
key: B marks the wavelength, from one wave to the next one like it. A marks the amplitude, from the flat line up to the crest. (4-PS4-1)
The amplitude grew. The crests are much taller in the second drawing. The wavelength stayed the same, which is worth pointing out if the student misses it. (4-PS4-1)

title: Ripples, Colour and Signals
desc: modelling how light reflects from an object into the eye so the object can be seen
dir: Answer out loud or in writing. You may draw arrows.
text: Two apples sit on the sorting table under the barn lamp, one red and one green. When the lamp is switched off the barn is completely dark.
qs: Draw or tell the path the light takes when a sorter sees the red apple. Name every place it goes.
In the completely dark barn the apples have not moved. Why can nobody see them?
key: Light leaves the lamp, travels to the apple, reflects off the apple, and travels into the eye. All three legs are needed. (4-PS4-2)
With the lamp off there is no light to reflect off them, so no light reaches anybody's eye. An object has to send light to the eye to be seen. (4-PS4-2)

title: Ripples, Colour and Signals
desc: comparing two solutions that use patterns to send information
dir: Read the two systems. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The pickers are spread across the far rows and need three messages from the barn: bring a load in, take a break, and come to the barn now. System How a message
qs: Name the pattern that carries the information in each system.
A picker is working in the far rows where trees block the view of the barn. Which system reaches them, and why?
key: In the bell system the pattern is how many rings and how long they go on. In the flag system the pattern is which colour is flying. An agreed pattern standing for a message is what transfers the infor
The bell, because sound travels around and through the trees while a flag needs a clear line of sight. (4-PS4-3)

title: A Chute That Does Not Bruise
desc: defining a design problem with criteria for success and constraints
dir: Read the situation, then answer out loud or in writing.

qs: State the problem in one sentence, in your own words.
Write two criteria: how will the crew know the new chute works?
key: Something like: apples need to reach the crate without being bruised. A problem statement, not a solution. (3-5-ETS1-1)

Any two testable criteria: fewer than one bruised apple in twenty, apples still reach the crate without being carried by hand, the chute is no slower than the old one, one person can work it. (3-5-ETS

title: A Chute That Does Not Bruise
desc: generating and comparing solutions against the criteria and constraints
dir: Study the three designs. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: Three designs for the chute. Design What it is Materials Build time 1 line the chute with an old blanket a blanket short 2 add three gentle bends so apples slow
qs: Which design breaks a constraint? Name the constraint.
Compare designs 1 and 2 against the criteria. Which do you expect to bruise fewer apples, and why?
key: Design 3. It needs a belt and a motor to buy, and there is no money, and two days is longer than the one morning available. (3-5-ETS1-2)

Either, argued from the criteria. The blanket softens the landing at the end, while the bends take speed out along the whole way down, so less energy is left at the bottom. A student who says both tog

title: A Chute That Does Not Bruise
desc: planning a fair test with controlled variables and naming a failure point

title: Autumn Sky

The sun is only 8 light-minutes away and Betelgeuse is about 550 light-years away. That enormous difference in distance more than cancels out the difference in light given off. (5-ESS1-1)

title: Water for the Orchard

key: About one, the groundwater bucket, plus a splash from lakes and rivers. The 97 ocean buckets are salty and the 2 ice buckets are frozen solid and far away. (5-ESS2-2)
About 3% is fresh. Of that, only about 1% of all water, the groundwater, plus a trace in lakes and rivers is easy to reach, so roughly 1% of all Earth's water. (5-ESS2-2)

Roots hold the soil in place and the leaves and stems slow the rain before it hits the ground, so less soil is loosened and carried away. The cover also lets more water soak in instead of running off.

dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Here are 6.
key: Say: Show me one way to split these 6 into two groups. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 3 + 3 = 6. (a drawing with two groups, or an equation, that makes 6)
Say: Now show me a different way. (a second pair of parts that make 6. The same two numbers in the other order do not count as different.)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: showing a number from 11 to 19 as a ten and some more and recording it
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Look at the full ten frame and the extra ones.
key: Say: Show 13 as a ten and some more. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 13 = 10 + 3. (a drawing of a ten and 3 more, or the equation)
Ask: How many ones are left after the ten? (3)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: seeing a teen number as ten and some more
dir: Look at the boxes. Answer out loud.
key: Top box. Say: The frame holds ten pumpkins. How many pumpkins in all? (13. Look for the student to start from ten and count on: ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen.)
Say: So 13 is ten and how many more? (3)

title: Which One
desc: comparing two objects directly by height, by weight, and by length
dir: Look at each pair. Answer out loud.
key: First box. Say: Which sunflower is taller? (the one on the left)
First box. Say: Now tell me about the other one, using the word shorter. (The one on the right is shorter.)

title: Three Piles
desc: sorting pictures into groups, counting each group, and ordering the groups by how many
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
key: Say: These got mixed up. Put them into groups in your head: leaves, corn, and pumpkins. How many leaves? (5)
Say: How many ears of corn? (3)

title: Shed Shapes
desc: naming shapes of objects in a picture and telling where things are
dir: Look at the shed. Answer out loud.
key: Say: What shape is the roof of the shed? (triangle)
Say: What shape is the sun? (circle)

title: Flat or Solid
desc: telling flat shapes from solid shapes
dir: Look at the two rows. Answer out loud.
key: Say: One of these rows is flat shapes. Which row? (the top row: the circle, the square, and the triangle)
Say: Which row is solid things you could hold? (the bottom row: the ball, the box, and the pumpkin)

title: What Living Things Need
desc: telling what plants and animals need to stay alive
dir: Look at each row. Answer out loud.
text: A pumpkin vine and a field mouse both live in the patch. Living things need certain things to stay alive.
qs: The pumpkin vine needs two of these to grow. Which two? Water, sunlight, or a lantern?
The field mouse needs two of these. Which two? Food, water, or a song?
key: water and sunlight. A lantern is not something a vine needs.
food and water. A song is not something a mouse needs.

title: Weather in the Patch
desc: describing a weather pattern from a week of observations
dir: Look at the week of weather. Answer out loud.
text: Here is one week of weather in the pumpkin patch. Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri
qs: How many windy days were there?
How many days had rain instead of wind?

title: Weather in the Patch
desc: telling how a living thing changes its surroundings to get what it needs
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A field mouse wants a dry place to sleep out of the wind.
qs: The mouse chews a small hole in an old pumpkin and lines the inside with dry grass. Did the mouse change the pumpkin, or did the pumpkin change the mouse?
Tell me one way an animal changes a place so it can live there.
key: The mouse changed the pumpkin. It made a hole and added grass that were not there before.
Any sensible answer: a bird builds a nest, a rabbit digs a burrow, an ant digs tunnels, a spider spins a web, a beaver piles up sticks.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Land
desc: matching animals to the places that give them what they need
dir: Match each animal to the place it lives. Answer out loud.
text: Animals live near the patch. Each one lives in one place. It gets what it needs. Here are the places. The pond. A burrow under the hedge. A nest high in a tree.
qs: Where does the rabbit live?
Where does the frog live?
key: a burrow under the hedge. Accept a hole in the ground.
the pond. Accept the water.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Land
desc: telling what a weather forecast is for
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Before the pumpkins are picked, the farmer listens for a frost warning.
qs: Why does she listen for a frost warning? To find out if a very cold night is coming, or to find out who won a game?
What could the farmer do if a very cold night was coming?
key: to find out if a very cold night is coming.
Any sensible answer: cover the pumpkins with cloth, pick them early, bring them into the shed.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Land
desc: telling one way people can take better care of the land and water
dir: Answer out loud.
text: At the end of the season there is a big pile of old vines and leaves.
qs: One helper puts the pile in the compost heap, where it rots and feeds the soil. The other pushes the pile into the creek. Which choice takes better care of the land and the water?
Tell me one more thing people can do to take care of a creek or a field.
key: putting the pile in the compost heap. Pushing it into the creek blocks the water and makes a mess downstream.
Any sensible answer: pick up litter, turn off the tap, do not pour things in a creek, plant something, carry your trash home.

title: Pushes and Pulls
desc: telling a push from a pull, and comparing a hard push with a gentle one
dir: Answer out loud. Let the student say the word push or pull first.
text: A push moves something away from you. A pull brings it toward you.
qs: You tug a pumpkin stem toward you to twist it off the vine. Is that a push or a pull?
You roll a big pumpkin along the ground away from you. Is that a push or a pull?
key: a pull
a push

title: Pushes and Pulls
desc: deciding whether a change made a thing move faster or in a new direction
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The helpers rolled the same pumpkin down two chutes and counted how far it rolled past the end. Chute How far the pumpkin rolled a bare wooden chute 7 steps a c
qs: Which chute sent the pumpkin farther?
A pumpkin is rolling straight ahead. You set a board in its path at a slant. What does the board do to the pumpkin?
key: the bare wooden chute, 7 steps
It turns the pumpkin and sends it off a new way. The board changed the direction the pumpkin was rolling.

title: Sun and Shade
desc: telling what sunlight does to the things it shines on
dir: Answer out loud. If you can, feel a sunny spot and a shady spot together first.
text: Two flat stones sit in the patch all morning. One is out in the open. One is under the corn rows.
qs: By the middle of the day, one stone is warm and one is cool. Which one is warm, the stone in the open or the stone under the corn?
Why is that stone warm? Because the sun shines on it, or because it is a bigger stone?
key: the stone out in the open
because the sun shines on it

title: Sun and Shade
desc: designing and drawing something that keeps a spot cooler
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: The water bucket is here. It is by the patch gate. It gets warm by noon. Draw something over the bucket to make shade, like a board on two posts, a straw hat la
qs: Draw your shade over the water bucket.
Tell me how your shade keeps the water cooler.
key: Any cover drawn ABOVE the bucket, or a tall plant drawn on the sunny side of it. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one still counts. A cover drawn under the bucket is not shade: ask
Something like: it blocks the sun, the sun cannot reach the water, it puts the bucket in a shadow.

title: Solving a Problem
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking about it
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem? The sign tips over in the wind, or the sign is painted orange?
Ask me a question about the sign that would help you fix it.
key: The sign tips over in the wind.
Any real question: how strong is the wind, how heavy is the sign, how tall is it, is there a post to tie it to. A statement is not a question, so ask once more.

title: Solving a Problem
desc: drawing something whose shape would solve the problem
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw something that would hold the sign up in the wind, like a rope tying it to the post, two legs on the back, or a heavy stone at the bottom.
qs: Draw the thing you would build.
Tell me what you drew and how it keeps the sign standing.
key: Anything that would hold a sign up: a rope or a tie, legs or a brace on the back, a stone or a sandbag at the bottom, a post driven into the ground. The three examples are in the direction, so copying
Naming it is what shows intent. Something like: the rope holds it to the post, the legs stop it tipping, the stone is heavy so the wind cannot move it.

title: Solving a Problem
desc: comparing test results from two fixes for the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Tess tried two fixes and counted how many times the sign tipped over in one day. Fix Times the sign tipped a rope tied to the post 0 a stone leaned against it 5
qs: Which fix kept the sign standing better?
What on the chart tells you that?
key: the rope tied to the post
Because the sign tipped 0 times with the rope and 5 times with the stone. The reason has to come from the chart, not from liking ropes.

title: Rules and Doing Right
desc: following rules, knowing what happens when they are broken, and naming an honest choice
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What did Dev choose to do? Ask the farmer first, or pick the pumpkin without asking?
Another rule in the patch is walk, do not run between the rows. What might happen if someone runs?
key: He asked the farmer first.
They could trip, step on a vine, or knock a pumpkin over. Any real consequence counts.

title: Maps and Places
desc: telling land from water on a map, using position words, and naming places in a neighborhood
dir: Look at the map. Answer out loud.
text: Here is a map of the pumpkin patch. the shed the corn rows the scarecrow
qs: Every map uses color to tell you things. On a map, which color means water, and which color means land?
The shed is at the top of the map. The corn rows are at the bottom. Which one is at the top?
key: Blue means water. Green or brown means land. Pointing to each one as they say it counts.
the shed

title: Left and Right
desc: telling where things are with left and right, near and far, and in front and behind
dir: Look at each picture. Point or answer out loud.
text: A B C
key: Ask: Look at picture A. Point to the one on the left. (the pumpkin)
Ask: Point to the one on the right. (the cat)

title: Our Flag and Long Ago
desc: recognizing the flag as a symbol of the country
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Our country has a flag. Our state has one too. The California flag is white. It has a red stripe. The stripe is along the bottom. It has a red star. The star is
qs: Our country has a flag. What colors do you see on the one in the picture?
Our state has its own flag as well. What animal is walking on the flag of California?
key: red, white, and blue. Naming two of the three counts.
a bear, the grizzly bear. Accept bear. A state flag and a state animal are state symbols, which is the other half of this standard. (HSS-K.2)

title: Our Flag and Long Ago
desc: telling what a holiday honors and how life long ago was different from life today
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Long ago there were no light switches.
qs: Long ago, how did people light a room at night, with a lantern or with an electric lamp?
How do you light a room at night today?
key: a lantern. Accept a candle or a fire.
Any real answer: flip a switch, a lamp, a ceiling light, a flashlight. Naming today's way is the then-and-now half of this standard.

title: Corn Row Sounds
desc: blending, isolating, and segmenting sounds and telling long from short vowels in spoken words
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the sounds and words out loud.
text: Listen. Then say it.
key: Blend: /v/ /ī/ /n/ (vine)
Blend: /s/ /t/ /a/ /k/ (stack)

title: First Sound
desc: isolating and pronouncing the initial sound in spoken single-syllable words
dir: Listen to the word. Say just the first sound.
qs: What is the first sound in van?
What is the first sound in jam?
key: The sound /v/. Say the sound, not the letter name.
The sound /j/. Say the sound, not the letter name.

title: Words on the Vine
desc: reading words with digraphs, blends, double letters, endings, and two syllables
dir: Read each word out loud. The last one is a silly word. Just sound it out.
key: Count each word read correctly. sneck is a silly word: listen for sn and the ck ending.
Watch for: ck and double letters (duck, bell, fluff, chill), blends at the start and end (drift, stump), ng and nk (swing, honk), ending -s (rocks), two parts (basket), tricky word (have).

title: Silent E and Vowel Teams
desc: reading words with final e and common vowel teams that make long vowel sounds
dir: Read each word out loud.
key: Mark each word read correctly. The first four use a silent e (long vowel with a silent e at the end). The last four use a vowel team (two vowels that work together, such as ai, ee, oa, ea).
If the student says the short vowel sound for a silent e word (for example cap for cape), mark it wrong.

title: How Many Parts?
desc: using the rule that every syllable has a vowel sound to find the number of syllables in a printed word
dir: Read the word to yourself. Tell how many syllables, or parts, it has. Clap it if that helps.
text: pencil sun window hen
key: Point to “pencil”. How many syllables? (2)
Point to “sun”. How many syllables? (1)

title: Frosty Morning Read
desc: a 72-word decodable story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: Frost Frost is on the grass. It is crisp and wet. Val has on a thick red vest. She runs up the hill. The pumpkin patch is at the top. Crunch, crunch, crunch! Th
key: 72 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Note pace, expression (Crunch, crunch, crunch!), and whether the student rereads to fix a mistake.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: Frost Frost is on the grass. It is crisp and wet. Val has on a thick red vest. She runs up the hill. The pumpkin patch is at the top. Crunch, crunch, crunch! Th
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the story about? What happened first?” (a summary or answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: The Big Pumpkin Job
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about a story the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the story. Then listen to each question and answer out loud.
text: A Big Job Jill had the best pumpkin. But it was so big! Can Jill lift it? No! She ran to get Russ. Russ had a red wagon. Jill and Russ set the pumpkin in the wa
qs: What did Jill have?
Who did Jill run to get?
key: The best pumpkin (a big pumpkin)
Russ

title: How a Pumpkin Grows
desc: using a picture chart to answer a question in writing
dir: Look at the chart. Write 1 sentence on your paper and hold it up.
text: How does a pumpkin start? What comes next? Use the chart.
key: Finds the answer on the chart. Your help is fine: point to step 1 and read the question again
Writes an answer that uses the chart: it starts as a seed, and next comes a sprout

title: Remember and Tell
desc: recalling information from experiences to answer a question
dir: Think about what happened to you. Tell your teacher your answer out loud. You can draw it, too.
qs: Think about breakfast. What did you eat today or yesterday? Tell me about it.
Think about the weather today. What did you see or feel outside? Tell me.
key: Names a real food or meal from experience.
Gives one real detail about today’s weather from their own experience. (They may draw first, then tell. Write down what they say if you want a record.)

title: Pumpkin Facts
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about pumpkins. Then listen to each question and answer out loud.
text: Pumpkins A pumpkin sits on a stem. The stem is long. It has thick skin. Sun and wet mud help it get big. A pumpkin can get as big as a dog! Cut it open. You wil
qs: What kind of skin does a pumpkin have?
What helps a pumpkin get big?
key: Thick skin
The sun and wet mud (both, or one with a prompt)

title: Patch Writer
desc: an informative piece with facts about fall
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write about fall. Tell 2 facts about fall. leaf the air the harvest Write 2 or 3 sentences.
key: Names the topic: fall (W.1.2)
Gives at least 2 facts about fall, such as leaves drop, the air gets cool, or crops are picked (W.1.2)

title: Patch Writer
desc: a narrative about finding the biggest pumpkin
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write a story about the day you find the biggest pumpkin ever. Tell what happens first, next, and last. First Next Last Write 2 or 3 sentences.
key: Tells 2 or more events in order (W.1.3)
Includes some details about what happened (W.1.3)

title: Sentence Count
desc: finding sentences by their capital letters and end marks
dir: Look at the sentences. Answer out loud.
text: Ducks swim in the pond. Look at them go!
qs: How many sentences do you see? How can you tell?
Read the first word of the last sentence. What kind of letter does it start with?
key: 2 sentences. Each one starts with a capital letter and ends with an end mark
Look. It starts with a capital (uppercase) L

title: Scarecrow Fix It
desc: spoken grammar items (past tense, this and these, pronoun I, because, where words, asking sentences)
dir: Listen to your teacher read each one. Say your answer out loud.
qs: Today I pick a pumpkin. Yesterday I ____ a pumpkin.
Which sounds right? This pumpkins are big. These pumpkins are big.
key: picked (past tense)
The second one: these, because there is more than one pumpkin

title: Which Word Fits?
desc: using indefinite pronouns such as everyone, anyone, someone, something, and nothing
dir: Listen to the sentence. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? I have ___ to tell you. (something / anyone)
Which word fits? ___ is asleep. The room is quiet. (Everyone / Nobody)
key: something. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)
Nobody. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)

title: Whose Is It?
desc: using possessive nouns to show who owns something
dir: Listen. Say the answer. For the last one, you can point to the right one on paper.
qs: Lily has a ball. Whose ball is it?
The boy has a coat. Whose coat is it?
key: Lily’s ball. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)
the boy’s coat. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)

title: Commands and Big Feelings
desc: producing imperative (command) and exclamatory sentences in response to prompts
dir: Listen. Say your answer out loud in a full sentence.
qs: Tell a friend to wash their hands. Say it as a command.
You get a surprise present! Say one sentence that shows a big feeling.
key: A command such as “Wash your hands.”
An exclamation, for example “Wow, I love it!”

title: Print the Alphabet
desc: printing all upper- and lowercase letters
dir: On your paper, print each big letter and its small letter. Print them in order. Hold up your paper when you finish.
text: A a B b C c D d E e F f G g H h I i J j K k L l M m N n O o P p Q q R r S s T t U u V v W w X x Y y Z z
key: Look at the paper. Mark each letter pair where both the capital and the small letter are formed correctly and sit on the line. Letters may be uneven. Count a pair when each letter can be told from the
Check the tall letters (b, d, f, h, k, l, t), the letters that drop below the line (g, j, p, q, y), and the look-alikes (b and d, p and q).

title: Sunflower Listen
desc: asking and answering questions about a text read aloud
dir: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about sunflowers. Then answer out loud.
text: Listen.
key: Ask: What does a young sunflower turn to face? (the sun)
Ask: Who eats sunflower seeds? (birds and people; one is enough)

title: Tell Me About a Friend
desc: describing a person and what they do together with relevant details
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly.
text: Tell me about someone you like to play with. Who is it? What do you do together? How do you feel when you play?
key: Names the person and gives 2 or more details about who they are or what they are like (SL.1.4)
Names 1 or more things they do together and gives 1 or more details about it, all about this one person (SL.1.4)

title: Two-Step Directions
desc: giving, restating, and following simple two-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear, say it back, and give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do what your teacher says. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once, without repeating: “Point to the floor, then point to the ceiling.” (does both steps, in the right order)
Say once, without repeating: “Close your eyes, then count to three out loud.” (does both steps, in the right order)

title: Person, Place, Thing, Event
desc: describing a person, a place, a thing, and an event with relevant details, and saying ideas and feelings clearly
dir: Listen to your teacher. Tell about each one. Use lots of details.
text: Tell about a person, a place, a thing, and something that happened.
key: Say: “Tell me about a person who helps you.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the person, such as who they are, what they look like, or what they do)
Say: “Tell me about a place you go with your family.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the place, such as what is there or what you do there)

title: Which One Wins
desc: a short opinion piece with a reason and a closing
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Which would you rather take home from the patch: a pumpkin or a sunflower? Write 2 or 3 sentences. Tell which one you pick, tell why, and end it.
key: Names what the writing is about and states an opinion, such as: I would take home a pumpkin. (W.1.1)
Gives a reason for the opinion, such as: because I can grow seeds from it. (W.1.1)

title: Harvest Wagon Math
desc: addition and subtraction word problems within 20, with the unknown in different places
dir: Listen to each story problem. You can draw on your paper. Say your answer.
qs: 7 pumpkins are on the vine. 6 more pumpkins are on the wagon. How many pumpkins in all?
12 ducks are at the pond. 4 ducks swim away. How many ducks are left?
key: 13 pumpkins (7 + 6 = 13)

title: Hay Bale Hops
desc: counting on and counting back or up to add and subtract
dir: Count out loud like you are hopping on hay bales. Say each answer.
qs: Start at 9. Count on 4. Where do you land? What adding sentence is that?
Start at 15. Count back 3. Where do you land? What take away sentence is that?
key: Counts 14, 13, 12. Lands on 12. 15 - 3 = 12

title: Hay Bale Stacks
desc: tens and ones in two-digit numbers
dir: Look at the stacks. Each tall stack is 1 ten. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at Stack A. How many tens? How many ones? What number is it?
Look at Stack B. How many tens? How many ones? What number is it?
key: 3 tens and 4 ones. The number is 34
5 tens and 0 ones. The number is 50

title: Harvest Count
desc: reading a picture graph with three categories and asking and answering questions about it
dir: Look at the picture graph. Answer out loud.
qs: How many sunflowers did we pick?
How many more sunflowers than corn?
key: 9 sunflowers

title: Make a Graph
