desc: organizing and representing data with up to three categories, and answering questions about the total and about how many more or less
dir: Look at the list. Make a tally chart or a picture graph on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: Ten kids told us their favorite colors. blue red blue green blue red blue green blue red
key: A chart or graph with red 3, blue 5, green 2. Each item is counted once. Tally marks, pictures, or squares all work. Labels are on each group.
10 (the total of all three groups)

title: Corn Row Tricks
desc: using turn-around facts and making ten as strategies to add
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
qs: 5 + 9 = 14. So what is 9 + 5?
True or silly? 6 + 7 is the same as 7 + 6.
key: 14. Knows it without counting because the numbers just switch places
True. The order does not change the total. Both make 13

title: Count the Whole Patch
desc: counting to 120 from a number other than 1, and reading and writing numerals
dir: Count out loud. Then read the numbers.
text: Start at 108. Count out loud to 120.
key: Counts 108, 109, 110 and on to 120 with no skips. Listen at 109 to 110 and at 119 to 120.
Reads the three cards: eighty-seven, one hundred three, one hundred twenty.

title: Add It On
desc: adding a one-digit number and a multiple of ten to a two-digit number
dir: Look at the blocks. Answer out loud. You can use your paper.
qs: The wagon holds 34 pumpkins. 5 more go in. How many now?
Start with 34 again. 20 more pumpkins go in. How many now?
key: 39. Adds 5 ones to 4 ones, so the tens stay at 3.
54. Adds 2 tens to 3 tens, so the ones stay at 4.

title: Take Tens Away
desc: subtracting multiples of ten from multiples of ten
dir: Answer out loud. The blocks can help.
key: 40. 7 tens take away 3 tens is 4 tens.
30. 9 tens take away 6 tens is 3 tens.

title: How Many Blocks
desc: measuring length with same-size units laid end to end
dir: Look at the two vines. The blocks are all the same size. Answer out loud.
qs: How many blocks long is vine A?
How many blocks long is vine B?
key: 5 blocks. The blocks are end to end with no gaps, so counting them gives the length.
3 blocks

title: Patch Clock
desc: telling and writing time to the hour and half hour
dir: Look at the clocks. Say the time. Then write it on your paper.
qs: Clock A: what time is it? Write it.
Clock B: what time is it? Write it.
key: 3 o'clock. Writes 3:00
Half past 7, or seven thirty. Writes 7:30

title: Share It Fair
desc: halves and fourths of circles and rectangles, and comparing the size of the parts
dir: Look at the three pictures. Answer out loud.
key: Picture 1. Ask: This circle is cut into 2 equal parts. What do we call one of those parts? (a half)
Picture 2. Ask: This rectangle is cut into 4 equal parts. What do we call one of those parts? (a fourth, or a quarter)

title: Copy a Squirrel
desc: naming the job an animal body part does, then designing a tool that copies it to solve a human problem
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer the first out loud. Draw the second on your paper and hold it up.
text: A squirrel has stretchy pouches. They are inside its cheeks. It can fill them with acorns. A dozen will fit. It can still run and climb. Every foot is free. A w
qs: How do cheek pouches help a squirrel carry a lot of acorns at once?
Draw something the worker could wear that copies the squirrel's cheek pouches.
key: The acorns ride inside the squirrel instead of in its paws, so all four feet stay free for running and climbing. Any answer about carrying while keeping the feet or hands free counts.

Any wearable holder: an apron with a front pocket, a pouch on a belt, a sack hung on a strap, a bag tied at the waist. A basket carried in the hands is partial, so ask what the squirrel's trick really

title: Squirrel Parents
desc: finding a pattern in what a parent animal does and what the young do in answer, and saying how it helps the young
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What do the young do every morning after the parent gives her soft chuckle?
What do the young do once the parent starts digging in the grass?
key: They come down the trunk after her. Every morning is what makes it a pattern.
They crowd in and dig in the same spot she chose.

title: Squirrel Parents
desc: making observations that young plants and animals are like their parents but not exactly like them
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
text: A pumpkin seedling and the grown pumpkin plant it came from. A young squirrel and its parent.
qs: Name one way the pumpkin seedling is like the grown pumpkin plant.
Name one way the seedling is not exactly like the grown plant.
key: Both are green plants with leaves on a stem, both grow from the ground. Any likeness counts.
The seedling is tiny, it has only two leaves, it has no vine and no pumpkin. Any difference counts.

title: Stars Over the Patch
desc: finding a pattern in a log of sky observations and using it to predict what comes next
dir: Look at the star log. Answer out loud.
text: At eight o'clock on four clear nights the farmer wrote down where one group of bright stars was. Night Where the star group was at eight o'clock Monday just ove
qs: Where was the star group at eight o'clock on every one of the four nights?
Friday is clear too. Where do you predict the star group will be at eight o'clock?
key: just over the barn roof
just over the barn roof again

title: Stars Over the Patch
desc: relating the number of hours of daylight to the time of year from observations made across a year
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The farmer wrote down the time the sun went down on the first day of three months in a row. Month Time the sun went down October 6:30 November 5:00 December 4:3
qs: In which of the three months did the sun go down earliest?
Is the sun going down earlier or later as the months go by?
key: December, at 4:30
earlier each month

title: Sound in the Patch
desc: planning an investigation showing that a shaking material makes sound and that a sound can make a material shake
dir: If you have a dry gourd or a jar with seeds in it, shake it first. Either way, answer out loud.
text: Put a handful of dry pumpkin seeds in a jar and shake it hard. Then hold the jar still. Now lay a small scrap of paper on top of an upside down metal pan. Bang
qs: What has to happen to the seeds inside the jar before you hear anything?
Hold the jar perfectly still. Is there any sound? Say why.
key: They have to move, knock about, shake against the glass and each other.
No sound. Nothing is moving or shaking, and with no shaking there is no sound.

title: In the Dark Shed
desc: accounting for why an object in darkness can be seen only when light shines on it
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The tool shed at the edge of the patch has no window and the door is shut.
qs: A big orange pumpkin is sitting in the shed with the door shut. Can you see it? Say why or why not.
What has to happen before anyone can see it?
key: No. There is no light in the shed, and a thing can only be seen when light shines on it and comes back to your eyes.
Light has to reach it: a lamp or a flashlight switched on, or the door opened so daylight gets in.

title: In the Dark Shed
desc: using test results to tell what happens when different materials are put in the path of a beam of light
dir: Look at the test results. Answer out loud.
text: In the dark shed one flashlight beam was pointed at four things, and what it did was written down. What was put in the beam What the beam did a clear plastic ba
qs: Which thing stopped the beam completely?
Which thing let only a little light through?
key: the thick wooden plank
the dry corn husk

title: Across the Big Field
desc: designing a device that uses light or sound to send a message over a distance too far to shout
dir: Draw your answer on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: The pumpkin field is wide and the wagon driver waits at the far gate. Shouting does not carry that far across open ground.
qs: Draw a device that tells the driver at the far gate to bring the wagon over. It has to use light or sound.
What did you draw, and does it send its message with light or with sound?
key: Any device that carries light or sound across the field: a bell, a horn, a whistle, a drum, a bright lamp raised on a pole, a lamp flashed on and off.
Names it and says which one it uses.

title: Fix the Tipping Barrow
desc: naming a problem people want to change, asking a question about it, and saying what to observe first
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem the workers want to change?
Ask me a question about this problem that would help you solve it.
key: The wheelbarrow leans and a pumpkin rolls off when three are loaded in.
Any real question: how heavy is a pumpkin, where in the barrow are they put, is the ground bumpy, how wide is the barrow, which side does it lean to. A statement is not a question, so ask once more.

title: Fix the Tipping Barrow
desc: making a simple drawing of a fix and explaining how the shape of the object makes it work
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up. Then answer out loud.
text: Draw a better wagon or barrow for carrying three pumpkins out of the field.
qs: Draw your fix.
Point to the part that keeps the pumpkins in and tell me its shape.
key: Any real fix: a wider box, a rim or wall round the edge, two or four wheels instead of one, dips or hollows for each pumpkin to sit in, a strap across the top.
Names a shape: a tall rim all the way round, a wide flat bottom, round hollows, a low box.

title: Which Wagon Worked
desc: comparing the data from tests of two objects built to solve the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two wagons were tested down the same bumpy row, twelve pumpkins in each, three trips each. Wagon Pumpkins that rolled off, out of 12 a flat bed with no rim 7 a
qs: Which wagon worked better in the test?
Use the two numbers in the chart to tell me how you know.
key: the bed with a tall rim
Not one pumpkin out of 12 rolled off the wagon with the rim, and 7 out of 12 rolled off the flat bed. The numbers have to be in the answer.

title: Being a Good Neighbor
desc: telling a right from a responsibility and naming responsibilities that come with living in a community
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Think about the park, the sidewalk, and the crossing near where you live. They belong to everybody. There is an old saying. People call it the Golden Rule. Trea
qs: Anybody in town is allowed to play at the public park. Is being allowed to use it a right or a responsibility?
Picking up your own wrapper before you leave the park is something you do. Is that a right or a responsibility?
key: a right
a responsibility

title: The Patch Map
desc: giving an exact grid location, describing a relative location, and telling a physical feature from a built one
dir: Look at the map grid. Answer out loud.
text: A map of the pumpkin patch, drawn on a grid. 1 2 3 A B C the hill the scarecrow the pumpkin rows the farm stand the old oak The top of this map is north. The bo
qs: Find the farm stand. Give its exact spot on the grid, the letter and the number.
Where is the hill compared to the farm stand? Use north, south, east or west.
key: C2. Both parts are needed.
North of the farm stand and west of it. Both directions are needed for a full answer, and north west counts.

title: The Patch Map
desc: naming built features of a familiar place and recognizing that people in one place come from many different places
dir: Answer out loud.
text: On harvest day the table is full. It is the long table. It is at the patch. It is covered with food. The families brought it. They came from many different plac
qs: Does everyone who lives in one town come from the same place? Say how the long table shows the answer.
Name two buildings people made in your own town, and say what each one is for.
key: No. The families came from many different places, and the food they brought is all different.
Any two built places with a use: a school for learning, a store for buying food, a library for borrowing books, a fire station, a post office.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: telling the difference between an ordinary object and a national symbol, and naming a national tradition
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The Liberty Bell is very old. The bell is in Philadelphia. It cracked a long time ago. It is not rung any more. But people still come to look. They come from al
qs: The Liberty Bell is cracked and nobody rings it. So why do people still travel a long way to see it?
What is the difference between an ordinary bell on a school door and a symbol like the Liberty Bell?
key: Because it stands for something: the start of the country and the idea of being free. A symbol does its work even when it is broken.
The school bell is only a bell, used for ringing. The Liberty Bell stands for an idea that is bigger than the object itself.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: comparing everyday life long ago with life today and telling what changed from what stayed the same
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Getting water on a farm. Long ago Today where it came from a well dug in the yard a pipe that runs to the house how it was carried hauled up in a bucket on a ro
qs: Long ago, where did a farm family get its water?
Where does water come from in a house today?
key: From a well dug in the yard, hauled up in a bucket on a rope.
Out of a tap, through a pipe that runs to the house.

title: Corn Row Words
desc: reading words with vowel teams, r-controlled vowels, two syllables, a prefix, a suffix, and an irregular spelling
dir: Read each word out loud. The last two are silly words. Just sound them out.
key: Read each word. sharb and troid are silly words: listen for the ar sound and the oi sound.
Watch for: tch and r-controlled vowels (patch, corn), vowel teams (leaf, bright, soil), two syllables (pumpkin, scarecrow), a prefix and a suffix (unload, seedless), an irregular word (people).

title: Two-Part Long Vowel Words
desc: decoding regularly spelled two-syllable words with long vowels
dir: Read each word out loud. Each word has two parts.
key: Mark each word read correctly. Each word has two syllables and at least one long vowel sound, such as pa-per, mu-sic, o-pen.
If the student breaks the word into syllables and then says it smoothly, count it correct.

title: Read the Lines
desc: decoding words with long vowels, vowel teams, prefixes, and suffixes in connected text
dir: Read each line out loud.
text: My tiny pony went to the lake. The lady painted a cozy cabin.
key: Line 1: “My tiny pony went to the lake.” (every word read correctly)
Line 2: “The lady painted a cozy cabin.” (every word read correctly)

title: Read the Story
desc: a 97-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: On Friday afternoon a strong wind blew. It came across the pumpkin patch. It lifted the old straw hat right off the scarecrow. Jada watched the hat spin over th
key: 97 words. Mark each missed word and each self-correction on the passage in the record sheet.
Note pace and expression in your notes.

title: Story Questions
desc: asking and answering when, where, why, how, and what questions about a story
dir: Look back at the story if you need to. Then answer each question out loud.
text: The Scarecrow’s Hat (click to open or close the story) On Friday afternoon a strong wind blew. It came across the pumpkin patch. It lifted the old straw hat rig
qs: When did the wind blow across the pumpkin patch?
Where did the hat land?
key: On Friday, in the afternoon
In the mud (past the corn rows)

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: On Friday afternoon a strong wind blew. It came across the pumpkin patch. It lifted the old straw hat right off the scarecrow. Jada watched the hat spin over th
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the text about? Tell me two things you remember.” (an answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: Barn Door Tale
desc: retelling a fable in order and telling its lesson
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the fable. Then tell it back in your own words and answer out loud.
text: Goat and the Bag of Seeds Goat found a bag of sunflower seeds by the fence. Hen had dropped it on her way home. Goat’s tummy growled. “No one saw me find it,” h
qs: Tell what happened at the beginning of the story.
Tell what Goat did next.
key: Goat found a bag of sunflower seeds that Hen had dropped. He was hungry, and nobody saw him find it.
He thought about it for a long time. Then he took the bag to the coop and asked Hen if it was hers.

title: Scarecrow’s Notebook
desc: a short narrative with events in order, details, time words, and an ending
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write a story about a time you lost something or found something. It can be real or made up. Tell what happened in order. Tell what you did and how you felt. Wr
key: Tells about one event or a short set of events in order
Includes details about actions, thoughts, or feelings

title: Scarecrow’s Notebook
desc: a short informative piece with a topic sentence, facts, and a closing
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write to teach a friend about fall. Start by telling what you are writing about. Give 2 or more facts. End with a closing sentence. Write 4 sentences. Facts you
key: Starts with a sentence that names the topic (fall)
Gives 2 or more facts about fall

title: From Seed to Pumpkin
desc: asking and answering what, when, and how questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about pumpkins. Then answer each question out loud.
text: How a Pumpkin Grows A pumpkin starts as a flat white seed. Farmers plant the seeds in late spring. By then the soil is warm. In about a week, a green sprout pus
qs: What does a pumpkin seed look like?
When do farmers plant pumpkin seeds?
key: Flat and white
Late spring (when the soil is warm)

title: Look at the Patch Sign
desc: gathering information from a sign and recalling an experience to answer questions
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the sign. Then say the first two answers out loud. Write number 3 on your paper and hold it up. Then say number 4.
qs: A friend asks, “When is the patch open?” Use the sign to tell them.
Why should you wear boots to the patch?
key: On Saturday and on Sunday (the weekend)
Because of the mud. The sign says the field is muddy.

title: Listen Up
desc: describing key ideas and details from a text read aloud
dir: Listen first. Then answer your teacher’s questions out loud.
text: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about sunflowers.
key: Ask: “What does a young sunflower do during the day?” (turns its head to follow the sun)
Ask: “Where are the seeds on a sunflower?” (in the big brown middle of the flower)

title: Tell Me a Story
desc: telling about an experience in order, with facts and details, in clear complete sentences
dir: Tell your story out loud. Say what happened first, next, and last.
text: Tell me about a time you got muddy, wet, or messy. Where were you? How did it happen? What did you do next? First Next Last
key: Tells what happened in an order that makes sense
Gives facts that fit the story (where, when, who, or what)

title: Longer Directions
desc: following three- and four-step oral directions, requesting clarification when something is not understood, and giving multi-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear. Ask a question if you are not sure what to do. Then give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do the steps in order. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once: “Draw a tree, draw a sun above it, and color the sun yellow.” (does all three steps in order)
Say once: “Hold up your hand, count to five out loud, wave, and put your hand down.” (does all four steps in order)

title: Plan and Tell a Story
desc: planning and delivering a short narrative presentation that recounts an event with details, a logical sequence, and a conclusion
dir: Pick one idea. Plan what you will say: the start, the middle, and the end. Then tell your story out loud.
text: Pick one: a day at the park or the beach, a time you learned a skill, or a time you were proud. Beginning Middle End
key: Plans first: says or draws what will happen at the start, the middle, and the end before telling (give about one minute to plan)
Tells one event with enough detail (who, where, and what happened)

title: Say It Right
desc: spoken grammar items (irregular past tense, irregular plural, reflexive pronoun, adverb, putting words in order)
dir: Say each answer out loud.
qs: Today the pumpkins grow. Last summer the pumpkins ____.
One goose, two ____.
key: grew
geese

title: Write It Right
desc: written conventions (capital letters in a place name, an apostrophe to show who owns something, a comma in a letter closing, spelling a vowel team word)
dir: Write each answer on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Fix this sentence: the pumpkin patch is near lake tahoe
The hat belongs to the farmer. Write the missing word: the ____ hat
key: The pumpkin patch is near Lake Tahoe. (capital T at the start, capital L and T in Lake Tahoe, and a period)
farmer’s (apostrophe before the s)

title: Capital Letters
desc: capitalizing holidays, product names, and geographic names
dir: Listen while your teacher reads each sentence. Write it again with the right capital letters. Hold up your paper when you finish.
qs: Fix the capital letters: people clean up on earth day.
Fix the capital letters: we drove through texas.
key: People clean up on Earth Day.
We drove through Texas.

title: Use a Dictionary
desc: using a beginning dictionary and ABC order to check and correct spellings
dir: Listen. Answer out loud. If you have a beginning dictionary, you may use it.
qs: Put these words in ABC order: zebra, lion, bear.
The guide words are map and net. Would the word moon be on this page? Tell why.
key: bear, lion, zebra
Yes. moon comes after map and before net.

title: Group Words
desc: using collective nouns
dir: Listen. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? A group of players on a ball field is called a ___. (team / flock)
Which word fits? A group of wolves is called a ___. (pack / school)
key: team. (A collective noun names a group.)
pack. (A collective noun names a group.)

title: Which Pumpkin Wins
desc: a short opinion piece with a reason and a closing
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Harvest Hill sells small pumpkins and big pumpkins. Which one is the better buy? Write 3 sentences. Say which one you think is better, give one reason, and end
key: Opens by naming what the writing is about and states an opinion, such as: The small pumpkin is the better buy.
Gives at least one reason that goes with the opinion, such as: it is easier to carry, or you can buy two for the price of one big one.

title: Pumpkin Rows
desc: finding the total of arrays up to 5 by 5 and writing it as a sum of equal addends
dir: Look at the rows. Say how many in all. Write your adding sentences on your paper and hold them up.
qs: How many pumpkins in all? Write an adding sentence for the rows.
How many sunflowers in all? Write an adding sentence for the rows.
key: 10 pumpkins. 5 + 5 = 10 (also correct: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10)
12 sunflowers. 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 (also correct: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12)

title: Hundreds, Tens, Ones
desc: telling what the digits of a three-digit number stand for (hundreds, tens, and ones)
dir: A farmer counts seeds with blocks. Answer out loud. Write number 4 on your paper and hold it up.
qs: What number do the blocks show?
Think about the number 586. What is the 8 worth?
key: 243 (2 hundreds, 4 tens, 3 ones)
80, or 8 tens

title: Name That Number
desc: reading and writing numbers to 1000 as numerals, number names, and expanded form
dir: Say the first answer out loud. Write the others on your paper and hold them up.
qs: Read this number out loud: 417
Write this number with digits: five hundred eight
key: four hundred seventeen
508 (watch for 58 or 5008)

title: Harvest Wagon Problems
desc: one-step and two-step addition and subtraction word problems within 100 with the unknown in different places
dir: Listen while your teacher reads each problem. Solve it on your paper. You can draw or write a number sentence. Say your answer.
qs: A wagon holds 30 pumpkins. 18 are orange. The rest are white. How many pumpkins are white?
Tess picked 26 ears of corn. Luis picked 17 more ears than Tess. How many ears did Luis pick?
key: 12 white pumpkins (18 + □ = 30, or 30 - 18 = 12)
43 ears of corn (26 + 17 = 43)

title: Hay Bale Count
desc: skip-counting by 5s, 10s, and 100s and counting past 500
dir: Count out loud.
qs: Skip count by 5s from 85 to 120.
Skip count by 10s from 275 to 335.

title: Count by 2s
desc: skip-counting by 2s within 1000
dir: Count out loud by 2s.
qs: Count by 2s starting at 100. Say the next five numbers.
Count by 2s from 24 to 40. Say all the numbers.

title: Wagon Load Graph
desc: making a bar graph with four categories from a table and solving compare and put-together problems from it
dir: Use the table. Tell your teacher how tall to make each bar. Then answer the questions out loud.
qs: Build the bar graph. Tell your teacher where each bar should stop.
How many more loads of pumpkins than loads of corn?
key: Bars stop at Pumpkins 7, Corn 4, Squash 6, Hay 2. Click the squares the student says. If a bar is wrong, ask the student to check the table before you fix it.

title: Draw a Picture Graph
desc: drawing a picture graph from a data set with four categories and solving put-together, take-apart, and compare problems
dir: Look at the table. Draw a picture graph on your paper. Use one picture for each 1. Then answer out loud.
text: Ways to get to school: number of kids Choice Number of kids Walk 3 Bus 7 Car 5 Bike 2
qs: Draw a picture graph of the table. Give it a title and label each row.
How many kids chose Walk and Bus together?
key: A picture graph with 3 symbols for Walk, 7 symbols for Bus, 5 symbols for Car, 2 symbols for Bike. Each symbol stands for 1, the symbols are the same size and lined up, and the rows are labeled.

title: Measure the Harvest
desc: measuring length with a ruler and choosing the right measuring tool
dir: Answer out loud. For the last one, get a ruler and measure.
qs: Look at the ruler. How long is the ear of corn?
A sunflower is taller than you. Which tool is better for measuring it: a ruler or a yardstick?
key: 6 inches
A yardstick. A sunflower is much longer than a ruler. (A measuring tape or a meter stick is also a good choice.)

title: Odd or Even
desc: telling odd from even and writing an even number as a sum of two equal addends
dir: Look at the two rows. Answer out loud. Write the last answer on your paper.
qs: Row A: is the number of pumpkins odd or even? How do you know?
Row B: odd or even? How do you know?
key: 13, odd. Pairing them up leaves one over, or counting by twos does not land on 13.
8, even. Every pumpkin has a partner, or counting by twos lands on 8.

title: Three Digit Loads
desc: adding and subtracting within 1000 with regrouping, and explaining the regrouping
dir: Solve on your paper. Tell your teacher the answer and how you got it.
qs: Last fall the patch sold 345 pumpkins. This fall it sold 128. How many is that in all?
The barn had 406 seed packets. The patch sold 172 of them. How many packets are left?

title: What Time
desc: telling time to five minutes and writing times with a.m. and p.m.
dir: Look at the clocks. Say each time. Then write the last answer on your paper.
qs: Clock A: what time is it?
Clock B: what time is it?
key: 10:20, or twenty past ten
1:45, or quarter to two, or forty-five past one

title: Count the Money
desc: finding the value of a group of coins and solving a money problem with dollars
dir: Look at the coins. Answer out loud.
qs: How much money is here? Use the cents sign when you write it.
The sign says a small pumpkin costs 2 dollars. You pay with this 5 dollar bill. How much change do you get back?
key: 84¢ (2 quarters is 50¢, 3 dimes is 30¢, 4 pennies is 4¢: 50 + 30 + 4 = 84)

title: Time Facts
desc: knowing relationships of time such as minutes in an hour, days in a month, and weeks in a year
dir: Listen. Answer out loud.
qs: Which month has fewer days: February or July?
How many minutes are in half an hour?
key: February (28 or 29 days; July has 31)
30 minutes

title: Shapes in the Barn
desc: naming shapes by their number of sides and faces, and drawing a quadrilateral
dir: Look at the three shapes. Answer out loud. Then draw on your paper.
qs: Shape 1: how many sides does it have? What is it called?
Shape 2: how many sides does it have? What is it called?
key: 5 sides and 5 angles. It is a pentagon.
6 sides and 6 angles. It is a hexagon.

title: Three Pumpkin Seedlings
desc: reading the results of a plant test and planning a fair test of one thing a plant needs
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Then answer out loud.
text: Three pumpkin seedlings were started in cups in the barn and checked after three weeks. Cup What it got How it looked after three weeks 1 water, no sunlight (ba
qs: Which cup grew into the healthiest seedling, and what did it get?
Cup 1 was watered every single day. Why did it turn almost white?
key: Cup 2. It got both sunlight and water.
It was kept at the back of the barn with no sunlight. Water on its own is not enough. A plant needs sunlight to make its food and to go green.

title: Three Pumpkin Seedlings
desc: making a simple model that does the job an animal does when it moves seeds
dir: Draw your model on your paper. Then tell your teacher about it.
text: A squirrel picks up seeds. They are at the edge of the patch. It carries them off. It buries them in the soft dirt. It never comes back for some. Some of the bu
qs: Draw your model. Label the part that holds the seed and the part that puts it under the dirt.
Which animal job does your model copy, and why does burying the seed matter to the plant?
key: Any model with a holding part and a digging or dropping part: a spoon on a stick, a cup with a hole, a scoop with a flap, tongs and a trowel. The two labelled parts are what to look for.
It copies an animal that carries seeds away and buries them. Burying matters because the seed is in the soil where it can get water and grow, instead of lying on top where it dries out or gets eaten.

title: The Pond and the Hay Field
desc: comparing the kinds of living things found in two different habitats
dir: Listen while your teacher reads both lists. Answer out loud.
text: Two children looked for living things in two places at the farm, for twenty minutes in each place. The pond at the edge of the patch The dry hay field 2 kinds o
qs: How many kinds of living things are on the pond list?
Name one living thing from the pond list that could not live in the hay field, and say why.
key: 8. Two frogs, three water plants, one water beetle, one duck and one dragonfly.
Any sensible pick with a reason: a frog would dry out in the hay field because its skin has to stay wet, a water plant needs its roots in water, a water beetle swims and there is no water to swim in.

title: One Afternoon, or Thousands of Years
desc: using two sources as evidence that some Earth events happen quickly and some happen slowly
dir: Listen while your teacher reads both notes. Answer out loud.
text: Two notes about the land around the patch, from two different places. Where it came from What it says a photograph with a date written on the back One cloudburs
qs: Which note tells about a change to the land that happened quickly?
Which note tells about a change that took thousands of years?
key: The photograph with the date, the channel cut in a single afternoon.
The museum card, the hills wearing down over thousands of years.

title: One Afternoon, or Thousands of Years
desc: telling where water is found on Earth and whether it is solid or liquid
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Water turns up in more places on this farm than you would think.
qs: Name three places on this farm or nearby where you would find water.
Most of the water on Earth is in the ocean and it is salty. Name a place where the water is fresh instead.
key: Any three: the pond, the well, the creek, the trough, the rain barrel, rain in the clouds, dew or frost on the grass, under the ground, inside the pumpkins.
A pond, a creek, a well, a river, a lake, rain. Fresh water is the kind people and animals can drink.

title: Holding the Field, and a Map of It
desc: comparing two things put in place to stop wind from changing the shape of the land
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: After harvest, dry wind lifts the loose soil off the big field and carries it away. Two ways of stopping it were tried, and the soil that blew into a ditch at t
qs: Which one kept the most soil on the field?
How do you know, using the numbers in the chart?
key: leaving the old corn stalks standing
Only 2 buckets blew away with the stalks standing, 6 buckets blew away with the young pines, and 12 buckets blew away off the bare field. The reason must come from the numbers.

title: Holding the Field, and a Map of It
desc: making a model of an area that shows the shapes of the land and the bodies of water in it
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up.
text: Make your own model map of the land around the patch. Put in the hill behind the barn, the flat bottom field, the creek, and the pond. Add a key that says which
qs: Draw your model map with the hill, the flat field, the creek and the pond on it.
Show me your key. Which parts are land and which parts are water?
key: All four on the page and told apart by shape or colour: the hill as a bump or as rings, the flat field left flat, the creek as a line, the pond as a closed shape.
Points to each part and reads the key. The key is what makes this a model and not just a picture.

title: Sorting the Barn Shelf
desc: describing materials by properties you can see or feel and sorting them into groups
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Four things off the barn shelf, and what was noticed about each one. Item Material What was noticed a seed pail metal hard, shiny, cold, holds water a feed sack
qs: Sort the four items into a group that holds water and a group that water runs through.
Which two items are hard? Which two bend?
key: Holds water: the metal pail, the glass jar, the rubber boot. Water runs through: the burlap sack.
Hard: the metal pail and the glass jar. Bend: the burlap sack and the rubber boot.

title: Sorting the Barn Shelf
desc: using test data to choose the material that suits a job
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The scarecrow at the end of the rows needs a new coat. Three materials were pinned out in the field through a week of wind and rain. Material Still dry undernea
qs: Which material should the scarecrow's coat be made of?
Which two pieces of the chart make you sure?
key: the oiled canvas
It was still dry underneath and it was not torn by the wind after a week. Both columns have to be used, not just one.

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: telling how a thing built from a few pieces can be taken apart and built into something new
dir: Answer out loud. You may draw if it helps.
text: A hay feeder is in the barn. It is made of 10 flat slats. It has 4 corner posts. Screws hold it together. They are held with screws. The screws were taken out.
qs: The feeder is gone. Are the slats and posts gone too? What is stacked by the door?
Build something new in your head out of those 10 slats and 4 posts. What is it, and how do the pieces go together?
key: No. All 10 slats and all 4 posts are still there, and the screws. They are the same pieces, just not screwed together as a feeder any more.

Any real thing from 10 slats and 4 posts: a bench, a small table, a gate, a crate, a bookshelf, a frame for a seed bed. Listen for how the pieces join, because that is the evidence the same set of pie

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: arguing with evidence that some heating and cooling changes can be undone and some cannot
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two things happened in the farmhouse on the same cold morning. What happened A pail of water left out overnight was a solid block of ice by morning. Pumpkin see
qs: Bring the pail of ice into the warm kitchen. What happens to it?
Put the roasted seeds back out in the cold. Do they turn back into soft pale seeds?
key: It melts back into water. Warming undoes the freezing.
No. They stay brown, hard and nutty. Cold does not bring the soft pale seeds back.

title: The Rolling Pumpkins
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking a question about it
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the note. Answer out loud.
text: The pumpkins ride to the barn. They ride in a flat wagon bed. It has no sides. The track between the rows is bumpy. On every bump the pumpkins roll about. They
qs: What is the problem the children want to fix? Say it in one sentence.
Ask one question that would help you fix it.
key: The pumpkins roll around in the wagon bed on the bumps and fall off the edge. Naming the rolling, not the walking behind, is the problem.

Any real question: how many pumpkins fit in the wagon, how big are they, how bumpy is the track, how fast does the wagon go, how high would a side need to be. A statement is not a question, so ask onc

title: The Rolling Pumpkins
desc: drawing a design and telling how its shape does the job
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw something that would keep the pumpkins still in the wagon bed. Think hard about its shape.
qs: Draw your fix.
Tell me how the shape of what you drew stops the pumpkins rolling.
key: Any design that could really hold pumpkins: sides or a rail around the wagon bed, a tray of round dips or rings, straw packed between them, crates that each hold one, a net over the top.
The shape is the part being checked. Something like: a round dip holds a round pumpkin so it cannot roll, the sides stop it going over the edge, the straw fills the gaps so nothing can move.

title: The Rolling Pumpkins
desc: comparing test results from two designs built for the same problem
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Both fixes were tried over the same bumpy track, with 20 pumpkins each time. Fix Pumpkins that fell off Pumpkins with a new dent a tray with 20 round dips 0 1 a
qs: Which fix worked better?
How do you know? Use both columns.
key: the tray with 20 round dips
No pumpkins fell off with the tray and only 1 was dented, while 2 fell off the railed wagon and 7 were dented. Both columns have to be used, not just the falling off.

title: Farming Then and Now
desc: telling things that happened long ago from things that happened in the last day or two
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the four lines. Answer out loud.
text: Four lines from the notice board by the barn door. Line What it says 1 When this farm was new, two oxen pulled the plow and it took a week to turn one field. 2
qs: Which two lines tell about things that happened long ago?
Which two tell about things that happened in the last day or two?
key: Lines 1 and 3, the oxen and the plow, and drying or salting food.
Lines 2 and 4, the tractor this morning and loading the wagon yesterday.

title: Where Things Are in the Patch
desc: giving an exact place on a map with a letter and a number, and using north, south, east, west and between
dir: Look at the map. Answer out loud.
text: The patch and the fields around it, drawn in nine squares. North is at the top. 1 2 3 A corn rows walnut trees hay field B pumpkin patch scarecrow barn C pond w
qs: Give the exact square the scarecrow is in, using its letter and its number.
What is directly north of the scarecrow?
key: B2
the walnut trees, in square A2

title: Rules, Money and the Pumpkin Stand
desc: telling who makes rules at each level here, and how another country chooses a leader differently
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The farm follows rules. They come from more than one place. A government does three jobs with a law. It makes the law. It carries the law out, which is the job
qs: Who leads a city? A mayor, or a farmer?
A state law says a school bus must stop at every railway crossing. Why would a government make a law like that?
key: a mayor
To keep people safe. Any answer about safety counts. Laws are made to protect people.

title: Rules, Money and the Pumpkin Stand
desc: telling goods from services, spending a set amount of money, and naming a producer and a consumer
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the price list. Answer out loud.
text: The pumpkin stand price list. What is on offer Price a small pumpkin 45 cents a bag of walnuts 30 cents a jar of jam 40 cents a hay wagon ride round the field 2
qs: Three things on this list are goods and one is a service. Which one is the service, and how do you know?
You have 70 cents and you want all four. Name what you would buy and what you would have to give up.
key: The hay wagon ride. It is something done for you to enjoy, not a thing you take home.

Any pair or set that comes to 70 cents or less: walnuts and jam is 70 cents, pumpkin and the ride is 65 cents, pumpkin and walnuts is 75 cents and is too much. The giving up is the part to listen for,

title: Someone Who Made a Difference
desc: telling what one person from the past did, naming a character strength, and saying how it helped others
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about him. Answer out loud.
text: Louis Pasteur was a scientist in France. In his day people did not know. They did not know why milk went bad. They did not know why wine spoiled. Pasteur looked
qs: What did Louis Pasteur find out about why milk goes bad?
Which word fits him best from what you read: patient, careless, or greedy? Say why.
key: Tiny living things too small to see were doing it, and heating the milk and then cooling it quickly killed them so the milk stayed good longer.
patient. Any reason taken from the text: he kept working on the same idea for years, he looked closely under a microscope instead of guessing.

title: Sunflower Words
desc: reading longer words with prefixes and suffixes
dir: Read each word out loud. Look for a part you know at the start or the end of the word.
key: Read each word: sunflower, scarecrow, preheat, misplace, thankful, darkness, disappear, enjoyment, washable, direction, unbreakable, rediscover.

Watch for: compound words (sunflower, scarecrow), prefixes pre-, mis-, dis-, un-, re- (preheat, misplace, disappear, unbreakable, rediscover), suffixes -ful, -ness, -ment, -able (thankful, darkness, e

title: What Does the Ending Mean?
desc: identifying and knowing the meaning of common derivational suffixes and decoding words with Latin suffixes
dir: Read each word. Tell what the ending means and what the whole word means.
text: darkness thankful homeless gently
qs: What does the ending mean in darkness? What does darkness mean?
What does the ending mean in thankful? What does thankful mean?
key: -ness: the state of being dark.
-ful: full of thanks.

title: Tricky Words
desc: reading grade-appropriate irregularly spelled words
dir: Read each word out loud. Some of these words do not follow the usual rules.
key: Mark each word read correctly. These words do not follow the usual spelling patterns, so the student has to know them by sight.

title: Into the Corn Maze
desc: a 262-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: The Corn Maze The corn maze at Miller Farm had tall green walls and paths that twisted in every direction. Dev and his friend Rosa ran in at two o’clock. “We wi
key: 262 words, not counting the title. Time 1 minute and mark errors and self-corrections on your own copy. Let the student finish the passage.

Fall grade 3 benchmark: about 83 words correct per minute (Hasbrouck and Tindal 2017, fall 50th percentile). The passage length is set from the highest grade 3 figure on that same table, the spring 90

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice and let the rhymes show.
text: Bedtime Moon The moon looks down from the dark night sky. It watches the clouds as they wander by. It lights up the road and the sleeping town. Then it says goo
key: 35 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm and expression at the ends of lines: a pause at the end of each line or where the punctuation is.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: The Corn Maze The corn maze at Miller Farm had tall green walls and paths that twisted in every direction. Dev and his friend Rosa ran in at two o’clock. “We wi
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: Maze Questions
desc: asking and answering story questions using the exact words in the text
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud. Look back at the story to prove each answer.
text: The Corn Maze The corn maze at Miller Farm had tall green walls and paths that twisted in every direction. Dev and his friend Rosa ran in at two o’clock. “We wi
qs: How did Rosa know they were going in circles? Which sentence tells you?
What did Dev use to find the way out? Why did it work? Use the story.
key: They kept passing the same broken stalk. Points to “We have passed this broken stalk three times.” (RL.3.1)
The scarecrow’s red hat. It worked because the scarecrow stands at the exit and the hat shows above the corn, so walking toward the hat leads out. (RL.3.1)

title: Hay Wagon Sayings
desc: literal and nonliteral meanings of phrases in a story
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud.
text: The Biggest Pumpkin Lena rode the harvest wagon past a sea of orange pumpkins. She picked the biggest one she could find. “This thing weighs a ton!” she groaned
qs: The story says “a sea of orange pumpkins.” Is there real water in the pumpkin patch? What does the phrase tell you?
Lena says, “This thing weighs a ton!” Does the pumpkin really weigh a ton? What does she mean?
key: No. It means there are so many pumpkins that they spread out as far as she can see, like a sea. (RL.3.4)
No. She means it is very heavy. (RL.3.4)

title: Mixed-Up Scarecrow
desc: fixing spoken grammar mistakes (plurals, verb tense, agreement, comparing words, pronouns)
dir: The scarecrow mixed up his words. Each sentence has one mistake. Say the whole sentence the right way.
qs: The geeses flew over the corn.
My friends likes the hay ride.
key: The geese flew over the corn. (L.3.1, irregular plural noun)
My friends like the hay ride. (L.3.1, subject-verb agreement)

title: Hay Bale Builder
desc: spoken grammar items (joining sentences, past tense, comparing words, abstract nouns)
dir: Answer out loud. Say whole sentences.
qs: Join these two sentences into one. Use so or because: The wagon was full. We walked back.
Change this sentence so it happened yesterday: The farmer drives the wagon. We sing.
key: The wagon was full, so we walked back. Or: We walked back because the wagon was full. (L.3.1, conjunctions and compound or complex sentences)
The farmer drove the wagon, and we sang. Both verbs are needed. (L.3.1, irregular past tense verbs)

title: Each Other
desc: using reciprocal pronouns such as each other and one another correctly
dir: Choose the word that fits. Say it or write it.
qs: The two friends told ___ jokes. (each other / one another)
All the players cheered for ___. (each other / one another)
key: each other
one another or each other

title: Write It in Cursive
desc: writing legibly in cursive or joined italics with margins and correct spacing between letters in a word and words in a sentence
dir: On your paper, write this sentence in cursive or joined writing. Leave a margin and keep space between your words.
text: Write this sentence: We walked along the beach at sunset.
key: Letters are joined within each word (cursive or joined italics, not separate print letters)
Letters are formed so another person can read them

title: What Does the Word Do?
desc: explaining the function of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs in particular sentences
dir: Read the sentence. Then answer out loud. Tell what job each word does.
qs: Read: “The small dog barked loudly.” What does the word dog do in this sentence? What kind of word is it?
What does the word small do in the sentence? What kind of word is it?
key: Dog is a noun. It names the animal the sentence is about.
Small is an adjective. It tells about the dog (what kind).

title: Follow the Sun
desc: questions about an informational text answered with the exact words in the text
dir: Read the text. Then answer out loud. Look back at the text to prove each answer.
text: Follow the Sun A young sunflower does something surprising. It moves. In the morning, its bud faces east, where the sun comes up. All day, the bud slowly turns
qs: Which way does a young sunflower face in the morning? Read the sentence that tells you.
Why does a young sunflower follow the sun? Which sentence tells you?
key: East. Reads “In the morning, its bud faces east, where the sun comes up.” (RI.3.1)
To get more light so it can grow faster. Points to “Facing the sun gives the young plant more light, and more light helps it grow faster.” (RI.3.1)

title: Ask and Answer
desc: asking and answering questions to show understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers
dir: Read the text to yourself or out loud. Then ask your teacher questions about it. Answer your teacher’s questions with words from the text.
text: Honey bees live in a hive. Each bee has a job. Some bees care for the eggs. Some collect nectar from flowers. Nectar is a sweet liquid. The bees turn the nectar
key: Say: “Ask me one question about the text that the text can answer.” (asks a real question; you answer it from the text)
Say: “Ask me a second question that starts with why or how.” (asks a real question that needs more than one word to answer)

title: Patch Writer
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Write to teach someone how a pumpkin grows. Use the picture chart. Write 5 or 6 sentences. 1. A seed goes into warm soil → 2. A sprout comes up → 3. A
key: Introduces the topic: how a pumpkin grows (W.3.2)
Develops the topic with facts from the chart in order (seed in warm soil, sprout, vine with flowers, small green pumpkin, big ripe pumpkin) and adds at least one detail (W.3.2)

title: Patch Writer
desc: a narrative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: You grow a pumpkin so big that it will not fit in the harvest wagon. Write the story of how you get it home. Write 5 or 6 sentences. First Next After that Final
key: Sets up the situation and who is in the story (W.3.3)
Events happen in a clear order, with time words such as first, next, after that, finally (W.3.3)

title: Pumpkin Notes
desc: taking brief notes from a text and sorting them into given categories
dir: Read the text. Write your notes on your paper and hold it up.
text: Pumpkins Pumpkin seeds are planted in late spring, when the soil is warm. The vines need plenty of sunshine and water. They also need room to spread out, becaus
key: Needs box: two facts, such as warm soil, sunshine, water, room to spread out. (W.3.8, sorts evidence into the given category)
Uses box: two facts, such as pies, bread, and soup, roasted seeds for a snack, food for pigs and chickens, a fall decoration. (W.3.8, sorts evidence into the given category)

title: Remember and Take Notes
desc: recalling information from experience and taking brief notes on a source, sorting the evidence into categories
dir: Write on your paper. First, remember a time from your own life and write about it. Then take notes on the text and sort them.
text: Read the text. Take brief notes. Sort your notes into two groups: Birds and Fish. A robin builds a nest of twigs and grass. A hawk hunts mice from the sky. A tr
qs: Think about a time you learned something new. Write two or three sentences about it.
Take brief notes on the text. Write short notes, not whole sentences. (for example: nest of twigs, hunts mice)
key: Names something learned and tells how or when.
Short notes in the student’s own words, not copied sentences.

title: Scarecrow Talk
desc: telling about an experience or a topic with facts and details, speaking clearly
dir: Pick A or B. Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly, and do not rush.
text: A: Tell about the best day you ever spent outside. B: Teach me about a food you know how to make. Say your topic Give 3 facts or details Tell what you saw, hear
key: Gives facts that fit the topic or the experience (SL.3.4)
Adds relevant, descriptive details, such as what it looked, sounded, or felt like (SL.3.4)

title: The Better Job
desc: a short opinion piece with reasons, linking words, and a closing
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Miller Farm needs help this fall. Which job would you rather have: riding the wagon out to pick pumpkins, or working the gate where visitors come in? Write 4 se
key: Names the topic and states an opinion, such as: I would rather work the gate. (W.3.1)
Gives two reasons that support the opinion, not two ways of saying the same thing. (W.3.1)

title: Two Looks at One Seed
desc: comparing the key points of two texts on the same topic
dir: Read both short texts. Then answer out loud.
text: From the Farm Notebook We plant our sunflower seeds in May, once the nights stay warm. By late summer each flower head holds more than 1,000 seeds. We keep some
key: Ask: What point do both texts make about one sunflower head? (It holds more than 1,000 seeds. Both texts say it.) (RI.3.9)

Ask: What does the Farm Notebook tell you that the Bird Club Notes do not? (The seeds are planted in May, some are kept to plant again, and the rest are pressed into cooking oil. Any one of these coun

title: How the Maze Is Made
desc: main idea and supporting details of a text read aloud
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. The words are not on your screen. Then answer out loud.
key: Read the text out loud once. Read it a second time only if the student asks.
Ask: What is the main idea? (How Miller Farm builds its corn maze: the whole maze is planned and cut long before fall.) (SL.3.2)

title: Read the Chart
desc: determining main ideas and supporting details from information presented visually and quantitatively
dir: Look at the chart. Answer your teacher’s questions out loud.
text: Ways to travel: number of students Choice Students Bus 6 Car 10 Bike 3 Walk 9
qs: What is the main idea of this chart? Tell it in one sentence.
Which choice did the most students pick? How many?
key: The chart shows how many students chose each kind of ways to travel. The most popular is Car.
Car, 10

title: Pumpkin Weigh-In
desc: rounding whole numbers to the nearest 10 and 100
dir: Say each answer out loud.
qs: The dot is at 43. Which ten is 43 closer to? Round 43 to the nearest ten.
Round 78 to the nearest ten.
key: 43 is closer to 40, so it rounds to 40. Partial: 50 rounds up when 43 sits below the halfway mark and does not count. (3.NBT.A.1)
80. Partial: 70 rounds down when the ones digit is 8 and does not count. (3.NBT.A.1)

title: Hay Bale Floors
desc: finding area by counting squares, adding parts, and multiplying side lengths
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
qs: Picture A: Each small square is 1 square unit. What is the area of the barn floor? Tell two ways to find it.
Picture B: Find the area of Part 1 and the area of Part 2. Then find the area of the whole floor.
key: 21 square units. Two ways, such as counting every square, adding the rows 7 + 7 + 7, or multiplying 3 × 7. Partial: the area right with only one way given is approaching. (3.MD.C.7)
Part 1 is 4 × 5 = 20 square units. Part 2 is 4 × 4 = 16 square units. The whole floor is 20 + 16 = 36 square units, the same as 4 × 9. Partial: the two parts right with no total given is approaching.

title: Harvest Wagon Loads
desc: two-step word problems solved with an equation that uses a letter
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work and hold it up.
qs: A wagon has 4 rows of pumpkins with 5 pumpkins in each row. Then 6 pumpkins roll off. How many pumpkins are still on the wagon? Write an equation with a letter for the number you do not know. Then solve.
Omar picks 18 small pumpkins and 12 big pumpkins. He packs all of them into crates with 5 pumpkins in each crate. How many crates does he fill? Write an equation with a letter. Then solve.
key: Problem 1 equation with a letter, such as 4 × 5 − 6 = p, or 4 × 5 = 20 and 20 − 6 = p. Partial: the right answer with no letter for the unknown is approaching. (3.OA.D.8)
Problem 1 answer: 14 pumpkins. Partial: 20 stops at the rows and leaves the 6 out, so it is approaching. (3.OA.D.8)

title: Patch Plans
desc: finding the area of shapes made of two rectangles by adding the parts
dir: Look at the pictures. Solve on your paper and hold it up. Then tell how you did it.
qs: Picture A: Each small square is 1 square unit. Break the garden into two rectangles. What is the area of the whole garden?
Picture B: This corn maze has no squares to count. Break it into two rectangles and find its area.
key: 18 square units. Two rectangles, such as 2 × 3 = 6 and 6 × 2 = 12, or 2 × 5 = 10 and 4 × 2 = 8. Partial: the two rectangles right with no total given is approaching. (3.MD.C.7)
23 square meters. Two rectangles, such as 3 × 5 = 15 and 4 × 2 = 8, or 7 × 2 = 14 and 3 × 3 = 9. Partial: the two rectangles right with no total given is approaching. (3.MD.C.7)

title: Does It Make Sense?
desc: estimating and checking whether answers to two-step problems make sense
dir: Estimate first. Then solve on your paper and hold it up.
qs: On Saturday, 287 people came to the pumpkin patch. On Sunday, 412 people came. Of all those people, 95 rode the hay wagon. About how many people did not ride the wagon? Round each number to estimate. Do not find the exact answer yet.
Now find the exact answer. Is it close to your estimate?
key: About 600 people, from 300 + 400 − 100. Partial: any rounding that lands near 600 counts, and the exact answer alone is approaching, since an estimate was asked for. (3.OA.D.8, estimates by rounding)
604 people. 287 + 412 = 699, then 699 − 95 = 604. Yes, 604 is close to 600. Partial: 699 stops before the wagon riders are taken off and is approaching. (3.OA.D.8)

title: What a Product Means
desc: telling what a product means as a number of equal groups
dir: Look at the crate. Answer out loud. You can write on your paper.
qs: Crate A holds 3 rows with 7 pumpkins in each row. Write the multiplication fact. Then tell me what 3 x 7 means in this crate.
Tell me a patch story for 5 x 6. What does each number stand for in your story?
key: 3 x 7 = 21. It means 3 groups with 7 pumpkins in each group, which is 21 pumpkins in all. The number of pumpkins in all is the key part. Partial: the fact right with no meaning given is approaching. (

A story with 5 equal groups of 6, or 6 equal groups of 5, 30 pumpkins in all, such as 5 wheelbarrows with 6 pumpkins in each. The student has to say which number is the groups and which is how many ar

title: What a Quotient Means
desc: telling what a quotient means, as the size of each share and as the number of shares
dir: Answer out loud. Tell me what the answer counts. You can write on your paper.
qs: 24 pumpkins go into 4 crates with the same number in each crate. Write the division fact. Then tell me what 24 divided by 4 means.
Now a different story with the same two numbers. 24 pumpkins go into crates with 4 pumpkins in each crate. What does 24 divided by 4 tell you this time?
key: 24 divided by 4 = 6. It means 24 pumpkins split into 4 equal groups, with 6 in each group. Saying it the other way, how many are in each of the 4 crates, also counts. Partial: the fact right with no m

6 again, but this time the 6 is the number of crates, not the number in each crate. The size of each share is the number given here, so the answer counts the shares. Partial: 6 right with nothing said

title: Equal Parts
desc: naming the unit fraction for one equal part of a shape and reading a fraction of a whole
dir: Look at the two pictures. Answer out loud.
qs: Picture 1 is a garden bed cut into 6 equal parts. What fraction of the whole bed is one part?
What fraction of the bed is shaded? Tell me what the top number means and what the bottom number means.
key: 1/6. One of 6 equal parts of the whole bed. Partial: 6 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.G.A.2)

3/6. The 6 is how many equal parts the whole is cut into. The 3 is how many of those parts are counted. Partial: the fraction right with only one of the two numbers explained is approaching. (3.NF.A.1

title: On the Line
desc: placing and naming a fraction on a number line
dir: Look at the number line. Answer out loud.
qs: The line from 0 to 1 is cut into 4 equal parts. What fraction does one of those parts show?
What fraction is the dot sitting on? How do you know?
key: 1/4. The whole from 0 to 1 is cut into 4 equal lengths, so one length is 1/4. Partial: 1/4 right with no account of the equal lengths is approaching. (3.NF.A.2)
3/4. It is 3 of those 1/4 lengths away from 0. Partial: 3/4 right with no count of lengths from 0 is approaching. (3.NF.A.2)

title: Same or Not
desc: equivalent fractions and comparing fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator
dir: Look at the two bars. They are the same length. Answer out loud.
qs: Bar 1 shows 1/2 shaded and Bar 2 shows 2/4 shaded. Is 1/2 equal to 2/4? How do you know?
Which is greater, 3/4 of a bar or 1/4 of the same bar? How do you know?
key: Yes, they are equal. The bars are the same length and the same amount is shaded. Partial: saying yes with no reason from the bars is approaching. (3.NF.A.3)
3/4. The pieces are the same size, and 3 pieces is more than 1 piece. Partial: naming 3/4 with no reason is approaching. (3.NF.A.3)

title: Compare With Symbols
desc: comparing fractions with the same numerator or denominator, recording the results with the symbols >, =, or <, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know. You can draw a model.
qs: Compare 5/6 and 1/6 with >, = or <.
Compare 3/5 and 3/8 with a symbol. Tell how you know.
key: 3/5 > 3/8. Same numerator, and fifths are bigger than eighths.

title: Measure the Stems
desc: reading and adding to a line plot of lengths measured to the half inch, and generating measurements of real objects with a ruler
dir: Look at the line plot. Each X is one pumpkin stem. Answer out loud. For the last one, get a ruler and measure.
qs: How many stems were exactly 3 inches long?
Which length came up the most?
key: 2 stems. Partial: counting the Xs above a different mark does not count. (3.MD.B.4)
3 1/2 inches, with 4 Xs. Partial: the length right with no count of Xs is approaching. (3.MD.B.4)

title: Sense, Brain, Act
desc: using a model to show how an animal takes in information, processes it, and responds
dir: Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your model on your paper and hold it up.
text: A barn owl sits still on a beam above the straw. Something rustles below. She tips her head one way, then the other, then drops straight down.
qs: Which sense took in the information about the mouse? Which body part did that work?
Why did the owl tip her head twice before she dropped? What was going on inside her?
key: Hearing, with her ears. The rustle is a sound. (3-LS1-1)
Her brain was working out where the sound was coming from. Turning her head gave the brain a second helping of information to compare, and then it decided where to drop. (3-LS1-1)

title: Many Eyes Are Better
desc: building an argument from data that forming a group helps animals survive
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Crows feed in the stubble beside the patch. A class watched single crows and flocks of crows for the same number of hours. Crows Seconds spent head-up watching,
qs: Which crows spent more of every minute watching instead of eating?
Make an argument that feeding in a flock helps a crow survive. Use a number from the table.
key: the crow feeding alone, 34 seconds out of 60 against 9 (3-LS2-1)

The claim yes, with the numbers attached: a crow in the flock only watched for 9 seconds a minute, so it had more time to eat, and flocks were surprised once against six times. A yes with no number is

title: Passed Down and Shaped
desc: reading trait data for parents and offspring, naming the variation, and telling when the surroundings shaped a trait
dir: Look at both tables. Answer out loud.
text: Table 1: a deeply ribbed orange pumpkin and five pumpkins grown from its seeds. Pumpkin Skin Weight in kg parent orange, deep ribs 7 A orange, deep ribs 5 B ora
qs: Every pumpkin in Table 1 is orange with deep ribs, the same as the parent. Where did that come from?
The weights are all different. What is that difference called. Does it mean one of them grew from a different parent?
key: It was inherited from the parent plant. A trait the parent has and every offspring has is passed down. (3-LS3-1)
Variation. They all still grew from that parent: inherited traits vary from one offspring to the next, so a group of similar organisms is not identical. (3-LS3-1)

title: Clues in the Road Cut
desc: reading fossil data to say which organisms lived in a place and what the place was like
dir: Look at the table of rock layers. Answer out loud.
text: A new road was cut through the ridge above the patch, and the cut shows three layers of rock. A class listed what they found in each. The top layer is the young
qs: Name two organisms that once lived where this ridge now stands.
Was the middle layer once a pond or once dry grassland? Use the fossils as your evidence.
key: Any two the table names: a grass, a grasshopper, a cattail, a frog, a pond snail, a fern, a turtle. (3-LS4-1)
A pond. Cattails, frogs and pond snails need standing water, and naming them is the evidence. An answer with no fossil named is not yet using the data. (3-LS4-1)

title: A Useful Difference
desc: explaining how a variation among individuals of one species gives an advantage
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Field mice live in the dark soil at the edge of the patch. Owls hunt them at night. A class live-trapped mice, recorded coat color, and marked and released them
qs: Which mice were still around after two months?
Explain why a dark coat is an advantage for a mouse on this dark soil. Use the table.
key: the dark brown mice, 31 out of 40 against 9 (3-LS4-2)

A dark coat on dark soil is hard for a hunting owl to pick out, so fewer dark mice are caught, 31 still found against 9. The explanation has to lean on the data, and it has to tie the coat to the soil

title: Who Survives, and What Would Help
desc: arguing from data who can survive in a changed habitat, then judging the merit of a solution
dir: Read the table. Answer out loud.
text: The pond at the corner of the patch holds water most years. After a hot dry autumn it shrank to a wet patch of mud. A class checked it every two weeks. Living t
qs: Which living thing survived well after the pond shrank? Give the evidence.
Which one could not live there at all. Which one managed but not well?
key: The mud snails. There were more of them than in any other year, so the change suited them. (3-LS4-3)
The pond turtles could not survive there at all, none were found. The cattails survived less well, still growing but with fewer new shoots. (3-LS4-3)

title: A Season of Weather
desc: reading and making a graphical display of typical weather for one season
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your graph on your paper and hold it up.
text: Rain measured at the patch in each week of the autumn season. Week Rain in mm 1 5 2 10 3 30 4 45 5 50 6 60
qs: What is happening to the rain across the autumn season?
Which half of the season is wetter, the first three weeks or the last three? Use the numbers.
key: It is rising week by week, from 5 mm up to 60 mm. (3-ESS2-1)
the last three, 155 mm against 45 mm. Accept a correct comparison even if the student only names the bigger numbers rather than adding them. (3-ESS2-1)

title: Two Parts of the World
desc: combining information to describe the climates of two different regions of the world
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Two regions of the world, with their rain split between the two halves of the year. Region Summer rain Winter rain Summer temperature a coastal region with dry
qs: Which region gets rain all year round?
In which region would a farmer have to water crops in summer. What in the table tells you?
key: the rainforest region, 120 cm in summer and 130 cm in winter (3-ESS2-2)
the coastal region with dry summers, because it gets only 4 cm of summer rain (3-ESS2-2)

title: Ready for the Wind
desc: making a claim about the merit of a design that reduces the impact of a weather hazard
dir: Answer out loud.
text: An autumn windstorm can tear the broad vine leaves. It can roll small pumpkins into the ditch. The farmer stacks straw bales two high. They run along the west e
qs: Which weather hazard is the bale wall meant to reduce?
Make a claim. Does the bale wall have merit? Give your reason.
key: wind, which tears the leaves and rolls the fruit (3-ESS3-1)

Yes, with a reason attached: the bales break the force of the wind before it reaches the vines, and the gaps let some air through so the wall is not pushed over. A yes with no reason is not yet a clai

title: Balanced or Not
desc: planning an investigation of balanced and unbalanced forces acting on an object
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A wheelbarrow loaded with pumpkins stands on the sloped path to the barn. One worker holds the handles and the barrow does not move.
qs: The slope pulls the barrow downhill and the worker holds it back. Are the forces on it balanced or unbalanced? How do you know?
The worker shifts her grip and the barrow creeps downhill. What changed about the forces?
key: Balanced. She is holding back exactly as hard as the slope pulls, and the barrow standing still is the evidence. (3-PS2-1)
The hold got weaker than the pull of the slope, so the forces became unbalanced and the barrow moved downhill. (3-PS2-1)

title: Predict the Next Roll
desc: using a pattern in motion data to predict where an object will be later
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: A small pumpkin rolls down a long plank ramp. The class marked where its front edge was after each half second. Half seconds Distance down the ramp 1 10 cm 2 40
qs: Is the pumpkin covering the same distance in every half second, or more each time? Use the numbers.
Look at how much is added each half second: 30, then 50, then 70. What distance would you predict at the fifth half second?
key: More each time. The gaps grow: 10, then 30 more, then 50 more, then 70 more. A pumpkin speeds up as it rolls down. (3-PS2-2)
250 cm, because the next added amount in the pattern is 90, and 160 plus 90 is 250. Accept any answer the student reaches by continuing the pattern and explaining it. (3-PS2-2)

title: Ask About the Pull
desc: asking questions about cause and effect in magnetic interactions between objects not touching
dir: Answer out loud. Your two questions have to be questions, not statements.
text: A steel washer sits on top of a wooden table. A magnet is slid along underneath the table top, and the washer slides across the table, following it. The magnet
qs: The magnet is under the table and the washer is on top. They never touch. What does that tell you about this force?
What two questions could you test to find out more about it?
key: The force acts across a distance and straight through the wood, with no contact between the objects. (3-PS2-3)

Any two real investigable questions: how thick can the table be before it stops working, does a stronger magnet pull a heavier washer, does a brass washer follow, how fast can the magnet move before t

title: A Problem for a Magnet
desc: defining a design problem that magnets can solve, with criteria for success and constraints
dir: Answer out loud. For the third one you may write your two sentences on your paper.
text: The patch gate has to swing shut on its own. Then no deer wander in. But the old latch needs two hands. The gate is often left open.
qs: Put the problem into one sentence beginning: The problem is.
Why is a magnet a sensible idea for a latch? Would a magnet hold a wooden gate post to a wooden gate?
key: A problem statement about a gate latch that shuts and holds on its own without two hands. The problem has to be about the latch, not about the deer. (3-PS2-4)

A magnet pulls steel across a small gap, so the gate can be pulled shut and held closed with no hands and no moving catch. Wood on wood will not work, because a magnet does not pull on wood, so a stee

title: Three Ways to Do It
desc: comparing several possible solutions against stated criteria and constraints
dir: Look at the table and the three rules. Answer out loud.
text: Pumpkins have to get from the field to the stand across soft ground. Three ways are tried. Design Pumpkins per trip Sinks into soft ground? Pumpkins cracked out
qs: Which design carries the most pumpkins in one trip?
Which design passes all three rules? Explain from the table.
key: the wide-wheeled wagon, 14 a trip (3-5-ETS1-2)

The wide-wheeled wagon. It carries 14, stays on top of soft ground, and cracks only 2 out of 30. Another choice counts only if the student argues it against all three rules using the table. (3-5-ETS1-

title: Make the Test Fair
desc: judging whether a test is fair, naming controlled variables, and identifying a failure point
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two wagon wheels were tested to see which one rolls better on soft ground. Wheel Load in the wagon Route narrow wheel 14 pumpkins across the soft field wide whe
qs: Can you trust what this test shows? Why or why not?
Name two things that have to match for the test to be fair.
key: No. Two things were different at once, the load and the route, so sinking cannot be pinned on the wheel. (3-5-ETS1-3)
Any two controlled variables: the same load, the same route, the same distance, the same wagon, the same ground conditions. (3-5-ETS1-3)

title: Maps and Places
desc: using a map grid and a table to describe physical and human features and where they sit
dir: Use the map grid and the table. Answer out loud.
text: A map grid of the farm and the land around it. North is the top row. west middle east north woods pond corn maze middle ridge pumpkin field barn south creek bri
qs: What lies directly east of the pumpkin field?
Which two directions do you walk to get from the pumpkin field to the corn maze?
key: the barn (HSS-3.1)
north and east, in either order. The corn maze sits in the north row and the east column. Partial: one of the two directions is approaching. (HSS-3.1)

title: The First Nations Here
desc: describing how the American Indian nations of California used the plants of their own place long ago, their folklore, and how a nation is part of the state today
dir: Answer out loud. Use what is on the screen and what you have learned.
text: Tule is a tall reed. It grows thick along California rivers and marshes. Nations here cut and dried it. They bundled it into boats. Those boats floated two or t
qs: The screen names one plant and three things nations made from it. Name the plant, say where it grows, and name all three things.
A nation’s folklore was told out loud and not written down. What had to happen in every single generation for those stories to last. What did the stories carry?
key: Tule, a tall reed, which grows thick along California rivers and marshes. From it nations made boats that floated two or three people, mats, and the walls of houses. Partial: the plant and two of the

Somebody had to tell them to the children, and the children had to learn them well enough to tell them later, so the telling had to happen again in every generation. The stories carried the nation’s o

title: A Town Over Time
desc: sequencing local historical events and describing the mark each period left on the land
dir: Look at the timeline. Answer out loud.
text: A timeline for the town of Creek Landing. Year What happened 1851 a ferry starts crossing the creek where the water runs shallow 1880 the marsh east of the cros
qs: Put these three in order, earliest first: the bridge, the ferry, the canning plant.
Which event changed the marsh. What did it do to it?
key: ferry, bridge, canning plant. Partial: two of the three in the right order is approaching. (HSS-3.3)
the draining in 1880, which turned the marsh into grain fields. Partial: naming the draining with no account of what it did to the marsh is approaching. (HSS-3.3)

title: Rules, Laws and Government
desc: telling rules from laws and naming the basic parts and levels of United States government
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The corn maze has a rule on a sign. Stay on the marked paths. The state has a law for a business. The business is open to the public. It must keep a clear way o
qs: What is the difference between the maze’s own rule and the state law?
Why do we have laws at all? Give one reason.
key: The maze rule is set by the farm and applies in the maze. The state law is made by a government, applies to every business in the state, and the government decides what happens when it is broken. Part

Any sound reason: to keep people safe, to settle disagreements fairly, so everyone knows what to expect, to protect people’s things and rights. Partial: saying laws are the rules with no reason for ha

title: Choices and the Local Economy
desc: basic economic reasoning about scarce money, trade-offs, goods and services
dir: Look at the price list. Answer out loud.
text: The farm sells pumpkins and cider at the stand, and it also sells rides on the hay wagon. A family comes with 20 dollars. What they want Price a large pumpkin 9
qs: Can the family buy all three with 20 dollars? Work it out.
They decide on the pumpkin and the cider. What have they given up. What is the name for the thing you give up when you choose?
key: No. 9 plus 7 plus 8 is 24 dollars, and they have 20. Partial: saying no with no total worked out is approaching. (HSS-3.5)
