They gave up the two hay wagon rides. The idea is a trade-off, or opportunity cost: picking one thing means doing without another, because money is limited. The idea matters more than the term at this

title: Hay Bale Word Stack
desc: reading long words with prefixes, roots, and suffixes
dir: Read each word out loud. The last two are made-up words. Just sound them out.
key: Read each word. Count a word as correct when the student reads it right on the first try or fixes it without help.
The last two are made-up words. Listen for the chunks: un-prost-a-ble and re-grump-tion.

title: Read the Sentences
desc: reading multisyllabic words accurately in context using letter-sound correspondences, syllable patterns, and word parts
dir: Read each sentence out loud. Take your time with the long words.
text: The scientist carefully recorded the temperature every afternoon. An unexpected thunderstorm interrupted the basketball tournament.
key: Listen for these six words read correctly in the sentences: scientist, carefully, temperature, unexpected, thunderstorm, tournament. Mark each one.
A word that is self-corrected on a second try counts as correct. Note words the student breaks into syllables to decode.

title: Read by the Scarecrow
desc: a 193-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: The corn maze at Dunmore Farm had one rule. Stay with your partner. Nell and Carmen broke it in the first five minutes. “Left is faster,” Nell said, and she mar
key: 193 words. Time 1 minute and mark errors and self-corrections on your own copy.
Fall grade 4 benchmark: about 94 words correct per minute (50th percentile).

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice. Let the rhythm and the rhymes show.
text: The Night Train Down the track with a clickety-clack, The night train rolls and never looks back. Past sleeping towns and a silver lake, It hums a song for the
key: 42 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm, pauses at the end of lines or punctuation, and a voice that fits the mood of the poem.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: The corn maze at Dunmore Farm had one rule. Stay with your partner. Nell and Carmen broke it in the first five minutes. “Left is faster,” Nell said, and she mar
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: Prove It
desc: questions answered with details and examples from a story
dir: Answer out loud. Look back at the story and point to the details that prove your answer.
text: The corn maze at Dunmore Farm had one rule. Stay with your partner. Nell and Carmen broke it in the first five minutes. “Left is faster,” Nell said, and she mar
qs: How did Nell find her way out of the maze? Give two details from the story.
True or false: Carmen got lost too. Prove it with details from the story.
key: She heard the squeaking harvest wagon and remembered from the map that the wagon road ran beside the exit. At each turn she picked the path that made the squeak louder. (explicit)
False. Carmen was already out. She was sitting on a hay bale with two cups of cider, and she said going right really was faster. (inference)

title: Word Detective
desc: meanings of words and phrases in a story, including one from mythology
dir: Look back at the story. Answer out loud.
text: Look back at the story The corn maze at Dunmore Farm had one rule. Stay with your partner. Nell and Carmen broke it in the first five minutes. “Left is faster,”
qs: The story says the walk “turned into an odyssey.” The word comes from Odysseus, a hero in Greek myths. His trip home took ten years. What does odyssey mean in this story? Which details help you?
What does “her pride held her tongue” mean?
key: A long, wandering trip with many troubles. Details: a short walk took much longer, she passed the same bent stalk three times, and her water ran out. (allusion to mythology)
She did not want to admit she was lost, so she stayed quiet and did not call for help.

title: Corn Maze Listen
desc: retelling a text read aloud in their own words
dir: Listen to your teacher read. Then tell it back in your own words.
text: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about how a corn maze is made. Then tell it back in your own words.
key: Tells the main idea: the maze is planned and cut early, while the corn is short, and then the corn grows tall around the paths.

Includes 2 or more key details: corn is planted in spring; a designer draws the maze on a computer; a tractor cuts the paths when the corn is about knee high; a GPS unit tells the driver where to turn

title: Say It in Your Own Words
desc: paraphrasing information presented visually and quantitatively
dir: Look at the chart. Tell your teacher what it shows in your own words. Do not read it word for word.
text: Trees planted at school Item Amount Grade 3 12 trees Grade 4 20 trees Grade 5 25 trees
qs: Tell what the chart is about in your own words.
Tell two important facts from the chart in your own words.
key: A paraphrase of the main point in the student’s own words (not reading the numbers aloud in order).
Two accurate facts or comparisons put in new words (for example, which is greatest or smallest and about how much).

title: Sunflower Notebook
desc: taking notes in their own words, sorting the notes, and listing sources
dir: Read the two sources. Write your notes on your paper and hold it up.
text: You are gathering facts for a report about sunflowers. Source 1 (book page): Sunflowers on the Move A young sunflower does something surprising. Its bud follows
qs: Write three notes. Use both sources. Keep them short and use your own words.
Sort your notes. Write a heading above each note: How Sunflowers Move or Sunflower Seeds.
key: Three short notes that use both sources, in the student’s own words and not copied sentences. Examples: young buds turn to follow the sun; grown flowers face east; one head can have over 1,000 seeds.

Each note sits under the heading that fits. Facts about following the sun and facing east go under How Sunflowers Move. Facts about tiny flowers, seeds, harvest, snacks, oil, and birdseed go under Sun

title: Scarecrow Says Fix It
desc: spoken grammar items (relative adverbs, progressive tense, modal words, fragments, prepositional phrases, confused words)
dir: Say each sentence out loud the correct way.
qs: This is the patch ____ we found the biggest pumpkin. (where, when, or why)
Tomorrow at noon, we ____ on the hay wagon. (ride) Start with will be.
key: where (relative adverb)
will be riding (progressive tense)

title: Cursive Writing
desc: writing fluidly and legibly in cursive or joined italics
dir: Write this sentence on your paper in cursive or joined writing. Write smoothly and keep it neat.
text: Write this sentence: We practiced our spelling words every single morning.
key: Letters are joined within words (cursive or joined italics)
Writing is legible: another reader can read each word

title: Patch Writer
desc: an opinion writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Would you rather grow one giant pumpkin or one hundred tiny pumpkins? Write your opinion. Write 5 to 7 sentences. State your opinion Give reasons with facts or
key: Introduces the topic and states an opinion
Gives reasons supported by facts and details

title: Patch Writer
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: How does a pumpkin grow from a seed to harvest? Write to explain it. Use facts from the chart. Write 5 to 7 sentences. Introduce your topic Give facts, details,
key: Introduces the topic clearly
Develops the topic with facts and details from the chart, such as the seed sprouting in about a week, vines spreading, bees carrying pollen, or harvest after 3 to 4 months

title: Patch Writer
desc: a narrative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: The harvest wagon gets stuck in the mud on the busiest day of fall. Write the story of what happens next. Write 5 to 7 sentences. Start by telling who is in the
key: Sets up the situation and introduces a narrator or characters
Events unfold in a clear order, with transition words like at first, suddenly, a while later, at last

title: Harvest Report
desc: giving a short report out loud in an organized way with facts and details
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly and take your time.
text: Give a one-minute report. Pick a topic you know a lot about: an animal, a sport, a game, or a hobby. Teach me about it. Name your topic Three facts A detail for
key: Reports in an organized way: names the topic, gives the facts in an order that makes sense, and wraps it up
Gives facts that fit the topic

title: Prove It from the Text
desc: explaining what an informational text says and drawing an inference from it
dir: Read Source 1. Then answer out loud. Point to the words that prove each answer.
text: Source 1 (book page): Sunflowers on the Move A young sunflower does something surprising. Its bud follows the sun. In the morning the bud faces east. All day it
key: Ask: Which way does a fully grown sunflower face all day? Read the sentence that proves it. (East. Reads: A grown sunflower faces east all day.) (RI.4.1)
Ask: What does a young bud do between sunset and sunrise? Read the sentence. (It swings back to the east to wait for sunrise.) (RI.4.1)

title: Put the Two Together
desc: using information from two texts on one topic to explain the topic
dir: Read both sources. Then answer out loud using facts from both.
text: Source 1 (book page): Sunflowers on the Move A young sunflower does something surprising. Its bud follows the sun. In the morning the bud faces east. All day it
qs: Using both sources, tell me in two or three sentences. A sunflower head goes from following the sun to becoming birdseed. How? Use at least one fact from each source.

Source 1 says a grown sunflower faces east. So the morning sun warms it and more bees visit it. Source 2 says what one head is really made of. Put the two together. A bee lands on one sunflower head. How many flowers is it visiting? What does that mean for the number of seeds that head can make?
key: Say: Using both sources, tell me in two or three sentences. A sunflower head goes from following the sun to becoming birdseed. How? Use at least one fact from each source. (Looks for a fact from Sourc

Say: Source 1 says a grown sunflower faces east. So the morning sun warms it and more bees visit it. Source 2 says what one head is really made of. Put the two together. A bee lands on one sunflower h

title: Pumpkins on the Vine
desc: multiplication as a comparison (times as many)
dir: Say 1 and 2 out loud. Write 3, 4, and 5 on your paper and hold it up. Then explain number 6.
qs: Look at the pumpkins. Row B has how many times as many pumpkins as Row A? Say a multiplication equation that shows it.
42 = 6 × 7. Say it two ways. Use the words “times as many” each time.
key: 4 times as many. 12 = 4 × 3. Partial: 9 more is a difference and not a multiplicative comparison, so it does not count.
42 is 6 times as many as 7. 42 is 7 times as many as 6. Partial: one of the two ways given is approaching.

title: Sunflower Fractions
desc: explaining and making equivalent fractions
dir: Look at the two bars. Answer out loud. Write numbers 2 and 3 on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Do the two bars show the same amount? Explain. Talk about the number of pieces and the size of the pieces.
Fill in the missing number: 5/6 = ?/12
key: Yes. The second bar has 3 times as many pieces, and each piece is one third as big, so the shaded amount is the same. Partial: saying yes with nothing said about the size of the pieces is approaching.
10 (5/6 = 10/12). Or: double the top and the bottom of 5/6 to get 10/12.

title: Harvest Wagon Weigh-In
desc: sizes of measurement units and changing a larger unit to a smaller unit
dir: Answer out loud. Use the table for number 2. For number 5, explain how you know.
qs: Which is more: 1 liter of cider or 500 milliliters of cider? How do you know?
Finish the table. How many ounces are in 3 pounds? How many are in 5 pounds?
key: 1 liter. A liter is 1,000 milliliters, so it is twice as much as 500 milliliters. Partial: naming the liter with no change into millilitres is approaching.
48 ounces and 80 ounces. Partial: one of the two rows right is approaching.

title: Pumpkin Pie Compare
desc: comparing fractions with different numerators and denominators
dir: Answer out loud and tell how you know. Write number 2 on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Which is greater: 3/5 or 7/10? How do you know?
Write >, <, or = to make it true: 4/6 ____ 4/5
key: 7/10. 3/5 is the same as 6/10, and 6/10 is less than 7/10. Partial: naming 7/10 with no common denominator shown is approaching.
4/6 is less than 4/5. Both have 4 pieces, but sixths are smaller pieces than fifths. Or: compare both with 1 whole, since 4/5 is 1/5 short and 4/6 is 2/6 short.

title: Compare With Symbols
desc: comparing fractions with different numerators and denominators, recording the results with symbols, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know.
qs: Compare 7/10 and 3/5 with a symbol.
Compare 1/3 and 3/8 with a symbol. Tell how you know.

title: Fence the Patch
desc: area and perimeter of rectangles
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work and hold it up. For number 5, explain how you know.
qs: The farmer puts a fence all the way around the pumpkin patch. How many meters of fence does the farmer need?
The farmer covers the whole patch with straw. How many square meters of ground get covered?
key: 40 meters (12 + 8 + 12 + 8). Or: 2 × 12 + 2 × 8 = 40. Partial: 20 adds only one of each side and does not count.
96 square meters (12 × 8). Partial: 96 with no square unit named is approaching.

title: Seed Count Place Value
desc: comparing the value of two digits in one number, and rounding a multi-digit number
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
text: 4,400 The patch counted 23,681 sunflower seeds in one head basket.
qs: Look at 4,400. How does the value of the 4 in the thousands place compare with the value of the 4 in the hundreds place?
Round 23,681 to the nearest thousand.
key: It is 10 times as much. The first 4 is worth 4,000 and the second 4 is worth 400, and 4,000 is 10 times 400. Partial: naming the two values with no comparison is approaching. (4.NBT.A.1)
24,000. 681 is more than 500, so it rounds up. Partial: 23,000 rounds down when the hundreds digit is 6 and does not count. (4.NBT.A.3)

title: Decimal Patch
desc: writing fractions with denominators 10 and 100 as decimals, and comparing two decimals
dir: Look at the two pictures. Answer out loud. Write the first two answers on your paper.
qs: The grid has 100 equal squares. Write the shaded part as a fraction and as a decimal.
The bar has 10 equal parts. Write the shaded part as a fraction and as a decimal.
key: 37/100 and 0.37. Partial: one of the fraction and the decimal given is approaching. (4.NF.C.6)
3/10 and 0.3. Partial: one of the fraction and the decimal given is approaching. (4.NF.C.6)

title: Compare Decimals
desc: comparing two decimals to hundredths, recording the results with the symbols >, =, or <, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know. You can use a number line or a grid.
qs: Compare 0.62 and 0.6 with a symbol. Tell how you know.
Compare 0.8 and 0.79 with a symbol.

title: Angles in the Barn
desc: sorting figures by right angles and parallel sides, and naming a right triangle
dir: Look at the three figures. Answer out loud.
qs: Which figure is a right triangle? How do you know?
Figure 2 has one pair of parallel sides. Which two sides are they, and what does parallel mean?
key: Figure 1. It is a triangle and it has one right angle, the square corner at the bottom left. Partial: naming the figure with no reason is approaching. (4.G.A.2)

The top side and the bottom side. Parallel means the two lines run the same direction and stay the same distance apart, so they would never meet. The two slanted sides are not parallel. Partial: namin

title: Triangles by Their Sides
desc: classifying triangles as equilateral, isosceles, or scalene by their side lengths
dir: Answer out loud. For the drawing questions, draw on your paper.
qs: Draw a triangle with all three sides equal. What is it called?
Draw a triangle with exactly two equal sides. What is it called?
key: Equilateral. The drawing has three sides that look the same length.
Isosceles

title: Special Four-Sided Shapes
desc: classifying quadrilaterals as rhombus, trapezoid, parallelogram, rectangle, or square by parallel sides, equal sides, and angles
dir: Answer out loud. Draw if you need to.
qs: A shape has two pairs of parallel sides and four right angles. List two names for it.
A shape has four equal sides and four right angles. What is it?
key: Rectangle and parallelogram (a square works if the sides are equal)
A square (also a rhombus, a rectangle, and a parallelogram)

title: Vine and Owl
desc: arguing that named plant and animal structures do a job that supports survival, growth or reproduction
dir: Look at the two living things. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: A pumpkin vine runs along the ground at the edge of the patch. An owl roosts in the oak above it. A vine grows curling tendrils that wrap around anything they t
qs: Name the job of the tendrils and the job of the seeds.
The owl has hollow bones inside its body and soft fringed edges on its wing feathers. Pick one and build an argument for how it supports the owl's survival.
key: Tendrils grip stems, fences and other plants, which anchors the vine and keeps it from being dragged or rolled. Seeds carry the next generation of plants, so they support reproduction. (4-LS1-1)

Hollow bones make the owl light, so it needs less energy to stay in the air. Fringed feather edges make the wing quiet, so the owl can hear faint sounds while flying and is not heard by what it hunts.

title: Vine and Owl
desc: modelling the path from sense organ to brain to response in an animal
dir: Read what happens, then answer. You may draw your model.
text: A mouse rustles the dry leaves at the edge of the patch. The owl on the branch turns its head toward the sound. It waits. Then it glides down to the row of pump
qs: Which sense took in the information first, and which body part took it in?
The owl turned its head and waited before it moved. What was its brain doing in that moment?
key: Hearing, taken in by the ears. The owl's face funnels sound toward them, which is worth noting if the student mentions it. (4-LS1-2)

Processing the information: working out where the sound came from and whether to respond, and choosing the response. Turning the head is itself a response that gathers better information first. (4-LS1

title: The Well Pit
desc: reading rock layers and the fossils in them as evidence of landscape change
dir: Study what the diggers found. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: A new well was dug at the edge of the patch. The diggers wrote down each layer as they went down. Layers pile up newest on top. Depth What the layer is Fossils
qs: Which layer formed first, and how does the chart show it?
Clam shells and shark teeth sit 3 to 6 metres down. What was this spot like when that layer formed?
key: The coarse gravel at 6 to 8 metres, because layers build up from the bottom and everything above it landed later. (4-ESS1-1)
It was under salt water. Clams and sharks live in the sea, so the ocean reached this spot at that time. (4-ESS1-1)

title: The Well Pit
desc: using measurements to compare the rate of erosion under different conditions
dir: Look at the measurements. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: Soil washes out of the furrows every time the field is watered. The crew set up four identical slopes of soil and ran the same amount of water over each, then m
qs: Which pair of slopes shows what steepness does? Say the numbers and what they show.
Which cover worked best on the steep slope. By how much compared with bare soil?
key: Slopes 1 and 2, both bare soil: 30 grams gentle and 94 grams steep. Only the steepness changed, so steeper ground erodes faster. (4-ESS2-1)
Clover roots, 8 grams instead of 94 grams. That is 86 grams less, or about a tenth of the bare soil loss. (4-ESS2-1)

title: The Sea Floor and the Hill
desc: interpreting map data to describe patterns in Earth's features
dir: Study the depth readings. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: A map of the ocean floor gives the depth every 20 kilometres straight out from the beach. Distance from shore Depth 20 km 40 m 40 km 85 m 60 km 120 m 80 km 160
qs: Describe the pattern in the depths from 20 km out to 80 km out.
Something changes between 80 km and 100 km. Describe it using the numbers.
key: The depth increases slowly and evenly, about 40 metres deeper for each 20 kilometres out. (4-ESS2-2)
The depth jumps from 160 metres to 1,900 metres in the same 20 kilometres, far more than any step before it. The gentle slope ends and the floor drops away steeply. (4-ESS2-2)

title: The Sea Floor and the Hill
desc: generating and comparing solutions that reduce the impact of a natural Earth process
dir: Read the two plans. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: Heavy rain sends mud sliding off the bare hill above the pumpkin patch and across the farm road. The farm can do one thing before the rains. Plan What it does C
qs: Name a third way of your own to reduce the mud on the road.
Compare plan A and plan B. Which would you pick. What in the chart backs you up?
key: Any workable idea: lay straw bales or a fence across the slope to catch mud, dig a ditch above the road, move the road, cover the bare hill with straw mulch, build a small basin at the bottom to colle
Either plan, judged on the chart. Plan A works this winter but costs the most and needs a machine. Plan B costs almost nothing and keeps improving but will not hold much the first year. A student who

title: Running the Water Pump
desc: describing where energy and fuels come from and how their use affects the environment
dir: Study the chart. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The irrigation pump can be run four ways. Way to run it Natural resource behind it Runs out? One effect on the environment diesel engine oil pumped from undergr
qs: Pick two rows and trace each one back to the natural resource it starts from.
The farm says the windmill and the solar panels are free energy. Using the chart, say what that claim gets right and what it leaves out.
key: Any two read correctly: diesel from oil underground, mains electricity here from natural gas underground, the windmill from moving air, the panels from sunlight. (4-ESS3-1)

It is right that wind and sunlight cost nothing and do not run out. It leaves out that the tower and panels have to be built, take up space, and have effects of their own, such as noise and a hazard f

title: Wheelbarrow Ramp
desc: using evidence to explain how the speed of an object relates to its energy
dir: Look at the results. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The same loaded wheelbarrow was rolled down a plank three times and allowed to run into a sandbag at the bottom. Try Speed at the bottom Sandbag moved 1 1 metre
qs: What happens to the distance the sandbag moves as the speed goes up?
Which try put the most energy into the sandbag? Give the measurement that is your evidence.
key: It goes up, and by larger steps each time: 3 cm, 13 cm, 29 cm. (4-PS3-1)
Try 3. It moved the sandbag 29 cm, the farthest of the three, so it arrived with the most energy to give away. (4-PS3-1)

title: Wheelbarrow Ramp
desc: asking a question and predicting the energy change in a collision
dir: Answer out loud or in writing. A prediction needs a reason, not the right answer.
text: Two pumpkins of the same size roll along a flat board toward each other. One is rolling fast and one is barely moving. They are about to meet.
qs: Ask one question about this collision that a test could answer.
Predict what happens to each pumpkin's speed after they meet.
key: Any testable question: how far does the slow pumpkin get pushed back, does the thump get louder if the fast one is faster, do they both crack, what happens if the slow one is held still. (4-PS3-3)
The fast pumpkin slows down and the slow one is pushed backward or sideways and speeds up. Both halves make the full prediction. (4-PS3-3)

title: Energy at the Farm Stand
desc: matching observations to energy transferred by sound, light, heat or electric current
dir: For each observation, say how the energy travelled. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: Four things noticed at the farm stand on a cool morning. What was noticed 1 A metal spoon left standing in the pot of soup becomes hot at the handle. 2 The hand
qs: How did the energy travel in observation 1?
How did it travel in observation 2?
key: By heat, from the hot soup along the metal to the handle. (4-PS3-2)
By sound, through the air from the bell all the way to the gate. (4-PS3-2)

title: Energy at the Farm Stand
desc: designing, testing and improving a device that converts energy from one form to another
dir: Draw your device and label it. Then answer out loud or in writing.
text: The stand needs a signal that can be heard at the far end of the patch. There is no power at the stand. Design a device that turns one kind of energy into sound
qs: Draw and label your device. Show the energy going in and the sound coming out.
Name the kind of energy going in and the kind coming out.
key: Any labelled drawing with a path through it: a weight on a string that falls and swings a striker into a pipe, a crank turning a cam that taps a bell, a battery and wire running a buzzer. The labels a
Going in: motion of the falling weight or the crank, or electrical energy from the battery. Coming out: sound, plus some heat. Both forms named. (4-PS3-4)

title: Pond, Colour and Signals
desc: using a wave model to describe amplitude and wavelength and the effect on a floating object
dir: Look at the two drawings of the pond surface. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: A leaf floats on the irrigation pond. The crew drew the surface on a still morning and again when the wind picked up.
qs: Which letter marks the amplitude, and which marks the wavelength?
Compare the two drawings. Say what happened to the amplitude and what happened to the wavelength.
key: A marks the amplitude, the height from the flat line to the crest. B marks the wavelength, the distance from one crest to the next. (4-PS4-1)

Both got bigger. The crests are taller, so the amplitude grew, and the crests are farther apart, so the wavelength grew too. This pair is the one where both measurements change, so look for both. (4-P

title: Pond, Colour and Signals
desc: modelling how light reflects from an object into the eye so the object can be seen
dir: Answer out loud or in writing. You may draw arrows.
text: A lantern hangs in the barn over a pile of pumpkins. When it is switched off and the door is shut, the barn is completely dark.
qs: Draw or tell the whole path of the light when someone sees a pumpkin. Name each place it goes.
With the lantern off, the pumpkins are still there. Why can nobody see them?
key: Light leaves the lantern, travels to the pumpkin, reflects off it, and travels into the eye. All three legs are needed. (4-PS4-2)
There is no light in the barn to reflect off them, so no light reaches anybody's eye. Seeing needs light arriving at the eye. (4-PS4-2)

title: Pond, Colour and Signals
desc: comparing two solutions that use patterns to send information
dir: Read the two systems. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The crew at the far end of the patch needs three messages from the stand: a wagon is ready, come and eat, and bring more crates. System How a message is sent Ne
qs: Say what the pattern is in each system.
Which system suits a crew working 400 metres away at dusk? Use the chart in your reason.
key: In the card system the pattern is the number of dots showing. In the horn system it is the number of blasts and whether a blast is short or long. An agreed pattern standing for a message is what carri
The horn blasts. The chart says the card can only be read within about 50 metres and needs daylight, while the horn carries 600 metres and works at dusk. (4-PS4-3)

title: A Cart for Soft Ground
desc: defining a design problem with criteria for success and constraints
dir: Read the situation, then answer out loud or in writing.
text: The small cart sinks into the soft ground after watering. The crew has to unload it and pull it out. There is one afternoon, a pile of scrap wood, two old bicyc
qs: State the problem in one sentence, in your own words.
Write two criteria that would tell the crew the new cart works.
key: Something like: the cart needs to cross soft wet ground with a load without sinking in. A problem statement, not a solution. (3-5-ETS1-1)
Any two testable criteria: it crosses the wet row without sinking, it still carries at least a full load of pumpkins, one person can pull it, it fits between the rows. (3-5-ETS1-1)

title: A Cart for Soft Ground
desc: generating and comparing solutions against the criteria and constraints
dir: Study the three designs. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: Three designs for the cart. Design What it is Materials Build time 1 swap the narrow wheels for wide boards fixed as runners, like a sled two wide boards and ro
qs: Which design breaks a constraint? Name the constraint it breaks.
Compare designs 1 and 2 against the criteria. Which do you expect to sink less, and why?
key: Design 3. It has to be bought and there is no money, and a week is far longer than one afternoon. (3-5-ETS1-2)

Either, argued from the criteria. Both spread the load over more ground so it presses down less in any one spot. The runners are simplest but hard to pull on dry ground, while wider wheels still roll.

title: A Cart for Soft Ground
desc: planning a fair test with controlled variables and naming a failure point
dir: Answer out loud or in writing.
text: The crew wants to find out whether the runners or the wide wheels sink less. They have one wet row to test on.
qs: Plan the test. What will you measure?
Name two things you must keep the same for both carts so the test is fair.
key: Any measured outcome: how deep the track sinks in centimetres, how far the cart travels before it bogs down, how hard it is to pull measured with a spring scale. A number, not a feeling. (3-5-ETS1-3)
Any two: the same load weight, the same row and the same wetness, the same distance, the same person pulling, the same speed. Only the design under the cart should change. (3-5-ETS1-3)

title: Four California Rivers
desc: describing the physical and human geographic features that define places and regions in California
dir: Study the chart of four rivers. Answer out loud or in writing.
text: Four California rivers, where each one starts, and what people have built along it. River Starts in Flows through Built along it Sacramento mountains in the far
qs: Three of these rivers start in California mountains. Which one does not, and where does it come from?
The Sacramento and the San Joaquin both end up in the Central Valley. Why would a flat valley be where the big farming happens?
key: The Colorado. It starts in the Rocky Mountains, outside California. Partial: naming the Colorado with no account of where it starts is approaching. (HSS-4.1)

The valley is flat, has deep soil, and two large rivers run through it so water can be moved along canals. Flat land is easy to plough, plant and water. Partial: naming the flat land with nothing said

title: Land, Gold and a Constitution
desc: describing the social, political and economic life of California from the first peoples through the mission and rancho periods
dir: Read the chart, then answer out loud or in writing.
text: How land was held and used in three periods of early California. Period How land was held How people lived day to day First peoples, for thousands of years each
qs: The first peoples held land one way. The ranchos held it another. Name one big difference between them. Then use the note. A nation's own land mattered beyond what could be grown on it. Give one reason.
The chart names 21 missions along the coast. Why would they be built in a line near the coast rather than spread across the whole state?
key: The first peoples used and cared for an area as a nation and did not buy or sell it. Ranchos were granted to families as property that one family held, and could be passed on or sold. On the second ha
They were linked by one road, El Camino Real, and supplied by ship, so being near the coast and within reach of the next mission made travel and supply possible. The interior had no road and no port.

title: Land, Gold and a Constitution
desc: explaining the political and economic changes from the Bear Flag Republic through the Gold Rush to statehood
dir: Study the chart, then answer out loud or in writing.
text: How California was governed, and how mining changed, in six years. Year Government Mining 1846 settlers at Sonoma declared the Bear Flag Republic; the war with
qs: What did the delegates at Monterey do in 1849, and why was it needed before statehood?
Mining changed from hand tools to water cannons. Who could afford the later method, and what happened to the rivers?
key: They wrote a state constitution, the plan of government California would use. A territory needed a constitution and a government in place before Congress would admit it as a state. Partial: naming the

Companies with money and equipment, not individual miners. The washed hillsides filled the rivers with mud and gravel, which buried riverbeds and farmland downstream and ruined fishing. Partial: one o

title: Moving Water, Sharing Power
desc: tracing how California became an agricultural and industrial power since the 1850s
dir: Study the chart, then answer out loud or in writing.
text: Four water and power projects that changed California. Project What it did Los Angeles Aqueduct, finished 1913 carried water more than 300 kilometres from the e
qs: What do all four projects have in common?
Why would a city build an aqueduct 300 kilometres long instead of using water nearby?
key: They all move or store water, carrying it from where it falls or collects to where people want to use it. Partial: saying they are all about water with nothing said about moving it from where it falls

The water nearby was not enough for the number of people the city expected. Southern California has little rain, so the city reached to where snow and rain are plentiful. Partial: saying the city need

title: Moving Water, Sharing Power
desc: explaining the structures, functions and powers of local, state and federal government
dir: Study the chart, then answer out loud or in writing.
text: Which level of government holds which power. Power Held by running the public schools in a district local school board, under state law setting the state budget
qs: Why would printing money be a federal power rather than a state one?
Two rows in the chart are decided locally. Name them and say what makes them local matters.
key: Money has to be the same everywhere for trade to work. If each state printed its own, buying and selling across state lines would be a mess. One national currency needs one government in charge of it.

Running the schools in a district and setting speed limits on city streets. Both affect only the people in that place, and the people nearby know the local needs best. Partial: both rows named with no

title: Weigh-Off Warm-Up
desc: a 230-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud at your normal speed. Use your best reading voice.
text: The Weigh-Off All summer, Rohan had watered one pumpkin vine behind the shed at the community garden. He pulled every weed. He even slid a board under the pumpk
key: 230 words, not counting the title. Time 1 minute, mark the last word read, and count errors on your own copy. Let the student finish the story.
Fall grade 5 benchmark: about 121 words correct per minute (50th percentile).

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice. Let the rhythm and the mood show.
text: The Clockmaker In a narrow shop on a narrow street A clockmaker bends at his bench. He listens for each tiny beat And tightens a wheel with a wrench. The pendul
key: 53 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm, pauses at line ends and punctuation, and a voice that matches the mood.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: The Weigh-Off All summer, Rohan had watered one pumpkin vine behind the shed at the community garden. He pulled every weed. He even slid a board under the pumpk
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: The Weigh-Off
desc: quoting the story accurately to tell what it says and to back up inferences
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud. Read me the exact words from the story that prove each answer.
text: The Weigh-Off All summer, Rohan had watered one pumpkin vine behind the shed at the community garden. He pulled every weed. He even slid a board under the pumpk
qs: What did Rohan do to take care of his pumpkin? Read me two sentences from the story that tell you.
How did Rohan feel when he saw the other pumpkins? The story does not say it in one word. Read me the sentence that proves your answer.
key: Reads any two: “All summer, Rohan had watered one pumpkin vine behind the shed at the community garden,” “He pulled every weed,” or “He even slid a board under the pumpkin so it would not rot on the d
Discouraged, embarrassed, or let down. Quotes “Rohan stuffed his hands in his pockets and stared at the hay on the ground.” (RL.5.1, inference)

title: Hay Bale Signs
desc: fixing spoken grammar mistakes (verb tense shifts, perfect tenses, paired conjunctions)
dir: Each sign has one mistake. Say the whole sentence the right way.
qs: Last week we planted the seeds, water them, and waited.
Since June, the vines grown ten feet.
key: Last week we planted the seeds, watered them, and waited. (L.5.1, fixing a shift in verb tense)
Since June, the vines have grown ten feet. (L.5.1, present perfect tense)

title: Last Wagon of the Day
desc: explaining similes, metaphors, and words as they are used in a story
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Last Wagon of the Day By late afternoon, the pumpkin patch was a sea of orange. Vines crawled across the dirt like green ropes, and Camila had to step high to k
qs: “The pumpkin patch was a sea of orange.” What does this tell you about the patch? Is it a simile or a metaphor? How do you know?
“The sunflowers along the fence were tired guards.” How are the sunflowers like tired guards?
key: There were so many pumpkins that orange spread out in every direction, the way water does in a sea. It is a metaphor because it says the patch was a sea and does not use like or as. (RL.5.4, metaphor)
They stand tall in a row along the fence the way guards stand watch, and their heavy heads are bowed as if they are worn out. (RL.5.4, metaphor)

title: Harvest Writer
desc: an opinion writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: At the pumpkin weigh-off, should the top ribbon go to the heaviest pumpkin or to the best-looking pumpkin? Write your opinion. Give at least two reasons. Write
key: Introduces the topic and states an opinion clearly (W.5.1)
Gives reasons in an order that makes sense (W.5.1)

title: Harvest Writer
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Write to teach a reader about pumpkins. Use at least three facts from the fact box. Put them in an order that makes sense. Write 5 to 8 sentences. Fact box: pum
key: Introduces the topic clearly (W.5.2)
Groups related information in an order that makes sense (W.5.2)

title: Harvest Writer
desc: a narrative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: You and a friend walk into the corn maze. After three turns, every path looks the same. Then you notice a clue that might help you find the way out. Write the s
key: Orients the reader: sets up the situation and introduces the narrator or characters (W.5.3)
Events unfold in a clear order, with transition words such as at first, later, after that, finally (W.5.3)

title: Corn Maze Words
desc: spoken grammar items (interjections, prepositions, conjunctions, future perfect, both/and)
dir: Every word has a job. Answer out loud.
qs: “Whew, we finally found the way out of the corn maze!” Which word is the interjection? What does it show?
“The wagon rolled between the rows and through the gate.” Find two prepositions. What do they tell you?
key: Whew. It shows a feeling: relief. (L.5.1, interjection)
between and through. They tell where the wagon went. (L.5.1, prepositions)

title: Giant Pumpkin Notes
desc: notes in the student’s own words from two sources, a spoken summary, and a list of sources
dir: Read the two sources. Write your notes on your paper and hold it up.
text: Question: How do growers get a pumpkin to grow so big? Source 1 Giants of the Garden , a book by Rosa Castillo Giant pumpkins start with seeds saved from other
key: Writes 3 notes that answer the question and uses both sources, such as: seeds from giant pumpkins, keep only the best pumpkin on the vine, all food and water go to one fruit, water every day, shade it
Notes are short and in the student’s own words, not sentences copied from the sources. (W.5.8, paraphrases in notes)

title: Remember and Summarize
desc: recalling relevant information from experience, summarizing or paraphrasing information from a source in notes, and providing a list of sources
dir: Write on your paper. First write about your own experience. Then write a short summary of the text in your own words, and list where it came from.
text: Read this text, then summarize it. Bees do more than make honey. When a bee lands on a flower to drink nectar, grains of pollen stick to its legs. The bee carri
qs: Think about a time you worked with other people. Write three or four sentences about what each person did.
Write a summary of the text in your own words. Do not copy whole sentences.
key: Real experience with the roles of at least two people.
A short summary that states the main idea (bees help plants make seeds and fruit by carrying pollen) in the student’s own words.

title: Pumpkin Report
desc: reporting on a topic out loud with facts in a logical order and clear speech
dir: Plan for 1 minute. Then give your report out loud.
text: Give a short report, about 1 minute long, that teaches how a pumpkin grows. The fact cards are mixed up. Tell the facts in an order that makes sense, and add de
key: Starts by telling what the report is about (SL.5.4, reports on a topic)

Tells the facts in an order that makes sense: seeds are planted, the seed sprouts, yellow flowers open, bees carry pollen, a small green pumpkin grows, it turns orange and the stem hardens (SL.5.4, se

title: Memorize and Recite
desc: memorizing and reciting a poem or a section of a speech or historical document using rate, expression, and gestures appropriate to the selection
dir: Read this and practice it. Then turn away from the screen and say it by heart with a strong voice and gestures.
text: Gettysburg Address Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposit
key: Give the student about two minutes to study the beginning of the Gettysburg Address, then have them face away from the screen. (A different poem or speech the student has memorized is fine.)
Says it from memory with all the words in order (one prompt allowed)

title: Weigh-Off Word Stack
desc: reading unfamiliar multisyllabic words using syllable patterns and word parts
dir: Read each word out loud. Break it into parts if it helps.
key: The words are circumference, horticulture, unpredictable, measurement, cultivation, irresistible. Count each word read correctly.
Watch for: the prefixes circum- and un-, the roots cultiv- and hort-, and the suffixes -ment, -ation, -able and -ible.

title: Read the Sentences
desc: reading unfamiliar multisyllabic words accurately in context using letter-sound correspondences, syllable patterns, and morphology
dir: Read each sentence out loud. Take your time with the long words.
text: The independent journalist interviewed several witnesses about the unusual accident. Her determination impressed the entire editorial department.
key: Listen for these six words read correctly in the sentences: independent, journalist, interviewed, witnesses, determination, editorial. Mark each one.
A word that is self-corrected on a second try counts as correct. Note words the student breaks into syllables or word parts (roots and endings) to decode.

title: How a Weigh-Off Works
desc: summarizing a text read aloud
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. The words are not on your screen. Then summarize out loud.
text: Listen, then tell me the gist in two or three sentences.
key: Read the text out loud once. Read it again only if the student asks.
Sums it up in two or three sentences and gets the main point: a weigh-off is an orderly check and weighing of each pumpkin, and the heaviest one wins. (SL.5.2)

title: Two Giant Sources
desc: quoting accurately from an informational text and using two texts on one topic together
dir: Read both sources. Then answer out loud. Quote the exact words when you are asked to.
text: Source 1 Giants of the Garden , a book by Rosa Castillo Giant pumpkins start with seeds saved from other giant pumpkins. When small pumpkins form on the vine, t
key: Ask: Why does the grower cut off all but one small pumpkin? Quote the exact words that tell you. (Reads: Now the vine sends all of its food and water to a single fruit.) (RI.5.1)

Ask: Source 2 says a giant pumpkin can gain more than 30 pounds in one day. What does Source 1 tell you that helps explain how that is possible? (All of the vine's food and water goes to one fruit ins

title: Pumpkin Bread Shares
desc: fractions as division, with sharing problems that have fraction and mixed number answers
dir: Solve on your paper. Then tell your teacher your answers.
qs: Look at the picture. 4 loaves of pumpkin bread are shared equally by 6 friends. How much bread does each friend get?
Write 11 ÷ 4 as a fraction and as a mixed number.
key: 4/6 of a loaf, which is the same as 2/3 of a loaf. Or: 4 ÷ 6 written as a division counts equally. Partial: 6/4 reverses the share and does not count. (5.NF.B.3)
11/4 and 2 3/4. Partial: one of the two forms given is approaching. (5.NF.B.3)

title: Scarecrow’s Puzzles
desc: using and evaluating expressions with parentheses, brackets, and braces
dir: Solve each one on your paper. Then tell your teacher your answers.
key: 48. Add first: 12 × 4. Partial: 21 comes from multiplying before adding and does not count. (5.OA.A.1)
36. Work from the inside out: 4 + 5 = 9, then 15 − 9 = 6, then 6 × 6. Partial: 6 found by stopping at 15 − 9 is approaching. (5.OA.A.1)

title: Patch Parts
desc: multiplying a whole number by a fraction
dir: Look at the picture. Solve on your paper. Then tell your teacher your answers.
qs: 1/4 of the 12 pumpkins will be sold today. How many pumpkins is that?
key: 3 pumpkins. 12 split into 4 equal groups is 3 in each group. Or: 1/4 × 12 = 12/4 = 3. (5.NF.B.4)

title: Tell a Story for the Product
desc: creating a story context for a product of a fraction and a whole number or of two fractions
dir: Tell your teacher a story that fits the multiplication. Then solve it. Show your work on paper.
qs: Tell a short story that fits (1/4) × 8. Then solve it.
Tell a short story that fits (3/5) × (1/2).
key: A story about 1/4 of 8 things. The answer is 2.
A story such as 3/5 of half a pie. The answer is 3/10.

title: Place Value Patch
desc: using the 10 times and 1/10 pattern between decimal places
dir: Look at the place value chart. Answer out loud. For number 4, write your number on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Look at the chart. The 2 in the tenths place is worth how many times as much as the 2 in the hundredths place?
The 2 in the thousandths place is worth what fraction of the 2 in the hundredths place?
key: 10 times as much. 0.2 is 10 × 0.02. Partial: naming the two values with no comparison is approaching. (5.NBT.A.1)
