title: Letter Sounds
desc: saying the most common sound for all 26 letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What sound does this letter make? Mark each correct sound.
For a, e, i, o and u the short sound is what is expected. The long sound is also correct.

title: Book Parts
desc: print concepts (finding the title, where to start, which way to read, and the first and last word of a line)
dir: Look at the page. Point or answer out loud.
text: The Snow Day I see the snow fall We can play in it
key: Say: This is a page from a book. Point to the title. (the big words in the banner at the top: The Snow Day. If the student cannot point on the screen, they can tell you where it is.)
Ask: Where do I start reading? Point to it. (the first word of the top line, on the left: I)

title: Snowy Sounds
desc: rhyming, clapping syllables, blending sounds, and saying the sounds in spoken words
dir: Listen to your teacher. Answer out loud.
key: Ask: Do sled and bed rhyme? (yes)
Ask: Tell me a word that rhymes with ice. (mice, nice, rice, dice, any rhyme, silly words count)

title: Word Trail
desc: reading high-frequency words and short vowel words
dir: Read each word out loud.
text: we go is me he and topHat log pup
key: Sight words the student should know by heart: we, go, is, me, he, and
Sounds out or reads: hat, log, pup

title: Little Snow Book
desc: reading a short emergent-reader book
dir: Point to each word and read it out loud.
text: I see snow. Snow is cold. I see a sled. My sled is fast. I sit on my sled. I can go fast. We go and go. I like the snow.
key: Count the words the student reads correctly, out of 31, and enter the number in the box. A word the student fixes without help counts. Write down the words that were missed.
Points or tracks left to right and top to bottom

title: Listen to the Fox Lines
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about story lines read aloud to the student
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the lines. Then answer out loud.
text: The fox sat on the ice. The fox got cold. The fox ran in the den. Ice is hard, cold water. A den is a hole. It is warm. An animal sleeps there.
qs: Read the three lines on the screen out loud to the student two times. Point under each word as you read. The student does not read them. Then ask: Where did the fox sit?
What did the fox do when it got cold?
key: On the ice
Ran in the den

title: Snow Day in the Village
desc: answering key detail questions about a story read aloud
dir: Put your eyes on your teacher and listen. Then answer out loud.
text: Listening time. Your teacher will read you a story about a snowy village.
qs: Who is the story about?
What did she pull on?
key: Mira
Her boots and her wool mittens

title: Animals in Winter
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about an informational text read aloud to the student
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the lines. Then answer out loud.
text: A bear naps in a den. A deer digs in the snow. A bird can fly far. Snow is soft. Snow is white. Snow is cold. It sits on the grass. It gets cold too.
qs: Read the three lines on the screen out loud to the student two times. Point under each word as you read. The student does not read them. Then ask: Where can a bear nap?
What can a deer dig in?
key: In a den
The snow

title: Warm Clothes Talk
desc: describing a familiar thing with details
dir: Tell your teacher out loud. Use lots of details.
text: Tell me what you wear when it is cold outside.
key: Describes the clothes, such as a coat, a hood, or thick socks
Adds more detail when you ask: What color is it? How does it feel? When do you wear it?

title: Snowy Word Play
desc: spoken grammar items (plural nouns, question words, complete sentences)
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say your answer out loud.
key: Say: One mitten, two ____. (mittens)
Say: One box, two ____. (boxes)

title: Winter Food Chart
desc: answering questions from a picture chart and from experience
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the chart. What does a bird eat?
Look at the chart. What does a squirrel eat?
key: Seeds. Uses the chart to answer
Nuts. Uses the chart to answer

title: Snow Facts
desc: an informative draw-and-write piece
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: sled pine tree hot cocoa Pick one: a sled, a pine tree, or hot cocoa. Draw it. Write its name. Then write or tell one thing about it.
key: Names what the picture and writing are about (W.K.2)
Gives at least one piece of information about it, such as: A sled goes down a hill (W.K.2)

title: Which Do You Like
desc: an opinion draw-and-write piece
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: hot cocoa warm soup Which do you like more on a cold day: hot cocoa or warm soup? Draw it. Then write or tell which one you like best.
key: Tells the topic: hot cocoa or warm soup (W.K.1)
States an opinion or preference, such as: I like warm soup (W.K.1)

title: My Cold Day
desc: a narrative draw-and-write piece
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Think of a day the weather got cold, windy, or rainy where you live. Draw what you did that day. Then write or tell what happened first and what happened next.
key: Tells about one thing that happened, or a few things that go together (W.K.3)
Tells the events in the order they happened (W.K.3)

title: Where Is It?
desc: using in, on, and under to tell where something is
dir: Look at each picture. Say your answer out loud.
key: Ask: Look at picture 1. Where is the rabbit? (in the box. in or inside counts)
Ask: Look at picture 2. Where is the rabbit? (on the table. on or on top counts)

title: Count Out Loud
desc: counting to 100 by ones and by tens
dir: Count out loud for your teacher.
text: The village is counting snowballs. Count out loud as high as you can. Then count again by tens.
key: Counts by ones. Stop the student at 100 and write the last number they said before any mistake.

title: How Many Trees
desc: counting objects, telling one more, and counting on from a given number
dir: Point to each tree and count out loud.
qs: How many pine trees? Count them.
If one more tree grows here, how many will there be?
key: 7, touching or pointing to each tree once
8, without going back and recounting

title: Count On
desc: counting on from a given number and telling the number that is one more
dir: Listen to your teacher. Count out loud.
text: Count with your teacher.
key: Say: Start at 7 and keep counting up. Stop at 12. (8, 9, 10, 11, 12. The student does not go back to 1.)
Say: Start at 11 and count up to 15. (12 to 15)

title: Two Snow Piles
desc: comparing two groups of objects (more and fewer)
dir: Count the snowballs in each box. Answer out loud.
qs: Which pile has more snowballs?
Which pile has fewer snowballs?
key: Pile A (7)
Pile B (4)

title: Sled Hill Math
desc: addition and subtraction word problems and facts within 10
dir: Listen to your teacher read each one. Use your fingers or draw. Then say the answer.
qs: 4 kids slide down the hill. 2 more kids come to slide. How many kids are sliding now?
7 snowballs sit in a row. 2 of them roll away. How many snowballs are left?
key: 6 kids
5 snowballs

title: Split the Snowballs
desc: breaking 6 and 9 into pairs of numbers
dir: Use your fingers or draw on your paper. Then tell your teacher.
qs: Show one way to make 6.
Show a different way to make 6.
key: First way to make 6: 0 and 6, 1 and 5, 2 and 4, or 3 and 3, shown with fingers, a drawing, or numbers
Second way to make 6 that is different from the first

title: Split It
desc: breaking a number up to 10 into two parts in more than one way and recording each way
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Here are 9.
key: Say: Show me one way to split these 9 into two groups. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 3 + 6 = 9. (a drawing with two groups, or an equation, that makes 9)
Say: Now show me a different way. (a second pair of parts that make 9. The same two numbers in the other order do not count as different.)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: showing a number from 11 to 19 as a ten and some more and recording it
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Look at the full ten frame and the extra ones.
key: Say: Show 17 as a ten and some more. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 17 = 10 + 7. (a drawing of a ten and 7 more, or the equation)
Ask: How many ones are left after the ten? (7)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones
dir: Look at the snowballs. Answer out loud.
qs: How many snowballs in all?
This number is ten and how many more?
key: 6 (16 is ten and 6 more)

title: Taller or Shorter
desc: comparing the heights of two objects
dir: Look at the two trees. Answer out loud.
qs: Which tree is taller?
Which tree is shorter?
key: Tree 1
Tree 2

title: Sort and Count
desc: sorting pictures into groups, counting each group, and comparing the counts
dir: Look at the pictures. Count out loud.
qs: How many pine trees? How many snowflakes? How many snow people?
Which group has the most?
key: 5 pine trees, 3 snowflakes, 2 snow people
Pine trees (5)

title: Heavy or Light
desc: comparing two objects by weight to say which is heavier and which is lighter
dir: Look at the scales. Answer out loud.
text: A B
key: Ask: Look at scale A. Which one is heavier? (the snowman. It is on the side that goes down.)
Ask: Which one is lighter? (the mitten)

title: Where Is It
desc: naming shapes and telling where they are (above, below, beside)
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud.
qs: Name each shape.
Which shape is above the square?
key: Triangle, square, rectangle, circle
Triangle

title: Flat or Solid
desc: telling flat shapes from solid shapes
dir: Answer out loud.
text: An icicle is a long, pointed piece of ice that hangs down from a roof.
qs: Is an icicle flat or solid?
Is a mug of cocoa flat or solid?
key: Solid
Solid

title: What Living Things Need
desc: telling what plants and animals need to stay alive
dir: Look at each row. Answer out loud.
text: A pine tree and a deer both live near the village. Living things need certain things to stay alive.
qs: The pine tree stays green all winter. It still needs two of these. Which two? Sunlight, water, or a sled?
The deer needs two of these. Which two? Food, water, or a mitten?
key: sunlight and water. A sled is not something a tree needs.
food and water. A mitten is not something a deer needs.

title: Weather in the Village
desc: describing a weather pattern from a set of observations
dir: Look at the chart of weather. Answer out loud.
text: Here is a week of weather in the snowy village. Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat
qs: How many snowy days were there?
How many days were sunny?

title: Weather in the Village
desc: telling how a living thing changes its surroundings to get what it needs
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A rabbit wants to reach the grass that is buried under the snow.
qs: The rabbit digs a tunnel through the snow to get to the grass. Did the rabbit change the snow, or did the snow change the rabbit?
Tell me one way you change a room when it gets cold.
key: The rabbit changed the snow. It dug a tunnel that was not there before.
Any sensible answer about changing a space on purpose: shutting the window, closing the door, turning the heat up, putting a blanket on the couch.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Land
desc: matching animals to the places that give them what they need
dir: Match each animal to the place it lives. Answer out loud.
text: Animals live near the village. Each one lives in one place. It gets what it needs. Here are the places. A den dug into the hillside. A birdhouse on a post. A pi
qs: Where does the hedgehog live?
Where does the red bird live?
key: a pile of leaves under a log. Accept under the leaves.
a birdhouse on a post. Accept the birdhouse.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Land
desc: telling what a weather forecast is for
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Every morning the village listens to the weather report before anyone opens a door.
qs: Why do they listen to the weather report? To find out how much snow is coming, or to hear a story?
What could the village do if a lot of snow was coming?
key: to find out how much snow is coming.
Any sensible answer: shovel early, stay home, put sand on the path.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Land
desc: telling one way people can take better care of the land and water
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two children finish their cocoa beside the frozen pond.
qs: One child carries her cup home to wash and use again. The other sets his cup down on the ice and walks away. Which choice takes better care of the pond?
Tell me one more thing people can do to keep a pond or a park clean.
key: carrying the cup home to wash and use again
Any sensible answer: pick up litter, carry your trash home, turn off the tap, do not pour things in the water, reuse a cup or a bag.

title: Pushes and Pulls
desc: telling a push from a pull, and telling what has to happen before a still thing will move
dir: Answer out loud. Let the student say the word push or pull first.
text: A push moves something away from you. A pull brings it toward you.
qs: You give a sled a shove to start it down the hill. Is that a push or a pull?
You open the cabin door by bringing the handle toward you. Is that a push or a pull?
key: a push
a pull

title: Pushes and Pulls
desc: deciding whether a change made a thing move faster or in a new direction
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two sleds were sent down the same hill and the helpers counted the steps each one slid at the bottom. Sled How far it slid a sled with waxed runners 15 steps a
qs: Which sled slid farther?
A sled is sliding straight down the hill. You drag your boot in the snow on one side of it. What happens to the way the sled is going?
key: the sled with waxed runners, 15 steps
It turns toward the boot, or it slows down. Either answer counts. Dragging on one side changed the way the sled was going.

title: Sun and Shade
desc: telling what sunlight does to the ground
dir: Answer out loud. If you can, feel a sunny spot and a shady spot together first.
text: Two patches of snow are here. Both sat in the yard. They sat there all day. One was out in the open. One was in the shade. It sat beside the cabin wall.
qs: By the afternoon one patch is almost gone and the other is still deep. Which one melted, the patch in the open or the patch in the shade?
What made that snow melt?
key: the patch out in the open
the sun. Accept the sun warmed it, or the sun made it warm enough to turn to water.

title: Sun and Shade
desc: designing and drawing something that keeps a spot cooler
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: The snowman stands by the gate. The afternoon sun is on it. It keeps slumping. Draw something over the snowman to make shade, like a roof of boards, a wide umbr
qs: Draw your shade cover over the snowman.
Tell me how your cover keeps the snowman colder.
key: Any cover drawn ABOVE the snowman. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one still counts. A screen drawn beside the snowman is partial: ask where the sun is coming from.
Something like: it blocks the sun, the sun cannot reach the snow, it puts the snowman in a shadow.

title: Solving a Problem
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking about it
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem? Melted snow makes a puddle by the door, or the door is painted blue?
Ask me a question about the puddle that would help you fix it.
key: Melted snow from people's boots makes a puddle by the door.
Any real question: how many people come in, how big is the puddle, is there a mat already, where could the water go. A statement is not a question, so ask once more.

title: Solving a Problem
desc: drawing something whose shape would solve the problem
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw something that would keep the floor by the door dry, like a tray with high sides for boots, a mat with deep bumps, or a bench to sit on while boots come of
qs: Draw the thing you would put by the door.
Tell me what you drew and how its shape keeps the water off the floor.
key: Anything that would catch or hold melted snow: a tray, a pan, a deep mat, a rack, a bench with a tray under it. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one earns credit.
Naming it is what shows intent. Something like: the sides hold the water in, the bumps catch the snow, the tray keeps it off the floor.

title: Solving a Problem
desc: comparing test results from two fixes for the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Rosa tried two fixes and counted the wet spots on the floor after one morning. Fix Wet spots on the floor a tray with high sides 2 a flat cloth mat 8
qs: Which fix kept the floor drier?
What numbers on the chart show that?
key: the tray with high sides
Because there were 2 wet spots with the tray and 8 with the flat mat. The reason has to come from the chart, not from liking trays.

title: Rules and Doing Right
desc: following rules, knowing what happens when they are broken, and naming an honest choice
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What did Nora choose to do? Tell the shed keeper about the broken strap, or put the snowshoes back and say nothing?
One rule at the shed is put things back where you found them. What might happen if nobody put things back?
key: She told the shed keeper about the broken strap.
The next person cannot find what they need, or things get lost. Any real consequence counts.

title: Maps and Places
desc: telling land from water on a map, using position words, and naming places in a neighborhood
dir: Look at the map. Answer out loud.
text: Here is a map of the snowy village. the village hall the woods the bridge
qs: On a map, water is one color and land is another. Which color would show the frozen creek, and which would show the woods?
On the map the woods are above the bridge and the village hall is below it. Which one is below the bridge?
key: Blue would show the creek, because blue means water. Green or brown would show the woods, because that means land.
the village hall

title: Left and Right
desc: telling where things are with left and right, near and far, and in front and behind
dir: Look at each picture. Point or answer out loud.
text: A B C
key: Ask: Look at picture A. Point to the one on the left. (the mitten)
Ask: Point to the one on the right. (the sled)

title: Our Flag and Long Ago
desc: recognizing the flag as a symbol of the country
dir: Answer out loud.
qs: Here is our country's flag. What shapes do you see on it?
Why do you think a town puts a flag up outside the village hall?
key: stars and stripes. Accept stars, lines, or a blue square with stars in it.
Any answer about the country: to show the town belongs to our country, to show we are proud of it, because it is our flag.

title: Our Flag and Long Ago
desc: telling what a holiday honors and how life long ago was different from life today
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Long ago there were no heaters in a house.
qs: Long ago, how did people keep a house warm on a cold night, with a wood fire or with a heater?
How does your home stay warm today?
key: a wood fire. Accept a stove or a fireplace.
Any real answer: a heater, a furnace, a vent in the wall, a wood stove, extra blankets. Naming today's way is the then-and-now half of this standard.

title: Snow Sounds
desc: blending and segmenting sounds in spoken words
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the sounds and words out loud.
key: Blend: /s/ /l/ /e/ /d/ (sled)
Blend: /m/ /e/ /l/ /t/ (melt)

title: Mitten Words
desc: reading words with digraphs, final e, vowel teams, endings, and two syllables
dir: Read each word out loud. The last two are silly words. Just sound them out.
key: Read each word out loud. flane and chud are silly words: listen for the silent e in flane and the ch in chud.
Watch for: digraphs (shed, chip), final e (pine, home), vowel teams (coat, feet), the -ed ending (packed), two syllables (mitten, cabin), and the tricky word (they).

title: Sled Hill Story
desc: a 75-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Look at the three pictures. Then read the story out loud in your best reading voice.
text: a sled a pine tree snow Tess had a new sled. It was red. Snow fell all night. It covered the big hill. In the morning Tess went out. She took her sled up the hi
key: 75 words. Mark errors and self-corrections on the large-print passage in the record sheet.
Point to the three pictures first so the words sled, pine tree, and snow are clear before the student reads.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: a sled a pine tree snow Tess had a new sled. It was red. Snow fell all night. It covered the big hill. In the morning Tess went out. She took her sled up the hi
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the story about? What happened first?” (a summary or answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: Print Detective
desc: the first word, capital letters, and end marks in sentences
dir: Look at the story. Answer out loud.
text: Tess had a new sled. It was red. Snow fell all night. It covered the big hill. In the morning Tess went out. She took her sled up the hill. At the top she saw N
qs: Find the sentence that begins with the word Snow. What do you notice about the first letter of that word? Does every sentence in this story start that way?
One sentence ends with a mark that is not a period. Find it and read that sentence. What is the mark called?
key: Shows the capital S in Snow and says a sentence begins with a capital letter. Yes, every sentence in the story starts with a capital letter (RF.1.1)
Reads the short sentence about the sled coming up and names the mark, exclamation mark or exclamation point (RF.1.1)

title: Story Questions
desc: key detail questions about a story
dir: Use the story above. Answer out loud.
qs: Where was Nico’s sled stuck?
What did Tess do when she saw Nico?
key: Under a pine tree. Just “under a pine tree” is correct; adding that it was at the top of the hill is also correct (RL.1.1)
She pulled the other end of his sled until it came free (RL.1.1)

title: Fix the Frost
desc: spoken grammar items (verb tense, pronouns, joining sentences, questions)
dir: Listen to your teacher read each one. Say your answer out loud.
qs: Today I skate. Yesterday I ____.
Today I shovel. Tomorrow I ____ shovel.
key: skated
will

title: Which Word Fits?
desc: using indefinite pronouns such as everyone, anyone, someone, something, and nothing
dir: Listen to the sentence. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? ___ in the bag is red. (Everything / Someone)
Which word fits? ___ came to the party, so the room was empty. (Nobody / Everybody)
key: Everything. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)
Nobody. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)

title: Whose Is It?
desc: using possessive nouns to show who owns something
dir: Listen. Say the answer. For the last one, you can point to the right one on paper.
qs: Ben has a kite. Whose kite is it?
The teacher has a pen. Whose pen is it?
key: Ben’s kite. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)
the teacher’s pen. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)

title: Commands and Big Feelings
desc: producing imperative (command) and exclamatory sentences in response to prompts
dir: Listen. Say your answer out loud in a full sentence.
qs: Tell me to open the door. Say it as a command.
You see a rainbow! Say one sentence that shows a big feeling.
key: A command such as “Open the door.” or “Please open the door.”
An exclamation such as “What a big rainbow!” or “Look how pretty it is!”

title: Hot Cocoa Chat
desc: describing a person and an event with details
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly.
text: Tell me about a time you played outside with someone. Who was with you? What did you do? How did you feel?
key: Names who was there and gives 1 or more details about them (SL.1.4)
Says what they did and where, with 2 or more details, all about this one time (SL.1.4)

title: Person, Place, Thing, Event
desc: describing a person, a place, a thing, and an event with relevant details, and saying ideas and feelings clearly
dir: Listen to your teacher. Tell about each one. Use lots of details.
text: Tell about a person, a place, a thing, and something that happened.
key: Say: “Tell me about someone you like to play with.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the person, such as who they are, what they look like, or what they do)
Say: “Tell me about a store or a park near your home.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the place, such as what is there or what you do there)

title: Winter Sleep
desc: key detail questions about an informational text
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about the groundhog. Then answer out loud.
text: Some animals sleep all winter. They do not wake up. In the fall a groundhog eats. It eats a lot of food. Then it digs a den. The den is under the ground. It sta
qs: What does a groundhog do in the fall?
Where does a groundhog sleep all winter?
key: It eats a lot of food (RI.1.1)
In a den it digs under the ground (RI.1.1)

title: Frozen Pond
desc: asking and answering questions about a text read aloud
dir: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about a frozen pond. Then answer out loud.
key: What happens to the top of a pond when the air gets very cold? (it turns to ice) (SL.1.2)
Where do the fish go once there is ice on top? (they still swim in the water under the ice) (SL.1.2)

title: Two-Step Directions
desc: giving, restating, and following simple two-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear, say it back, and give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do what your teacher says. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once, without repeating: “Stomp your feet three times, then sit down.” (does both steps, in the right order)
Say once, without repeating: “Put your hand on your head, then hop one time.” (does both steps, in the right order)

title: Opinion Writing
desc: an opinion writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Was Tess a good friend to Nico? Write what you think and tell why. Use the story. Write 2 or 3 sentences. Look back at the story Tess had a new sled. It was red
key: Names the story or the people in it (W.1.1)
States an opinion about Tess (W.1.1)

title: Facts Writing
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write about groundhogs. Tell 2 facts you learned from Winter Sleep. Write 2 or 3 sentences. Look back at Winter Sleep Some animals sleep all winter. They do not
key: Names the topic (W.1.2)
Gives at least 2 facts (W.1.2)

title: Story Writing
desc: a narrative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write about a cold day outside, or a day you helped someone. Tell what happened first, next, and last. First Next Last
key: Tells 2 or more events in order (W.1.3)
Includes some details about what happened (W.1.3)

title: Remember and Tell
desc: recalling information from experiences to answer a question
dir: Think about what happened to you. Tell your teacher your answer out loud. You can draw it, too.
qs: Think about a time you helped someone. Tell me what you did.
Think about getting ready for bed. Tell me two things you do.
key: Tells one real time and what they did.
Gives two real things the student does at bedtime. Any true answer counts. (They may draw first, then tell. Write down what they say if you want a record.)

title: Hop and Count
desc: counting on and back to add and subtract
dir: Answer out loud.
qs: Start at 9. Count on 4. Where do you land? What adding sentence is that?
Start at 15. Count back 3. What taking away sentence is that?

title: Big Numbers
desc: counting, reading, and writing numbers to 120
dir: Count and read out loud. Write your numbers on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Count out loud from 88 to 105.
Read these numbers out loud: 47, 101, 116.
key: Forty-seven, one hundred one, one hundred sixteen (1.NBT.A.1)

title: Stacks of Ten
desc: tens and ones in two-digit numbers
dir: Look at the blocks. Answer out loud.
qs: What number is this? How many tens and ones?
What does the 7 in 72 mean?
key: 53. 5 tens and 3 ones (1.NBT.B.2)
7 tens, or 70 (1.NBT.B.2)

title: Story Problems
desc: addition and subtraction word problems within 20
dir: Listen to each problem. You can draw on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
qs: Ruby rolled 14 snowballs. Some of them broke apart. Now she has 6 left. How many broke apart? Write a number sentence with a box for the number you don’t know.
Leo cleared 7 steps. Maya cleared 13 steps. How many more steps did Maya clear?

title: Smart Adding
desc: using properties of addition as strategies
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
qs: 9 + 5 = 14. So what is 5 + 9?
Add 3 + 8 + 7. Which two numbers would you add first? Why?
key: 14, knows without counting (1.OA.B.3)
18. Adds 3 + 7 to make 10, then 10 + 8 (1.OA.B.3)

title: What Was at the Start?
desc: solving addition and subtraction word problems within 20 where the start is unknown, using a symbol for the unknown number
dir: Listen to the story problem. You can draw. Write a number sentence with a box for the number you do not know. Say your answer.
qs: Some birds sat on a fence. Then 6 more birds came. Now there are 14. How many were on the fence at first? Write a number sentence with a box.
There were some cookies on a plate. Dad ate 3. Now there are 8. How many cookies were on the plate at the start? Write a number sentence with a box.
key: 11 cookies. □ - 3 = 8

title: Add It Up
desc: adding within 100
dir: Solve each one. Say 1 and 2 out loud. Show your work for 3 on your paper and hold it up.
key: 71, adds tens to tens (1.NBT.C.4)

title: Tens Away
desc: subtracting multiples of 10
dir: Solve each one. Tell how you know.
qs: 70 - 40. Show how you know.
key: 30, uses tens (7 tens take away 4 tens) and explains (1.NBT.C.6)

title: Winter Fun Graph
desc: finishing and reading a bar graph with three categories
dir: Tell your teacher how many squares to color for snowshoes. Then answer out loud.
text: 3 kids picked snowshoes. Finish the graph.
qs: How many kids are on the graph in all?
How many more kids picked the sled than the skates?
key: Snowshoes bar filled to 3. Click the squares as the student tells you.
8 + 5 + 3 = 16 kids in all

title: Make a Graph
desc: organizing and representing data with up to three categories, and answering questions about the total and about how many more or less

text: Ten kids told us their ways kids get to school. bus car walk bus bus car bus walk bus car
key: A chart or graph with walk 2, bus 5, car 3. Each item is counted once. Tally marks, pictures, or squares all work. Labels are on each group.
10 (the total of all three groups)

title: Measure It
desc: measuring length with same-size units
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
qs: How many cubes long is the sled?
Is the ski measured the right way? Why or why not?
key: 6 cubes (1.MD.A.2)
No. The cubes are not all the same size, so counting them does not tell how long the ski is. Units must be the same size (1.MD.A.2)

title: Cabin Clocks
desc: telling time to the hour and half hour
dir: Write the times for A and B on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Write the time on Clock A.
Write the time on Clock B.

title: Cut It Fair
desc: halves and fourths of circles and rectangles
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud. Draw the last one on your paper.
qs: What do we call the shaded part of the circle?
Which rectangle shows fourths? How do you know?
key: A fourth, a quarter, or one of four equal parts (1.G.A.3)
Rectangle A. Its four parts are the same size (1.G.A.3)

title: Copy a Fox Paw
desc: naming the job an animal body part does, then designing a tool that copies it to solve a human problem
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer the first out loud. Draw the second on your paper and hold it up.
text: A fox crosses packed snow. It does it all winter without slipping. Each paw has a bottom. It is covered in thick fur. Stiff hairs stick out. They are between th
qs: How do thick fur and stiff hairs on the bottom of a paw help a fox walk on slippery snow?
Draw a boot sole for the villagers that copies the bottom of the fox's paw.
key: The rough hairs catch and grip instead of sliding across the surface, the way a smooth sole does. Any answer about gripping or roughness counts.
Any sole drawn with grip: bumps, ridges, spikes, a rough or hairy surface, deep grooves. A smooth sole is partial, so ask what the bottom of the fox's paw is like.

title: Deer and Fawn
desc: finding a pattern in what a parent animal does and what the young do in answer, and saying how it helps the young
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What does the fawn do every time the deer walks ahead through deep snow?
What does the fawn do when the deer paws the snow away from the grass?
key: It follows, stepping in the tracks she has already made. Every time is what makes it a pattern.
It comes up beside her and eats the grass she uncovered.

title: Deer and Fawn
desc: making observations that young plants and animals are like their parents but not exactly like them
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
text: A young pine and the grown pine beside it. A fawn and the deer that is its parent.
qs: Name one way the young pine is like the grown pine.
Name one way the young pine is not exactly like the grown pine.
key: Both have green needles, both have a straight trunk, both stay green in winter. Any likeness counts.
The young one is much shorter, thinner, and has far fewer branches. Any difference counts.

title: The Sunset Log
desc: finding a pattern in a log of sky observations and using it to predict what comes next
dir: Look at the log. Answer out loud.
text: The village keeper writes down the time the sun goes down behind the ridge. Day Time the sun went down Monday 4:38 Tuesday 4:39 Wednesday 4:41 Thursday 4:42
qs: Is the sun going down a little earlier or a little later each day?
On Friday, do you predict the sun will go down before 4:42 or after it? Say how you know.
key: a little later each day. 4:38, 4:39, 4:41, 4:42
After 4:42. The times are growing by a minute or two each day, and a pattern that repeats lets you predict the next one.

title: The Sunset Log
desc: relating the number of hours of daylight to the time of year from observations made across a year
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Hours of daylight in the village, counted on one day in each of three months. Month Hours of daylight December 9 March 12 June 15
qs: Which of these three months has the fewest hours of daylight?
How many more hours of daylight does June have than December?
key: December, 9 hours
6 more hours. 15 take away 9

title: Bells and Shaking
desc: planning an investigation showing that a shaking material makes sound and that a sound can make a material shake
dir: If you have a small bell, ring it first. Either way, answer out loud.
text: Ring a small bell and then close your hand round it while it is still ringing. Now sprinkle a pinch of salt on a piece of plastic wrap stretched tight over a bo
qs: While the bell is ringing, what is the metal of the bell doing?
You close your hand round the bell. What happens to the sound, and why?
key: Shaking back and forth very fast. Buzzing, humming, vibrating, all count. A student who says the clapper is moving is partly right, so ask what the metal itself does.
The sound stops almost at once, because your hand holds the metal still and stops the shaking. No shaking, no sound.

title: The Dark Cabin
desc: accounting for why an object in darkness can be seen only when light shines on it
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The cabin shutters are closed for the night and the lamp is not lit. No light gets in.
qs: The sled is standing just inside the cabin door. Can you see it with the shutters closed and the lamp out? Say why or why not.
What has to happen before anyone can see the sled?
key: No. No light reaches the sled, and a thing can only be seen when light shines on it and bounces back to your eyes.
Light has to reach it: the lamp lit, a flashlight switched on, or a shutter opened to let light in.

title: The Dark Cabin
desc: using test results to tell what happens when different materials are put in the path of a beam of light
dir: Look at the test results. Answer out loud.
text: In the dark cabin one flashlight beam was pointed at four things and what it did was written down. What was put in the beam What the beam did a clear block of i
qs: Which thing let the most light through?
Which thing let the least light through?
key: the clear block of ice
the closed wooden shutter

title: The Far Cabin
desc: designing a device that uses light or sound to send a message over a distance too far to shout
dir: Draw your answer on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: One cabin stands alone across the valley. Snow lies deep between the two and nobody can shout that far.
qs: Draw a device that tells the far cabin that the path has been shovelled clear. It has to use light or sound.
Name the device you drew and say which one it uses, light or sound.
key: Any device that carries light or sound across the valley: a lamp set in the window, a lamp flashed on and off, a bell, a horn, a whistle, a drum.
Names it and says which one it uses.

title: Fix the Slipping Rope
desc: naming a problem people want to change, asking a question about it, and saying what to observe first
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem the children want to change?
What is one thing you would ask the children before you tried to fix it?
key: The rope slips out of a mittened hand partway up the hill.

Any real question: how thick is the rope, how slippery are the mittens, how heavy is the sled, how steep is the hill, where on the rope does the hand hold. A statement is not a question, so ask once m

title: Fix the Slipping Rope
desc: making a simple drawing of a fix and explaining how the shape of the object makes it work
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up. Then answer out loud.
text: Draw a better end for the sled rope, one a mittened hand will not lose.
qs: Draw your fix on the end of the rope.
Point to the part the hand holds and tell me its shape.
key: Any real fix: a loop to put a wrist through, a crossbar handle, a thick knot, a wooden grip, a strap round the hand.
Names a shape: a round loop, a straight bar across, a fat knot, a hooked grip.

title: Which Handle Worked
desc: comparing the data from tests of two objects built to solve the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two rope handles were tested with the same thick mittens, ten pulls up the same hill each. Handle Times it slipped, out of 10 a wrist loop 1 a fat knot 4
qs: Which handle worked better in the test?
Say how the numbers in the chart tell you that.
key: the wrist loop
The wrist loop slipped only 1 time out of 10 and the fat knot slipped 4 times out of 10. The numbers have to be in the answer.

title: The Village Meeting
desc: telling a right from a responsibility and naming the responsibility that comes with a shared decision
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.

Clearing the snow in front of your own door is a job you take on. Is that a right or a responsibility?
key: a right
a responsibility

title: The Village Map

qs: Find the bridge. Give its exact spot on the grid, the letter and the number.
Where is the pine wood compared to the bridge? Use words like above, below, left of, or right of.
key: C2. Both parts are needed.
Above the bridge and to the left of it. Up and over counts too.

title: The Village Map
desc: naming built features of a familiar place and recognizing that people in one place come from many different places
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Nine families live in this village. They came from six different places. In one house they sing. They sing in a language. None of the others speak it. At the vi
qs: Do the families in a small village all come from the same place? Say how the story shows the answer.
Name three things people built in the place where you live, and say what one of them is for.
key: No. Nine families came from six different places, and one house sings in a language the others do not speak.
Any three built things, with a use for one of them: a school for learning, a store for food, a road for travelling, a park, a bus stop, a library.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: telling what the parts of the national flag stand for and naming a tradition people share
dir: Answer out loud.

qs: How many stripes are on the flag of the United States, and what does each one stand for?
The country has far more than thirteen states now, but the number of stripes has never changed. What do you think the stripes are there to remind people of?
key: Thirteen stripes, one for each of the thirteen states the country started with.
The beginning of the country, the states it started with. Any answer about remembering how it began counts.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: comparing everyday life long ago with life today and telling what changed from what stayed the same
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.

qs: Long ago, where did people get the cold that kept their food?
Where does the cold come from today?
key: Blocks of ice cut out of the frozen pond and packed away in an ice house.
A machine in the kitchen, a refrigerator.

title: Mitten Word Flip
desc: reading words with long and short vowels, vowel teams, a prefix, a suffix, and irregular spellings

key: Read each word in order. shime and floot are made-up words: listen for the silent e long i sound and the oo team sound.
Watch for: long vs short vowel (slide, mitt), vowel teams (steep, glow, spoon), a compound word (snowball), prefix and suffix (refill, coldest), irregular words (could, again).

title: Two-Part Long Vowel Words
desc: decoding regularly spelled two-syllable words with long vowels
dir: Read each word out loud. Each word has two parts.
key: Mark each word read correctly. Each word has two syllables and at least one long vowel sound, such as pa-per, mu-sic, o-pen.
If the student breaks the word into syllables and then says it smoothly, count it correct.

title: Read the Lines
desc: decoding words with long vowels, vowel teams, prefixes, and suffixes in connected text
dir: Read each line out loud.

Line 2: “A student spoke to the ruler.” (every word read correctly)

title: Read by the Fire
desc: an 81-word grade-level fable read aloud

text: Deep snow covered the path to the pine woods. Hare wanted to visit her friend Badger. But the snow came up to her ears. She hopped and hopped and got nowhere. “

Note pace and expression in your notes.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression

text: Deep snow covered the path to the pine woods. Hare wanted to visit her friend Badger. But the snow came up to her ears. She hopped and hopped and got nowhere. “
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the text about? Tell me two things you remember.” (an answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: Snow Story Questions
desc: why and what questions about key details in a fable
dir: Look back at the story. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Hare and Badger Deep snow covered the path to the pine woods. Hare wanted to visit her friend Badger. But the snow came up to her ears. She hopped and hopped an
qs: Why could Hare not get to the pine woods by herself?
What did Badger’s wide snowshoes do to the snow?
key: The snow was so deep that it reached her ears, so hopping got her nowhere. (RL.2.1)
They pressed it down flat, which made a path that was easy to walk on. (RL.2.1)

title: Retell and Lesson
desc: retelling a fable and telling its lesson
dir: Tell the story in your own words. Then answer out loud.
qs: Tell me what happened in the story, from beginning to end.
What lesson does this story teach?
key: Retells in order: Hare set out to see Badger, the deep snow stopped her and she got tired, Badger came by on snowshoes and flattened a path, Hare walked behind him easily, and now the two friends clea
A job gets easier when you let a friend help, or friends should help each other. Accept any lesson the student ties to the story. (RL.2.2)

title: Ask About the Story
desc: asking and answering who, what, where, when, why, and how questions about key details in a story
dir: Listen to the story. Then ask your teacher questions about it, and answer your teacher’s questions.
text: Listen to the story. Then ask me questions.
key: Read the story out loud once: Mia packed a bag for the lake. She put in a towel, a snack, and a book. Her dad drove the car. At the lake, Mia saw a duck. She gave the duck a small piece of bread. The
Say: “Ask me a who, what, or where question about the story.” (asks a real question that the story answers, for example who flew the kite, or where was the girl)

title: Listen Up
desc: recounting and describing key details from a text read aloud
dir: Listen first. Then answer your teacher’s questions out loud.
text: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about a red fox in winter.
key: What does the fox do with its tail at night? (curls up and wraps the tail over its nose like a scarf)
Describe how the fox catches a mouse when snow covers the field. (it listens for the mouse moving under the snow, jumps high, and dives in nose first)

title: Listen and Answer
desc: what, where, when, and why questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about pond ice. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Pond Ice When the air gets very cold, the top of a pond turns to ice. The ice starts out thin and clear. It grows thicker on each cold night. Under the ice the
qs: What happens to the top of a pond when the air gets very cold?
Where do the fish swim while the pond is covered with ice?
key: It turns to ice (RI.2.1)
Slowly, near the bottom, under the ice (RI.2.1)

title: Find It and Write It
desc: gathering information from a text on the page to answer questions
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the Pond Ice text again. Then find your answers. Say the first two out loud. Write the last one on your paper and hold it up.
qs: What do frogs do all winter? Find the part of the text that tells you.
Does the water under the ice freeze too?
key: They rest in the mud and do not eat all winter. The student should point to or read that sentence (W.2.8)
No. Under the ice the water does not freeze (W.2.8)

title: Longer Directions
desc: following three- and four-step oral directions, requesting clarification when something is not understood, and giving multi-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear. Ask a question if you are not sure what to do. Then give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do the steps in order. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once: “Touch your nose, tap the table, and say your first name.” (does all three steps in order)
Say once: “Write the letter B, draw a line under it, draw a circle next to it, and color the circle red.” (does all four steps in order)

title: Ask About the Facts
desc: asking and answering who, what, where, when, why, and how questions about key details in an informational text
dir: Listen to the facts. Then ask your teacher questions about them, and answer your teacher’s questions.
text: Listen to the facts. Then ask me questions.
key: Read the text out loud once: A turtle has a hard shell on its back. The shell keeps the turtle safe. Sea turtles live in the ocean. They come to the beach to lay eggs in the sand. The eggs hatch in ab
Say: “Ask me a who, what, or where question about the facts.” (asks a real question that the text answers)

title: Remember and Write
desc: recalling information from experiences to answer a question in writing
dir: Think about what happened to you. Write one sentence on your paper for each question. Hold it up when you finish.
qs: Think about a game you played. Tell how you played it.
Think about a place you visited. Tell what you saw there.
key: Tells a real game and at least one rule or step. (a complete sentence)
Names a real place and tells at least one thing seen. (a complete sentence)

title: Say It Right
desc: spoken grammar items (irregular plural, irregular past tense, reflexive pronoun, making a sentence longer)
dir: Say each answer out loud.
qs: One goose, two ____.
Today I bring my sled. Yesterday I ____ my sled.
key: geese (L.2.1)
brought (L.2.1)

title: Write It Right
desc: written conventions (capital letters, an apostrophe in a contraction, a comma in a letter greeting, spelling a vowel team word)
dir: Write each answer on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Fix this sentence: the pond froze in january
Write did not as one short word.
key: The pond froze in January. (capital T, capital J, and a period) (L.2.2)
didn’t (with the apostrophe) (L.2.2)

title: Capital Letters
desc: capitalizing holidays, product names, and geographic names

qs: Fix the capital letters: we ate cake on new year’s day.
Fix the capital letters: the grand canyon is in arizona.
key: We ate cake on New Year’s Day.
The Grand Canyon is in Arizona.

title: Use a Dictionary

The guide words are ball and bug. Would the word bike be on this page? Tell why.

Yes. bike comes after ball and before bug.

title: Group Words

Which word fits? A group of singers is called a ___. (choir / swarm)
key: flock. (A collective noun names a group.)
choir. (A collective noun names a group.)

title: Adjective or Adverb?

qs: Which word tells how she writes: neat or neatly? “She writes ___.”
Which word describes the soup: warm or warmly? “The ___ soup tasted good.”
key: neatly
warm

title: Cabin Story Time

Uses descriptive details

key: Plans first: says or draws what will happen at the start, the middle, and the end before telling (give about one minute to plan)
Tells one event with enough detail (who, where, and what happened)

title: Write in the Cabin
desc: an opinion letter about the fable

text: Write a letter to Hare. Should she have asked Badger for help sooner? Tell her why, using the story. Write 3 or 4 sentences. Start with: Dear Hare End with: You

Gives a reason from the story (W.2.1)

title: Write in the Cabin
desc: an informative piece about pond ice
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.

title: Write in the Cabin

key: Tells about one event or a short set of events in order (W.2.3)
Includes details about actions, thoughts, or feelings (W.2.3)

title: Hundreds, Tens, Ones
desc: telling how many hundreds, tens, and ones are in a three-digit number and the value of a digit

What is the 2 worth?
key: 2 hundreds, 7 tens, and 4 ones (2.NBT.A.1)
200, or 2 hundreds (2.NBT.A.1)

title: Write the Number
desc: writing a number in expanded form and writing a number from its name

I say five hundred three. Write it as a number.
key: 503 (2.NBT.A.3). Watch for an answer of 53 or 5003.

title: Count the Snowy Miles

Skip count by 5s from 165 to 200.

title: Count by 2s

Count by 2s from 90. Say the next five numbers.

title: Snowflake Array

dir: Look at the snowflakes. Write your adding sentence on your paper and hold it up.
qs: How many snowflakes in all?
Write an adding sentence for them.
key: 15 snowflakes (2.OA.C.4)

title: Odd or Even

dir: Count the snowballs in each pile. Answer out loud. Write the double on your paper.

Is Pile B odd or even?
key: Pile A has 16: even, 8 + 8 (2.OA.C.3)
Pile B has 11: odd (2.OA.C.3)

title: Sled Count

54 - 29 = 25; answer 25 cups (2.OA.A.1)

The village had 80 bags of sand for the icy paths. The crew used 25 bags on Monday and 36 bags on Tuesday. How many bags are left?

title: Big Snow Numbers

Solve 600 - 245. Show how you did it.

355, regroups across the two zeros, or counts up from 245 (2.NBT.B.7)

title: Why Regroup?
desc: adding and subtracting within 1000 with place value, and explaining why a ten or hundred is composed or decomposed

the pine woods

The stream, the pond, the well, or melted snow. Fresh water is the kind people can drink.

There was only 1 hole with the gravel, 4 with the planks, and 11 with bare dirt. The reason must come from the numbers.

The wool mitten soaks water up. The rubber boot keeps water out.

title: Sorting the Warming Hut Basket

Which two pieces of the chart make you sure?

The room was 14 degrees with the plastic, which is warmer than the 10 degrees with cotton and the 8 degrees with nothing, and you could still see out through it. Both columns have to be used.

Any real thing from 2 long pieces and 5 flat ones: a bench, a shelf, a step, a sign, a small table, a bird feeder, a snow fence. Listen for how the pieces join, because that is the evidence the same s

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: arguing with evidence that some heating and cooling changes can be undone and some cannot

No. It stays black and crumbly. Cold does not bring the bread back.

title: The Firewood That Topples

Ask one question that would help you fix it.

Any real question: how high is the pile, how long are the logs, is the ground flat, which side does it lean to, how much wood has to fit. A statement is not a question, so ask once more.

title: The Firewood That Topples

Tell me how the shape of what you drew holds the logs in.

The shape is the part being checked. Something like: the two end posts stop the ends sliding out, the walls hold the sides in, the floor keeps the bottom logs off the snow, the roof keeps the snow off

The pile never spilled and no logs were too wet, while the other one spilled once and left 9 logs too wet to light. Both columns have to be used, not just the spilling.

Lines 1 and 3, the mail truck this morning and clearing the pond yesterday.

the sled hill, in square A2

the people the state votes for. Accept: the state lawmakers, the legislature, with the governor leading the state.
