Tell a story problem for 3 × 7.
key: 4 × 5 = 20: 4 rows (groups) of 5 snowflakes, 20 in all. 5 × 4 = 20 read as 5 columns of 4 is also correct. Partial: the equation right with no meaning for each number is approaching. (3.OA.A.1)
A story with 3 equal groups of 7, or 7 groups of 3, 21 in all. Partial: a story with the right numbers but no equal groups is approaching. (3.OA.A.1)

title: Divide
desc: explaining division as equal shares or equal groups
dir: Say your story problem out loud.
qs: Tell a story problem for 24 ÷ 4. What does the answer mean in your story?
30 mittens are packed into bags with 5 mittens in each bag. Write the division equation. What does the answer count?
key: A story where 24 things are shared into 4 equal groups, or put into groups of 4. Partial: a story with the right numbers but no equal sharing is approaching. (3.OA.A.2)
Says the 6 is the number in each group, or the number of groups, to match the story. Partial: naming 6 with no match to the story is approaching. (3.OA.A.2)

title: Tell a Story for a Quotient
desc: interpreting a whole-number quotient as the number in each share and as the number of shares
dir: Tell your teacher a story that fits the division. Do it two ways.
qs: Tell a story where 18 ÷ 3 means the number of objects in each share.
Tell a story where 18 ÷ 3 means the number of shares.
key: 18 things shared among 3; each gets 6.
18 things in groups of 3; there are 6 groups.

title: Snowy Rounding
desc: rounding to the nearest 10 and 100
dir: Say each answer out loud.
qs: Round 43 to the nearest 10.
Round 276 to the nearest 10.
key: 40. Partial: 50 rounds up when the ones digit is 3 and does not count. (3.NBT.A.1)
280. Partial: 270 rounds down when the ones digit is 6 and does not count. (3.NBT.A.1)

title: Shovel Crew
desc: two-step word problems with an equation and an estimate
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work and hold it up.
qs: The warming hut has 3 racks of snowshoes with 9 pairs on each rack. Right now 7 pairs are out on the trail. How many pairs are on the racks? Write an equation with a letter for the unknown. Then solve.
The shovel crew cleared 176 feet of path on Monday and 238 feet on Tuesday. Then new snow drifted over 85 feet of it. How many feet are still clear? Estimate first. Then solve.
key: Problem 1 equation with a letter: 3 × 9 − 7 = p, or 3 × 9 = 27 and 27 − 7 = p. Partial: the right answer with no letter for the unknown is approaching. (3.OA.D.8)
Problem 1 answer: 20 pairs. Partial: 27 stops at the racks and leaves the 7 out, so it is approaching. (3.OA.D.8)

title: Skating Rink
desc: finding area by counting tiles and by multiplying
dir: Look at the rink. Answer out loud.
qs: Each small square is 1 square unit. What is the area of this rink? How did you find it?
A cabin rug is 8 feet long and 4 feet wide. What is its area?
key: 21 square units. Partial: 21 with no square unit named is approaching. (3.MD.C.7)
Counts the tiles or rows, or multiplies 7 × 3. Partial: counting the tiles one at a time counts here, and the multiplying is the thing to note. (3.MD.C.7)

title: Area Models and L-Shapes
desc: relating area to multiplication and addition, using the distributive property with area models, and finding areas of rectilinear figures by adding non-overlapping rectangles
dir: Draw on your paper. Show your work. Tell how you know.
qs: Draw a rectangle 5 units by 6 units. Find its area two ways: by counting squares and by multiplying.
Break a 5 by 6 rectangle into 5 × 4 and 5 × 2. Write the equation that shows they match.
key: 30 square units both ways

title: Equal Shares
desc: naming fractions and unit fractions of a whole
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud.
qs: Shape A: What fraction is shaded? What fraction is one part?
Shape B: Is this shape split into thirds? Why or why not?
key: 2/3 is shaded. Partial: 2 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.NF.A.1)
One part is 1/3. Partial: naming 3 parts with no fraction for one part is approaching. (3.NF.A.1)

title: Equal Parts
desc: splitting a shape into equal parts and naming the unit fraction
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up. Then answer out loud.
qs: On your paper, draw a rectangle and split it into 8 equal parts. What fraction of the whole is each part?
Now draw a circle and split it into 3 equal parts. What fraction of the whole circle is each part?
key: Draws 8 parts that are about equal in area. Partial: 8 parts drawn that are plainly not equal in area is approaching. (3.G.A.2)
Each part is 1/8. Partial: 8 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.G.A.2)

title: Number Line
desc: fractions on a number line
dir: Look at the number lines. Answer out loud.
qs: Line 1: What fraction is at the dot?
Line 2: Which letter is at 5/8?
key: 2/3. Partial: 2 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.NF.A.2)

title: Compare Fractions
desc: equivalent fractions and comparing fractions
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know. For the last one, write the fraction on your paper and hold it up.
qs: 1/2 = ?/6. How do you know?
Which is greater: 4/6 or 2/6?
key: 3/6. Explains with a picture, same size, or same point on a number line. Partial: 3/6 right with no explanation is approaching. (3.NF.A.3)
4/6: same size parts, more of them. Partial: naming 4/6 with no reason is approaching. (3.NF.A.3)

title: Compare With Symbols
desc: comparing fractions with the same numerator or denominator, recording the results with the symbols >, =, or <, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know. You can draw a model.
qs: Compare 2/8 and 6/8 with >, = or <.
Compare 1/3 and 1/4 with a symbol. Tell how you know.
key: 1/3 > 1/4. Same numerator, so the smaller denominator means bigger parts.

title: Fractions on a Number Line
desc: representing a fraction on a number line diagram by partitioning 0 to 1 into equal parts and marking off lengths
dir: Draw on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
qs: Draw a number line from 0 to 1. Cut it into 8 equal parts. Mark and label 3/8.
Mark 1/8 on the same line.
key: 8 equal parts. 3/8 is marked 3 parts from 0.
1/8 is the end of the first part.

title: Measure It
desc: measuring lengths to the nearest half and fourth of an inch, including generating measurements of real objects with a ruler
dir: Look at the rulers. Each ruler shows inches. Say each length out loud. For the last one, get a ruler and measure.
text: An icicle is a stick of ice. These two broke off the cabin roof.
qs: How long is icicle A?
How long is icicle B?
key: 1 1/2 inches. The icicle ends on the half-inch mark between 1 and 2. Partial: 1 inch or 2 inches rounds to a whole and is approaching. (3.MD.B.4)
2 3/4 inches. The icicle ends on the last small mark before 3. Partial: 3 inches rounds to a whole and is approaching. (3.MD.B.4)

title: Plot It
desc: showing measurement data on a line plot marked in fourths of an inch
dir: Tell your teacher where each X goes. Your teacher will click for you.
text: Four more icicles were measured. Put all six icicles on the line plot. Icicle C D E F Length in inches 2 1/2 1 3/4 2 1/2 3
qs: Where does the X go for each icicle: A, B, C, D, E, and F?
key: How to mark: click above a number on the line plot to add an X as the student tells you. Use Undo last X to fix a click.

Halves and fourths: one X above 1 1/2 for icicle A, one above 1 3/4 for icicle D, and two stacked above 2 1/2 for icicles C and E. Partial: three of the four Xs placed right is approaching. (3.MD.B.4)

title: Sense, Brain, Act
desc: using a model to show how an animal takes in information, processes it, and responds
dir: Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your model on your paper and hold it up.
text: A snowshoe hare is nibbling bark. She is at the edge of the village. A twig cracks behind her. Her long ears swing back. She holds perfectly still for a moment.
qs: Which body part took in the information about the crack?
She held still for a moment before she ran. What was happening inside her in that moment?
key: Her ears, which swung toward the sound. An ear is a sense organ for sound. (3-LS1-1)
Her brain was processing the information: working out where the sound came from and choosing between holding still and running. (3-LS1-1)

title: Warmer Together
desc: building an argument from data that forming a group helps animals survive
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Chickadees roost in tree holes on winter nights. A ranger measured the air inside the holes just before dawn and weighed the birds in the morning. Birds in the
qs: Which hole was warmer before dawn?
Make an argument that roosting in a group helps a chickadee survive a winter night. Use a number from the table.
key: the hole with six birds, 6 C above zero against 5 C below (3-LS2-1)

The claim yes, with the numbers attached: the group kept the air 11 degrees warmer and each bird lost only 3 percent of its weight against 8 percent alone, so a bird in a group has more left to get th

title: Passed Down and Shaped
desc: reading trait data for parents and offspring, naming the variation, and telling when the surroundings shaped a trait
dir: Look at both tables. Answer out loud.
text: Table 1: a pair of sled dogs with upright ears, and their four pups. Dog Ears Weight at one year, in kg parent 1 upright 26 parent 2 upright 22 pup A upright 21
qs: Every pup has upright ears, like both parents. Where did that trait come from?
The pups do not all weigh the same at one year. What is that difference called. Does it mean one of them is not from this litter?
key: It was inherited from the parents. A trait both parents have and every offspring has is passed down. (3-LS3-1)
Variation. They are all still littermates: inherited traits vary from one offspring to the next, so a group of similar organisms is not identical. (3-LS3-1)

title: Clues Under the Village
desc: reading fossil data to say which organisms lived in a place and what the place was like
dir: Look at the table of rock layers. Answer out loud.
text: Workers digging a well below the village cut through three layers of rock and saved the fossils from each. The top layer is the youngest. Layer Fossils found to
qs: Name two organisms that once lived where this snowy village now stands.
Was the bottom layer a warm wet place or a cold snowy one? Use the fossils as your evidence.
key: Any two the table names: a pine, a deer, a swamp plant, a turtle, a palm, a crocodile-shaped animal. (3-LS4-1)
Warm and wet. Palms and crocodile-shaped animals live in warm wet places, and naming them is the evidence. An answer with no fossil named is not yet using the data. (3-LS4-1)

title: A Useful Difference
desc: explaining how a variation among individuals of one species gives an advantage
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Snowshoe hares have wide back feet that spread their weight on soft snow. A ranger measured feet and followed tracks through deep snow. Hares Back foot width Ho
qs: Which hares sank less into the snow?
Explain why wide back feet are an advantage for a hare in deep snow. Use the table.
key: the wide-footed hares, 3 cm against 11 cm (3-LS4-2)
Wide feet spread the hare’s weight so it stays near the surface and can run instead of struggling, and 17 of 20 chases ended in escape against 6. The explanation has to lean on the data. (3-LS4-2)

title: Who Survives, and What Would Help
desc: arguing from data who can survive in a changed habitat, then judging the merit of a solution
dir: Read the table. Answer out loud.
text: One winter stayed so mild that the village pond froze for only two weeks instead of three months. The ranger recorded what she found. Living thing What happened
qs: Which two living things survived well in that mild winter? Give the evidence for one of them.
Which one could not survive there at all that winter?
key: The cattails, which spread further than in any recorded year, and the bark beetles, many more of which survived. Either one with its evidence counts. (3-LS4-3)
the snow fleas, since the ice they live on barely formed (3-LS4-3)

title: A Season of Weather
desc: reading and making a graphical display of typical weather for one season
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your graph on your paper and hold it up.
text: Snow measured at the village in each month of winter, in centimeters. Month Snowfall in cm first 35 second 60 third 75 fourth 40
qs: Which month of winter is the snowiest here?
About how much snow does a typical winter month bring? Use the table.
key: the third month, 75 cm (3-ESS2-1)
About 50 cm. Anything from 40 to 60 counts if the student used the numbers. The point is a typical value for the season, not one single month. (3-ESS2-1)

title: Two Parts of the World
desc: combining information to describe the climates of two different regions of the world
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Two places at about the same distance from the middle of the globe: one high in the mountains, one on the coast. Region Winter average Summer average Snow in a
qs: Which region has the colder winter. By about how many degrees?
Both places sit about the same distance from the middle of the globe. So what is making their climates different?
key: the mountain village, about 15 degrees colder in winter, 6 below zero against 9 above (3-ESS2-2)
Height above the sea. The mountain village is 1,800 m up and the city is near sea level, and air is colder higher up. Being next to the ocean also steadies the city’s temperature. (3-ESS2-2)

title: Ready for the Snow Load
desc: making a claim about the merit of a design that reduces the impact of a weather hazard
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Heavy wet snow can pile a meter deep on a flat roof. It can crack the beams underneath. Every new house in the village has a steep roof. It is built that way in
qs: Which weather hazard is the steep roof meant to reduce?
Make a claim. Does a steep roof have merit? Give your reason.
key: heavy snow piling up and cracking the roof beams (3-ESS3-1)
Yes, with a reason attached: snow slides off a steep slope instead of piling up, so the weight never builds on the beams. A yes with no reason is not yet a claim. (3-ESS3-1)

title: Balanced or Not
desc: planning an investigation of balanced and unbalanced forces acting on an object
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A loaded sled sits part way up the packed hill. A rope runs from the sled to a post at the top. The sled does not move.
qs: The hill pulls the sled down and the rope holds it up. Are the forces on it balanced or unbalanced? How do you know?
The rope is untied. What happens, and what changed about the forces?
key: Balanced. The rope pulls back exactly as hard as the hill pulls down, and the sled standing still is the evidence. (3-PS2-1)
The sled slides down the hill. Now nothing balances the downhill pull, so the forces are unbalanced. (3-PS2-1)

title: Predict the Next Flag
desc: using a pattern in motion data to predict where an object will be later
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Small flags are planted every 10 m along the flat track below the hill. A rider on a sled is timed as she passes each flag. Flag Seconds since the start 1 2 2 4
qs: Say what pattern you see in the table.
Which flag will she reach at 14 seconds? How do you know?
key: One flag every 2 seconds, the same time for each one. She is moving at a steady speed. (3-PS2-2)
flag 7, because 14 seconds divided into 2-second steps is seven flags. The reason has to be the pattern, not a guess. (3-PS2-2)

title: Ask About the Pull
desc: asking questions about cause and effect in magnetic interactions between objects not touching
dir: Answer out loud. Your two questions have to be questions, not statements.
text: A compass is set on the workbench in the village shed. The steel snow shovel is carried past. The compass needle swings. It settles back once the shovel is away
qs: The shovel never touches the compass, yet the needle swings. What does that tell you about this force?
Give me two questions about it that an experiment could answer.
key: The force acts across a distance, with no contact between the objects. (3-PS2-3)

Any two real investigable questions: how close does the shovel have to be, does a bigger steel tool swing the needle further, does an aluminum shovel do anything, does holding the shovel still keep th

title: A Problem for a Magnet
desc: defining a design problem that magnets can solve, with criteria for success and constraints
dir: Answer out loud. For the third one you may write your two sentences on your paper.
text: The small steel screws from the skate blades drop into the deep snow by the pond bench. Nobody can find them. The next skater has a loose blade.
qs: Tell me the problem in a single sentence that starts: The problem is.
Why is a magnet a sensible idea here? Would the same tool find a dropped plastic lace tip in the same snow?
key: A problem statement about finding small steel screws lost in deep snow. The problem has to be about the lost screws, not about the skates being old. (3-PS2-4)
The screws are steel, and a magnet pulls steel without touching it, so it can lift them out of snow where you cannot see them. A plastic lace tip is not pulled by a magnet, so no. (3-PS2-4)

title: Three Ways to Do It
desc: comparing several possible solutions against stated criteria and constraints
dir: Look at the table and the three rules. Answer out loud.
text: Hands get cold on the hill, so three mitten designs are tried. Each one was worn for an hour. Design Hand temperature after an hour Can you grip a rope? Wet thr
qs: Which design kept the hand warmest?
Which of the three meets every rule? Back it up with the table.
key: the wool mitten inside a coated shell, 31 C (3-5-ETS1-2)
The wool mitten inside a coated shell. It holds 31 C, lets you grip, and stays dry. Another choice counts only if the student argues it against all three rules using the table. (3-5-ETS1-2)

title: Make the Test Fair
desc: judging whether a test is fair, naming controlled variables, and identifying a failure point
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two waxes were tested to see which one makes a sled run faster. Wax Rider weight Start point on the hill wax A 30 kg halfway up wax B 45 kg at the very top
qs: Is this a fair test? Say why.
What two things would you make the same before testing again?
key: No. Two things were different at once, the rider weight and the start point, so a faster run cannot be pinned on the wax. (3-5-ETS1-3)
Any two controlled variables: the same rider, the same start point, the same sled, the same snow and weather, the same push or no push at the start. (3-5-ETS1-3)

title: Maps and Places
desc: using a map grid and a table to describe physical and human features and where they sit
dir: Use the map grid and the table. Answer out loud.
text: A map grid of the village and the valley around it. North is the top row. west middle east north high pass pine forest sled hill middle frozen creek village squ
qs: What lies directly north of the village square?
Which two directions do you walk to get from the village square to the stone bridge?
key: the pine forest (HSS-3.1)
south and west, in either order. The stone bridge sits in the south row and the west column. Partial: one of the two directions is approaching. (HSS-3.1)

title: The First Nations Here
desc: describing how the American Indian nations of California moved with the seasons and stored food long ago, and how a nation is part of the state today
dir: Answer out loud. Use what is on the screen and what you have learned.
text: Nations in California often moved with the seasons. They would spend part of the year in the foothills. They would spend part higher up. They stored dried food
qs: The screen says nations often moved with the seasons. Where did they spend part of the year. Where the rest of it? Name the two things they stored dried food in.
People here moved with the seasons. They stored dried food. What does that tell you? How had they planned for winter?
key: Part of the year in the foothills and part of it higher up. They stored dried food in baskets and in granaries. Partial: the two places right with only one of the two containers named, or the two cont

They planned ahead around the seasons: they knew when and where food could be gathered, and they put some away for the months when little grows. Listen for planning tied to the local land, not a memor

title: A Town Over Time
desc: sequencing local historical events and describing the mark each period left on the land
dir: Look at the timeline. Answer out loud.
text: A timeline for the village of Pine Hollow. Year What happened 1857 a pack trail is cut over the high pass 1884 a logging camp opens, and the slope above the cre
qs: Put these three in order, earliest first: the ski lift, the pack trail, the road.
Which event changed the slope above the creek. What did it do to it?
key: pack trail, road, ski lift. Partial: two of the three in the right order is approaching. (HSS-3.3)
the logging camp in 1884, which cleared the trees off the slope. Partial: naming the logging camp with no account of what it did to the slope is approaching. (HSS-3.3)

title: Rules, Laws and Government
desc: telling rules from laws and naming the basic parts and levels of United States government
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The sled hill has a rule on a board. One sled on the run at a time. The county has a law about snowfall. Every homeowner must clear the walk in front of the hou
qs: What is the difference between the hill’s own rule and the county law?
Who do you think made the county’s snow-clearing law. Who would enforce it?
key: The hill rule is set by whoever runs the hill and applies there. The county law is made by a government, applies to every homeowner in the county, and the government decides what happens when it is br
The county’s elected lawmakers, usually a board of supervisors or a council, made it, and county workers or officers enforce it. Accept any answer that puts lawmaking with elected representatives and

title: Choices and the Local Economy
desc: basic economic reasoning about scarcity, trade-offs, goods and services
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: When the pass closes in a storm, no delivery truck reaches the village until it is plowed. Here is what the village store charged for milk in one winter. Week P
qs: In which week was milk more expensive. What had happened to the number of jugs?
Why would fewer jugs push the price up? Use the idea that there is not enough to go around.
key: week 2, 6 dollars, and the store had only 5 jugs instead of 40. Partial: the week named with no account of the number of jugs is approaching. (HSS-3.5)

With only 5 jugs and many people wanting milk, milk is scarce, and buyers will pay more for the few there are. Accept scarcity explained in the student’s own words. Partial: saying the price goes up w

title: Snowshoe Word Flip
desc: reading long words with prefixes, roots, and suffixes
dir: Read each word out loud. The last two are made-up words. Just sound them out.
key: Read each word. unbrantable and misploration are made-up words: listen for the prefix, the middle, and the suffix (un-brant-a-ble, mis-plor-a-tion).

Watch for: prefixes (over-, dis-, in-, trans-, under-, re-, mis-), roots (therm, meter, photo, graph, geo, port), suffixes (-ed, -ment, -ly, -tion, -ible), and whether the student breaks long words in

title: Read the Sentences
desc: reading multisyllabic words accurately in context using letter-sound correspondences, syllable patterns, and word parts
dir: Read each sentence out loud. Take your time with the long words.
text: The captain announced that the expedition would depart at midnight. A mysterious package arrived at the lighthouse yesterday.
key: Listen for these six words read correctly in the sentences: captain, expedition, midnight, mysterious, package, lighthouse. Mark each one.
A word that is self-corrected on a second try counts as correct. Note words the student breaks into syllables to decode.

title: Read in the Cabin
desc: a 182-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: Marisol had never seen snow until her family moved to Pine Hollow. On her first morning in the village, every roof was white and the air was so still she could
key: 182 words. Time 1 minute and mark errors and self-corrections on your own copy.

Midyear grade 4 benchmark: about 120 words correct per minute (50th percentile, Hasbrouck and Tindal 2017 winter norms). The LP 1 game used the fall figure of 94, so expect the midyear bar to be highe

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice. Let the rhythm and the rhymes show.
text: Ocean Morning The sun climbs up from the edge of the sea, And paints every wave in gold for me. The gulls cry out as they wheel and glide, Riding the wind on th
key: 51 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm, pauses at the end of lines or punctuation, and a voice that fits the mood of the poem.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: Marisol had never seen snow until her family moved to Pine Hollow. On her first morning in the village, every roof was white and the air was so still she could
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: Prove It
desc: questions answered with details and examples from a story
dir: Answer out loud. Look back at the story for details.
text: Marisol had never seen snow until her family moved to Pine Hollow. On her first morning in the village, every roof was white and the air was so still she could
qs: How did Marisol feel when she put one blade on the ice? Give details from the story.
Why did Keisha drag a wooden chair onto the pond? Use a detail from the story.
key: Afraid, or sure she was going to fall. Details: she stopped after one blade touched the ice, she whispered “I can’t,” and she said “I will fall.” (RL.4.1, explicit)
So Marisol would have something to hold on to and push. Detail: Keisha says “Push this. The chair will not let you tip over.” (RL.4.1, inference)

title: Word Meanings
desc: meanings of words and phrases in a story, including one from mythology
dir: Look back at the story. Answer out loud.
qs: The story says “Stopping was her Achilles heel.” What does that mean? Who was Achilles?
What does the story mean when it says the pond “had frozen into a smooth gray mirror”?
key: Stopping was the one thing she was weak at. Achilles was a hero in Greek myths who was strong everywhere except his heel, so an Achilles heel means a person’s one weak spot. (RL.4.4, allusion to mytho
The ice was so flat and shiny that it reflected the light like a mirror. The pond is not really a mirror. (RL.4.4)

title: Use the Text
desc: questions answered with details from informational texts
dir: Read both texts to yourself. Then answer out loud.
text: Text 1: A Blanket of Snow Fresh snow is not solid ice. It is made of tiny crystals with pockets of air trapped between them. All that trapped air is a poor path
qs: What makes snow a poor path for heat? Give a detail from Text 1.
Why would a vole be easier for an owl to catch after the snow melts? Use details from Text 2.
key: The pockets of air trapped between the tiny crystals. Text 1 says fresh snow is not solid ice. (RI.4.1, explicit)
With the snow gone, nothing hides the vole, so the owl could see it instead of having to listen for an animal it cannot see. (RI.4.1, inference)

title: Put It Together
desc: putting together information from two texts on the same topic
dir: Think about both texts. Answer out loud.
qs: Use both texts. Explain why living under the snow instead of on top of it helps a vole get through a cold winter.
One winter is bitterly cold but hardly any snow falls. Use a fact from Text 1 and a fact from Text 2. Give two different reasons that winter would be harder on a vole.
key: Uses Text 2: the vole chews tunnels between the snow and the ground, eats grass stems, roots, and bark there, and the snow hides it from an owl or a fox. (RI.4.9)
Connects to Text 1: trapped air keeps the ground under deep snow near 32 degrees even when the air above is far below freezing, so the tunnels are much warmer than the open air. (RI.4.9)

title: Field Notes
desc: taking notes in their own words, sorting the notes, and listing sources
dir: Look back at the two texts. Write your notes on your paper and hold it up.
text: You are gathering facts for a report about how deep snow changes winter for small animals. Look back at the two texts Text 1: A Blanket of Snow Fresh snow is no
qs: Write two notes about snow and voles, one from each text. Keep them short and use your own words.
Sort your notes. Write a heading above each note: How Snow Works or Animals Under the Snow.
key: Two short notes, one from each text, in the student’s own words and not copied sentences. Examples: trapped air keeps the ground warm; voles tunnel under snow and eat stems. (W.4.8: gathers informatio

Each note sits under the heading that fits. Text 1 facts (crystals, trapped air, ground near 32 degrees) go under How Snow Works. Text 2 facts (tunnels, nibbling stems and bark, hidden from owls) go u

title: Snowflake Listen
desc: paraphrasing a text read aloud
dir: Listen to your teacher read. Then tell it back in your own words.
text: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about how a snowflake is made. Then tell it back in your own words.
key: Tells the main idea: a snowflake grows from a crystal that forms on a speck of dust in a cold cloud. (SL.4.2)

Includes 2 or more key details: the crystal has six sides so arms grow from six corners; it falls through layers of colder or wetter air; each layer changes how the arms grow; no two fall the same pat

title: Say It in Your Own Words
desc: paraphrasing information presented visually and quantitatively
dir: Look at the chart. Tell your teacher what it shows in your own words. Do not read it word for word.

title: Shovel the Grammar

was shoveling (L.4.1, progressive tense)

title: Cursive Writing

text: Write this sentence: Please write neatly so that everyone can read your work.

Writing is legible: another reader can read each word

title: Warming Hut Report
desc: reporting on a topic out loud in an organized way with facts and details

Gives facts that fit the animal and the question (SL.4.4)

title: Write by the Window

Gives reasons supported by facts and details (W.4.1)

title: Write by the Window
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.

key: Introduces the topic clearly (W.4.2)
Develops the topic with facts, details, or examples from the texts, such as trapped air, warmer ground, tunnels, or hiding from owls (W.4.2)

title: Pine Tree Count

qs: In 8,800, how does the 8 in the thousands place compare to the 8 in the hundreds place?
A 3 in the tens place is worth 30. In which place would a 3 be worth 10 times as much. What would it be worth there?
key: It is 10 times as much. 8,000 is 10 times 800. Partial: naming the two values with no comparison is approaching.
The hundreds place, where it would be worth 300. 300 is 10 times 30. Partial: naming the place with no value given is approaching.

title: Snow Gauge Rounding

Round 46,382 to the nearest hundred.
key: 46,000. Partial: 47,000 rounds up when the hundreds digit is 3 and does not count.
46,400. Partial: 46,300 rounds down when the tens digit is 8 and does not count.

title: Times as Many Sleds

45 = 9 × 5. Or: 9 × 5 = 45 written the other way round counts equally.

title: Units

key: 5,000 mL. Or: 5 × 1,000 = 5,000. Partial: 500 uses hundreds instead of thousands and does not count.
240 seconds. Or: 4 × 60 = 240. Partial: 240 with no unit named is approaching.

Perimeter: 34 meters (12 + 12 + 5 + 5). Or: 2 × 12 + 2 × 5 = 34. Partial: 60 given as the perimeter is the area and does not count.

B and D. Partial: one of the two blocks named is approaching.

The run from the very top, at 7 metres each second, because it pushed the bales 49 cm, farther than either other run. (4-PS3-1)

key: B marks the amplitude, the height from the flat line to the crest. A marks the wavelength, the distance from one crest to the next. (4-PS4-1)
The amplitude grew. A larger amplitude in a sound wave is heard as a louder sound. The wavelength stayed the same, so the note is the same pitch. (4-PS4-1)

Snow reflects much more of the light that falls on it, so far more light reaches the eye from snow than from dark ground, which absorbs most of the light instead. (4-PS4-2)

qs: The salt cannot be seen in the puddle. Is it gone? What is the evidence?
Use the idea of particles too small to see to explain where the salt went.
key: It is not gone. The puddle tastes salty, which shows the salt is still there, and the puddle weighs the water plus the salt. (5-PS1-1)
The salt broke into particles far too small to see and spread out among the water particles, so it is mixed all through the puddle rather than sitting in one visible pile. (5-PS1-1)

H is the baking soda, because it dissolves in water while the crushed limestone, J, does not. (5-PS1-3)

key: 480 g. The snow melted into less space but no matter left the sealed jar, so the weight is unchanged. Taking up less room is not the same as weighing less. (5-PS1-2)
520 g. The salt dissolved and spread out among the water particles. Nothing left the jar, so the total weight is the same. (5-PS1-2)

Where did nearly all the new wood and needle material come from?
key: The tree gained 189 kg. The soil lost 11 kg. (5-LS1-1)
From air and water. Carbon dioxide from the air and water taken up by the roots are built into the tree using energy from sunlight. (5-LS1-1)

qs: It is January and there is no grass growing. Where did the energy in today's milk come from?
Explain why cutting and storing hay is really a way of storing something else.
key: From last summer's sunlight. The hay captured and stored it, the cow ate the hay, and some of that energy is in the milk. (5-PS3-1)
It is a way of storing energy that came from sunlight. The hay holds the energy the grass captured in summer so it can be used months later. (5-PS3-1)

title: Under the Snow

Decomposers broke it down once the soil warmed, releasing gases into the air and minerals into the soil. (5-LS2-1)

title: Icicles and Sleds

No. The pull is still straight down. The hillside is in the way and pushes back, so the only movement left is along the slope. Over a cliff edge it would fall straight down. (5-PS2-1)

Because landlords were paid by the room and the demand was desperate, so filling every square foot was profitable and no law said otherwise. What changed it was regulation: housing laws requiring wind

title: Find the Letter
desc: matching a spoken letter name to its printed form (12 cards, 6 uppercase and 6 lowercase)
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
key: Say: Here are twelve letter cards from the supply crate. I will say a letter name. Point to the card with that letter.
Say: Point to the letter q. (top row, fourth card)

title: Uppercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 uppercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts.

title: Lowercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 lowercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
b, d, p and q are the ones to watch. Write down which way a mix-up went, such as said d for b.

title: First Sound Check
desc: saying the first sound of a pictured word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the first sound.
key: Model first: Dog. The first sound in dog is /d/. Now you try.
Point to the tent. Say: Tent. A tent is a cloth house you sleep in on a trip. What is the first sound in tent? (/t/)

title: Rhyme Radio
desc: making a rhyme for a given word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say a word that rhymes.
key: Model first: Ice, mice, rice. They rhyme. They sound the same at the end.
Point to the whale. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with whale. (tail, pail, sail, nail, mail, zail)

title: Slow Radio Voice
desc: blending syllables and sounds into a word with picture support
dir: Listen to the slow radio voice. Say the whole word.
key: Say: The radio voice is very slow today. Put the parts together and tell me the word. The pictures can help you, but they are mixed up.
Say with a pause between the parts: ice ... berg. (iceberg, the big chunk of floating ice in the second picture)

title: Pip and the Flags
desc: questions about the character, the order of three events, and what happens next in a story read aloud
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Pip and the Flags
key: If picture supports are on, point to the picture before you read. Say: A science team is camping on the snow. They push little flags into the snow so they can find their way. The tall pole with cups o
Read the story out loud. Stop at the bold note, right after Pip comes to the stack of crates.

title: Crate Labels
desc: matching a spoken letter name to its printed lowercase form
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
key: Say: Every crate has a small letter painted on it. I will say a letter name. Point to the crate with that letter.
Say: Point to the letter d. (second crate from the left)

title: Dot Jumps In
desc: questions about the character, the problem, the order of events, and what happens next in a story read aloud
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Dot Jumps In
key: If picture supports are on, point to the picture before you read. Say: This flat piece of ice floating on the sea is called an ice floe. Penguins rest on it and jump off it to swim. The small grey pen
Read the story out loud. Stop at the bold note, right after Dot looks down at the water.

title: Seal Holes
desc: making an inference, making a connection, and asking a question about an informational text read aloud
dir: Listen to your teacher read about seals. Then answer out loud.
key: Read the facts out loud. If picture supports are on, point to the pictures first and follow the arrows. Say: The seal swims under the ice near some fish. Next it scrapes the ice with its front teeth.

Ask: Why is that hole so important to the seal? What would happen if the hole froze shut? (The seal breathes air, so it has to come up to the top for a breath. With the hole frozen shut it could not g

title: Expedition Notes
desc: writing the letter for a beginning sound (w, b, c, g)
dir: Listen for the sound. Write the letter on your paper and hold it up.
key: Point to the wave. Say: Wave starts with /w/. Write the letter that makes the /w/ sound. Hold it up. (w or W)
Point to the boot. Say: Boot starts with /b/. Write the letter for /b/. (b or B)

title: Radio Check
desc: asking questions to get missing information and to confirm understanding
dir: Your teacher is calling on the radio. Ask questions until you know what to do.
key: Say: You are at base camp. I will call you on the radio, but part of my message will be missing. Ask me questions until you know what to do.

Message 1. Say in a radio voice: Base camp, please bring the bag out to the tent. Look for: asks a question about which bag or which tent (there are three tents and two bags). If the child does not as

title: Mystery Bag
desc: asking questions and follow-up questions to find out information
dir: Something is in the bag on the sled. Ask your teacher questions to find out what it is.
key: Your secret: a camera is in the bag. Do not tell.
Say: One thing is packed in this bag. Ask me questions to find out what it is. You can ask things like: Is it alive? What do you do with it?

title: Name the Gear
desc: naming objects, actions, and describing words from pictures
dir: Look at each picture. Answer out loud.
key: Picture 1. Say: What is this? (a backpack, a pack, or a bag)
Picture 2. Say: This tool has a needle that always points one way, so you can tell which way to walk. What is it called? (a compass. This is a harder word. Accept compass only.)

title: Dogs or Skis
desc: sharing an opinion with a reason, a description, and an explanation
dir: Pick one. Tell your teacher why.
key: Say: On the expedition you can ride on a sled pulled by a team of dogs, or you can travel on skis, long flat boards strapped to your boots that slide over the snow. Which way would you rather go? Tell
Look for: tells an opinion (picks one).

title: Label Your Sled
desc: writing letters to label a drawing
dir: Draw one thing you would pack on your sled. Write letters to tell what it is. Hold it up.
key: Say: Here are three things the team packed. Draw one thing you would pack on your own sled. Then write a word or some letters to tell what it is. Hold it up and tell me what you wrote.
Look for: writing that is separate from the drawing (letters or marks that look like letters, not only a picture).

title: Pack the Sleds
desc: counting 10 or more real objects one by one where the teacher can see, then counting groups of 10, 13, 11, and 15 objects one by one on the screen
dir: First count some small things from near you. Then count the pictures on the screen.
key: Start with real things, before the screen. Say: Go and get ten small things you can hold, like spoons, blocks, socks or crayons, and set them on the table where I can see them. Then say: Move each one

Say: Push them back into a pile, add a few more, and count the whole lot again the same way. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down

title: Sled Loads
desc: comparing two groups by counting (more, same, fewer)
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
key: Box 1. Say: Are there more penguins or more fish? How do you know? (More penguins. 8 penguins and 5 fish.)
Box 2. Say: Are there more tents, more flags, or the same number of each? (The same. 6 tents and 6 flags.)

title: Ice Camp Shapes
desc: naming, describing, and drawing circles, squares, rectangles, and triangles
dir: Look at the camp. Answer out loud. Then draw a shape on your paper.
key: Say: Here is the camp drawn with shapes. What shape is the purple tent? (triangle)
Say: Look at the front of the blue crate. What shape is it? (square)

title: Trail Patterns
desc: extending repeating patterns and naming the part that repeats
dir: Look at each row. Say what comes next.
key: Row 1. Say: Flag, tent, flag, tent, flag, tent, flag. What comes next? (a tent)
Row 2. Say: Look at this row. What comes next? (a fish. The pattern is fish, fish, seal.)

title: Which Pile Has More?
desc: comparing two mixed-up groups by counting (more, fewer, same)
dir: These are all mixed up. Count them and answer out loud.
key: Say: These are not in rows, so you have to count carefully. Box 1 and box 2: are there more fish or more ice cubes? (More fish. 10 fish and 8 ice cubes.)
Say: So which box has fewer, box 1 or box 2? (Box 2, the ice cubes. 8 is fewer than 10.)

title: Animal Count
desc: reading, copying, and adding to a tally chart with three groups
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud. Then make marks on your paper.
key: Say: The team keeps a chart of the animals they see. Each straight mark means one animal. How many whales did they see? (3. The whale row has 3 marks.)
Say: Which animal did they see the most? (Penguins. 8 marks, more than the 5 seals and the 3 whales.)

title: Base Camp Map
desc: position words (between, on top of, next to, below, near and far)
dir: Look at the camp. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Here is the base camp. What is between the tent and the dog? (the red flag on its pole)
Say: What is on top of the sled? (the wooden crate)

title: Number Cards
desc: naming the numerals 1 to 10
dir: Say the name of each number.
key: Say: The team writes a number on every box at camp. What number is this? Click Next after each one.
Correct means the child says the number name. Write down the ones missed. Watch for 6 and 9 mixed up.

title: Line Up the Poles
desc: ordering five objects by height
dir: Look at the flag poles. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Five trail flags stand along the trail. Which pole is the tallest? (B)
Say: Which pole is the shortest? (A)

title: Sort the Supplies
desc: sorting one group by what the things are and another group by size, and saying the rule
dir: Look at the tray and the boots. Answer out loud.
key: Point to the tray. Say: Put these supplies into groups. How many groups did you make? Tell me your rule. (3 groups by what they are: 4 fish, 3 ice cubes, 2 trail flags. Any rule the child can say and
Say: How many are in each of your groups? (4 fish, 3 ice cubes, 2 flags)

title: Uppercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 uppercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts.

title: Lowercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 lowercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
b, d, p and q are the ones to watch. Write down which way a mix-up went, such as said d for b.

title: Letter Sounds
desc: saying the most common sound for all 26 letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What sound does this letter make? Mark each correct sound.
For a, e, i, o and u the short sound is what is expected. The long sound is also correct.

title: Two Lines
desc: print concepts (where to start, where to go at the end of a line, counting words and letters)
dir: Look at the two lines. Answer out loud.
text: We camp on the ice. The sled is red. The four pictures are a tent, a snowflake, a flag, and a sled.
key: Say: I want to read this. Ask: Where do I start, at the tent, the snowflake, the flag, or the sled? (the tent. Reading starts at the top on the left.)
Say: I read the top line and I stop at the snowflake. Ask: Where do I go next? (to the flag, the start of the next line)

title: Book Parts
desc: print concepts (finding the title, where to start, which way to read, and the first and last word of a line)
dir: Look at the page. Point or answer out loud.
text: The Ice Camp A seal is on the ice It can nap there
key: Say: This is a page from a book. Point to the title. (the big words in the banner at the top: The Ice Camp. If the student cannot point on the screen, they can tell you where it is.)
Ask: Where do I start reading? Point to it. (the first word of the top line, on the left: A)

title: Rhyme Floes
desc: hearing rhymes, making a rhyme, and clapping syllables
dir: Listen to your teacher. Answer out loud.
text: An iceberg is a huge piece of ice that floats in the sea.
key: Ask: Do snow and go rhyme? (yes)
Ask: Do whale and seal rhyme? (no)

title: Put It Together
desc: blending spoken sounds and saying the first, last, and all sounds in a word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Put these sounds together: /s/ /u/ /n/. (sun)
Say: Put these sounds together: /f/ /l/ /a/ /g/. (flag)

title: Pip on the Ice
desc: asking and answering questions about key details in a story read aloud to the student
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the lines. Then answer out loud.
text: Pip is a seal. Pip sits on the ice. The sun is hot. Pip dips in the sea. A seal can swim. It swims in the sea. The sea is cold. It can nap on the ice.
key: Read the four lines on the screen out loud to the student two times. Point under each word as you read. The student does not read them. Ask: Who is the story about? (Pip, a seal)
Ask: Where does Pip dip? (in the sea)

title: Sound Flags
desc: saying the sounds of letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: The student says the most common sound for each letter: r /r/, A as in apple, s /s/, k /k/, i as in it, N /n/, b /b/, o as in octopus, w /w/, g /g/. The letter name is not needed here.
The long sound for A or i is also fine. Write down any sounds that were missed.

title: Sled Words
desc: reading high-frequency words and short vowel words
dir: Read each word out loud.
text: the my see can it map bed fin tub
key: High-frequency words the student should know by sight: the, my, see, can, it
Sounds out or reads: map, bed, fin, tub

title: Radio Call
desc: answering questions about key details in a text read aloud and asking for help
dir: Put your eyes on your teacher and listen. Then answer out loud.
text: Listening time. Your teacher will read you a report from the ice camp.
key: Ask: Where did the team land? (on a flat field of snow)
Ask: How many tents did they put up? (four)

title: Little Camp Book
desc: reading a short emergent-reader book with purpose and understanding
dir: Point to each word and read it out loud.
text: I see the camp. I see a tent. It is red. I see a sled. A dog can pull. The dog can run. I sit on the sled. I like the camp. A camp has tents. People sleep there
key: Count the words the student reads correctly, out of 32, and enter the number in the box. A word the student fixes without help counts. Write down the words that were missed.
Points or tracks under each word, left to right and top to bottom

title: Whale Watch
desc: asking and answering questions about key details in an informational text about whales
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the lines. Then answer out loud.
text: A whale is in the sea. A whale is big. A whale is not a fish. It comes up for air. It goes up to the top. Whales can sing.
key: Read the six lines on the screen out loud to the student two times. Point under each word as you read. The student does not read them. Ask: Where does a whale live? (in the sea. Line 1.)
Ask: What does a whale come up for? (air. Line 4. The read-aloud also says a whale breathes air, so ask this before you read the longer text aloud.)

title: Camp Talk
desc: spoken grammar items (plural nouns, question words, position words in complete sentences)
dir: Look at the picture. Listen to your teacher. Say your answer out loud.
key: Say: One tent, two ____. (tents)
Say: One dish, two ____. (dishes)

title: Draw and Write
desc: an informative draw-and-write piece about a piece of camp gear
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: tent a dog and a sled warm boots Pick one: a tent, a sled, or warm boots. Draw it. Write its name. Then write or tell one thing about it. Dogs can pull a sled.
key: Names what the drawing and writing are about: a tent, a sled, or warm boots. The student may say it, label the picture, or write a letter or word for it.
Gives at least one piece of true information about it, such as: You sleep in a tent. Dogs pull the sled. Boots keep your feet warm.

title: Field Notes
desc: answering questions from a picture chart and from experience
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the chart. What do we use to carry the food crates?
Look at the chart. What do we use to go fast on the snow?
key: The sled. Uses the chart to answer.
The skis. Uses the chart to answer.

title: Tell Me More
desc: describing a familiar place with details
dir: Tell your teacher out loud. Use lots of details.
text: Tell me about a place where you like to play.
key: Names the place and tells something about it
Adds a detail when you ask: What do you see there?

title: Best at the Ice Camp
desc: an opinion draw-and-write piece naming the topic and stating a preference
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: a seal a whale a sled dog Which one is the best to watch at the ice camp: a seal, a whale, or a sled dog? Draw your pick. Write its name. Then tell me why you p
key: Tells the reader what the writing is about, such as: This is about the best animal to watch. The student may say it, label the drawing, or write a letter or word for it.
States an opinion by picking one and saying so, such as: I like the whale best.

title: One Thing I Did
desc: a narrative draw-and-write piece about one event, told in order, with a reaction
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: boots snow outside Think of one thing you did outside. Draw it. Write about it. Then tell me what happened.
key: Tells about one thing that really happened, not a list of many things.
Tells what happened in order. Listen for order words such as first, then, next, after that. If none come, ask once: What happened first? What happened next?

title: Up the Trail
desc: counting out loud by ones
dir: Count out loud. Start at 1. Go as high as you can.
text: The team put flags in the snow to mark the trail to the weather station. Count out loud as you walk up the trail.
key: Say: Start at 1 and count as high as you can. Check: counts 1 to 20 in order with no skips.
Keeps going from 20 to 40 and gets across each new ten (29 to 30, 39 to 40).

title: Ten Crates a Sled
desc: counting by tens
dir: Count by tens out loud.
text: Each sled carries 10 crates. Count by tens to 100.
key: Say: Count the crates by tens as the sleds go by. Check: says 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 with no help.
Keeps going: 60, 70, 80, 90, 100. Write the last number said in order.

title: More or Fewer
desc: comparing two groups of objects (more, fewer, the same)
dir: Look at the two groups. Answer out loud.
key: Card 1. Ask: Are there more crates or more fish? (fish. 8 is more than 6.)
Card 2. Ask: Which group has fewer, the flags or the tents? (the tents. 5 is fewer than 7.)

title: One for Each
desc: matching and counting to tell which group has more, fewer, or the same
dir: Look at the boxes. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the top box. Is there a fish for every seal?
In the top box, which has more: the seals or the fish?
key: Yes. There are 5 seals and 7 fish, so 2 fish are left over.
The fish (7 is more than 5)

title: Long and Tall
desc: comparing two objects to tell which has more or less of an attribute and describing the difference
dir: Look at the two poles and the two sleds. Answer out loud.
text: Both sleds start at the same dotted line, so you can see which one is longer.
key: Ask: Which flag pole is taller? (Pole 2)
Ask: Which flag pole is shorter? (Pole 1)

title: Heavy or Light
desc: comparing two objects by weight to say which is heavier and which is lighter
dir: Look at the scales. Answer out loud.
text: A B
key: Ask: Look at scale A. Which one is heavier? (the polarBear. It is on the side that goes down.)
Ask: Which one is lighter? (the fish)

title: Camp Shapes
desc: naming shapes of objects and telling where they are (above, below, beside)
dir: Look at the camp made of shapes. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Each part of the camp is a shape. Ask: Name the shape of the sun, the tent, the sled, and the crate. (circle, triangle, rectangle, square)
Ask: Which shape is above the tent? (the circle, the sun)

title: How Many Fish
desc: counting a group and telling how many, and knowing the count does not change when the things move or the counting starts somewhere else
dir: Look at the two boxes. Count out loud and answer.
text: The second box holds the same fish as the first box. They are just moved around.
key: Point to the first box. Say: Count these fish out loud. How many fish are there? (8. The last number said is the answer. If the student counts correctly and then cannot say how many, write that down:
Point to the second box. Say: These are the same 8 fish, moved around. How many fish are in this box? (8, without counting them again. Counting again and getting 8 is a partial answer; note it.)

title: Count On
desc: counting on from a given number and telling the number that is one more
dir: Listen to your teacher. Count out loud.
text: Count with your teacher.
key: Say: Start at 3 and keep counting up. Stop at 8. (4, 5, 6, 7, 8. The student does not go back to 1.)
Say: Start at 12 and count up to 16. (13 to 16)

title: Fish and Flags
desc: solving addition and subtraction word problems within 10
dir: Listen to your teacher. Use the ten frames if you want. Answer out loud.
text: Pip fish flags You can count on your fingers, draw, or open the ten frames.
key: Say: Pip caught 4 fish in the morning and 3 more fish after lunch. How many fish did Pip catch in all? (7)
Say: There were 9 fish on the ice. A bird carried 2 of them away. How many fish were left? (7)

title: Two Sleds
desc: breaking 7 into two parts in more than one way and saying the number sentence
dir: Look at the seven crates and the two sleds. Answer out loud.
key: Say: All 7 crates go on these two sleds. Tell me one way to split them. How many on Sled A and how many on Sled B? (Any pair that makes 7: 6 and 1, 5 and 2, 4 and 3, 3 and 4, 2 and 5, 1 and 6, or 7 an
Say: Now tell me a different way. (Any other pair that makes 7. It must be a new pair, not the same one turned around unless the student says so.)

title: Split It
desc: breaking a number up to 10 into two parts in more than one way and recording each way
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Here are 7.
key: Say: Show me one way to split these 7 into two groups. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 3 + 4 = 7. (a drawing with two groups, or an equation, that makes 7)
Say: Now show me a different way. (a second pair of parts that make 7. The same two numbers in the other order do not count as different.)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: showing a number from 11 to 19 as a ten and some more and recording it
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Look at the full ten frame and the extra ones.
key: Say: Show 12 as a ten and some more. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 12 = 10 + 2. (a drawing of a ten and 2 more, or the equation)
Ask: How many ones are left after the ten? (2)

title: Teen Crates
desc: seeing a teen number as one ten and some more ones
dir: Look at the sled and the crates on the snow. Answer out loud.
key: Say: A full sled carries 10 crates. This sled is full, and there are more crates on the snow beside it. How many crates are there in all? (14. 10 on the sled and 4 on the snow.)
Say: So 14 is one full sled of ten and how many more? (4 more)

title: Sort the Finds
desc: sorting things into groups, counting each group, and putting the groups in order by how many
dir: Look at the box. Answer out loud.
key: Say: The team put everything it found into one box. Sort these into groups by what they are. How many groups do you get? (3 groups: fish, snowflakes and flags.)
Say: How many are in each group? (6 fish, 4 snowflakes, 3 flags)

title: Flat or Solid
desc: telling a flat two-dimensional shape from a solid three-dimensional one
dir: Look at the four boxes. Answer out loud.
key: Say first: A flat shape is a drawing on a page. It lies down flat. A solid shape is thick, and you could hold it in your hands. Then ask: Which boxes have a flat shape? (1 and 3)
Ask: Which boxes have a solid thing? (2 and 4, the crate and the ball)

title: What Living Things Need at Camp
desc: telling what an animal and a plant need to stay alive
dir: Look at both pictures. Answer out loud.
text: A penguin lives out on the shore. A bean sprout grows in a cup on the tent windowsill.
qs: A penguin stays alive by getting two of these. Which two? Fish to eat, water to drink, or a sled?
The bean sprout in the cup stays alive by getting two of these. Which two? Light, water, or a flag?
key: fish to eat and water to drink. A sled is not something a living thing needs.
light and water. A flag is not something a plant needs.

title: Weather at the Ice Camp
desc: describing a weather pattern from a week of recorded observations
dir: Look at the week on the board. Count out loud.
text: The team writes the weather on the board every morning. Here is one week. Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat
qs: Count the days it snowed. How many?
Count the sunny days. How many?

title: Weather at the Ice Camp
desc: telling how a living thing changes its surroundings to get what it needs
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A seal has to come up for air, but the sea is roofed over with thick ice.
qs: The seal scrapes at one spot with its claws and keeps a round hole open in the ice so it can breathe. Did the seal change the ice, or did the ice change the seal?
Tell me one way you change the snow or the dirt outside when you want to play.
key: The seal changed the ice. It made a hole that was not there before and it keeps the hole open.
Any sensible answer about changing a space on purpose: digging a hole, piling snow into a wall, stamping a path, clearing sticks off a spot, making a track to slide on.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Ice
desc: matching animals to the places that give them what they need
dir: Match each animal to the place it lives. Answer out loud.
text: Look at these animals. Each one lives in one place. It gets what it needs. Here are the places. A nest of pebbles. It is on the shore. The open sea. A den dug i
qs: Where does the penguin keep its eggs?
Where does the narwhal live?
key: a nest of pebbles on the shore
the open sea. Accept the water or under the ice.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Ice
desc: telling what a weather forecast is for and how people use one to get ready
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Before dark the team listens to the forecast for tonight.
qs: The forecast says strong wind and heavy snow tonight. Should the team tie the tents down now, or wait until the wind starts shaking them?
What is a forecast for? To tell what the weather will probably do next, or to tell what the weather did last year?
key: tie the tents down now, before the wind comes. Getting ready early is the whole point of a forecast.
to tell what the weather will probably do next

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Ice
desc: telling one way people can take better care of the land and water
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The team is packing up to leave the ice.
qs: One person carries the empty cans back to the ship. One person leaves the cans sitting on the snow. Which choice takes better care of the ice and the water?
The team used a whole barrel of water washing dishes. Tell me one way they could use less next time.
key: carrying the empty cans back to the ship
Any sensible answer: wash in a small bowl instead of under a running tap, scrape the plates first, use the same rinse water twice, turn the tap off while scrubbing.

title: Pushes and Pulls on the Ice
desc: telling a push from a pull, and comparing a hard push with a gentle one
dir: Answer out loud. Do not say push or pull for the student.
text: A push moves something away from you. A pull brings it along with you.
qs: You put both hands on a heavy supply crate and shove it across the snow away from you. Is that a push or a pull?
The dog team is hitched in front of the sled and runs ahead. The sled comes along behind. Is the sled being pushed or pulled?
key: a push
pulled

title: Pushes and Pulls on the Ice
desc: deciding from test results whether a change made a thing move farther or in a new direction
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The team gave the same crate the same shove on two kinds of ground and counted the steps it slid. Ground Steps the crate slid smooth ice 9 deep soft snow 2
qs: Which ground let the crate slide farther?
A sled is gliding straight toward the tent. You give it a shove on its side. What happens to the way it is going?
key: smooth ice, 9 steps. Deep snow only let it go 2.
It turns and goes a new way, so it no longer heads at the tent. A push from the side changes the direction.

title: Sun and Shade on the Snow
desc: telling what sunlight does to a surface it shines on
dir: Answer out loud. If you can, stand in a sunny spot and a shady spot together first.
text: Two dark mats are here. Both are laid on the snow. Both went out together. It was the same time. One is in the open sunlight. One is in the shadow. The tent mak
qs: Both mats started out just as cold. One hour later one mat feels warm. Which one, the mat in the sunlight or the mat in the shadow?
The snow under the warm mat has started to melt. The snow under the other mat has not. What did the melting?
key: the mat in the sunlight
the sunlight. Accept the sun. It warmed that mat, and the warm mat melted the snow. Accept any answer that names the sun as the warmer.

title: Sun and Shade on the Snow
desc: designing and drawing a cover that keeps a spot out of the sunlight
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: Here is a crate of fish. The fish is frozen. It is sitting on the sled. The sunlight is bright. The fish starts to thaw. Draw something that keeps the sunlight
qs: Draw your sun cover over the crate.
Point to where the sunlight is coming from and tell me how your cover keeps it off the crate.
key: Any cover drawn ABOVE or OVER the crate. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one still counts. A wall drawn only beside the crate is partial: ask where the sunlight is coming from.
Something like: it blocks the sun, the sun cannot get to the crate, it puts the crate in a shadow.

title: Solving a Problem at Camp
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking a question about it
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem? The wind blows the trail flags flat, or the flags are orange?
Ask me one question about the flags that would help you fix this.
key: The wind blows the trail flags flat.
Any real question: how deep do they go in, how hard does the wind blow, how long are the sticks, could two flags hold each other up, is the snow soft there. A statement is not a question, so ask once

title: Solving a Problem at Camp
desc: drawing something whose shape would solve the problem
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw something that would hold a trail flag up in strong wind, like a deeper hole, a wide foot at the bottom, or stones piled around the stick.
qs: Draw your fix.
Tell me what you drew and how its shape keeps the flag standing.
key: Anything that would steady a stick: a deeper hole, a wide base or foot, a pile of stones or packed snow around it, a second stick tied across, guy lines. The three examples are in the direction, so co
Naming it is what shows intent. Something like: the stones hold the bottom, the deep hole grips it, the wide foot does not tip.

title: Solving a Problem at Camp
desc: comparing test results from two fixes for the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The team tried two fixes and counted how many flags were still standing after the wind. Fix Flags still standing pushed in deep with stones at the base 10 pushe
qs: Which fix worked better?
How do you know?
key: pushed in deep with stones at the base
Because 10 flags were still standing with the stones and only 2 were standing the other way. The reason has to come from the chart, not from liking stones.

title: Rules and Doing Right
desc: following rules, knowing what happens when they are broken, and naming an honest choice
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What did Juno choose to do? Tell the leader what happened, or hang the telescope back up and say nothing?
One rule at camp is sign for a tool before you take it. What might go wrong if nobody signed for anything?
key: She told the leader what happened.
Nobody would know where things were, two people would want the same tool, something could be lost and nobody would know. Any real consequence counts.

title: Maps and Places
desc: telling land from water, using position words on a map, and naming places in a town
dir: Look at the globe, then the map. Answer out loud.
text: Look at the globe. Blue stands for water. Green and brown stand for land. Look at the camp map. The tent is at the top. The bottom has the fishing hole. The mid
qs: Look at the globe. Is there more water or more land?
On the camp map, which one is at the top, the tent or the fishing hole?
key: more water. The blue covers more of the globe than the green and brown do.
the tent

title: Left and Right
desc: telling where things are with left and right, near and far, and in front and behind
dir: Look at each picture. Point or answer out loud.
text: A B C
key: Ask: Look at picture A. Point to the one on the left. (the seal)
Ask: Point to the one on the right. (the fish)

title: Our Flag and Long Ago
desc: recognizing the flag as a symbol of the country
dir: Answer out loud.
qs: The team plants this one at base camp. What is it called?
Our flag stands for our whole country. Name one place at school or in your town where you have seen it.
key: a flag. Accept the flag of our country or the American flag.
Any real place: a school, a post office, a park, outside a building, on a coin, at a game.

title: Our Flag and Long Ago
desc: telling how life long ago was different from life today, and what a commemorative holiday is for
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Long ago there were no radios and no phones.
qs: Long ago, how did a traveler send news back home, with a letter carried on a ship for many months, or with a radio?
How would you send news to somebody far away today?
key: with a letter carried on a ship
Any real answer: a phone call, a message, a video call, an email, a letter in the mail. Naming today's way is the then-and-now half of this standard.

title: Ice Camp Sounds
desc: blending, segmenting, and isolating sounds, counting syllables, and telling long from short vowels in spoken words
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the sounds and words out loud.
text: Listen. Then say it.
key: Blend these sounds: /f/ /l/ /a/ /g/ (flag)
Blend these sounds: /s/ /k/ /ē/ (ski)

title: First Sound
desc: isolating and pronouncing the initial sound in spoken single-syllable words
dir: Listen to the word. Say just the first sound.
qs: What is the first sound in log?
What is the first sound in pig?
key: The sound /l/. Say the sound, not the letter name.
The sound /p/. Say the sound, not the letter name.

title: Middle Sound
desc: isolating and pronouncing the medial vowel sound in spoken single-syllable words
dir: Listen to the word. Say just the middle sound.
qs: What is the middle sound in rub?
What is the middle sound in fan?
key: The short vowel sound /u/.
The short vowel sound /a/.

title: Base Camp Words
desc: reading words with digraphs, blends, final e, vowel teams, r-controlled vowels, endings, and two syllables
dir: Read each word out loud. The last one is a silly word. Just sound it out.
key: Count each word read correctly. vope is a silly word: listen for the long o that the final e makes.

Watch for: th (thin), ck ending (neck), blend (swim), double letters (pass), final e (cave, note), vowel teams (seal, deep), r-controlled ur (fur), the -ed ending said as /t/ (jumped), two syllables (

title: How Many Parts?
desc: using the rule that every syllable has a vowel sound to find the number of syllables in a printed word
dir: Read the word to yourself. Tell how many syllables, or parts, it has. Clap it if that helps.
text: button pig kitten tent
key: Point to “button”. How many syllables? (2)
Point to “pig”. How many syllables? (1)

title: Camp on the Ice
desc: a 75-word polar story read aloud
dir: Look at the three pictures. Then read the story out loud in your best reading voice.
text: tents at camp dogs that pull a sled a flag marks the way Camp on the Ice Our camp sits on thick ice. We sleep in red tents. The sun is up all day. It is up all
key: 75 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Point to the three pictures first so tents, sled dogs, and flag are clear before the student reads.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: tents at camp dogs that pull a sled a flag marks the way Camp on the Ice Our camp sits on thick ice. We sleep in red tents. The sun is up all day. It is up all
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the story about? What happened first?” (a summary or answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: The Hat in the Wind
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about a story the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the story. Then listen to each question and answer out loud.
text: The Hat in the Wind Rosa and Pim work at the camp. The camp is on the ice. The wind took Pim's red hat. Rosa ran to help him look. They dug in the soft snow. Th
qs: What did Pim lose?
Who ran to help Pim look?
key: His red hat. The wind took it
Rosa

title: Seals on the Ice
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about seals. Then listen to each question and answer out loud.
text: Seals A seal lives in the cold sea. It has thick fat. The fat keeps it warm. A seal can hold its breath for a long time. It swims down deep. There it can find f
qs: What keeps a seal warm?
What does a seal swim down deep to find?
key: Its thick fat
Fish

title: Sentence Spotter
desc: finding sentences by their first word, capital letter, and end mark
dir: Look at the sentences. Answer out loud.
text: The dogs pull the sled. Can you see the flag?
qs: How many sentences do you see? How can you tell?
Read the first word of the second sentence. What kind of letter does it start with?
key: 2 sentences. Each one starts with a capital letter and ends with an end mark
The word is Can. It starts with a capital, or uppercase, C

title: Camp Fix It
desc: spoken grammar items (plural nouns, subject and verb match, pronouns, time words, describing words)
dir: Listen to your teacher read each one. Say your answer out loud.
qs: Which sounds right? The dog pull the sled. Or: The dogs pull the sled.
One tent, two ____.
key: The second one. More than one dog goes with the verb pull
tents

title: Which Word Fits?
desc: using indefinite pronouns such as everyone, anyone, someone, something, and nothing
dir: Listen to the sentence. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? ___ is happy today. (Everybody / Nothing)
Which word fits? I heard ___ in the dark. (something / everyone)
key: Everybody. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)
something. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)

title: Whose Is It?
desc: using possessive nouns to show who owns something
dir: Listen. Say the answer. For the last one, you can point to the right one on paper.
qs: Ana has a drum. Whose drum is it?
The duck has a pond. Whose pond is it?
key: Ana’s drum. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)
the duck’s pond. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)

title: Commands and Big Feelings
desc: producing imperative (command) and exclamatory sentences in response to prompts
dir: Listen. Say your answer out loud in a full sentence.
qs: Tell me to sit down. Say it as a command.
Your team wins the game! Say one sentence that shows a big feeling.
key: A command such as “Sit down.”
An exclamation, for example “We won!” or “That was so fun!”

title: Print the Alphabet
desc: printing all upper- and lowercase letters
dir: On your paper, print each big letter and its small letter. Print them in order. Hold up your paper when you finish.
text: A a B b C c D d E e F f G g H h I i J j K k L l M m N n O o P p Q q R r S s T t U u V v W w X x Y y Z z
key: Look at the paper. Mark each letter pair where both the capital and the small letter are formed correctly and sit on the line. Letters may be uneven. Count a pair when each letter can be told from the
Check the tall letters (b, d, f, h, k, l, t), the letters that drop below the line (g, j, p, q, y), and the look-alikes (b and d, p and q).

title: Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow
desc: using verbs to show past, present, and future
dir: Listen. Say the sentence the new way.
qs: Say this sentence about yesterday: “Today I help my mom.”
Say this sentence about tomorrow: “Today I help my mom.”
key: Yesterday I helped my mom.
Tomorrow I will help my mom.

title: Sky Lights Listen
desc: asking and answering questions about a text read aloud
dir: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about lights in the night sky. Then answer out loud.
text: Listen.
key: Ask: What two colors glow in the sky? (green and pink)
Ask: Where does the light come from? (tiny bits of energy from the sun)

title: Tell Me About It
desc: describing a thing with relevant details
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly.
text: Tell me about something you wear or use when you are cold. What is it? What does it look like? How does it help you?
key: Names the thing and gives 2 or more details about it (SL.1.4)
Gives 2 or more details about what it looks like, and they stay on this one thing (SL.1.4)

title: Two-Step Directions
desc: giving, restating, and following simple two-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear, say it back, and give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do what your teacher says. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once, without repeating: “Tap the table two times, then tap your knees.” (does both steps, in the right order)
Say once, without repeating: “Stand up, then touch the wall.” (does both steps, in the right order)

title: Person, Place, Thing, Event
desc: describing a person, a place, a thing, and an event with relevant details, and saying ideas and feelings clearly
dir: Listen to your teacher. Tell about each one. Use lots of details.
text: Tell about a person, a place, a thing, and something that happened.
key: Say: “Tell me about a grown-up you know well.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the person, such as who they are, what they look like, or what they do)
Say: “Tell me about the place where you sleep.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the place, such as what is there or what you do there)

title: Radio Call
desc: using a provided chart to answer a question in writing
dir: Look at the chart. Write 1 sentence on your paper and hold it up.
text: The team is far out on the ice and needs help from the ship. What will they use? Use the chart.
key: Finds the answer in the chart. Your help is fine: read the two columns out loud and point to the first row
Writes a sentence drawn from the chart, such as: They will use the radio

title: Remember and Tell
desc: recalling information from experiences to answer a question
dir: Think about what happened to you. Tell your teacher your answer out loud. You can draw it, too.
qs: Think about the weather today. What did you see or feel outside? Tell me.
Think about your favorite place to play. Tell me what you do there.
key: Gives one real detail about today’s weather from their own experience.
Names a place and at least one thing they do there. (They may draw first, then tell. Write down what they say if you want a record.)

title: Camp Journal
