desc: an opinion piece about a dogsled or skis
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Would you rather cross the snow on a dogsled or on skis? Write what you think and tell why. a dogsled team skis Write 2 or 3 sentences.
key: Names the topic: riding a dogsled or going on skis (W.1.1)
States an opinion, which one the student would pick (W.1.1)

title: Camp Journal
desc: an informative piece with facts about a polar camp
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write about a polar camp. Tell 2 facts about it. The pictures can help. tents keep out the wind dogs pull the sleds colder than a freezer Write 2 or 3 sentences
key: Names the topic: a polar camp (W.1.2)
Gives at least 2 facts, such as people sleep in tents, dogs pull the sleds, or the air is very cold (W.1.2)

title: Trail Story
desc: a narrative about a day at camp with two sequenced events, detail, a time word, and closure
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write a story about one day at the ice camp. Tell 2 things that happened, in the order they happened. the tents the trail flags Write 2 or 3 sentences.
key: Tells 2 or more things that happened, in an order that makes sense (W.1.3)
Adds some detail about what happened, such as what it looked like or who was there (W.1.3)

title: Flag Hops
desc: counting on and counting back or up to add and subtract
dir: Count out loud like you are hopping from flag to flag. Say each answer.
text: The team puts a flag in the snow to mark the way back to camp.
qs: Start at 8. Count on 5. Where do you land? What adding sentence is that?
Start at 16. Count back 4. Where do you land? What take away sentence is that?

title: Crate Count
desc: counting, reading, and writing numerals to 120 and counting objects
dir: Count and read out loud. Write your numbers on your paper and hold it up.
text: Supplies come to camp in crates. A crate is a big box.
qs: Count out loud from 96 to 112.
Read these numbers out loud: 58, 103, 119.
key: Fifty-eight, one hundred three, one hundred nineteen

title: Sled Load Problems
desc: addition and subtraction word problems within 20, with the unknown in different places
dir: Listen to each story problem. You can draw on your paper. Say your answer.
text: A sled is pulled over the snow. Boxes and bags on the sled hold the camp food.
qs: The team packs 8 boxes of food on one sled and 7 boxes on the other sled. How many boxes in all?
There were 13 bags of dog food. The dogs ate 5 bags. How many bags are left?

title: Smart Adding
desc: using turn-around facts and making ten as strategies to add
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
qs: 7 + 8 = 15. So what is 8 + 7?
Pim says 6 + 9 is easier if he turns it around and thinks 9 + 6. Is that OK? What is the total?
key: 15. Knows it without counting because the two numbers just switch places
Yes, that is fine. The order does not change the total. Both make 15

title: Split It Even
desc: halves and fourths of circles and rectangles
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud. Draw the last one on your paper.
qs: Shape A is cut into 2 equal parts. What do we call the shaded part?
Look at Shape B. How many equal parts is it cut into? What do we call one of those parts?
key: One half, or half of the circle
4 equal parts. One part is a fourth, or a quarter

title: Tens and Ones
desc: reading a two-digit number as tens and ones
dir: Look at the blocks. Answer out loud.
qs: Each tall bar is one ten and each little square is one. What number do the blocks show?
In the number 53, what does the 5 stand for?
key: 47. Four tens and seven ones
5 tens, which is 50

title: Loading Up
desc: adding within 100, including a two-digit number plus ones and plus a multiple of ten
dir: Solve on your paper. Say your answer and tell how you got it.
text: More crates come to camp and go on the sled.
qs: There were 24 crates at camp. The plane brought 8 more. How many crates now?
There were 35 crates at camp. The plane brought 20 more. How many crates now?
key: 32 crates. 24 + 8 = 32. Adding the ones makes 12, so a new ten is made
55 crates. 35 + 20 = 55. Three tens plus two tens is five tens, and the 5 ones stay

title: Taking Tens Off
desc: subtracting a multiple of ten from a multiple of ten
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
text: Crates leave camp ten at a time.
qs: 60 crates were at camp. 20 crates went out on sleds. How many crates are left?
key: 40 crates. 6 tens take away 2 tens is 4 tens

title: Block Long
desc: measuring length as a whole number of same-size units laid end to end
dir: Look at the blocks under the ski and the rope. Answer out loud.
qs: How many blocks long is the ski?
How many blocks long is the rope?
key: 7 blocks
4 blocks

title: Camp Clocks
desc: telling and writing time to the hour and the half hour on analog and digital clocks
dir: Look at the two clocks. Answer out loud. Write the last one on your paper.
qs: What time does Clock A show?
What time does Clock B show?
key: 3 o'clock, or 3:00
Half past 7, or 7:30. The hour hand sits between the 7 and the 8, which tells you the hour is still 7

title: What We Saw
desc: reading a bar graph with three categories: total, how many in each, and how many more
dir: Look at the graph. Answer out loud.
qs: How many animals did the team see in all?
How many more seals than birds did they see?
key: 17. 8 seals plus 5 fish plus 4 birds
4 more. 8 seals take away 4 birds

title: Make a Graph
desc: organizing and representing data with up to three categories, and answering questions about the total and about how many more or less
dir: Look at the list. Make a tally chart or a picture graph on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: Ten kids told us their favorite snacks. cheese carrot cheese pretzel cheese cheese carrot pretzel carrot cheese
key: A chart or graph with pretzel 2, cheese 5, carrot 3. Each item is counted once. Tally marks, pictures, or squares all work. Labels are on each group.
10 (the total of all three groups)

title: Copy a Seal Flipper
desc: naming the job an animal body part does, then designing a tool that copies it to solve a human problem
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer the first out loud. Draw the second on your paper and hold it up.
text: A seal moves fast through the water. It has flippers. They are wide, flat and smooth. One sweep of a flipper pushes water. It pushes a lot of water. It goes bac
qs: Why does a wide flat flipper push a boat or a body through water better than a thin one?
Draw a paddle for the team that copies the shape of the seal's flipper.
key: It pushes against more water at once. A thin shape slips through the water instead of pushing it. Any answer about catching or pushing more water counts.
Any paddle drawn wide and flat on the end: an oar with a broad blade, a flat board on a handle, a spoon shape. A thin stick is partial, so ask what a flipper looks like.

title: Penguin Parents
desc: finding a pattern in what a parent animal does and what the young do in answer, and saying how it helps the young
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What do the two parents take turns doing?
What does the chick do when the returning parent calls?
key: One stays and keeps the chick warm on its feet while the other walks to the water for food, and then they swap. Both halves count.
It answers with a whistle of its own.

title: Penguin Parents
desc: making observations that young plants and animals are like their parents but not exactly like them
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
text: A penguin chick and a grown penguin. A young seal and the seal that is its parent.
qs: Name one way the penguin chick is like the grown penguin.
The chick is covered in soft grey fluff and the grown penguin has smooth black and white feathers. Does that mean the chick is not a penguin? Say why.
key: Both have two feet, a beak, wings held close, and both stand upright. Any likeness counts.
No. It is a penguin, and it is like its parent in the big ways, but young animals are not exactly like their parents. The fluff will be replaced by feathers as it grows.

title: The Star Over Camp
desc: finding a pattern in a log of sky observations and using it to predict what comes next
dir: Look at the log. Answer out loud.
text: On four clear nights the team looked for one bright star and wrote down where it was. Night At nine at night At midnight first night over the north marker over
qs: Where was the bright star at nine at night on all four nights?
Did it move between nine at night and midnight?
key: over the north marker
No. The log shows it in the same place at both times on every night.

title: The Star Over Camp
desc: relating the number of hours of daylight to the time of year from observations made across a year
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Hours of daylight at the camp, counted on one day in each of three months. Month Hours of daylight January 5 April 13 July 20
qs: Which month on the chart had the fewest hours of daylight?
How many more hours of daylight did July have than January?
key: January, 5 hours
15 more hours. 20 take away 5

title: Sound on the Ice
desc: planning an investigation showing that a shaking material makes sound and that a sound can make a material shake
dir: If you have a rubber band and a cup, try the first part. Either way, answer out loud.
text: Stretch a rubber band over the open top of a cup. Pluck it and put a fingertip on it while it sounds. Now turn the camp radio up and rest your fingers lightly o
qs: What do you feel on your fingertip while the rubber band is sounding?
Hold the rubber band still. What happens to the sound?
key: A buzz or a tickle. The band is shaking back and forth very fast.
The sound stops, because the shaking has stopped. No shaking, no sound.

title: Inside the Dark Tent
desc: accounting for why an object in darkness can be seen only when light shines on it
dir: Answer out loud.
text: In the long dark month the tent flap is tied shut and the lamp is off. No light gets in.
qs: The compass is lying on the floor of the tent. Can you see it in there? Say why or why not.
What would have to change in that tent before the compass could be seen?
key: No. There is no light in the tent, and a thing can only be seen when light shines on it and comes back to your eyes.
Light has to reach it: the lamp switched on, a flashlight, or the flap opened to let daylight in.

title: Inside the Dark Tent
desc: using test results to tell what happens when different materials are put in the path of a beam of light
dir: Look at the test results. Answer out loud.
text: One flashlight beam was pointed at four things in the dark tent and what it did was written down. What was put in the beam What the beam did a clear slab of ice
qs: Which of the four let the most light through?
Which thing let none through at all?
key: the clear slab of ice
the wooden crate lid

title: Camp to the Ridge
desc: designing a device that uses light or sound to send a message over a distance too far to shout
dir: Draw your answer on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: Two of the team are up on the ridge, far above the camp. The wind takes away a shout before it gets halfway.
qs: Draw a device at the camp that tells the pair on the ridge that supper is ready. It has to use light or sound.
Describe your device to me and tell me whether light or sound carries the message.
key: Any device that carries light or sound up the slope: a lamp raised on a pole, a lamp flashed on and off, a horn, a bell, a whistle, a mirror catching the sun.
Names it and says which one it uses.

title: Fix the Frozen Bottles
desc: naming a problem people want to change, asking a question about it, and saying what to observe first
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem the team wants to change?
Ask me one question that would tell you more about why it happens.
key: The water bottles freeze overnight in the supply tent.

Any real question: how cold does the tent get, how many bottles freeze, where in the tent are they kept, how full are the bottles, how long does it take. A statement is not a question, so ask once mor

title: Fix the Frozen Bottles
desc: making a simple drawing of a fix and explaining how the shape of the object makes it work
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up. Then answer out loud.
text: Draw something that keeps the water bottles from freezing in the night.
qs: Draw what you would make.
Point to the part that keeps the cold out and tell me its shape.
key: Any real fix: a thick sleeve round each bottle, a padded box they all go in, a bag stuffed with cloth, bottles kept inside a sleeping bag, bottles packed close together under a blanket.
Names a shape: a thick wrap all the way round, a deep padded box, a closed bag, a tight bundle.

title: Which Sleeve Worked
desc: comparing the data from tests of two objects built to solve the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two bottle sleeves were tested on the same night, eight bottles in each. Sleeve Bottles frozen by morning, out of 8 a thick wool sleeve 1 a thin plastic sleeve
qs: Which sleeve worked better in the test?
Which numbers in the chart make you say that?
key: the thick wool sleeve
Only 1 bottle out of 8 froze in the wool sleeve and 6 out of 8 froze in the plastic one. The numbers have to be in the answer.

title: The Camp Agreement
desc: telling a right from a responsibility and connecting the agreement of a small group to the rules of a town
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: Name one thing from the agreement that every person gets.
Name one thing from the agreement that every person has to do.
key: A hot meal, a dry place to sleep, or a turn to speak at the morning meeting. Those are the rights.
Writing their own gear into the log, or not going past the flag line alone. Those are the responsibilities.

title: The Camp Map
desc: giving an exact grid location, describing a relative location, and telling a physical feature from a built one
dir: Look at the map grid. Answer out loud.
text: A map of the camp, drawn on a grid. 1 2 3 A B C the ice ridge the bay the tents the flag line the supply store The top of this map is north. The bottom is south
qs: Find the supply store. Give its exact spot on the grid, the letter and the number.
Where is the bay compared to the supply store? Use north, south, east or west.
key: C3. Both parts are needed.
North of the supply store. The student may add that it is in the same column, which is a strong answer.

title: The Camp Map
desc: naming built features of a familiar place and recognizing that people in one place come from many different places
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Ten people are at this camp. They grew up in seven different states. Two grew up in other countries. At supper they each told the others. Each one named one foo
qs: Do the people working side by side at this camp all come from the same place? Say how you know.
Think of the place you live. Name three things there that people built, and say what one of them does for the people who live there.
key: No. They grew up in seven different states and two other countries.
Any three built things, with a use for one: a school teaches children, a hospital takes care of sick people, a store sells food, a road lets people travel, a park gives a place to play.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: telling why a country keeps one shared symbol and naming a custom that goes with it
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The team carried a flag with them. It was a United States flag. They put it up outside. It went outside the main tent. The same flag flies outside post offices.
qs: The country keeps a famous paper from 1776 safe. What is it called, and what did it say?
Why would a team working far from home carry the flag of their country with them?
key: The Declaration of Independence. It said this country would make its own decisions instead of being ruled from far away. Accept that it is the paper that started our country. (HSS-1.3)
To show where they come from, and because the flag stands for their country even when they are far away.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: comparing everyday life long ago with life today and telling what changed from what stayed the same
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Sending word home from somewhere far away. Long ago Today how word travelled a letter carried by ship a radio or a satellite call how long it took many weeks a
qs: Long ago, how did word from a far away team get home?
How does word get home today?
key: A letter carried by ship, taking many weeks.
By radio or a satellite call, in a few seconds.

title: Crate Word Flip
desc: reading words with silent e, vowel teams, r-controlled vowels, two syllables, a prefix, a suffix, and an irregular spelling
dir: Read each word out loud. The last two are made-up words. Just sound them out.
key: Read each word in order. drook and flarn are made-up words: listen for the oo team sound and the ar sound.

Watch for: silent e long o and a short vowel (froze, chest), r-controlled or (north), vowel teams and diphthongs (tail, crowd, flew), a compound word (campsite), a prefix and a suffix (unpack, windy),

title: Two-Part Long Vowel Words
desc: decoding regularly spelled two-syllable words with long vowels
dir: Read each word out loud. Each word has two parts.
key: Mark each word read correctly. Each word has two syllables and at least one long vowel sound, such as pa-per, mu-sic, o-pen.
If the student breaks the word into syllables and then says it smoothly, count it correct.

title: Read the Journal Page
desc: a 102-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: Mira woke up in a tent at base camp. Base camp is where the team sleeps and keeps its food. The air was so cold. Her breath made little clouds. Her job today wa
key: 102 words. Mark each missed word and each self-correction on the passage in the record sheet.
Note pace and expression in your notes.

title: Journal Questions
desc: asking and answering who, what, why, and how questions about key details in a story
dir: Look back at the story if you need to. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Marking the Trail (click to open or close the story) Mira woke up in a tent at base camp. Base camp is where the team sleeps and keeps its food. The air was so
qs: Who pulled the sled up the ridge?
What did she pack on the sled?
key: Mira
Twelve red flags

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: Mira woke up in a tent at base camp. Base camp is where the team sleeps and keeps its food. The air was so cold. Her breath made little clouds. Her job today wa
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the text about? Tell me two things you remember.” (an answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: Ice Floe Facts
desc: asking and answering what, who, how, and why questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about ice floes. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Ice Floes The sea near the poles gets very cold. The top of the water freezes. The ice cracks into flat pieces that float. A flat piece of floating sea ice is c
qs: What is an ice floe?
Who climbs onto floes to rest?
key: Sea ice that has cracked into a flat piece and floats on the water
Seals

title: Say It Right
desc: spoken grammar items (irregular past tense, irregular plural, reflexive pronoun, adverb, word order, joining two sentences)
dir: Say each answer out loud.
qs: Today the dogs run on the trail. Yesterday the dogs ____.
One foot, two ____.
key: ran
feet

title: Write It Right
desc: written conventions (capital letters in place names and months, an apostrophe for a possessive and a contraction, a comma in a letter greeting, spelling two patterns)
dir: Write each answer on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Fix this sentence: we flew over the arctic ocean in may
The tent belongs to the pilot. Write the missing word: the ____ tent
key: We flew over the Arctic Ocean in May. (capital W to start, capital A and capital O in the ocean name, capital M in the month, and a period)
pilot’s (apostrophe before the s)

title: Capital Letters
desc: capitalizing holidays, product names, and geographic names
dir: Listen while your teacher reads each sentence. Write it again with the right capital letters. Hold up your paper when you finish.
qs: Fix the capital letters: we had a picnic on independence day.
Fix the capital letters: lake tahoe is in nevada and california.
key: We had a picnic on Independence Day.
Lake Tahoe is in Nevada and California.

title: Use a Dictionary
desc: using a beginning dictionary and ABC order to check and correct spellings
dir: Listen. Answer out loud. If you have a beginning dictionary, you may use it.
qs: Put these words in ABC order: jump, hop, skip.
The guide words are rain and sand. Would the word rock be on this page? Tell why.
key: hop, jump, skip
Yes. rock comes after rain and before sand.

title: Group Words
desc: using collective nouns
dir: Listen. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? A group of ants is called a ___. (colony / school)
Which word fits? A group of puppies born together is called a ___. (litter / flock)
key: colony. (A collective noun names a group.)
litter. (A collective noun names a group.)

title: Expedition Story
desc: a short narrative with events in order, details about actions and feelings, time words, and an ending
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: You are on the polar team. One morning you step out of your tent and find animal tracks in the snow. Write a story about what happens next. Tell what happened i
key: Tells about one event or a short set of events in order
Includes details about actions, thoughts, or feelings

title: Listen Up
desc: recounting and describing key ideas and details from a text read aloud
dir: Listen first. Then answer your teacher’s questions out loud.
text: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read a radio report about lights in the polar sky.
key: Ask: “What do people call the lights that move across the sky near the North Pole?” (the northern lights)
Ask: “Describe what the glow can look like.” (a curtain blowing in the wind; green and pink waves of light)

title: Tell Me About It
desc: telling about an experience in order, with facts and details, in clear complete sentences
dir: Tell about it out loud. Say what happened first, next, and last.
text: Tell me about a time you had to get ready for cold weather or hot weather. Where were you going? What did you put on or pack? What happened? First Next Last
key: Tells what happened in an order that makes sense
Gives facts that fit (where, when, who, or what)

title: Longer Directions
desc: following three- and four-step oral directions, requesting clarification when something is not understood, and giving multi-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear. Ask a question if you are not sure what to do. Then give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do the steps in order. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once: “Pick up your paper, fold it in half, and put it on your head.” (does all three steps in order)
Say once: “Stand up, hop two times, spin once, and sit down.” (does all four steps in order)

title: Plan and Tell a Story
desc: planning and delivering a short narrative presentation that recounts an event with details, a logical sequence, and a conclusion
dir: Pick one idea. Plan what you will say: the start, the middle, and the end. Then tell your story out loud.
text: Pick one: a time you made something, a time you visited a place, or a day you spent with a friend. Beginning Middle End
key: Plans first: says or draws what will happen at the start, the middle, and the end before telling (give about one minute to plan)
Tells one event with enough detail (who, where, and what happened)

title: Trail Sign Reading
desc: applying grade-level phonics and word-analysis skills to decode words in text
dir: Read each line out loud. Sound out any word that is tricky.
text: The sled dogs turned north and climbed the icy ridge. We unpacked three crates and stacked them beside the tent. The frozen sea looked silver in the moonlight.
key: Line 1: listen for the r-controlled or in north, the long i and the y that says long e in icy, and the dge ending in ridge.
Line 2: listen for the prefix un in unpacked, the ed ending on unpacked and stacked, the ee team in three, and the two syllables with silent e in beside.

title: Weather Station Log
desc: gathering information from a provided log and recalling information from experience to answer questions
dir: Use the log to answer. Say the first two answers out loud. Write number 3 on your paper and hold it up. Then say number 4.
text: At the weather station every temperature is below zero. On the thermometer, the numbers below zero are colder. 20 below zero is colder than 9 below zero.
qs: Use the log. Which day was the coldest?
Which days had strong wind?
key: Wednesday, at 20 below zero
Tuesday and Thursday

title: Two Shovels
desc: recounting a short story and naming the lesson it teaches
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the story. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Two Shovels Nils wanted the path to the weather station cleared before breakfast. He picked up a shovel and started at one end. The snow was soft and deep. By n
qs: Retell this story. Tell me the beginning, the middle, and the end.
What lesson does this story teach?
key: Nils shovelled the path alone and had only half of it done by noon. The next morning Ada brought a second shovel. They worked from both ends and finished quickly. Count it correct when the three parts
A job goes faster when people share the work. Any wording of that idea counts, such as: two people working together finish sooner.

title: Sled or Snowmobile
desc: a short opinion piece with the topic, an opinion, a reason, a linking word, and an ending
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Which is the better way to move gear across the snow at base camp: a dogsled or a snowmobile? Write what you think and tell why. Write 2 or 3 sentences. I think
key: Names the topic the writing is about: the best way to move gear across the snow
States an opinion, which of the two the student would pick

title: What Is at Base Camp
desc: a short informative piece with the topic, two facts, one definition, and an ending
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write about base camp for someone who has never seen one. Tell 2 facts about it and explain what one polar word means. Write 2 or 3 sentences. Base camp is One
key: Names the topic: base camp, or what a polar team keeps at base camp
Gives at least 2 true facts, such as the team sleeps there, the food is kept there, tents are put up there, or the weather station log is kept there

title: Load the Sleds
desc: one-step addition and subtraction word problems within 100 with the unknown in different places
dir: Listen while your teacher reads each problem. Solve it on your paper. You can draw or write a number sentence. Say your answer.
text: The team is packing sleds at base camp. A sled is a flat box on runners that the team pulls across the snow.
qs: A sled can carry 40 kilograms. The team loads 26 kilograms of food. How many more kilograms can the sled carry?
The team skied 23 kilometers on Monday and 34 kilometers on Tuesday. How many kilometers in all?
key: 57 kilometers (23 + 34 = 57)

title: Depth Soundings
desc: adding and subtracting within 1000 with a place value strategy and relating it to a written method
dir: Solve each one on your paper. Show your work and hold it up. Say your answer.
text: A sounding tells how deep the water is under the ship. The team writes every sounding and every mile in a logbook.
qs: The ship sailed 348 kilometers on Monday and 275 kilometers on Tuesday. How far did it sail in all? Show how you added.
The team must travel 500 kilometers to reach the ice shelf. They have gone 236 kilometers. How many kilometers are left?
key: 623 kilometers (348 + 275 = 623). Listen for hundreds with hundreds, tens with tens, ones with ones, and for making a new ten and a new hundred.
264 kilometers (500 - 236 = 264). This one needs two decomposes, so watch the work.

title: Flags on the Trail
desc: counting within 1000 and skip-counting by 2s, 5s, 10s, and 100s
dir: Count out loud.
text: The team plants a flag on the trail every 5 kilometers, so the counting goes 5, 10, 15, and on.
qs: Skip count by 5s from 70 to 110.
Skip count by 10s from 430 to 500.

title: Ration Count
desc: two-step addition and subtraction word problems within 100
dir: Each problem has two steps. Solve it on your paper and say your answer.
text: Rations are the food the team packs for each day. Fuel is what the camp stove burns to melt snow into water.
qs: The team had 45 ration bars. They ate 17 bars the first week and 12 bars the second week. How many bars are left?
One dogsled carries 8 crates. A second dogsled carries 9 crates. The team unloads 6 crates at the weather station. How many crates are still on the sleds?

title: Measure the Ice
desc: measuring length with a ruler and choosing the right measuring tool
dir: Answer out loud. For the last one, get a ruler and measure.
text: An ice core is a round stick of ice the team drills out and measures. A snow tube holds a sample of snow.
qs: Look at the first ruler. How long is the ice core?
Look at the second ruler. How long is the snow tube?
key: 5 inches
9 centimeters

title: Logbook Check
desc: subtracting and adding three-digit numbers with decomposing and composing, and finding an error in a written method
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work and hold it up.
qs: One depth reading was 740 meters. The next reading was 358 meters. How much less deep was the second reading?
The team pulled 567 kilograms of gear on the first sled and 276 kilograms on the second sled. How many kilograms in all?
key: 382 meters (740 - 358 = 382). Two decomposes are needed here.

title: Odd or Even
desc: deciding whether a group is odd or even and writing an even number as a sum of two equal addends
dir: Count each group. Answer out loud. Write the last one on your paper.
qs: Count the crates. Is that number odd or even? How do you know?
Count the snow samples. Is that number odd or even?
key: 13, odd. Pairing them up leaves one crate with no partner, and counting by 2s skips over 13.
16, even. Every snow sample has a partner.

title: Crates in Rows
desc: finding the total in a rectangular array and writing it as a sum of equal addends
dir: Look at each block of crates. Answer out loud and write the equation on your paper.
qs: Yard A. How many crates in all? Write an addition equation with equal addends.
Yard B. How many crates in all? Write an addition equation with equal addends.
key: 20 crates. 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20, one addend for each of the 4 rows. 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 20 by columns is also correct.
12 crates. 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 by rows, or 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 by columns.

title: Four Hundred Six
desc: reading a three-digit number from blocks, writing it in expanded form, and writing its number name
dir: Look at the blocks. Answer out loud. Write the last two on your paper.
qs: Each big square is a hundred, each tall bar is a ten, and each little square is a one. What number do the blocks show?
Write that number in expanded form.
key: 406. Four hundreds, no tens, and six ones. If the student says 46, point at the empty tens place and ask what belongs there. (2.NBT.A.1)
400 + 6. Writing 400 + 0 + 6 is also correct. (2.NBT.A.3)

title: Camp Clocks
desc: telling time to the nearest five minutes, using a.m. and p.m., and knowing minutes in an hour
dir: Look at the two clocks. Answer out loud.
qs: What time does Clock A show?
What time does Clock B show?
key: 4:15, or a quarter past 4
9:45, or a quarter to 10. The hour hand sits close to the 10, but it has not passed it, so the hour is still 9.

title: Time Facts
desc: knowing relationships of time such as minutes in an hour, days in a month, and weeks in a year
dir: Listen. Answer out loud.
qs: How many minutes are in 2 hours?
Name a month that has 31 days.
key: 120 minutes (60 + 60)
January, March, May, July, August, October, or December

title: Coins in the Pocket
desc: finding the value of a set of coins and solving a money problem with the cent symbol
dir: Look at the coins. Answer out loud.
qs: Mira still has these coins in her coat pocket from home. How much money is that in all?
On the way home she spends 40¢ at the airfield counter. How much does she have left?
key: 67¢. Two quarters make 50¢, the dime makes 60¢, the nickel makes 65¢, and the two pennies make 67¢.
27¢ (67¢ - 40¢ = 27¢). Look for the ¢ symbol in the written answer.

title: Draw the Core Graph
desc: drawing a bar graph with a single-unit scale from a table and answering questions about it
dir: Look at the table. Draw the graph on your paper and hold it up. Then answer out loud.
qs: Draw a bar graph of this table on your paper. Give it a title, label the three days, and number the side by ones.
How many more cores were drilled on Tuesday than on Wednesday?
key: A bar graph with three bars, 6 for Monday, 9 for Tuesday and 4 for Wednesday, a title, the days labelled, and a side scale counting by ones. A picture graph with one symbol for each core is also corre

title: Draw a Picture Graph
desc: drawing a picture graph from a data set with four categories and solving put-together, take-apart, and compare problems
dir: Look at the table. Draw a picture graph on your paper. Use one picture for each 1. Then answer out loud.
text: Favorite snacks: number of kids Choice Number of kids Cheese 4 Carrots 3 Crackers 6 Popcorn 5
qs: Draw a picture graph of the table. Give it a title and label each row.
How many kids chose Cheese and Carrots together?
key: A picture graph with 4 symbols for Cheese, 3 symbols for Carrots, 6 symbols for Crackers, 5 symbols for Popcorn. Each symbol stands for 1, the symbols are the same size and lined up, and the rows are

title: Camp Shapes
desc: naming shapes by their number of sides and angles, drawing a shape to a given attribute, and naming a cube
dir: Look at the five shapes. Answer out loud. Draw the middle one on your paper.
qs: Name shapes A, B, C and D.
Draw a shape that has exactly 6 angles. What is that shape called?
key: A is a triangle (3 sides, 3 angles), B is a quadrilateral (4 sides, 4 angles), C is a pentagon (5 sides, 5 angles), D is a hexagon (6 sides, 6 angles).
A closed shape with exactly 6 straight sides and 6 angles. It is called a hexagon. The drawing does not have to be neat or regular.

title: Three Trays in the Camp Hut
desc: reading the results of a plant test and planning a fair test of one thing a plant needs
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Then answer out loud.
text: The team grows cress in trays in the camp hut, because nothing green grows outside. Three trays were started on the same day. Tray What it got After ten days A
qs: Which tray grew best, and what did it get?
Tray C got water every day. Why did nothing in it turn green?
key: Tray A. It got both the lamp light and water.
The lamp was switched off, so it had no light. A plant needs light to make its food, and that is also what makes it green.

title: Three Trays in the Camp Hut
desc: making a simple model that does the job an animal does when it moves pollen
dir: Draw your model on your paper. Then tell your teacher about it.
text: The polar summer is short. Bumblebees crawl over the low arctic flowers. Pollen sticks to the hairs on their bodies. It rubs off again. That happens on the next
qs: Draw your model. Label the part that the pollen sticks to.
Which animal job does your model copy, and why does your model need a rough or hairy part instead of a smooth one?
key: Any model with a rough, hairy or fuzzy carrying part: a bottle brush, a woolly sock on a stick, a pipe cleaner, a strip of felt. The labelled carrying part is what to look for.
It copies a bee carrying pollen between flowers. A rough or hairy part catches and holds the tiny grains, and a smooth part would let them slide straight off, so nothing would get carried.

title: The Rocky Shore and the Snow Plain
desc: comparing the kinds of living things found in two different habitats
dir: Listen while your teacher reads both lists. Answer out loud.
text: The team wrote down every living thing they found in two places, spending one hour in each. The rocky shore The snow plain inland 4 kinds of seaweed 1 kind of l
qs: How many kinds of living things are on the rocky shore list?
Which place has more different kinds of living things?
key: 12. Four seaweeds, two mosses and lichens, one seal, three seabirds and two shore creatures.
the rocky shore

title: Minutes, or Thousands of Years
desc: using two sources as evidence that some Earth events happen quickly and some happen slowly
dir: Listen while your teacher reads both notes. Answer out loud.
text: Two notes about this coast, from two different places. Where it came from What it says the camp radio log At eleven in the morning a crack opened right across t
qs: Which note tells about a change that happened in minutes?
Which note tells about a change that took thousands of years?
key: The radio log, the crack opening across the floe in a few minutes.
The handbook chapter, the valley scraped out by a glacier over thousands of years.

title: Minutes, or Thousands of Years
desc: telling where water is found on Earth and whether it is solid or liquid
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Almost everything the team can see is water in one form or another.
qs: Name three places around this camp where you would find water.
The sea here is salty. Where does the team get fresh water from instead?
key: Any three: the sea, the sea ice, the glacier, the snow on the ground, a melt pool, clouds, frost on the gear.
By melting snow or glacier ice, which is fresh and not salty. Accept: a stream of melt water.

title: Holding the Camp Ground, and a Map of It
desc: comparing two things built to stop wind from changing the shape of the ground
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Wind scours the snow out from under the tents and leaves bare holes. Two screens were tried and the depth of the holes was measured after three windy days. What
qs: Which screen held the ground best?
How do you know, using the numbers in the chart?
key: the wall of cut snow blocks
The holes were only 4 centimeters deep behind the snow wall, 12 centimeters behind the canvas, and 30 centimeters with nothing there. The reason must come from the numbers.

title: Holding the Camp Ground, and a Map of It
desc: making a model of an area that shows the shapes of the land and the bodies of water in it
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up.
text: Make your own model map of the coast around base camp. Put in the high ice cap, the flat plain, the bay, and the melt stream that runs down to it. Add a key tha
qs: Draw your model map with the ice cap, the flat plain, the bay and the melt stream on it.
Show me your key. Which parts are land or ice and which parts are liquid water?
key: All four on the page and told apart by shape or colour: the ice cap high, the plain left flat, the bay as an opening of water in the coast, the stream as a line.
Points to each part and reads the key. The key is what makes this a model and not just a picture.

title: Sorting the Expedition Kit
desc: describing materials by properties you can see or feel and sorting them into groups
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Four things out of a kit crate, and what the team wrote about each one. Item Material What they wrote a mug steel hard, shiny, gets very cold to hold a sock woo
qs: Sort the four items into a hard group and a group that bends.
Two of them keep the cold away from your skin. Which two, and what do they have in common?
key: Hard: the steel mug and the glass thermometer tube. Bends: the wool sock and the rubber boot sole.
The wool sock and the rubber boot sole. Both of them bend, and both are worn next to the body rather than held. Accept any answer that groups them by being soft or bendy rather than by being metal or

title: Sorting the Expedition Kit
desc: using test data to choose the material that suits a job
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The team needs a facing for the bottom of a sled runner. Three materials were each dragged 100 meters over cold snow with the same load. Facing Pull needed Afte
qs: Which facing should go on the runner?
Which two pieces of the chart make you sure?
key: the hard plastic strip
It needed only a light pull and it had no damage after 100 meters. Both columns have to be used, not just one.

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: telling how a thing built from a few pieces can be taken apart and built into something new
dir: Answer out loud. You may draw if it helps.
text: The weather station has a mast. It is made of 3 metal poles. It has 6 clamps. The team unclamped it. They laid the poles flat. They did it before a storm came t
qs: The mast is gone. Are the poles and clamps gone too? What is lying flat on the snow?
Build something new in your head out of those 3 poles and 6 clamps. What is it, and how do the pieces go together?
key: No. All 3 poles and all 6 clamps are still there. They are the same pieces, just not clamped together as a mast any more.

Any real thing from 3 poles and 6 clamps: a tripod to hang a pot over a stove, a flag pole, a frame for a tent door, a drying rack, a marker for the trail. Listen for how the pieces join, because that

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: arguing with evidence that some heating and cooling changes can be undone and some cannot
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two things happened on the camp stove within an hour of each other. What happened A pot of packed snow was heated and became a pot of water. A pan of oats was c
qs: Set the pot of water outside the tent. What happens to it?
Set the pan of porridge outside the tent. Does it turn back into dry loose oats?
key: It freezes into ice, and heating it again would melt it back.
No. It stays thick porridge. It goes cold and hard but it is still porridge, not dry loose oats.

title: The Thermometer That Blows Over
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking a question about it
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the note. Answer out loud.
text: The thermometer has to stand outside the tent. It stands there all day. Then the team can write down the temperature. They do it every hour. It stands on three
qs: What is the problem the team wants to fix? Say it in one sentence.
Ask one question that would help you fix it.
key: The thermometer stand blows over in the wind, so readings get missed. Naming the falling over, not the missed readings alone, is the problem.

Any real question: how heavy is the thermometer, how deep do the legs go, how hard does the wind blow, how wide are the legs apart, is the snow soft or packed. A statement is not a question, so ask on

title: The Thermometer That Blows Over
desc: drawing a design and telling how its shape does the job
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw a stand that would hold the thermometer up in a strong wind. Think hard about its shape.
qs: Draw your stand.
Tell me how the shape of what you drew keeps it standing.
key: Any design that could really stand in wind: three or four legs spread wide, a wide flat base, a box of packed snow around the foot, long legs pushed deep, guy lines out to pegs.
The shape is the part being checked. Something like: the wide legs make it hard to tip, the heavy base holds the bottom down, the deep legs cannot pull out, the lines pull it from all sides at once.

title: The Thermometer That Blows Over
desc: comparing test results from two designs built for the same problem
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Both stands were used for five windy days. Stand Times it fell over Readings missed wide legs set in a block of packed snow 0 0 three thin legs with guy lines 2
qs: Which stand worked better?
How do you know? Use both columns.
key: the wide legs set in a block of packed snow

text: A bare rock ridge rises out of the ice near base camp. The team chipped samples from three layers and listed the fossils. The top layer is the youngest. Layer F
qs: Name two organisms that once lived where this ice-covered ridge now stands.
The middle layer has ferns, a tree trunk and beetles. What kind of place was this then? Use the fossils as your evidence.
key: Any two the table names: a fern, a tree, a beetle, coral, a clam. (3-LS4-1)
A forest, warm enough for trees and ferns and insects to live. Naming the fossils is the evidence. An answer with no fossil named is not yet using the data. (3-LS4-1)

title: A Useful Difference
desc: explaining how a variation among individuals of one species gives an advantage
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Penguins swim after fish. The team measured flippers and counted catches on a hundred dives. Penguins Flipper length Top swimming speed Fish caught in a hundred
qs: Which penguins caught more fish?
Explain why a longer flipper is an advantage for a penguin here. Use the table.
key: the longer-flippered penguins, 51 fish against 22 (3-LS4-2)
Longer flippers give more speed, 9 km an hour against 6, and a faster swimmer catches more of the fish it chases, 51 against 22. The explanation has to lean on the data. (3-LS4-2)

title: Who Survives, and What Would Help
desc: arguing from data who can survive in a changed habitat, then judging the merit of a solution
dir: Read the table. Answer out loud.
text: The sea ice near base camp formed six weeks later than usual and broke up early. The team recorded what they found through the season. Living thing What happene
qs: Which living thing survived well that season? Give the evidence.
Name the one that could not survive at all and the one that survived less well.
key: The floating plankton. There was far more of it, because open water let light in. (3-LS4-3)
The ice algae could not survive at all, none were found. The seals survived less well, fewer counted and resting on rocks instead of ice. (3-LS4-3)

title: A Season of Weather
desc: reading and making a graphical display of typical weather for one season
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your graph on your paper and hold it up.
text: Average temperature at base camp, month by month, through the polar summer. Month Average temperature first 14 C below zero second 6 C below zero third 2 C belo
qs: Which month of the polar summer is the warmest here?
Does any month in this table rise above freezing? What does that tell you about this season?
key: the third month, 2 C below zero (3-ESS2-1)
No. Every month is below zero, so even in summer the typical day here stays below freezing and ice does not all melt. (3-ESS2-1)

title: Two Parts of the World
desc: combining information to describe the climates of two different regions of the world
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Two regions of the world, one at the bottom of the globe and one at its middle. Region Warmest month Coldest month Hours of daylight in midwinter this polar reg
qs: Which region has almost the same temperature all year?
In the polar region there are zero hours of daylight in midwinter. How does that help explain how cold it gets?
key: the region on the middle line of the globe, 31 C at the warmest and 27 C at the coldest (3-ESS2-2)
With no sunlight at all for weeks, nothing is warming the ground or the air, so the heat keeps leaving and the temperature falls much lower. (3-ESS2-2)

title: Ready for the Blizzard
desc: making a claim about the merit of a design that reduces the impact of a weather hazard
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A blizzard wind can tear a tent off the ice. It takes minutes. Before the storm season the team cuts snow blocks. They build a curved wall on the windward side.
qs: Which weather hazard is the snow wall meant to reduce?
Make a claim. Does the snow wall have merit? Give your reason.
key: blizzard wind, which can tear a tent loose (3-ESS3-1)
Yes, with a reason attached: the wall takes the force of the wind before it reaches the tent, and a curved wall turns the wind around the sides. A yes with no reason is not yet a claim. (3-ESS3-1)

title: Balanced or Not
desc: planning an investigation of balanced and unbalanced forces acting on an object
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A loaded sledge sits on flat ice. Two team members pull from the front and two hold a rope at the back. Everyone pulls and the sledge stays put.
qs: Are the forces on the sledge balanced or unbalanced? How do you know?
The two at the back let go. What happens, and what changed about the forces?
key: Balanced. The front pull and the back pull are equal and opposite, and the sledge staying still is the evidence. (3-PS2-1)
The sledge moves forward. Nothing balances the front pull now, so the forces are unbalanced. (3-PS2-1)

title: Predict the Next Marker
desc: using a pattern in motion data to predict where an object will be later
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Orange markers stand every 100 m along the trail out from camp. A team member on skis is timed as she passes each one. Marker Minutes since camp 1 3 2 6 3 9 4 1
qs: Describe the pattern in the table.
She is heading for marker 8. At what time should she pass it. How do you know?
key: One marker every 3 minutes, the same time for each one. She is moving at a steady speed. (3-PS2-2)
24 minutes, because eight markers at 3 minutes each is 24. The reason has to be the pattern, not a guess. (3-PS2-2)

title: Ask About the Pull
desc: asking questions about cause and effect in magnetic interactions between objects not touching
dir: Answer out loud. Your two questions have to be questions, not statements.
text: The team’s compass points the same way every morning, until someone sets the iron camp stove down beside it. Then the needle swings toward the stove and stays t
qs: The stove never touches the compass, yet the needle moves. What does that tell you about this force?
Ask two questions about it that you could actually investigate.
key: The force acts across a distance, with no contact between the objects. (3-PS2-3)

Any two real investigable questions: how far away does the stove have to be before the needle goes back, does a smaller iron object do it, does an aluminum pot do anything, does a thicker mitten betwe

title: A Problem for a Magnet
desc: defining a design problem that magnets can solve, with criteria for success and constraints
dir: Answer out loud. For the third one you may write your two sentences on your paper.
text: Steel tent pegs get pulled loose in a blizzard. They are buried under new snow. Digging with a shovel takes an hour. A sharp spade can slice a tent line.
qs: Define the problem in one sentence. Begin it: The problem is.
Why is a magnet a sensible idea here? Would the same tool find a buried nylon line?
key: A problem statement about finding buried steel tent pegs under new snow without cutting the lines. The problem has to be about finding the pegs, not about the storm. (3-PS2-4)
The pegs are steel, and a magnet pulls steel without touching it, so it can find and lift a peg from under snow. A nylon line is not pulled by a magnet, so no. (3-PS2-4)

title: Three Ways to Do It
desc: comparing several possible solutions against stated criteria and constraints
dir: Look at the table and the three rules. Answer out loud.
text: Three boot designs were worn for a full day out on the ice. Design Toe temperature after a day Weight of the pair Grip on bare ice heavy insulated boot 21 C 2.6
qs: Which design keeps toes warmest?
Which design clears all three rules? Explain with the numbers.
key: the heavy insulated boot, 21 C (3-5-ETS1-2)
The insulated boot with a studded sole. Toes at 19 C, 1.8 kg, and good grip. Another choice counts only if the student argues it against all three rules using the table. (3-5-ETS1-2)

title: Make the Test Fair
desc: judging whether a test is fair, naming controlled variables, and identifying a failure point
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two tent peg shapes were tested to see which one holds better in snow. Peg Snow Pull used to test it flat blade peg hard packed snow a steady pull by one person
qs: Does this test prove anything? Say why.
Name two things to keep the same so the test is fair.
key: No. Two things were different at once, the snow and the kind of pull, so holding better cannot be pinned on the shape. (3-5-ETS1-3)
Any two controlled variables: the same snow, the same kind and size of pull, the same depth driven in, the same angle, the same temperature. (3-5-ETS1-3)

title: Maps and Places
desc: using a map grid and a table to describe physical and human features and where they sit
dir: Use the map grid and the table. Answer out loud.
text: A map grid of the ground around base camp. North is the top row. west middle east north ice ridge weather post snowfield middle open water base camp radio mast
qs: What lies directly east of base camp?
Which two directions do you travel to get from base camp to the penguin colony?
key: the radio mast (HSS-3.1)
south and west, in either order. The penguin colony sits in the south row and the west column. Partial: one of the two directions is approaching. (HSS-3.1)

title: The First Nations Here
desc: describing how the American Indian nations of California used the rivers and traded long ago, and how a nation governs itself today
dir: Answer out loud. Use what is on the screen and what you have learned.
text: Some California nations lived along rivers. They caught salmon and other fish. They dried them on racks in the sun and wind. They traded dried fish with other n
qs: The screen says river nations dried their fish. How did they dry it. Who did they trade the dried fish to?
People here were drying fish and trading it. What does that tell you about how they lived? What does it tell you about working with other nations?
key: They dried the fish on racks in the sun and the wind. They traded the dried fish to nations living away from the water. Partial: one of the two halves answered is approaching. (HSS-3.2)

They used what their own place gave them, and they traded with nations who had other things, so nations were connected to each other and not living apart. Listen for the local land and the trade link.

title: A Town Over Time
desc: sequencing local historical events and describing the mark each period left on the land
dir: Look at the timeline. Answer out loud.
text: A timeline for the town of Frost Harbor. Year What happened 1862 a wharf is built in the sheltered part of the bay 1891 an ice house opens, and a pond is dug to
qs: Put these three in order, earliest first. The ice house. The dredging of the bay. The wharf.
Which event changed the shape of the bay bottom. What did it do?
key: wharf, ice house, dredging of the bay. Partial: two of the three in the right order is approaching. (HSS-3.3)
the dredging in 1958, which cut the bay bottom deeper so larger ships could come in. Partial: naming the dredging with no account of what it did to the bay is approaching. (HSS-3.3)

title: Rules, Laws and Government
desc: telling rules from laws and naming the basic parts and levels of United States government
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The expedition has a rule: nobody leaves camp alone. Back home there is a law about boats. A boat must carry one life jacket for every person aboard.
qs: What is the difference between the expedition’s rule and the life jacket law?
Why do we have laws at all? Give one reason.
key: The expedition rule is set by the team leader and applies to the team. The law is made by a government, applies to everyone with a boat, and the government decides what happens when it is broken. Part
Any sound reason: to keep people safe, to settle disagreements fairly, so everyone knows what to expect, to protect people’s rights and property. Partial: saying laws are the rules with no reason for

title: Choices and the Local Economy
desc: basic economic reasoning about scarcity, trade-offs, goods and services
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Only one supply flight a month reaches the camp, and it can carry 300 kg. The team wants all of this. What they want Weight fuel for the stove 150 kg fresh food
qs: Can the flight carry all three? Work it out.
They load the fuel and the fresh food. What have they given up. What is the name for the thing you give up when you choose?
key: No. 150 plus 120 plus 60 is 330 kg, and the flight carries 300 kg. Partial: saying no with no total worked out is approaching. (HSS-3.5)
They gave up the spare radio. The idea is a trade-off, or opportunity cost: picking one thing means doing without another, because space and weight are limited. The idea matters more than the term at

title: Crate Word Flip
desc: reading long words with prefixes, roots, and suffixes
dir: Read each word out loud. The last two are made-up words. Just sound them out.
key: Read each word in order. Count a word correct when the student reads it right the first time or fixes it without help.
unflemmable and disgrantion are made-up words. Listen for the chunks: un-flem-ma-ble and dis-grant-ion.

title: Read the Sentences
desc: reading multisyllabic words accurately in context using letter-sound correspondences, syllable patterns, and word parts
dir: Read each sentence out loud. Take your time with the long words.
text: The architect designed a spectacular library with enormous windows. Our neighborhood celebrated the beginning of the harvest festival.
key: Listen for these six words read correctly in the sentences: architect, spectacular, library, neighborhood, celebrated, harvest. Mark each one.
A word that is self-corrected on a second try counts as correct. Note words the student breaks into syllables to decode.

title: Read the Run
desc: a 163-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: The radio crackled at six in the morning, and Tova was already dressed. Her boots stood by the tent door, stuffed with dry socks so they would not freeze stiff.
key: 163 words. Time 1 minute and mark errors and self-corrections on your own copy.
Midyear grade 4 benchmark: about 120 words correct per minute (50th percentile, Hasbrouck and Tindal 2017 winter norms).

title: Prove It
desc: questions about the dogsled story answered with details and examples from the text
dir: Answer out loud. Look back at the story and point to the details that prove your answer.
text: Look back at the story The radio crackled at six in the morning, and Tova was already dressed. Her boots stood by the tent door, stuffed with dry socks so they
qs: Why were Tova's boots stuffed with dry socks? Use a detail from the story.
How do you know the dogs were eager to run? Give two details from the story.
key: So the boots would not freeze stiff. The story says they stood by the tent door, stuffed with dry socks for that reason. (explicit)
They waited in their harnesses breathing little clouds, they did not bark, and they leaned, which means they were already pulling forward. (inference)

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice. Let the rhythm and the rhymes show.
text: Winter Fields The fields lie quiet under snow, Where only the footprints of foxes go. The fence posts wear their caps of white, And the sky grows pink in the fa
key: 46 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm, pauses at the end of lines or punctuation, and a voice that fits the mood of the poem.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: The radio crackled at six in the morning, and Tova was already dressed. Her boots stood by the tent door, stuffed with dry socks so they would not freeze stiff.
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: Reading the Ice
desc: questions answered with details and examples from an informational text
dir: Read the text to yourself. Then answer out loud using the text.
text: Reading the Ice Snow that falls on a polar ice sheet does not melt. New snow presses down on old snow, year after year, until the bottom layers turn to solid ic
qs: What is an ice core? Use details from the text.
A team finds a gray band in a core. What does that tell them about that year? Use the text.
key: A long round stick of ice drilled out of an ice sheet. The text explains that new snow presses down on old snow year after year until the bottom layers become solid ice. (explicit)
A volcano put ash in the sky that year. The text gives that as what a gray band means. (explicit)

title: Two Night Stories
desc: questions about two stories answered with details and examples from each text
dir: Read both stories to yourself. Then answer out loud and point to the details that prove your answer.
text: Story 1: The Midnight Shift Jonah drew the midnight shift, which meant two hours of sitting up in the cook tent while the rest of the team slept. His one job wa
qs: Story 1. What were Jonah's two jobs on the midnight shift? Use the story.
Story 1. Why did Jonah tie a rope from the tent pole to his belt? Give details from the story.
key: Two jobs: keeping the stove going, and listening to the radio. The story names both. (explicit)
So he could find his way back to the tent. The story says the spare cans were forty steps away and that in blowing snow forty steps can turn into a lost person. (inference)

title: Four Animal Texts
desc: putting together information from two texts on the same topic, over two different topics
dir: Read all four texts to yourself. Then answer out loud. Use facts from both texts of a pair in each answer.
text: Emperor penguins live near the South Pole. Texts 1 and 2 are both about that bird. Text 1: The Huddle Emperor penguins raise their chicks in the coldest months
qs: Use Texts 1 and 2. Explain how an emperor penguin lives through the coldest months of the year.
A penguin's feathers and fat already hold heat in very well. Use Texts 1 and 2 to explain why standing in a huddle is still worth doing.
key: From Text 2: about 100 feathers per square inch that overlap and lock out wind and water, a fat layer as thick as a book, blood to the feet and flippers warmed on the way back, and eating until almost

Text 2 says a penguin still loses heat fast through its feet and flippers and that it has only the fat it stored to live on. Text 1 says the huddle is more than 20 degrees warmer inside and that the s

title: Radio Vote
desc: a short opinion piece with a reason and a closing sentence
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: One hour of daylight is left. The team can do one job today: dig out the supply crates buried by last night's storm, or ride to the weather station for one more
key: States an opinion about which job the team should do today
Gives a reason supported by a fact or detail, such as the three days of food, the daily reading, or tomorrow's storm

title: Whale Watch Notes
desc: taking notes in their own words, sorting the notes, and listing sources
dir: Read the two sources. Write your notes on your paper and hold it up.
text: You are gathering facts for a report on whales that stay in the far north all year. Source 1 (field guide): Narwhals and Belugas Narwhals and belugas are whales
qs: Write three notes. Use both sources. Keep them short and use your own words.
Sort your notes. Write a heading above each note: Living Under the Ice or How Researchers Listen.
key: Three short notes that use both sources, in the student's own words and not copied sentences. Examples: no back fin so they can swim under ice; they need a crack or hole to breathe; a hydrophone is le

Each note sits under the heading that fits. Facts about fins, breathing holes, and danger go under Living Under the Ice. Facts about hydrophones, squeaks and clicks, and matching sounds by computer go

title: Fix the Field Log
desc: spoken grammar items (relative pronouns, progressive tense, modal words, order of adjectives, run-ons, confused words)
dir: Say each sentence out loud the correct way.
qs: The scientist ____ fixed the radio works at the weather station. (who or which)
Right now the dogs ____ in the snow. (rest) Start with are.
key: who (relative pronoun for a person)
are resting (progressive tense)

title: Cursive Writing
desc: writing fluidly and legibly in cursive or joined italics
dir: Write this sentence on your paper in cursive or joined writing. Write smoothly and keep it neat.
text: Write this sentence: The old lighthouse stood bravely against the storm.
key: Letters are joined within words (cursive or joined italics)
Writing is legible: another reader can read each word

title: Base Camp Writer
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: How does the team stay warm and safe at base camp? Write to explain it. Use facts from the chart. Write 5 to 7 sentences. Introduce your topic Give facts, detai
key: Introduces the topic clearly

Develops the topic with facts and details from the chart, such as two tent layers holding still air, melting snow for water, ropes between tents, face checks for frostbite, radio calls every six hours

title: Base Camp Writer
desc: an opinion writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Should the expedition travel by dogsled or by snowmobile? Write your opinion. Use facts from the chart. Write 5 to 7 sentences. State your opinion Give reasons
key: Introduces the topic and states an opinion
Gives reasons supported by facts and details from the chart, such as speed, food or fuel, thin ice, or breaking down in deep cold

title: What the Words Mean
desc: explaining what words and phrases mean as they are used in a text, including a name that alludes to a character from an old story
dir: Read the short piece. Then answer out loud.
text: Ravi calls the biggest husky on the team Atlas, after the giant in the old Greek stories who held up the whole sky on his shoulders. Atlas runs closest to the s
qs: Why is Atlas a good name for that dog? Use what the piece tells you about the giant in the old Greek stories.
The story says the sled flew. The sled has no wings, so what does flew mean here?
key: In the old stories Atlas carried the heaviest load there was, the whole sky. This dog runs where the pull is hardest and never slacks his line, so he carries the heaviest share of the work. (RL.4.4, a
It means the sled went very fast. The writer uses flew to show speed, not that the sled left the ground. (RL.4.4)

title: The Midnight Sun
desc: paraphrasing portions of a text read aloud
dir: Put your pencil down and listen. Then say each answer in your own words.
text: Listening time. Your teacher will read a short report about daylight at the poles. The horizon is the line where the sky seems to meet the ground.
key: Ask: Put the first part in your own words. Why does the sun stay up all day and all night for part of the year? (Because the earth is tilted, and for part of the year that half of the world leans towa
Ask: Put the middle part in your own words. What happens for the other part of the year? (The same tilt leans that half away from the sun, so the sun never comes up at all.) (SL.4.2)

title: Say It in Your Own Words
desc: paraphrasing information presented visually and quantitatively
dir: Look at the chart. Tell your teacher what it shows in your own words. Do not read it word for word.
text: Books read in a month Item Amount Class A 40 books Class B 55 books Class C 30 books
qs: Tell what the chart is about in your own words.
Tell two important facts from the chart in your own words.
key: A paraphrase of the main point in the student’s own words (not reading the numbers aloud in order).
Two accurate facts or comparisons put in new words (for example, which is greatest or smallest and about how much).

title: Fox Report
desc: reporting on a topic in an organized way with facts and descriptive details
dir: Give a one-minute report out loud. Speak clearly and not too fast.
text: Give a short report on the arctic fox for someone who has never heard of one. Use the two texts. Start by saying what your report is about Group your facts: fir
key: Organized: opens by naming the topic, groups the facts rather than jumping about, and finishes (SL.4.4)

Uses appropriate facts from the texts, such as the coat that turns white in fall, small round ears and nose, no shivering until near 40 below, listening for lemmings under the snow, jumping and punchi

title: Moving Camp
desc: a short narrative with an orientation, ordered events, description or dialogue, and a conclusion
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Write the story of the day the team packed up base camp and moved it to a new spot on the ice. You are on the team. Write 5 or 6 sentences. Start by telling who
key: Orients the reader: who is in the story and where and when it takes place (W.4.3)
Events unfold in a natural order, with transitional words such as first, after that, by then, finally (W.4.3)

title: Depot Count
desc: how a digit is worth 10 times what the same digit is worth one place to its right
dir: Answer out loud. Explain how you know.
text: A depot is a pile of supplies the team leaves out on the ice to pick up later. Every depot has a count board.
qs: In 9,900, how does the 9 in the thousands place compare to the 9 in the hundreds place?
A 4 in the hundreds place is worth 400. In which place would a 4 be worth 10 times as much. What would it be worth there?
key: It is worth 10 times as much. The 9 in the thousands place is 9,000 and the 9 in the hundreds place is 900, and 9,000 is 10 times 900. Partial: naming the two values with no comparison is approaching.
The thousands place, where a 4 would be worth 4,000. 4,000 is 10 times 400. Partial: naming the place with no value given is approaching.

title: Round the Log
desc: rounding multi-digit whole numbers to a given place
dir: Say each answer out loud.
text: The radio operator reports round numbers, not exact ones, so the base ship can write them down fast.
qs: Round 38,471 to the nearest thousand.
Round 38,471 to the nearest hundred.
key: 38,000. Partial: 39,000 rounds up when the hundreds digit is 4 and does not count.
38,500. Partial: 38,400 rounds down when the tens digit is 7 and does not count.

title: Fuel Drum Compare
desc: comparing fractions with different numerators and denominators
dir: Answer out loud and tell how you know. Write numbers 2 and 5 on your paper and hold them up.
text: Fuel runs the camp stove. The team writes down how full each drum is as a fraction.
qs: Which is greater: 2/3 of a drum or 5/8 of a drum? How do you know?
Write >, <, or = to make it true: 3/4 ____ 9/12
key: 2/3. Using twelfths does not work here, so use twenty-fourths: 2/3 is 16/24 and 5/8 is 15/24. Or: 2/3 is 1/3 from a whole and 5/8 is 3/8 from a whole, and 1/3 is the smaller gap. Partial: naming 2/3 w
3/4 = 9/12. Multiplying the top and bottom of 3/4 by 3 gives 9/12. Partial: the equals sign right with no reason is approaching.

title: Compare With Symbols
desc: comparing fractions with different numerators and denominators, recording the results with symbols, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know.
qs: Compare 4/9 and 1/2 with a symbol.
Compare 5/6 and 3/4 with a symbol.

title: Times As Many
desc: reading a multiplication equation as a comparison and writing a comparison as an equation
dir: Answer out loud. Write the equations on your paper and hold them up.
text: A dogsled travels about 10 kilometers in an hour. A snowmobile travels about 30 kilometers in an hour.
qs: Write a multiplication equation that compares the two speeds, and say it in words.
Read 35 = 5 × 7 as a comparison. Say it two different ways.
key: 30 = 3 × 10. In words: the snowmobile goes 3 times as fast as the dogsled. 10 × 3 = 30 is the same equation. Partial: the equation right with no words given is approaching. (4.OA.A.1)
35 is 5 times as many as 7, and 35 is 7 times as many as 5. Partial: one of the two ways given is approaching. (4.OA.A.1)

title: Same Amount of Fuel
desc: explaining and generating equivalent fractions with a visual model
dir: Look at the two drums. Answer out loud.
qs: What fraction of Drum A is shaded? What fraction of Drum B? Do the two drums hold the same amount of fuel?
Explain why multiplying the top and the bottom of 3/4 by 2 does not change how much fuel that is.
key: 3/4 of Drum A and 6/8 of Drum B, and yes, they are the same amount. The drums are the same size and the shaded lengths match. Partial: both fractions right with no answer about the amounts is approach
Multiplying by 2 on the top and the bottom cuts every part in half, so there are twice as many parts and twice as many of them shaded. The pieces are smaller and there are more of them, so the amount

title: Snow Gauge
desc: writing fractions with denominators 10 and 100 as decimals, locating a decimal on a number line, and comparing two decimals to hundredths
dir: Look at the line. Answer out loud. Write the last one on your paper.
text: The snow gauge measures the depth of new snow in parts of a meter.
qs: Monday's gauge read 62/100 of a meter. Write that as a decimal. Point to about where it would sit on the line.
Tuesday's gauge read 0.6 of a meter. Write that as a fraction with 10 on the bottom, and again with 100 on the bottom.
key: 0.62, and it sits just past the sixth tick after 0, a little short of 0.7. Partial: 0.62 right with no place found on the line is approaching. (4.NF.C.6)
6/10 and 60/100. Partial: one of the two fractions given is approaching. (4.NF.C.6)

title: Units on the Trail
desc: knowing relative sizes of units and expressing a larger unit in a smaller one, including a conversion table
dir: Answer out loud. Make the table on your paper and hold it up.
text: Flags stand every 100 meters along the route, and the weather station is at flag twenty-two.
qs: How far is the weather station from camp in meters? Give that distance in centimeters too.
A ration crate weighs 5 kilograms. How many grams is that?
key: 2,200 meters, because 22 flags at 100 meters each is 22 × 100. In centimeters that is 220,000, because 1 meter is 100 centimeters. Partial: the metres right with no centimetres given is approaching. (
5,000 grams, because 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams. Partial: 500 uses hundreds instead of thousands and does not count. (4.MD.A.1)

title: Pounds and Ounces
desc: knowing the relative sizes of pounds and ounces, converting a larger unit to a smaller unit, and recording equivalents in a table
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work.
qs: A puppy weighs 5 pounds. How many ounces is that?
How many ounces are in 2 pounds?
key: 80 ounces (5 × 16)
32 ounces

title: Tent Floors
desc: applying the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles, including finding an unknown side
dir: Solve on your paper and hold it up. Say each answer out loud.
qs: What is the area of this floor? What is its perimeter?
